# Getting Started

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/

<div class="dox-hero" markdown>

<img class="dox-hero__mascot" src="assets/mascot.png" alt="Doxie, the Dox mascot" width="140" height="137">

# Fast backends<br>in Dart

<p class="dox-hero__lead"><strong>Everything your Dart backend needs.</strong></p>

<p class="dox-hero__lead">
Dox is a web backend framework for Dart.
It has routing, an ORM, migrations, validation, auth and a CLI in one place.
It runs one isolate per CPU core and builds to a small native binary.
</p>

<p class="dox-hero__actions" markdown>
[Build your first API](tutorial/index.md){ .md-button .md-button--primary }
[GitHub](https://github.com/dartondox/dox){ .md-button }
[Blog](/blog/){ .md-button }
</p>

</div>

<div class="dox-hero__code" markdown>

```dart
Route.get('/blogs', BlogController.index); // (1)!

enum Status { active, draft }

@Dto() // (2)!
class BlogFilter {
  final Status status; // ?status=active, else 422
  const BlogFilter({required this.status});
  static const DtoSchema<BlogFilter> schema =
      $BlogFilterDto; // (3)!
}

class BlogController {
  static Future<List<Blog>> index(
    BlogFilter query, // (4)!
  ) async {
    return Blog()
        .where('status', query.status.name)
        .get(); // (5)!
  }
}
```

1.  A route points to a static method. Dox needs no reflection and no list of controllers.
2.  `@Dto()` marks an input class. `build_runner` makes the checks from the fields and their types.
3.  The generated schema. The OpenAPI docs use the same schema.
4.  Ask for the DTO as a parameter. Dox reads the query (or the body), checks it, and gives you a typed object. Bad input gets a `422` before your code runs.
5.  The ORM. The same code runs on Postgres, MySQL and SQLite. Postgres and MySQL use native drivers.

</div>

</div>

Your code is plain Dart. The speed comes from the native server. It runs
on the isolate's own thread, so a request never waits for another thread.
See [Performance](digging-deeper/performance.md) for every route and how
it was run.

## Run it in two minutes

You need [Dart](https://dart.dev/get-dart) 3.13 or newer, and nothing else.
The starter project uses SQLite, so there is no database to install.

```bash
dart pub global activate dox             # install the CLI
dox create my_app                            # download the starter project
cd my_app
dart pub get
dox s                                        # start the server
```

Open a second terminal and call the first route:

```bash
curl localhost:3000/ping
```

```text
pong
```

That is a Dox app. Next, follow the [tutorial](tutorial/index.md). It adds a
model, a database table, validation, login and a Docker image, one short step
at a time.

!!! note "The CLI is not found?"
    `dart pub global activate` puts `dox` in `$HOME/.pub-cache/bin`.
    Add that folder to your `PATH`. See [Installation](getting-started/installation.md).

## What you get

<div class="grid cards" markdown>

-   :material-lightning-bolt: **Fast by default**

    A native HTTP server, one isolate per CPU core and streamed bodies.
    `dox build` makes one native binary. See [Performance](digging-deeper/performance.md).

-   :material-database-outline: **ORM and query builder**

    Models, relations, migrations and transactions for Postgres, MySQL/MariaDB and SQLite.
    Postgres and MySQL use native drivers. See [Database](database/index.md).

-   :material-check-decagram-outline: **Typed validation**

    Write a `@Dto` class. Dox checks the input and gives your controller a typed object.
    See [Validation](the-basic/validation.md).

-   :material-file-document-outline: **OpenAPI**

    OpenAPI 3.1 docs and a Scalar docs page, made from your routes and DTOs.
    See [`dox_openapi`](packages/openapi.md).

-   :material-folder-outline: **File storage**

    Local disk and S3 behind one API, with signed URLs. See [`dox_storage`](packages/storage.md).

-   :material-cached: **Cache**

    Memory, file and Redis cache with tags and locks. See [`dox_cache`](packages/cache.md).

-   :material-access-point: **Real time**

    [Socket.IO](packages/socketio.md), with Redis for many servers.

-   :material-shield-lock-outline: **Security**

    JWT [authentication](security/authentication.md), [CORS](security/cors.md),
    [encryption](security/encryption.md) and [hashing](security/hashing.md).

-   :material-console: **CLI**

    Create projects, controllers, models and migrations. Run, build and migrate.
    See [CLI reference](reference/cli.md).

</div>

- Want to help? Read [Contribute](community/contribute.md).

# Installation

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/getting-started/installation/

# Installation

This page shows how to install the Dox CLI, make a new project and start the server.

Dox needs **Dart 3.13** or newer.

## Install the CLI

The `dox` CLI makes projects, runs the server and makes files for you. Install it with pub:

```bash
dart pub global activate dox
```

Check that it works:

```bash
dox version
```

!!! warning "`dox: command not found`"
    The shell can not find the CLI, because the pub `bin` folder is not in your `PATH`.
    Add this line to `~/.bashrc` or `~/.zshrc`, then open a new terminal:

    ```bash
    export PATH="$PATH":"$HOME/.pub-cache/bin"
    ```

## Create a new project

Use `dox create` with the name of your app:

```bash
dox create new_blog
```

It downloads the newest release of [dox-sample](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-sample), the starter project. To get one exact release, add `--version` with a release tag of dox-sample.

It also makes your `.env` file from `.env.example`, with a new random `APP_KEY`. Then get the packages:

```bash
cd new_blog
dart pub get
```

The starter project uses SQLite, so there is no database to install. The file `db/dox.sqlite` is created at the first start. To use Postgres or MySQL instead, change `DB_CONNECTION` and the `DB_*` values in `.env`. See [Database](../database/index.md).

!!! info "Add Dox to an existing Dart project"
    If you already have a Dart project, add the packages you need with `dart pub add`:

    ```bash
    dart pub add dox_core dox_orm dox_migration
    dart pub add dev:dox_builder dev:build_runner
    ```

## Start the server

Start the server in dev mode:

```bash
dox s
```

`dox s` does two things:

- It runs `dart run bin/server.dart`. When you change a file in `lib/app/`, it hot reloads the new code, so no restart is needed. For routes, providers, config and other start-up code, it restarts the server.
- It runs `dart run build_runner watch`, so generated files stay up to date.

At each start it also runs the new migrations in `db/migration`. The server uses the port in `APP_PORT` in the `.env` file (`3000` by default). Check that it works:

```bash
curl localhost:3000/ping
```

```text
pong
```

These options change `dox s`:

- `dox s --ignore-build-runner` skips the builder.
- `dox s --no-reload` turns hot reload off.

To start the server without the CLI, run `dart run bin/server.dart`.

## Start the server with Docker

The starter project has a Docker setup. This starts the app, a queue worker and a Postgres database:

```bash
docker compose up -d --build
```

The app and the worker always use the Postgres service. They set `DB_CONNECTION` and `DB_NAME` themselves. The database port is open on this machine only (`127.0.0.1`), not on the network.

If you want only the database in Docker, and the app with `dox s`, run `docker compose up -d postgres`. Then set `DB_CONNECTION=postgres` and `DB_NAME=dox` in `.env`.

!!! tip "Production"
    Do not use `dox s` or `dart run` in production.
    Build a native binary with `dox build`. See [Deployment](../digging-deeper/deployment.md).

## Run the code generator

Dox makes code for models and DTOs with `build_runner`. `dox s` already runs it. To run it alone:

```bash
dox build_runner:watch   # runs again on every file change
dox build_runner:build   # runs once
```

## AI agents

If you use an AI coding agent, give it the real API of each package. Run `dart run skills@ get` in your app after `dart pub get`. See [AI agents](ai-agents.md) for the skills, `AGENTS.md` and the llms files.

## Packages

Dox is split into packages, so you add only what you need:

| Package | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `dox` | the CLI |
| `dox_core` | HTTP server, routing, requests, responses, validation |
| `dox_orm` | query builder and models |
| `dox_migration` | database migrations |
| `dox_auth` | Login with access tokens, JWT or sessions |
| `dox_builder`, `dox_annotation` | code generation for models, DTOs and the container |
| `dox_validation` | [typed validation schemas](../packages/validation.md) |
| `dox_openapi` | [OpenAPI docs](../packages/openapi.md) |
| `dox_storage` | [file storage: local, S3](../packages/storage.md) |
| `dox_cache` | [cache: memory, file, Redis](../packages/cache.md) |
| `dox_cache_database` | [cache in a database table](../packages/cache.md#database-store) |
| `dox_socketio` | [Socket.IO server](../packages/socketio.md) |
| `dox_queue` | [background jobs](../digging-deeper/queue.md) |
| `dox_queue_database` | [queue in a database table](../digging-deeper/queue.md#database-driver) |
| `dox_scheduler` | [scheduled tasks](../digging-deeper/scheduler.md) |
| `dox_mailer` | [send email](../digging-deeper/mail.md) |
| `dox_view` | [HTML views](../the-basic/views.md) |
| `dox_inertia` | [Inertia.js pages](../the-basic/inertia.md) |
| `dox_http_native` | [native HTTP server](../digging-deeper/native-server.md) (Rust) |
| `dox_postgres_native`, `dox_mysql_native` | native drivers for [Postgres](../database/postgres-native.md) and [MySQL/MariaDB](../database/mysql-native.md) |

# AI agents

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/getting-started/ai-agents/

# AI agents

An AI coding agent must know the real Dox API. If it does not, it guesses class names and method names, and the code does not compile.

Dox gives the agent two sources:

- **Skills**: short guides that each package ships. The agent reads them while it writes code in your app.
- **`llms.txt` and `llms-full.txt`**: these docs as plain text files, for a chat or for a tool that has no skills.

## Skills

A skill is a `SKILL.md` file with the real API of one package and the steps for the usual tasks. Each Dox package ships its skill in its `skills/<name>/` folder.

The agent does not read all skills at the start. It reads a skill only when your task matches it. Thus the skills use little space in the memory of the agent.

A skill comes with the package. Thus it always agrees with the package version that your app uses.

These packages ship a skill:

| Package | Skill | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `dox_core` | `dox-core-guide` | routes, controllers, DTOs, serializers, middleware, providers, env config, CLI commands, HTTP tests |
| `dox_orm` | `dox-orm-guide` | models, queries, relations, pagination, transactions, factories, the switch to Postgres or MySQL |
| `dox_migration` | `dox-migration-guide` | migrations, table changes, seeders |
| `dox_validation` | `dox-validation-guide` | DTO rules, custom rules and messages, fluent schemas, database rules |
| `dox_auth` | `dox-auth-guide` | login and logout, JWT, session and access token guards, gates and policies |
| `dox_openapi` | `dox-openapi-guide` | the API docs at `/docs`, annotations for the OpenAPI document |
| `dox_cache` | `dox-cache-guide` | cache stores, `remember`, tags, cache locks, the cache in tests |
| `dox_queue` | `dox-queue-guide` | queue jobs, the worker, the Redis and database drivers, failed jobs, chains and batches |
| `dox_scheduler` | `dox-scheduler-guide` | scheduled tasks, cron frequencies, no double runs on many servers |
| `dox_storage` | `dox-storage-guide` | files and uploads, local, S3 and memory disks, signed URLs |
| `dox_mailer` | `dox-mailer-guide` | mail config, mailables, Markdown mail, queued mail, transports, mail in tests |
| `dox_socketio` | `dox-socketio-guide` | realtime events, rooms, socket login, the Redis adapter, broadcasts |
| `dox_view` | `dox-view-guide` | HTML pages with `.dox.html` templates, layouts, components, forms with CSRF |
| `dox_inertia` | `dox-inertia-guide` | Inertia.js pages with React, Vue or Svelte, shared props, Vite and SSR |
| `dox_mcp` | `dox-mcp-guide` | an MCP server: tools, a route with auth, sessions, OAuth sign-in |
| `dox_grpc` | `dox-grpc-guide` | gRPC services: the `.proto` file, the service class, status codes, deadlines |
| `dox_graphql` | `dox-graphql-guide` | a GraphQL API from annotations and ORM models, auth and limits |
| `ioredis` | `ioredis-guide` | Redis connections, commands, pipelines, transactions, pub/sub |

## Install the skills

The skills are not in your project until you install them. The [skills](https://pub.dev/packages/skills) tool copies them from your packages into the skills folder of your agent.

Run it in the root folder of your app, after `dart pub get`:

```bash
dart run skills@ get
```

The tool finds the skills of your packages. Then it asks which skills to install. To install all of them with no question, add `--all`:

```bash
dart run skills@ get --all
```

### Select your agent

The tool finds your agent from the folders in your project, for example `.claude/` or `.cursor/`. If it finds more than one agent, it installs the skills for each of them. If it finds none, it asks you.

To set the agent yourself, use `--agent`:

```bash
dart run skills@ get --all --agent claude
```

Each agent has its own skills folder:

| Agent | `--agent` | Skills folder |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Code | `claude` | `.claude/skills/` |
| Codex | `codex` | `.agents/skills/` |
| Cursor | `cursor` | `.cursor/skills/` |
| GitHub Copilot | `copilot` | `.github/skills/` |
| Cline | `cline` | `.cline/skills/` |
| OpenCode | `opencode` | `.opencode/skills/` |
| Antigravity | `antigravity` | `.agents/skills/` |
| Other agents | `generic` | `.agents/skills/` |

The tool does not find GitHub Copilot automatically. For Copilot, always use `--agent copilot`.

### Run it again after a package change

The installed skills are copies. They do not change when a package changes.

Run `dart run skills@ get` again after you add a package or update a package. The tool then installs the new skills. With `--all`, it also removes the skills of packages that you no longer use. Without `--all`, it asks first.

### Packages that come in through another package

The tool only reads the packages in your own `pubspec.yaml`. It does not see a package that comes in through a different package.

For example, `dox_cache` uses `ioredis`. If you use `ioredis` directly in your code, add it to your `pubspec.yaml`:

```bash
dart pub add ioredis
dart run skills@ get
```

### Make sure that it worked

List the installed skills:

```bash
dart run skills@ list
```

You can also look in the skills folder of your agent. For Claude Code, the `dox_core` skill is the file `.claude/skills/dox-core-guide/SKILL.md`.

If your tool has no support for skills, open the `SKILL.md` file as a normal file, or give it to the agent.

## AGENTS.md

A skill tells the agent how a package works. It does not tell the agent how your project is organized. The `AGENTS.md` file in the root folder of your app does that. Most coding agents read this file before they change code.

The starter project that `dox create` makes has an `AGENTS.md` file. It holds:

- what the project is, and the links to the llms files
- the command that installs the skills, and the list of skills
- the folder layout and the file names
- the `dox` commands that make files
- when to run the code generator, and which files are generated
- the conventions for routes, input, models, migrations, jobs, config and errors
- how to switch the database
- the checks to run before a change is done: `dart format .`, `dart analyze` and `dart test`
- a list of things that the agent must not do

This file is yours. Edit it when your app gets its own rules, for example a new folder or a rule for tests.

## llms.txt and llms-full.txt

Not every tool can read skills, and a chat does not see your project. For these, the docs site has two plain text files. They obey the [llms.txt](https://llmstxt.org) convention.

| File | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| [llms.txt](https://dartondox.dev/llms.txt) | The page list: a short description of Dox, then one line for each page with its title and its link. |
| [llms-full.txt](https://dartondox.dev/llms-full.txt) | All the docs as one Markdown file. |

### What is in the files

The docs build makes the two files again each time the docs change. Thus they always agree with this site.

- They hold the docs of the latest Dox version. The links in them go to `https://dartondox.dev/latest/`.
- They hold the docs pages, in the sequence of the menu of this site.
- In `llms-full.txt`, each page starts with its title and its link. Then comes the Markdown source of the page, with all its code examples.
- The blog and the docs of older Dox versions are not in the files.

### Use them

There are three ways to give the files to an agent:

1. **Paste the link.** In a chat agent that can open links, paste `https://dartondox.dev/llms-full.txt` and ask your question.
2. **Add a docs source.** Some editors let you add documentation by its link. If your editor has this feature, add the link of `llms-full.txt`.
3. **Download the file.** Save it, then point the agent at the file or attach it to the chat:

    ```bash
    curl -o dox-docs.md https://dartondox.dev/llms-full.txt
    ```

`llms-full.txt` is a large file. If your agent cannot hold it, give it `llms.txt`. The agent then opens only the pages that it needs.

## Skills or llms-full.txt

| | Skills | `llms-full.txt` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Use it for | code changes in your app | questions in a chat, or a tool with no skills |
| Size | small, one skill for each package | large, all the docs |
| Version | the package version of your app | the latest Dox version |
| How the agent gets it | automatically, when the task matches | you give it the link or the file |

For daily work in your app, install the skills and keep `AGENTS.md`. Use `llms-full.txt` when you ask about Dox out of your project, or when your tool cannot read skills.

# Add a package

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/getting-started/add-a-package/

# Add a package

`dox add` adds a Dox package to your app and sets it up.

Many packages need config files and `.env` keys. `dox add` writes them for you, so you do not set up each package by hand:

```bash
dox add orm
```

## What it does

`dox add orm` does three steps:

1. Runs `dart pub add dox_orm`. `orm` is short for `dox_orm`. The full name works too.
2. Runs `dart pub get`.
3. Runs the setup command of the package, `dox orm:install`.

The setup command writes the config files, adds the keys to `.env` and `.env.example`, and runs `build_runner` when the package needs it. At the end it prints what it did and the next steps.

A package with no setup command is only added, and `dox add` says so.

## Options

Words after the name go to the setup command, for example to pick a driver:

```bash
dox add orm --driver=postgres
```

`--dev` adds the package as a dev dependency.

## Safe to run twice

The setup command never overwrites a file and never changes a `.env` key that is already there. So you can run `dox add` again, and it only adds what is missing.

## Packages with a setup command

These packages have a setup command:

| Command | What it sets up |
| --- | --- |
| `dox add orm [--driver=sqlite\|postgres\|mysql]` | The ORM and migrations. See [Database](../database/index.md). |
| `dox add queue [--driver=database\|redis\|sync]` | Queued jobs and `bin/queue.dart`. `database` is the default and needs `dox add orm` first. See [Queue](../digging-deeper/queue.md). |
| `dox add scheduler` | Scheduled tasks and `bin/schedule.dart`. See [Scheduler](../digging-deeper/scheduler.md). |
| `dox add mailer [--transport=log\|smtp\|resend\|mailgun\|postmark\|ses]` | Mail. `log` is the default. See [Mail](../digging-deeper/mail.md). |
| `dox add cache [--store=file\|redis\|memory\|database]` | Cache stores. `database` needs `dox add orm` first. See [Cache](../digging-deeper/cache.md). |
| `dox add auth` | Access token auth. Needs `dox add orm` and a `User` model first. See [Authentication](../security/authentication.md). |
| `dox add storage [--disk=local\|s3]` | File storage. See [File storage](../digging-deeper/file-storage.md). |
| `dox add socketio [--broadcasting]` | Socket.IO, and broadcasting with the flag. See [Socket.IO](../packages/socketio.md). |
| `dox add view` | Views and `resources/views/`. See [Views](../the-basic/views.md). |
| `dox add inertia` | The server side of Inertia. It prints the Vite steps. See [Inertia](../the-basic/inertia.md). |
| `dox add mcp` | An MCP server with a sample tool. See [MCP](../packages/mcp.md). |
| `dox add grpc` | gRPC: a sample `.proto` file, a router with the health service and `APP_HTTP2` in `.env`. See [gRPC](../digging-deeper/grpc.md). |

The first `dox add orm` can download (or build) the Postgres and MySQL drivers once, also the one you do not use. After that, `pubspec.yaml` skips the unused drivers, so later builds do not get them.

To add a setup command to your own package, see [Package commands](../digging-deeper/package-commands.md#ship-an-install-command).


---

# Build a blog API

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/tutorial/

# Build a blog API

This tutorial takes you from an empty folder to a small blog API that runs as one native binary.

Every step has the full code and a `curl` command, so you can check your work after each step.

The finished project is on GitHub: [examples/blog-api](https://github.com/dartondox/dox/tree/main/examples/blog-api). CI builds it and runs its tests on every push, so the code on these pages always works.

## What you will build

You will build a JSON API for blog posts. Anyone can read posts, but only a logged in user can write them:

| Method | Path | Who | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `GET` | `/api/posts` | anyone | list all posts |
| `GET` | `/api/posts/{id}` | anyone | one post, or `404` |
| `POST` | `/api/posts` | logged in user | make a post (`201`, or `422` on bad input) |
| `PUT` | `/api/posts/{id}` | logged in user | change a post |
| `POST` | `/api/auth/register` | anyone | make an account, get a token |
| `POST` | `/api/auth/login` | anyone | log in, get a token |
| `GET` | `/api/auth/user` | logged in user | the user of the token |

## What you need

- Dart 3.13 or newer. Check it with `dart --version`.
- `curl`, to call the API.
- About 15 minutes.

You do not need Docker or a database server, because the app uses SQLite. SQLite keeps the whole database in one file in your project.

## The steps

1. [Create the project](01-create-project.md)
2. [Model and migration](02-model-and-migration.md)
3. [Routes and controller](03-routes-and-controller.md)
4. [Validation](04-validation.md)
5. [Login with dox_auth](05-auth.md)
6. [Test](06-test.md)
7. [Build and deploy](07-build-and-deploy.md)

## The finished project

This is the project at the end. Files that you make or change are marked with `*`. The template has more files, like queue, scheduler and storage, but this tree only shows the ones you need here.

```text
blog/
├── bin/
│   ├── migrate.dart              runs the dox migration:* commands
│   ├── server.dart               runs the migrations, starts the server
│   └── queue.dart, schedule.dart, seed.dart
├── db/migration/
│   ├── ..._create_posts_table.dart   *
│   ├── ..._create_users_table.dart
│   └── migrations.dart           the list of migrations (Dox writes it)
├── lib/
│   ├── app/http/controllers/
│   │   ├── auth.controller.dart  *
│   │   └── post.controller.dart  *
│   ├── app/dtos/
│   │   ├── login_user/login_user.dto.dart   *
│   │   ├── register_user/register_user.dto.dart *
│   │   └── save_post/save_post.dto.dart    *
│   ├── app/models/
│   │   ├── post/post.model.dart  *
│   │   └── user/user.model.dart
│   ├── config/
│   │   ├── app.dart              * adds the DTO list
│   │   ├── database.dart
│   │   └── env.dart              the .env keys, typed
│   ├── routes/api.dart           *
│   ├── providers/
│   │   ├── auth_provider.dart    *
│   │   └── orm_provider.dart
│   └── generated/
│       ├── container.g.dart      * generated
│       └── dtos.g.dart           * generated
├── test/http_test.dart           *
├── .env                          made by dox create
├── Dockerfile
└── pubspec.yaml                  * adds dox_auth
```

Start with [step 1: create the project](01-create-project.md).

# Step 1: Create the project

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/tutorial/01-create-project/

# Step 1: Create the project

In this step you make a new Dox project, start the dev server and call the first route.

## 1. Make the project

First install the `dox` command line tool. Then use it to make a project named `blog`:

```bash
dart pub global activate dox
dox create blog
cd blog
dart pub get
```

`dox create` downloads the [dox-sample](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-sample) template and names the package `blog`. So every import in this tutorial starts with `package:blog/`.

## 2. Look at the database settings

You do not need to change anything here. `dox create` made a `.env` file with a new random `APP_KEY`, and the template already uses SQLite:

```ini title=".env"
APP_PORT=3000
APP_KEY=<your new random key>

DB_CONNECTION=sqlite
DB_NAME=db/dox.sqlite
```

Dox makes the file `db/dox.sqlite` at the first start. SQLite does not use the other `DB_*` lines. The app reads these keys through the typed class in `lib/config/env.dart`. See [Environment variables](../digging-deeper/env.md).

!!! note "The folder must exist"
    Dox makes the database file when it is missing, but not its folder. If you set `DB_NAME=storage/blog.sqlite`, run `mkdir storage` first.

## 3. Start the server

Start the dev server:

```bash
dox s
```

`dox s` runs the code generator and the server. When you save a file in `lib/app/`, it hot reloads your code. When you change routes, config or other start-up code, it restarts the server.

The first start is slower, because it compiles the SQLite library. It also runs the migrations of the template. At the end you see this log line:

```text
[server] Server started at http://[::]:3000 with 8 isolate (native)
```

The number of isolates is the number of CPU cores on your machine.

## Check it

Call the `ping` route from a second terminal:

```bash
curl -i http://localhost:3000/api/ping
```

You should see:

```text
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
content-type: text/plain; charset=utf-8
...

pong
```

The route is in `lib/routes/api.dart`. The `ApiRouter` has the prefix `api`, so `/ping` is served at `/api/ping`.

## Next

[Step 2: Model and migration](02-model-and-migration.md)


---

# Step 2: Model and migration

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/tutorial/02-model-and-migration/

# Step 2: Model and migration

In this step you make the `posts` table with a migration, and a `Post` model to read and write it.

## 1. Make the model and the migration

Stop `dox s` first with `Ctrl+C`. You need to do this because `dox s` restarts the server when a new file appears, and the server runs new migrations at start. So it would run the new migration before you add the columns.

Now make the model and its migration:

```bash
dox make:model Post -m
```

This makes two files and updates one:

| File | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart` | the model (new) |
| `db/migration/<date>_create_posts_table.dart` | the migration (new) |
| `db/migration/migrations.dart` | the list of all Dart migrations. Dox writes it. Do not edit it. |

The `dox migration:*` commands run `bin/migrate.dart`, which the template already has.

## 2. Add the columns to the migration

A new migration has no columns yet. Open the new file in `db/migration` and add `title` and `body`:

```dart title="db/migration/2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table.dart"
// ignore_for_file: file_names
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

class CreatePostsTable extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.create('posts', (Table table) {
      table.id();
      table.string('title');
      table.text('body');
      table.timestamps();
    });
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.dropIfExists('posts');
  }
}
```

- `table.id()` makes an auto increment primary key.
- `table.timestamps()` makes `created_at` and `updated_at`. The model fills them for you.

## 3. Add the fields to the model

The model needs one field for each column you added:

```dart title="lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'post.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel(table: 'posts')
class Post extends PostGenerator {
  @override
  List<String> get hidden => <String>[];

  @Column()
  String? title;

  @Column()
  String? body;
}
```

Every column field is nullable, because a new `Post()` has no values yet. You do not declare `id`, `createdAt` and `updatedAt`, because they come from `PostGenerator`.

## 4. See how migrations run

You do not need to change anything here. The template's `bin/server.dart` already runs the migrations before the server starts:

```dart title="bin/server.dart"
import '../db/migration/migrations.dart';

void main() async {
  Dox().initialize(appConfig);

  await Migrator(
    migrations: migrations,
    config: databaseConfig.getConnectionConfig(),
  ).migrate();

  await Dox().startServer();
}
```

This also works in the native binary of [step 7](07-build-and-deploy.md).

## 5. Run the migration and the generator

Run the new migration now:

```bash
dox migration:run
```

```text
Migrating: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
Migrated: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
```

!!! tip "The migration ran too early?"
    If `dox s` was still running, the `posts` table may already exist without `title` and `body`. Run `dox migration:rollback`, then `dox migration:run` again.

The model also needs its generated file `post.model.g.dart`. `dox s` makes it while it runs. If `dox s` is not running, run the generator once:

```bash
dart run build_runner build
```

## Check it

See which migrations ran:

```bash
dox migration:status
```

You should see:

```text
Migration                                 Batch  Status
2023_07_16_131937700_create_users_table   1      Ran
2026_10_25_000000000_create_queue_tables  1      Ran
2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table      2      Ran
```

The first two come with the template. The server ran them at the first start in step 1.

Now start the server again with `dox s`.

## Next

[Step 3: Routes and controller](03-routes-and-controller.md)

# Step 3: Routes and controller

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/tutorial/03-routes-and-controller/

# Step 3: Routes and controller

In this step you add a controller and the routes to list, create and show posts.

## 1. Make the controller

A controller holds the code that answers a request. Make one for posts:

```bash
dox make:controller Post -r
```

`-r` makes a resource controller with the seven CRUD methods. You only need three of them now, so replace the file with this:

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/post.controller.dart"
import 'package:blog/app/models/post/post.model.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

@Inject()
class PostController {
  /// GET /api/posts
  Future<List<Post>> index(DoxRequest req) async {
    return Post().all();
  }

  /// POST /api/posts
  Future<DoxResponse> store(DoxRequest req) async {
    Post post = Post()
      ..title = req.input('title')
      ..body = req.input('body');
    await post.save();
    return response(post).statusCode(201);
  }

  /// GET /api/posts/{id}
  Future<Post> show(int id) async {
    Post? post = await Post().find(id);
    if (post == null) {
      throw NotFoundHttpException();
    }
    return post;
  }
}
```

What the code does:

- `@Inject()` puts the controller in the container, so Dox can make it for you. The code generator adds it to `lib/generated/container.g.dart`, and a new project already uses that file. So you change nothing else.
- When a method returns a model or a list of models, Dox sends it as JSON.
- `response(post).statusCode(201)` sets the status code.
- `show(int id)` gets the `{id}` from the URL. `/api/posts/abc` answers `404`, because `abc` is not an `int`.
- `req.input('title')` reads the input without any check. You add checks in [step 4](04-validation.md).

## 2. Add the routes

Routes connect a URL to a controller method. Open `lib/routes/api.dart` and add `Route.resource`:

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
import 'package:blog/app/http/controllers/api.controller.dart';
import 'package:blog/app/http/controllers/post.controller.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

class ApiRouter extends Router {
  @override
  String get prefix => 'api';

  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    Route.get('/ping', (ApiController c) => c.pong);

    Route.resource('posts', PostController);
  }
}
```

`Route.resource` makes one route for each method the controller has:

| Method | Path | Controller method |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `GET` | `/api/posts` | `index` |
| `POST` | `/api/posts` | `store` |
| `GET` | `/api/posts/{id}` | `show` |

The controller has no `update` or `destroy` yet, so those routes are not made. You do not need to register the router anywhere, because Dox finds every `Router` class by itself.

## 3. Start the server

If the server is not running, start it:

```bash
dox s
```

If it is already running, it restarts by itself when you save a file.

## Check it

Make a post:

```bash
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/posts \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Hello Dox","body":"My first post."}'
```

You should get `201` and the new post:

```text
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
...

{"id":1,"title":"Hello Dox","body":"My first post.","created_at":"2026-10-22T13:58:14.062215Z","updated_at":"2026-10-22T13:58:14.062215Z"}
```

List the posts:

```bash
curl http://localhost:3000/api/posts
```

```json
[{"id":1,"title":"Hello Dox","body":"My first post.","created_at":"2026-10-22T13:58:14.062215Z","updated_at":"2026-10-22T13:58:14.062215Z"}]
```

Show one post:

```bash
curl http://localhost:3000/api/posts/1
```

```json
{"id":1,"title":"Hello Dox","body":"My first post.","created_at":"2026-10-22T13:58:14.062215Z","updated_at":"2026-10-22T13:58:14.062215Z"}
```

Ask for a post that does not exist. You should get `404`:

```bash
curl -i http://localhost:3000/api/posts/99
```

```text
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
...

{"code":"not_found","message":"Not Found"}
```

## Next

[Step 4: Validation](04-validation.md)

# Step 4: Validation

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/tutorial/04-validation/

# Step 4: Validation

In this step you check the input of create and update with a `@Dto` class, so bad input gets a `422` answer and the controller does not run.

## 1. Make the DTO

A [DTO](../the-basic/dto.md) is a class that describes the input you expect, with a rule on each field. Make one:

```bash
dox make:dto SavePost
```

Create and update need the same fields, so one class is enough for both. Replace the file with this:

```dart title="lib/app/dtos/save_post/save_post.dto.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'save_post.dto.g.dart';

/// Typed, checked input. Run `dox build_runner:build` after a change.
@Dto()
class SavePost {
  @Trim()
  @Length(min: 3, max: 100)
  final String title;

  @Trim()
  @MinLength(10)
  final String body;

  const SavePost({required this.title, required this.body});

  static const DtoSchema<SavePost> schema = $SavePostDto;
}
```

- A field that is not nullable and has no default is required.
- The rules run from top to bottom. `@Trim()` removes spaces first, so an empty string then counts as missing.
- See [Validation](../the-basic/validation.md) for all rules.

## 2. Give the DTO list to the app

The code generator writes a list of all DTOs to `lib/generated/dtos.g.dart`. Dox needs this list, because it does not use reflection. Add two lines to `lib/config/app.dart`:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
import 'package:blog/generated/dtos.g.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  /// DTOs (generated list in lib/generated/dtos.g.dart)
  dtos: dtos,

  // ... the rest stays the same
);
```

## 3. Use the DTO in the controller

Now ask for `SavePost` as a parameter of the controller method. Dox checks the body and gives you a typed object. This version also adds `update`, so you can change a post:

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/post.controller.dart"
import 'package:blog/app/dtos/save_post/save_post.dto.dart';
import 'package:blog/app/models/post/post.model.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

@Inject()
class PostController {
  /// GET /api/posts
  Future<List<Post>> index(DoxRequest req) async {
    return Post().all();
  }

  /// POST /api/posts
  Future<DoxResponse> store(SavePost body) async {
    Post post = Post()
      ..title = body.title
      ..body = body.body;
    await post.save();
    return response(post).statusCode(201);
  }

  /// GET /api/posts/{id}
  Future<Post> show(int id) async {
    return _find(id);
  }

  /// PUT /api/posts/{id}
  Future<Post> update(int id, SavePost body) async {
    Post post = await _find(id);
    post
      ..title = body.title
      ..body = body.body;
    await post.save();
    return post;
  }

  Future<Post> _find(int id) async {
    Post? post = await Post().find(id);
    if (post == null) {
      throw NotFoundHttpException();
    }
    return post;
  }
}
```

You do not need to change the routes. `Route.resource` sees the new `update` method and adds `PUT` and `PATCH /api/posts/{id}`.

## 4. Run the generator

`dox s` runs the generator for you. If it is not running, run it once:

```bash
dart run build_runner build
```

It writes `lib/app/dtos/save_post/save_post.dto.g.dart` and `lib/generated/dtos.g.dart`.

## Check it

Send a title and a body that are too short:

```bash
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/posts \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Hi","body":"Short"}'
```

You should get `422` with one message for each field:

```text
HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Entity
content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
...

{"title":"The title must be between 3 and 100 characters","body":"The body must be at least 10 characters"}
```

Send an empty body:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/posts \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{}'
```

```json
{"title":"The title is required","body":"The body is required"}
```

Good input still gives `201`:

```bash
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/posts \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Second post","body":"Validation works now."}'
```

```text
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
```

Update the first post:

```bash
curl -X PUT http://localhost:3000/api/posts/1 \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Hello Dox (edited)","body":"My first post, edited."}'
```

```json
{"id":1,"title":"Hello Dox (edited)","body":"My first post, edited.","created_at":"2026-10-22T13:58:14.062215Z","updated_at":"2026-10-22T13:59:13.539886Z"}
```

# Step 5: Login with dox_auth

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/tutorial/05-auth/

# Step 5: Login with dox_auth

In this step you add register and login with a JWT token, so only a logged in user can create or change posts.

## 1. Add the package

`dox_auth` handles login and tokens. Add it to the project:

```bash
dart pub add dox_auth
```

## 2. Look at the users table

You need a user model and a `users` table to log in. You do not need to make them, because the template already has both. This is the `User` model:

```dart title="lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'user.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel(table: 'users', softDelete: true)
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @override
  List<String> get hidden => <String>['password'];

  @Column()
  String? name;

  @Column()
  String? email;

  @Column()
  String? password;
}
```

`password` is in `hidden`, so it is never in the JSON. This matters because the token holds the user as JSON, and anyone can read a JWT.

The `users` table already exists, because the server ran this migration at the first start in [step 1](01-create-project.md):

```dart title="db/migration/2023_07_16_131937700_create_users_table.dart"
class CreateUsersTable extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.create('users', (Table table) {
      table.id();
      table.string('name');
      table.string('email').unique();
      table.string('password');
      table.softDeletes();
      table.timestamps();
    });
  }
  // ...
}
```

`table.softDeletes()` makes the `deleted_at` column that `softDelete: true` needs. `email` is unique, so a second register with the same email fails.

## 3. Make the DTOs

Register and login each need their own input checks, so make two DTOs:

```bash
dox make:dto RegisterUser
dox make:dto LoginUser
```

Replace the register DTO with this:

```dart title="lib/app/dtos/register_user/register_user.dto.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart' hide Schema;

part 'register_user.dto.g.dart';

@Dto()
class RegisterUser {
  @Trim()
  @Length(min: 2, max: 50)
  final String name;

  @Trim()
  @Lowercase()
  @Email()
  @Unique('users', column: 'email')
  final String email;

  @MinLength(8)
  final String password;

  const RegisterUser({
    required this.name,
    required this.email,
    required this.password,
  });

  static const DtoSchema<RegisterUser> schema = $RegisterUserDto;
}
```

`@Unique` comes from `dox_orm`. It reads the database, so it runs after the other rules. `dox_orm` also has a class named `Schema`, so the import hides it.

Replace the login DTO with this:

```dart title="lib/app/dtos/login_user/login_user.dto.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'login_user.dto.g.dart';

@Dto()
class LoginUser {
  @Trim()
  @Lowercase()
  @Email()
  final String email;

  final String password;

  const LoginUser({required this.email, required this.password});

  static const DtoSchema<LoginUser> schema = $LoginUserDto;
}
```

## 4. Set up the auth provider

`dox_auth` needs to know which model to use and how to sign tokens. You tell it in a provider, which runs once in every isolate at start. Make this file:

```dart title="lib/providers/auth_provider.dart"
import 'package:blog/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:blog/config/env.dart';
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

/// Auth provider
/// --------------------------
/// Sets up JWT login with the User model.
/// Tokens are signed with APP_KEY and last 7 days.
class AppAuthProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Auth.initialize(
      AuthConfig(
        defaultGuard: 'api',
        guards: <String, AuthGuard>{
          'api': AuthGuard(
            driver: JwtAuthDriver(
              secret: SecretKey(env.appKey),
              expiresIn: const Duration(days: 7),
            ),
            provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
          ),
        },
      ),
    );
  }
}
```

You do not add the provider to a list. Dox finds it by itself, and the code generator adds it to `lib/generated/container.g.dart`.

## 5. Write the auth controller

This controller has the register, login and "who am I" routes:

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/auth.controller.dart"
import 'package:blog/app/dtos/login_user/login_user.dto.dart';
import 'package:blog/app/dtos/register_user/register_user.dto.dart';
import 'package:blog/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

@Inject()
class AuthController {
  /// POST /api/auth/register
  Future<DoxResponse> register(RegisterUser body) async {
    User user = User()
      ..name = body.name
      ..email = body.email
      ..password = await Hash.makeAsync(body.password);
    await user.save();

    String? token = Auth().login(user);
    return response(<String, dynamic>{
      'token': token,
      'user': user,
    }).statusCode(201);
  }

  /// POST /api/auth/login
  Future<Map<String, dynamic>> login(LoginUser body) async {
    Auth auth = Auth();
    String? token = await auth.attempt(<String, dynamic>{
      'email': body.email,
      'password': body.password,
    });
    if (token == null) {
      throw UnAuthorizedException(message: 'Wrong email or password');
    }
    return <String, dynamic>{'token': token, 'user': auth.user<User>()};
  }

  /// GET /api/auth/user
  User? user(DoxRequest req) {
    return req.auth?.user<User>();
  }
}
```

- `Hash.makeAsync()` makes a bcrypt hash of the password. You should never save a plain password. It runs in another isolate, so other requests do not wait.
- `Auth().attempt()` finds the user by email and checks the password. It gives a token, or `null`.
- `Auth().login(user)` gives a token without a password check. Register uses it, because the user was just made.

## 6. Protect the write routes

Reading posts stays public, but writing needs a login. So replace `Route.resource` with single routes, and put the write routes inside `Route.middleware`:

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
import 'package:blog/app/http/controllers/api.controller.dart';
import 'package:blog/app/http/controllers/auth.controller.dart';
import 'package:blog/app/http/controllers/post.controller.dart';
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

class ApiRouter extends Router {
  @override
  String get prefix => 'api';

  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    Route.get('/ping', (ApiController c) => c.pong);

    // Anyone can read posts.
    Route.get('/posts', (PostController c) => c.index);
    Route.get('/posts/{id}', (PostController c) => c.show);

    // Register and log in.
    Route.post('/auth/register', (AuthController c) => c.register);
    Route.post('/auth/login', (AuthController c) => c.login);

    // Only a logged in user can write posts.
    Route.middleware(<dynamic>[AuthMiddleware()], () {
      Route.get('/auth/user', (AuthController c) => c.user);
      Route.post('/posts', (PostController c) => c.store);
      Route.put('/posts/{id}', (PostController c) => c.update);
    });
  }
}
```

`AuthMiddleware` reads the `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header and loads the user. When the token is missing or wrong, it answers `401 Authentication failed`.

If you want a public route that still knows the user when there is a good token, use `AuthMiddleware(optional: true)`. It lets guests through.

## 7. Run the generator

`dox s` runs the generator for you. If it is not running, run it once:

```bash
dart run build_runner build
```

There is no new migration in this step, because the `users` table already exists.

## Check it

Register a user. You should get `201` with a token:

```bash
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/auth/register \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"Ann","email":"ann@example.com","password":"secret123"}'
```

```text
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
...

{"token":"eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIs...","user":{"id":1,"name":"Ann","email":"ann@example.com","created_at":"2026-10-22T14:01:07.827769Z","updated_at":"2026-10-22T14:01:07.827769Z"}}
```

Register with the same email again. You should get `422`:

```json
{"email":"The email has already been taken"}
```

Log in with a wrong password. You should get `401`:

```bash
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/auth/login \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"ann@example.com","password":"wrong"}'
```

```text
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
...

{"code":"unauthorized","message":"Wrong email or password"}
```

Now log in with the right password, and keep the token in a shell variable:

```bash
TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/auth/login \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"ann@example.com","password":"secret123"}' \
  | sed -E 's/.*"token":"([^"]+)".*/\1/')
echo $TOKEN
```

Try to make a post without a token. It is refused:

```bash
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/posts \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Third post","body":"Written with a token."}'
```

```text
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
...

{"code":"unauthorized","message":"Authentication failed"}
```

Send the same post with the token. Now it works:

```bash
curl -i -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/posts \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"title":"Third post","body":"Written with a token."}'
```

```text
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
...

{"id":3,"title":"Third post","body":"Written with a token.","created_at":"2026-10-22T14:01:08.094211Z","updated_at":"2026-10-22T14:01:08.094211Z"}
```

Ask who you are:

```bash
curl http://localhost:3000/api/auth/user -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
```

```json
{"id":1,"name":"Ann","email":"ann@example.com","created_at":"2026-10-22T14:01:07.827769Z","updated_at":"2026-10-22T14:01:07.827769Z"}
```

The answer has no `password`, because it is in `hidden`.

# Step 6: Test

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/tutorial/06-test/

# Step 6: Test

In this step you write one HTTP test for the list route and run it.

## 1. Write the test

A test calls your routes like a real client, so you know they still work after a change. The template has `test/http_test.dart`. Replace it with this:

```dart title="test/http_test.dart"
import 'package:blog/config/app.dart';
import 'package:blog/config/database.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/testing.dart';
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

import '../db/migration/migrations.dart';

void main() {
  late DoxTestClient client;

  setUpAll(() async {
    await Migrator(
      migrations: migrations,
      config: databaseConfig.getConnectionConfig(),
    ).migrate();
    client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig);
  });

  tearDownAll(() async {
    await client.close();
  });

  test('GET /api/posts gives a list', () async {
    TestResponse res = await client.get('/api/posts');
    res.expectStatus(200).expectJson(isA<List<dynamic>>());
  });
}
```

- `DoxTestClient.start` runs the app inside the test on a free port, so it does not clash with `dox s`.
- The test runs the migrations first, so it also works on an empty database.
- `package:test` is already in the `dev_dependencies` of the template.

## Check it

Run the test:

```bash
dart test test/http_test.dart
```

You should see:

```text
00:01 +1: All tests passed!
```

!!! tip "Use another database for tests"
    The test reads `.env`, so it uses `db/dox.sqlite`. To keep test data out of it, make a `.env.testing` file with `DB_NAME=test.sqlite`. `dart test` reads it on top of `.env`.

# Step 7: Build and deploy

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/tutorial/07-build-and-deploy/

# Step 7: Build and deploy

In this step you compile the app to one native binary, run it, and run it in Docker.

!!! warning "Never run production with `dox s` or `dart run`"
    They use the JIT compiler, which needs about 25 times more memory and starts slower. Build a native (AOT) binary for production.

## 1. Build the binary

Build the app:

```bash
dox build
```

```text
Built with build_runner/aot in 1s; wrote 0 outputs.
Running build hooks...Running link hooks...
Generated: /.../blog/build/bundle/bin/server
[Dox] Built build/bundle. Run it with: cd build/bundle && ./bin/server
```

`dox build` runs the code generator, then `dart build cli`. You get a `build/bundle` folder with everything the app needs:

| Path | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `bin/server` | the binary, about 10 MB. It needs no Dart SDK. |
| `bin/queue` | the [queue worker](../digging-deeper/queue.md). Run it as its own process. |
| `bin/schedule` | the [scheduler](../digging-deeper/scheduler.md). Run it as its own process. |
| `lib/` | native libraries from build hooks, like `libsqlite3`. Keep it next to `bin/`. |
| `db/` | your migrations. Your local SQLite file is not copied. |
| `.env.example` | a copy of the example env file. |

## 2. Run the binary

The binary reads `.env` from the folder you start it in, so copy yours there first. The `db` folder for the SQLite file is already in `build/bundle`.

```bash
cd build/bundle
cp ../../.env .env
./bin/server
```

```text
Migrating: 2023_07_16_131937700_create_users_table
Migrated: 2023_07_16_131937700_create_users_table
Migrating: 2026_10_25_000000000_create_queue_tables
Migrated: 2026_10_25_000000000_create_queue_tables
Migrating: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
Migrated: 2026_10_22_205345_create_posts_table
... "message":"Server started at http://[::]:3000 with 8 isolate (native)" ...
```

The migrations run again, because `db/dox.sqlite` is a new file in `build/bundle`. The migration list is compiled into the binary, so you do not need the source code.

On a server you can skip `.env` and set real environment variables instead. They win over `.env`.

## Check it

Call the binary from a second terminal:

```bash
curl http://localhost:3000/api/ping
curl http://localhost:3000/api/posts
```

```text
pong
[]
```

The list is empty, because this is a new database file. Stop the server with `Ctrl+C`.

## 3. Docker

If you deploy with Docker, the project already has a `Dockerfile`. It builds the same bundle and copies it into an empty (`scratch`) image:

```dockerfile title="Dockerfile"
FROM dart:stable AS build

# Resolve dependencies first, so this layer is cached.
WORKDIR /app
COPY pubspec.* ./
RUN dart pub get

COPY . .
RUN dart pub get --offline

# The dox CLI. `dox build` runs build_runner, then AOT-compiles
# bin/server.dart, bin/queue.dart and bin/schedule.dart with
# `dart build cli`. It puts all of them in build/bundle/bin, the native
# libraries in build/bundle/lib and the migrations in build/bundle/db.
# The queue worker and the scheduler run as their own processes:
# `/app/bin/queue work` and `/app/bin/schedule work`.
ARG DOX_VERSION=^3.2.0
RUN dart pub global activate dox "$DOX_VERSION"
RUN /root/.pub-cache/bin/dox build

# Lay out the final file tree:
# /app/bin/server, /app/bin/queue, /app/bin/schedule, /app/lib (native
# libraries), /app/db/migration, /app/storage and a writable /tmp
# (uploads bigger than 1 MB are streamed to a temp file).
RUN mkdir -p /out/app/storage /out/tmp \
  && chmod 1777 /out/tmp \
  && cp -r build/bundle/. /out/app/ \
  # the native HTTP server (Rust) needs libgcc_s, which /runtime/ does not have
  && LIBGCC=$(find / -name libgcc_s.so.1 -path '*lib*' | head -n 1) \
  && mkdir -p /out$(dirname $LIBGCC) && cp $LIBGCC /out$LIBGCC

# Minimal serving image: the AOT runtime files from the dart image
# (`/runtime/`) plus our bundle. No Dart SDK, no source code.
FROM scratch
COPY --from=build /runtime/ /
COPY --from=build /out/ /
WORKDIR /app

# Config comes from env variables. The image has no .env file,
# so secrets stay out of it.
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["/app/bin/server"]
```

Build and run the image. The image has no `.env` file, so pass the config as environment variables. `APP_KEY` must be exactly 32 characters, or the app does not start.

```bash
docker build -t blog .
docker run -p 3000:3000 \
  -e APP_KEY=$(openssl rand -hex 16) \
  -e DB_CONNECTION=sqlite \
  -e DB_NAME=storage/blog.sqlite \
  blog
```

!!! note "SQLite in Docker"
    The database file lives inside the container, so it is lost when the container is removed. Mount a volume for it: `-v blog-data:/app/storage`. For a busy app, use Postgres or MySQL. See [Database](../database/index.md).
