# Validation

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/the-basic/validation/

# Validation

Validation checks the request input with a typed [DTO](dto.md) class, so your controller only gets good data.

You write a class with `@Dto()` and put rules on its fields. Then you ask for it in your controller. Dox reads the request, checks it, and gives you a typed object. When the input is wrong, Dox answers `422` with the errors, and your controller does not run.

```dart title="lib/app/dtos/create_user/create_user.dto.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'create_user.dto.g.dart';

@Dto()
class CreateUser {
  @Trim()
  @Length(min: 3, max: 50)
  final String name;

  @Email()
  final String email;

  @MinLength(8)
  final String password;

  @Min(18)
  final int? age; // nullable, so optional

  const CreateUser({
    required this.name,
    required this.email,
    required this.password,
    this.age,
  });

  static const DtoSchema<CreateUser> schema = $CreateUserDto;
}
```

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/user.controller.dart"
class UserController {
  Future<User> store(CreateUser body) async {
    // body is already checked
    User user = User()
      ..name = body.name
      ..email = body.email
      ..password = await Hash.makeAsync(body.password);
    await user.save();
    return user;
  }
}
```

To create a DTO, register it with the app, and use it for the body, the query string or files, see [DTOs](dto.md). This page is about the rules and the error messages.

## Required and optional fields

The Dart type decides if a field is required, so you do not write `required` or `nullable`:

| Field | Key missing | Value `null` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `final String name;` | error `required` | error `required` |
| `final int? age;` | `null` | `null` |
| `final Role role;` with `this.role = Role.user` | `Role.user` | error `required` |

Rules on an optional field run only when it has a value. A default value is used only when the key is missing, and the rules do not check it.

### Empty strings and spaces

**An empty string counts as missing.** So a required `String` rejects `""`. Add `@AllowEmpty()` to keep `""`.

**Spaces are kept.** So `"   "` passes `required`, unless the field has `@Trim()`. To trim every text field of a DTO, use `@Dto(trim: true)`. Then `"   "` counts as missing.

If you want `""` to be `null` instead, use `@Dto(emptyStringsToNull: true)`.

### Using the default for bad values

Sometimes a bad value should not be an error. For example, `page=abc` in a list page should just give page 1. `@OrDefault()` turns a bad value into the default, with no error:

```dart
@OrDefault()
@NotIn(<int>[0])
final int page; // with this.page = 1, page=abc and page=0 give 1
```

The field needs a default, a nullable type or a `Maybe` type.

### Missing or `null`? (for PATCH)

In a PATCH request, a missing key means "do not change it", and `null` means "clear it". A `T?` field gives `null` for both. To know the difference, use `Maybe<T>`:

```dart
@Length(max: 500)
final Maybe<String?> bio; // default: const Maybe.missing()

// in the controller
if (body.bio.isPresent) {
  user.bio = body.bio.value; // can be null: the client cleared it
}
```

## Rules

Put rules on a field as annotations. They run from top to bottom, and the first rule that fails gives the error:

```dart
@Trim()
@Lowercase()
@Email()
@MaxLength(255)
final String email;
```

A rule on a list checks each item, like `@Email()` on a `List<String>`. Only the list rules check the list itself. For a few allowed values, use a Dart `enum`, or `@In(<String>['draft', 'published'])`.

These are the rules. Every rule, with its error code and message, is in [Validation rules](validation-rules.md):

| Kind | Annotations |
| --- | --- |
| Text | `@Length`, `@MinLength`, `@MaxLength`, `@Email`, `@Url`, `@Uuid`, `@Ulid`, `@Ip`, `@Regex`, `@In`, `@NotIn`, `@StartsWith`, `@EndsWith`, `@Alpha`, `@AlphaNumeric`, `@AlphaDash` |
| Change text | `@Trim`, `@Lowercase`, `@Uppercase`, `@AllowEmpty` |
| Numbers | `@Min`, `@Max`, `@Range`, `@Positive`, `@GreaterThan`, `@LessThan`, `@In`, `@NotIn` |
| Lists | `@MinItems`, `@MaxItems`, `@UniqueItems` |
| Dates | `@After`, `@Before`, `@AfterOrEqual`, `@BeforeOrEqual` |
| Other fields | `@Same`, `@Confirmed`, `@Different`, `@GreaterThanField`, `@GreaterThanOrEqualField`, `@LessThanField`, `@LessThanOrEqualField`, `@ProhibitedIf` |
| Present or missing | `@RequiredIf`, `@RequiredUnless`, `@RequiredWith`, `@RequiredWithout`, `@RequiredWithoutAll`, `@Filled`, `@Present`, `@Prohibited`, `@Accepted`, `@Declined` |
| Skip a field | `@ExcludeIf`, `@ExcludeUnless` |
| Files | `@MaxSize`, `@MinSize`, `@Mimes`, `@MimeTypes`, `@Image`, `@Dimensions` |
| Database | `@Unique`, `@Exists` |

## Checks across fields: `validate()`

Some checks need more than one field. Add a `validate(DtoErrors errors)` method to the DTO. Dox calls it after all field rules passed:

```dart
void validate(DtoErrors errors) {
  if (password != passwordConfirmation) {
    errors.add('password_confirmation', 'The passwords do not match');
  }
}
```

The key is the input key (snake_case). Use `_root` for an error about the whole body. `errors.has(key)` tells you if a key already has an error.

The method can be `async`. Do not throw for bad input. Add an error.

## Database rules: `@Unique` and `@Exists`

Sometimes you need to check the database, for example that an email is not taken yet. `@Unique` and `@Exists` do this. They come from `dox_orm`, so add `import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';` to the DTO file:

```dart
@Unique('users', column: 'email')
final String email;

@Exists('teams') // column defaults to id
final int teamId;
```

For an update, skip the row you are updating with `ignoreParam`:

```dart
// PUT /users/{id}
@Unique('users', column: 'email', ignoreParam: 'id')
final String email;
```

These rules read the database, so they run last. All options are in [Validation rules: database](validation-rules.md#database). The full order of checks is in [The order of checks](validation-rules.md#the-order-of-checks).

## The error response

When a check fails, Dox answers `422` with one message per field:

```json
{
  "email": "The email is not a valid email",
  "tags.0": "The tags may not be greater than 20 characters",
  "items.1.quantity": "The quantity must be greater than 0"
}
```

The key is the path to the value, with the input keys. List items use the index.

On a form post with a [session](session.md#validation-errors-and-old-input), Dox redirects back with the errors instead.

If you need another error shape, read `error.issues` of the `ValidationException` in your `ExceptionHandler`. Each issue has its `dottedPath`, its rule `code` (like `min_length`), its `message` and its `params`.

## Messages

Sometimes you want your own error text. You can change a message in three places. The first one wins.

On the rule:

```dart
@Email(message: 'Please check your email')
final String email;
```

On the DTO, by code or by `key.code`. Use `*` for list items, like `'tags.*.required'`:

```dart
@Dto(messages: <String, String>{
  'email.required': 'We need your email',
  'integer': 'The {field} must be a number',
})
```

For the whole app, with a `MessageResolver`. Use it for other languages:

```dart
class AppMessages extends MessageResolver {
  static const Map<String, Map<String, String>> _texts = <String, Map<String, String>>{
    'th': <String, String>{'required': 'กรุณากรอก {field}'},
  };

  @override
  String resolve(MessageRequest request) {
    String? template = _texts[request.locale]?[request.code]; // locale from Accept-Language
    if (template == null) {
      return super.resolve(request);
    }
    return format(template, request.params);
  }
}

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  validationMessages: AppMessages(),
  // ...
);
```

A message can use placeholders: `{field}` (the last key), `{value}`, and rule values like `{min}` and `{max}`.

### Names for `{field}`

By default `{field}` is the key, like `The first_name is required`. To show a nicer name, give attribute names on the DTO:

```dart
@Dto(attributes: <String, String>{'first_name': 'first name'})
class CreateUser { ... }
// The first name is required
```

Or for the whole app (and for fluent schemas), in the `MessageResolver`:

```dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  validationMessages: MessageResolver(
    attributes: <String, String>{'first_name': 'first name'},
  ),
  // ...
);
```

A key with no name still shows the key. Only the text changes. The key in the error response stays the same.

### Short rule names in message keys

Some error codes are long, like `min_length`. With the opt-in flag `laravelMessageKeys`, a message key can also use a short name. So `'name.min'` gives the message for the `min_length` error of `name`. Without the flag, only the full codes match. Set the flag in a provider's `setup()`, like the [other flags](../packages/validation.md#opt-in-flags):

```dart
Validator.flags = const ValidationFlags(laravelMessageKeys: true);
```

The error code in the response does not change: it is still `min_length`. These are the short names:

| Dox code | Short name |
| --- | --- |
| `min_length` | `min` |
| `max_length` | `max` |
| `length` | `size` |
| `length_between` | `between` |
| `start_with` | `starts_with` |
| `end_with` | `ends_with` |
| `alpha_numeric` | `alpha_num` |
| `greater_than` | `gt` |
| `less_than` | `lt` |
| `min_items` | `min` |
| `max_items` | `max` |
| `unique_items` | `distinct` |
| `min_size` | `min` |
| `max_size` | `max` |
| `mime_types` | `mimetypes` |
| `datetime` | `date` |

## Custom rules

If no built-in rule fits, write your own. Extend `Rule<T>`. `T` is the field type (or the item type, for a list):

```dart
class Slug extends Rule<String> {
  const Slug({super.message});

  @override
  String get name {
    return 'slug'; // the error code
  }

  @override
  String get defaultMessage {
    return 'The {field} must be a slug';
  }

  @override
  bool check(String value, RuleContext context) {
    return _pattern.hasMatch(value);
  }

  static final RegExp _pattern = RegExp(r'^[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*$');
}
```

Then use it like any rule:

```dart
@Slug()
final String slug;
```

- If the rule has values, add `final` fields and override `params`. They become placeholders.
- `context.lookup('other.key')` reads another input value.
- `context.sibling('key')` reads the raw input of a field next to this one, in the same object. For example, `context.sibling('password_confirmation')` in a rule on `password`. It gives `undefined` when the field is missing.
- If the rule needs the database, extend `AsyncRule<T>` and write `checkAsync`.

## Dynamic input

Sometimes the shape of the input is known only at runtime, like form fields from the database. Use a fluent schema for this:

```dart
Map<String, dynamic> data = await req.validateSchema(v.object(fields));
```

See [Fluent schemas](../packages/validation.md#fluent-schemas-for-dynamic-input). Use a DTO for everything else.

## Testing

To test the checks of a DTO, use `safeValidateMap` on its schema. See [DTOs: testing](dto.md#testing).

## Details

This section is for special cases. Most apps do not need it.

### Flags

- The flag `laravelErrors` sends `{"message": "...", "errors": {"field": ["..."]}}` as the error response. See [Core flags](../reference/app-config.md#core-flags).
- Three [opt-in flags](../packages/validation.md#opt-in-flags) change how DTOs are checked: get all errors at once, reject `[]` in a required list, and reject `""` in a `Maybe` field.

### Empty values and defaults

- `@Dto(trim: true)` works like `@Trim()` on each `String` field and on the text items of its lists and maps. A nested DTO uses its own `@Dto(trim:)`. The same is true for `@Dto(coerce:)`.
- With `@Dto(emptyStringsToNull: true)` and `@Dto(trim: true)`, blank text like `"  "` is `null` as well. Then `{"bio": ""}` clears a `Maybe<String?>` field. A required field still gets `required`. A field that is not nullable but has a default gets `required` too, because `null` is not a missing key.
- `@OrDefault()` works on any field, in a body or a query. A `Maybe` field gets `Maybe.missing()`. Errors from async rules (`@Unique`, `@Exists`, your `AsyncRule`) and from `validate()` are not dropped. They run later, on the built object, and still give `422`.

### Messages

- In `@Dto(messages:)`, a full dotted path works too, like `'address.city.required'`. It also reaches a nested DTO. A message in the nested DTO itself, like `'city.required'`, wins over it.
- A name for `{field}` is looked up by the dotted path (`address.city`), then with `*` for list items (`items.*.qty`), then by the field name (`city`).
- The names of the DTO win over the names of the `MessageResolver`. A nested DTO uses its own names first, then the names of the outer DTO.
- `MessageResolver.setAttributes(...)` adds names to a resolver. A custom resolver can override `attributeName(path)`.
- `{other}` and `{others}` (the other keys of rules like `@RequiredIf` and `@Same`) show their names too.
- `@Dto(attributes:)` needs one `build_runner` run.
- With `laravelMessageKeys`, the full code is tried first at each step of the lookup, then the short name. So `'name.min_length'` wins over `'name.min'`. A key with a path still wins over a key with only a code: `'name.min'` wins over `'min_length'`.
- Short names work in `@Dto(messages:)` and in a `MessageResolver`. A code that is already short (like `email` or `required`) needs nothing. With the flag on, a key `min` or `max` with no path fits text, list and file errors too, not only numbers.

# Validation rules

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/the-basic/validation-rules/

# Validation rules

This page lists every annotation you can put on a `@Dto` field, with its error code and default message.

Use it to look up a rule. To learn how DTOs work, read [Validation](validation.md) first.

How to read the tables:

- **Code** is the error code. Use it in `@Dto(messages: ...)` and in a `MessageResolver`.
- **Message** is the default English text. `{field}` is the last key of the path.
- Every annotation also takes `message:`. It wins over every other message.
- All limits include the limit itself, unless the table says "exclusive".
- On a `List<T>` field, a value rule checks each item. Only the list rules check the list itself.

## Type errors

You get these errors when a value does not fit the field type. They have no annotation.

| Code | When | Message |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `required` | a required field is missing, `null`, or `""` | `The {field} is required` |
| `string` | not a string | `The {field} must be a string` |
| `integer` | not a whole number | `The {field} must be an integer` |
| `numeric` | not a number (`double`, `num`) | `The {field} must be a number` |
| `boolean` | not a bool | `The {field} must be a boolean` |
| `date` | not an ISO 8601 date | `The {field} must be a date` |
| `in` | not a name of the enum | `The selected {field} is invalid. Valid options are {values}` |
| `array` | not a list | `The {field} must be an array` |
| `object` | not an object (nested DTO, `Map`) | `The {field} must be an object` |
| `file` | not a file | `The {field} must be a file` |
| `unrecognized_keys` | unknown key, with `@Dto(strict: true)` | `The {field} field is not allowed` |

## Text

Use these rules on `String` fields (and `List<String>` items):

| Annotation | Code | Message | JSON Schema |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `@Length(min: 3, max: 50)` | `length_between` | `The {field} must be between {min} and {max} characters` | `minLength`, `maxLength` |
| `@Length(min: 6, max: 6)` | `length` | `The {field} must be exactly {length} characters` | `minLength`, `maxLength` |
| `@MinLength(3)` | `min_length` | `The {field} must be at least {min} characters` | `minLength` |
| `@MaxLength(50)` | `max_length` | `The {field} may not be greater than {max} characters` | `maxLength` |
| `@Email()` | `email` | `The {field} is not a valid email` | `format: email` |
| `@Url()` | `url` | `The {field} must be a url` | `format: uri` |
| `@Uuid()` | `uuid` | `The {field} is invalid uuid` | `format: uuid` |
| `@Ulid()` | `ulid` | `The {field} must be a valid ULID` | `pattern` |
| `@Ip()` | `ip` | `The {field} must be an ip address` | `anyOf` `ipv4` / `ipv6` |
| `@Regex(r'[a-z]+')` | `regex` | `The {field} format is invalid` | `pattern` |
| `@In(['a', 'b'])` | `in` | `The selected {field} is invalid. Valid options are {values}` | `enum` |
| `@NotIn(['root'])` | `not_in` | `The {field} field cannot be {value}` | `not: {enum}` |
| `@StartsWith('dox')` | `start_with` | `The {field} must start with {prefix}` | `pattern` |
| `@EndsWith('.dev')` | `end_with` | `The {field} must end with {suffix}` | `pattern` |
| `@Alpha()` | `alpha` | `The {field} must be an alphabetic` | `pattern` |
| `@AlphaNumeric()` | `alpha_numeric` | `The {field} must be only alphabetic and number` | `pattern` |
| `@AlphaDash()` | `alpha_dash` | `The {field} must be only alphabetic, number, dash and underscore` | `pattern` |

- `@Length` has `min:` and `max:`. Both are optional, but you must give one.
  With only `min:` it acts like `@MinLength`, with only `max:` like `@MaxLength`.
- Length counts characters (Unicode code points). `é` counts as 1.
- `@Url()` needs `http` or `https` and a host.
- `@Uuid()` takes any version. Upper or lower case.
- `@Ulid()` takes 26 Crockford base32 characters, upper or lower case. The first one is `0` to `7`.
- `@Regex(pattern, {message})` must match the **whole** value. You do not need `^` and `$`.
  The regex is checked when the generator runs. A bad regex stops the build.
- `@Alpha()`, `@AlphaNumeric()` and `@AlphaDash()` use ASCII letters `a-z`, `A-Z`. `@AlphaDash()` also allows digits `0-9`, `-` and `_`.
- `@In` and `@NotIn` compare exactly (case matters).

## More text rules

These are also for `String` fields:

| Annotation | Code | Message | JSON Schema |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `@Json()` | `json` | `The {field} is not a valid json` | `contentMediaType: application/json` |
| `@Digits(6)` | `digits` | `The {field} must be {digits} digits` | `pattern` |
| `@DigitsBetween(4, 6)` | `digits_between` | `The {field} must be between {min} and {max} digits` | `pattern` |
| `@DateFormatted('Y-m-d')` | `date_format` | `The {field} must match the format {format}` | |
| `@HexColor()`, `@HexColor(short: true)` | `hex_color` | `The {field} must be a hex color like #1a2b3c` | `pattern` |
| `@Password(min: 8, ...)` | `password` | `The {field} must have {rules}` | `minLength` |

- `@HexColor()` takes `#` and 6 hex digits, in any case. `@HexColor(short: true)` also takes 3 digits, like `#abc`.
- `@Digits` and `@DigitsBetween` take only `0-9`. No sign, no dot. Use a `String` field, so leading zeros stay.
- `@DateFormatted` uses these letters:
  day `d`, `j`, `D` (`Mon`), `l` (`Monday`), `N`, `w`, `S` (`st`), `z`;
  month `m`, `n`, `M` (`Jan`), `F` (`January`), `t`;
  year `Y`, `y`, `L`;
  time `a`, `A`, `g`, `h`, `G`, `H`, `i`, `s`, `v`, `u`;
  time zone `e`, `T`, `P`, `p`, `O`, `Z`, `I`;
  full `U`, `c`, `r`.
  Put `\` before a letter to use it as text, like `Y-m-d\TH:i`. Any other letter stops the build (and throws an `ArgumentError` in `v.string().dateFormat()`). Other characters must be there as they are.
  `j`, `n`, `g`, `G`, `z` and `U` take no leading zero: `j/n/Y` rejects `01/02/2024`.
  `e` and `T` take any name that looks like a time zone. They do not check that it is a real one.
  The date must exist: `2023-02-29` fails. Names need the case shown (`Jan`, not `jan`). A day name must fit the date. The field stays a `String`. Use a `DateTime` field for ISO 8601 dates.
- `@Password` options: `min` (default 8), `letters`, `mixedCase` (one upper and one lower case letter), `numbers`, `symbols`. They are all off by default.
  Letters, numbers and symbols are Unicode, so `é` is a letter. `{rules}` lists the options you set, like `at least 8 characters, one number, and one symbol`, or `at least 8 characters and one number`.
  It does not check leaked passwords.

## Other fields

Sometimes a field depends on another field. For example, a password must match its confirmation, or a VAT number is required only for a company. These rules read another key of the same object.

The other key is the input key, like `account_type`, not the Dart name `accountType`. If you give the Dart name of a field with another key, the build stops.

| Annotation | Code | Message |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@Confirmed()` | `confirmed` | `The {field} confirmation does not match` |
| `@Same('email')` | `same` | `The {field} must match {other}` |
| `@RequiredIf('type', 'company')` | `required_if` | `The {field} is required when {other} is {values}` |
| `@RequiredWith(['phone'])` | `required_with` | `The {field} is required when {others} is present` |
| `@RequiredUnless('type', 'guest')` | `required_unless` | `The {field} is required unless {other} is {values}` |
| `@RequiredWithout(['email'])` | `required_without` | `The {field} is required when {others} is not present` |
| `@RequiredWithoutAll(['email', 'phone'])` | `required_without_all` | `The {field} is required when none of {others} are present` |
| `@Different('old_password')` | `different` | `The {field} and {other} must be different` |
| `@ProhibitedIf('type', 'guest')` | `prohibited_if` | `The {field} is prohibited when {other} is {values}` |
| `@GreaterThanField('min_price')` | `greater_than` | `The {field} must be greater than {min}` |
| `@GreaterThanOrEqualField('min_price')` | `min` | `The {field} must be greater than or equal {min}` |
| `@LessThanField('max_price')` | `less_than` | `The {field} must be less than {max}` |
| `@LessThanOrEqualField('max_price')` | `max` | `The {field} must be less than or equal {max}` |

- `@Confirmed` and `@Same` compare the raw input of both keys, so `@Trim` does not change the compare.
- `@Confirmed()` on `password` needs the key `password_confirmation` with the same value. The error is on `password`. Use `@Confirmed(other: 'password_again')` for another key.
  The DTO does not need a field for the confirmation key.
- Text and numbers match by text, both ways: `1234` matches `"1234"`, and `"1234"` matches `1234`.
- `@RequiredIf` and `@RequiredWith` work on a nullable field, a `Maybe` field or a field with a default. On an always-required field the build stops.
- `@RequiredIf('type', ['company', 'shop'])` takes a list: any of the values makes the field required. `"true"` matches `true`, `"1"` matches `1`. An enum value matches its name: `@RequiredIf('role', Role.admin)` matches `"admin"`.
- `@RequiredWith(['phone', 'email'])`: the field is required when any of the keys is there and not empty.
- `@RequiredUnless('type', 'guest')` makes the field required unless `type` is `guest`. A missing `type` counts as `null`, so the field is required then. It takes a list of values like `@RequiredIf`.
- `@RequiredWithout(['email'])`: the field is required when any of the keys is missing or empty. `@RequiredWithoutAll(['email', 'phone'])`: when all of them are missing or empty.
- `@RequiredUnless`, `@RequiredWithout` and `@RequiredWithoutAll` follow the same rules as `@RequiredIf`: a nullable, `Maybe` or default field, and input keys.
- `@Different('old_password')` needs a value that is not the same as the other key. It compares the raw input like `@Same`. A missing other key passes.
- `@ProhibitedIf('type', 'guest')` means: when `type` is `guest`, the field must be missing or empty. Empty is `null`, blank text, an empty list or an empty map. `0` and `false` fail. This is not the same as `@Prohibited()`, which fails on `null` and `[]`. It reads `type` and matches like `@RequiredIf`.
- `@GreaterThanField`, `@GreaterThanOrEqualField`, `@LessThanField` and `@LessThanOrEqualField` compare a value with another field. They are for `int`, `double` and `num` fields. They read the raw input of the other key: a number, or number text from a form. A missing other key (or one that is not a number) fails.
  `{min}` and `{max}` in the message are the other key. They use the codes of `@GreaterThan`, `@Min`, `@LessThan` and `@Max`.
- On a `List<T>` field, `@Different` checks the whole list, not each item. The field compare rules do not fit a list.
- Missing means: not there, `null`, blank text, an empty list or an empty map.
- They run in step 1, with the other "required" checks. `@Confirmed` and `@Same` run in step 2.

## Present or missing

Use these rules to check if a key is sent and has a value:

| Annotation | Code | Message |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@Filled()` | `filled` | `The {field} must have a value` |
| `@Present()` | `present` | `The {field} must be present` |
| `@Prohibited()` | `prohibited` | `The {field} is prohibited` |
| `@Accepted()` | `accepted` | `The {field} must be accepted` |
| `@Declined()` | `declined` | `The {field} must be declined` |

- `@Filled()`: a missing key passes. A key that is sent must have a value: not `null`, not blank text, not an empty list.
- `@Present()`: the key must be sent. Its value may be `null` or empty.
- `@Filled()` and `@Present()` are for a nullable, `Maybe` or default field, like `@RequiredIf`. They run in step 1.
- `@Prohibited()`: the key must be missing, or blank text like `""` or `"  "`. Any other sent value fails, also `null`, `[]`, `{}`, `0` and `false`. It reads the raw input, so it runs before the type check, in step 1. It is for a nullable, `Maybe` or default field.
- `@Accepted()` takes `true`, `1`, `"1"`, `"true"`, `"yes"` and `"on"`. `@Declined()` takes `false`, `0`, `"0"`, `"false"`, `"no"` and `"off"`. The text is case sensitive.
  Use them on a `bool` field with no default. Then a missing value fails with `required`. In a form, `yes` and `on` turn into `true` first. In a JSON body a `bool` field takes only `true` and `false`, unless the DTO has `@Dto(coerce: true)`.

```dart
@Accepted()
final bool terms;

@Present()
final String? note; // the key must be there, null is fine
```

## Skip a field

Sometimes a field only matters for some input. For example, a VAT number is only for a company. These rules skip the field for the other cases:

| Annotation | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `@ExcludeIf('type', 'person')` | when `type` is `person`, the field is skipped |
| `@ExcludeUnless('type', 'company')` | unless `type` is `company`, the field is skipped |

- A skipped field is not read and not checked. It gets its default, `null` or `Maybe.missing()`, as if it was not sent. The field is left out of the validated data.
- They read the raw input of the other key, and match like `@RequiredIf` (also with a list of values).
- `@ExcludeIf`: a missing other key does not skip. `@ExcludeUnless`: a missing other key counts as `null`, so the field is skipped.
- They are for a nullable, `Maybe` or default field. On an always-required field the build stops.
- The fluent schemas have `.excludeIf()` and `.excludeUnless()`. There the key is left out of the output. See [Skip a field](../packages/validation.md#skip-a-field).

```dart
final String type;

@ExcludeIf('type', 'person')
@MinLength(5)
final String? vatNumber; // not checked for a person
```

## Change text

These change the value before the rules run. For example, `@Trim` removes the spaces a user typed by mistake.

They always run in this order, wherever you put them: `@Trim`, then `@Lowercase` or `@Uppercase`, then the "empty string is missing" check.

| Annotation | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `@Trim()` | removes spaces at the start and the end |
| `@Lowercase()` | makes the text lower case |
| `@Uppercase()` | makes the text upper case |
| `@AllowEmpty()` | keeps `""` as a value. Without it, `""` counts as missing. |

They have no error and no JSON Schema output. `@Lowercase()` and `@Uppercase()` together stop the build.

## Bad value to default

Sometimes a bad value should just give the default, like `page=abc` in a list page:

| Annotation | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `@OrDefault()` | a bad value gives the default of the field (or `null`, or `Maybe.missing()`), not an error. |

- It drops type errors and the errors of the normal rules of the field.
- Errors from async rules (`@Unique`, `@Exists`, your `AsyncRule`) and from `validate()` are not dropped. They still give `422`.
- The field needs a default, a nullable type or a `Maybe` type. Else the build stops.

## Numbers

Use these rules on `int`, `double` and `num` fields (and list items):

| Annotation | Code | Message | JSON Schema |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `@Min(18)` | `min` | `The {field} must be greater than or equal {min}` | `minimum` |
| `@Max(100)` | `max` | `The {field} must be less than or equal {max}` | `maximum` |
| `@Range(1, 10)` | `between` | `The {field} must be between {min} and {max}` | `minimum`, `maximum` |
| `@Positive()` | `greater_than` | `The {field} must be greater than 0` | `exclusiveMinimum: 0` |
| `@GreaterThan(0.5)` | `greater_than` | `The {field} must be greater than {min}` (exclusive) | `exclusiveMinimum` |
| `@LessThan(100)` | `less_than` | `The {field} must be less than {max}` (exclusive) | `exclusiveMaximum` |
| `@In([1, 2, 3])` | `in` | `The selected {field} is invalid. Valid options are {values}` | `enum` |
| `@NotIn([0])` | `not_in` | `The {field} field cannot be {value}` | `not: {enum}` |

The values are `num`. `@Min(1.5)` on an `int` field stops the build. `@Range` checks that a number is between two values.

## Lists

Use these rules on `List<T>` fields. They check the list, not the items:

| Annotation | Code | Message | JSON Schema |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `@MinItems(1)` | `min_items` | `The {field} must have at least {min} items` | `minItems` |
| `@MaxItems(5)` | `max_items` | `The {field} may not have more than {max} items` | `maxItems` |
| `@UniqueItems()` | `unique_items` | `The {field} must not have duplicate items` | `uniqueItems: true` |

`@UniqueItems()` works for `String`, numbers, `bool`, enums and `DateTime`. On a list of DTOs it stops the build.

## Dates

Use these rules on `DateTime` fields:

| Annotation | Code | Message | JSON Schema |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `@After('2000-01-01')` | `after` | `The {field} must be a date after {date}` | `format: date-time` |
| `@Before('now')` | `before` | `The {field} must be a date before {date}` | `format: date-time` |
| `@AfterOrEqual('today')` | `after_or_equal` | `The {field} must be a date after or equal to {date}` | `format: date-time` |
| `@BeforeOrEqual('end_date')` | `before_or_equal` | `The {field} must be a date before or equal to {date}` | `format: date-time` |

- The value is one of:
    - an ISO 8601 date, like `'2000-01-01'`,
    - a word: `'now'` (the time of the request), `'today'`, `'tomorrow'` or `'yesterday'`. These are in UTC, and `'today'` is the start of the day,
    - the input key of another `DateTime` field of the same DTO, like `'start_date'`.
- With another field, the check uses its converted value. When that field has no value, the check passes.
- A text that is not a date, a word or a `DateTime` field stops the build.
- `@After` and `@Before` are exclusive: `@After('2000-01-01')` does not accept `2000-01-01T00:00:00Z`. `@AfterOrEqual` and `@BeforeOrEqual` accept the same time.
- Words and other fields need one `build_runner` run.

```dart
final DateTime startDate;

@After('start_date')
@BeforeOrEqual('tomorrow')
final DateTime endDate;
```

## Files

Use these rules on `RequestFile` and `List<RequestFile>` fields:

| Annotation | Code | Message | JSON Schema |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `@MaxSize('2MB')` | `max_size` | `The {field} may not be larger than {max}` | `maxLength` (bytes) |
| `@Mimes(['pdf', 'png'])` | `mimes` | `The {field} must be a file of type: {types}` | `contentMediaType` |
| `@Image()` | `image` | `The {field} must be an image` | `contentMediaType: image/*` |
| `@MinSize('10KB')` | `min_size` | `The {field} must be at least {min}` | `minLength` (bytes) |
| `@MimeTypes(['image/png', 'image/*'])` | `mime_types` | `The {field} must be a file of type: {types}` | `contentMediaType` |
| `@Dimensions(minWidth: 100, ratio: 3 / 2)` | `dimensions` | `The {field} has invalid image dimensions` | `contentMediaType: image/*` |

- `@MaxSize` and `@MinSize` units: `B`, `KB`, `MB`, `GB`. `1KB` = 1024 bytes. A bad size text stops the build.
- `@Mimes` takes file extensions. Dox finds the real type from the first bytes of the file.
  The file name extension must not name another type, or a type a browser runs (like `html` or `svg`).
  So `x.html` with GIF bytes does not pass. An empty or unknown extension is fine.
  For zip based types (like `docx` or `xlsx`), the file name extension must match too.
  For types without a byte signature (like `txt` or `csv`), it uses the file name extension.
- `@Image()` is `@Mimes(['jpg', 'jpeg', 'png', 'gif', 'webp', 'bmp'])`. No `svg`.
- `@MimeTypes` takes MIME types. Dox turns each one into file extensions, then checks the real bytes like `@Mimes`.
  It does not trust the content type the client sent.
  `image/*` means: jpg, jpeg, png, gif, webp, bmp, tif, tiff, ico, heic, heif, avif and psd. No `svg`.
  This is wider than `@Image()`, and browsers can not show most of the extra types.
  For images that browsers can show, use `@Image()` or list the MIME types.
  Write `image/jpeg`, not `image/jpg`. `image/jpg` is not a real MIME type, so it never matches.
  An unknown MIME type never matches.
- `@Dimensions` checks the width and height in pixels. Limits: `width`, `height` (exact), `minWidth`, `maxWidth`, `minHeight`, `maxHeight` and `ratio` (width / height, like `3 / 2`).
  Give at least one limit, or the build stops.
  It reads only the image header of PNG, GIF, WebP and JPEG files, never the whole file.
  Any other file, or a broken or cut short header, fails.
  For a JPEG over 1 MB, Dox reads the first 128 KB. A JPEG with more photo metadata than that before its size fails.
  A `ratio` passes when it is off by less than one pixel.
- The JSON Schema of a file is `{"type": "string", "format": "binary"}`, plus the keys above.

With fluent schemas, the same rules are on `v.file()`. Sizes there are in bytes, not text:

```dart
v.file()
    .maxSize(2 * 1024 * 1024) // 2 MB
    .mimeTypes(<String>['image/jpeg', 'image/png'])
    .dimensions(minWidth: 100, maxWidth: 2000);
```

The fluent methods are `maxSize(bytes)`, `minSize(bytes)`, `mimes(types)`, `mimeTypes(types)`, `dimensions(...)`, `image()` and `extensions(types)`.

## Database

These rules come from `dox_orm`. They read the database, so they run after all other checks passed:

| Annotation | Code | Message |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@Unique(table, {column, ignoreParam, ignoreColumn, connection})` | `unique` | `The {field} has already been taken` |
| `@Exists(table, {column, connection})` | `exists` | `The selected {field} is invalid` |

- `@Unique` column default: the input key. `@Exists` column default: `id`.
- They read the table, not the model. So soft-deleted rows count too.
- `ignoreParam: 'id'` skips the row where `ignoreColumn` (default `id`) equals the path param `{id}`.
- They add nothing to the JSON Schema.

See [Database rules](validation.md#database-rules-unique-and-exists).

In a fluent schema, use `v.string().unique('users', column: 'email')` and `v.int().exists('teams')`. See [Fluent schemas](../packages/validation.md#more-rules).

## Keys and DTO options

These options change how the whole DTO reads its input:

| Annotation | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `@Name('emailAddress')` | the input key for this field. Default: the field name in snake_case. |
| `@Dto()` | marks the class. |
| `@Dto(source: Source.query)` | where to read: `Source.auto` (default), `Source.query`, `Source.body`. |
| `@Dto(keyCase: KeyCase.field)` | keys: `KeyCase.snake` (default) or `KeyCase.field` (the Dart name as is). |
| `@Dto(strict: true)` | unknown keys are errors. Default `false`: they are dropped. |
| `@Dto(emptyStringsToNull: true)` | `""` is read as `null`, not as missing. Default `false`. |
| `@Dto(trim: true)` | trims every `String` field and text item, like `@Trim()` on each. Default `false`. |
| `@Dto(coerce: true)` | a JSON body may send text for numbers and bools, like a form. Default `false`. |
| `@Dto(messages: {...})` | messages by `code` or `key.code`. A dotted path like `address.city.required` or `tags.*.required` works too. A short rule name works too, like `name.min`. See [Short rule names](validation.md#short-rule-names-in-message-keys). |
| `@Dto(attributes: {...})` | the names shown for `{field}`, by key, like `{'first_name': 'first name'}`. See [Names for `{field}`](validation.md#names-for-field). |
| `@Describe('...')` | on a field: a short text for the `description` of the field in the JSON Schema. It does not change the checks. |

A `///` doc comment on a field becomes its `description` in the JSON Schema.
`@Describe` wins over the `///` comment. Use it when the text is for API users and MCP clients, not for the code.
The OpenAPI docs and MCP tools (`McpDtoTool`) show it.

```dart
@Describe('Category ID (see list_categories).') final int categoryId;
```

## Types in detail

This is how each field type reads input. The short table is in [Types](dto.md#field-types).

- **JSON is strict.** In a JSON body, `"18"` is not an `int`. You get the error `integer`. With `@Dto(coerce: true)`, JSON is read like form text for `int`, `double`, `num` and `bool`, and a `bool` also takes `1` and `0`.
- **Query and form data are text.** Dox turns the text into the field type first. If it can not, you get the type error.
- `int` takes `18` or `18.0`, never a fraction. `"4.5"` or `4.5` gives `integer`.
- `bool` in text takes `true`, `1`, `yes`, `on` and `false`, `0`, `no`, `off` (any case).
- `DateTime` takes `2024-01-31` or `2024-01-31T10:00:00Z`. A value without a time zone is read as UTC.
  The result is always UTC (`isUtc == true`). A number (timestamp) is not allowed.
- An `enum` matches the Dart name exactly. `"Admin"` does not match `Role.admin`. Custom wire values (like `"ADMIN"`) are not supported.
- `Object?` and `dynamic` take any value. They are not checked.
- `Map<String, dynamic>` must be an object. Its values are not checked.
- In query and form data, one value for a `List<T>` field gives a list with one item.
- In bracket keys, list indexes are sorted and packed: `items[3]` alone gives a list with one item.
- In query and form data, a list can have at most 1000 items, and keys can nest at most 10 levels. More gives `422` with the key `_root`.

## Body types

The content type of the body decides how Dox reads it:

| Body | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `application/json` (or any `+json` type) | read with strict JSON types |
| `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`, `multipart/form-data` | read as text, then converted |
| any other content type | `415 Unsupported Media Type` |
| JSON that is not valid | `400 Bad Request` |
| JSON that is not an object (like `[1, 2]`) | `422` with the key `_root` |

## The order of checks

Dox checks the input in four steps:

1. Read the input and convert types. Change text (`@Trim`, `@Lowercase`, `@Uppercase`). Find missing required fields.
2. The field rules, top to bottom. The first rule that fails stops the other rules of that field. So there is no `@Bail`. A fluent schema runs all rules, unless you add `.bail()`. See [Stop at the first error](../packages/validation.md#stop-at-the-first-error).
3. The `validate()` method (nested DTOs first, then the parent).
4. Async rules (`@Unique`, `@Exists`, your `AsyncRule`), one at a time, in field order.

Each step runs only when the step before it had no errors. So the database is never asked about input that is already wrong.

- Steps 1 and 2 run per DTO. So one answer can have a type error in `address` and a rule error in `items.1`.
- Inside one step, Dox collects the errors of all fields.
- A default value is not checked by the field rules. Async rules check the final value.

## What the generator checks

The build stops with a clear error when:

- a field is not `final`, or is not a parameter of the unnamed constructor,
- a field type is not supported (see [Types](dto.md#field-types)),
- a rule does not fit the field type (like `@Email()` on an `int`),
- a `Maybe<T>` field has no `const Maybe.missing()` default,
- `@RequiredIf`, `@RequiredWith`, `@RequiredUnless`, `@RequiredWithout`, `@RequiredWithoutAll`, `@Filled`, `@Present`, `@Prohibited`, `@ProhibitedIf`, `@ExcludeIf` or `@ExcludeUnless` is on a field that is always required,
- `@OrDefault()` is on a field that is always required (no default, not nullable and not a `Maybe`),
- a rule that reads another key (like `@RequiredIf`, `@Same`, `@Different`, `@ExcludeIf` or `@GreaterThanField`) names a Dart field (like `accountType`) instead of its input key (`account_type`),
- `@After`, `@Before`, `@AfterOrEqual` or `@BeforeOrEqual` has a text that is not a date, a word or another `DateTime` field,
- `@DateFormatted` has a letter it does not know,
- two `@Dto` classes in the app have the same name,
- the class is generic, or extends another class (other than `Object`).


---

# Controller

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/the-basic/controller/

# Controller

A controller holds the code that answers a route, so your route files stay short.

You could write all your code in route closures. But when an app grows, it is easier to group the code for one topic, like blogs, in one class. A controller can be a class method, a static method or a plain function.

## Writing controllers

### Basic controllers

Make a controller with the CLI:

```bash
dox make:controller Blog
```

It writes `lib/app/http/controllers/blog.controller.dart` with an empty `index` method. Fill it in:

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/blog.controller.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

@Inject()
class BlogController {
  String index(DoxRequest req) {
    return 'all blogs';
  }
}
```

Then point a route to the method:

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
Route.get('/blogs', (BlogController c) => c.index);
```

`@Inject()` puts the controller in the container. Run `dart run build_runner build` after you add one. The constructor can ask for services and repositories. See [Dependency injection](dependency-injection.md).

### Static methods

If a controller needs nothing from the container, a static method also works:

```dart
class AppController {
  static String ping(DoxRequest req) {
    return 'pong';
  }
}

Route.get('/ping', AppController.ping);
```

### Plain functions

A plain function works too:

```dart
String listBlog(DoxRequest req) {
  return 'all blogs';
}

Route.get('/blogs', listBlog);
```

## Resource controllers

Most models need the same routes: list, show, create, update and delete. A resource controller has the 7 methods that `Route.resource` uses, so one line of routes covers all of them.

Make one with `-r`:

```bash
dox make:controller Blog -r
```

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/blog.controller.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

/// Route: Route.resource('path', BlogController);
@Inject()
class BlogController {
  /// GET /resource
  Future<dynamic> index(DoxRequest req) async {}

  /// GET /resource/create
  Future<dynamic> create(DoxRequest req) async {}

  /// POST /resource
  Future<dynamic> store(DoxRequest req) async {}

  /// GET /resource/{id}
  Future<dynamic> show(DoxRequest req, int id) async {}

  /// GET /resource/{id}/edit
  Future<dynamic> edit(DoxRequest req, int id) async {}

  /// PUT|PATCH /resource/{id}
  Future<dynamic> update(DoxRequest req, int id) async {}

  /// DELETE /resource/{id}
  /// delete() gives the number of rows it deleted, so 0 is a 404:
  /// `if (await Blog().where('id', id).delete() == 0) throw NotFoundHttpException();`
  Future<dynamic> destroy(DoxRequest req, int id) async {}
}
```

Register it with one route:

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
Route.resource('blogs', BlogController);
```

You can delete the methods you do not need, because `Route.resource` skips them. See [Routing: resource routes](routing.md#resource-routes).

### API resource controllers

An API has no form pages. So `--api` makes the resource controller without `create` and `edit`:

```bash
dox make:controller Blog --api
```

### Resource controllers for a model

If the controller works with one model, use `--model`. It fills the methods with model code:

```bash
dox make:controller Blog --model=Blog
```

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/blog.controller.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/blog/blog.model.dart';

/// Route: Route.resource('path', BlogController);
@Inject()
class BlogController {
  /// GET /resource
  Future<dynamic> index(DoxRequest req) async {
    return Blog().all();
  }

  /// GET /resource/create
  Future<dynamic> create(DoxRequest req) async {}

  /// POST /resource
  /// create() takes only the fillable columns of Blog.
  /// Set fillable in the Blog model first. While it is empty, this throws.
  Future<dynamic> store(DoxRequest req) async {
    return Blog().create(req.body);
  }

  /// GET /resource/{id}
  /// Dox loads blog by the {id}. No row answers 404.
  Future<dynamic> show(DoxRequest req, Blog blog) async {
    return blog;
  }

  /// GET /resource/{id}/edit
  Future<dynamic> edit(DoxRequest req, Blog blog) async {
    return blog;
  }

  /// PUT|PATCH /resource/{id}
  /// update() takes only the fillable columns of Blog.
  /// Set fillable in the Blog model first. While it is empty, this throws.
  Future<dynamic> update(DoxRequest req, Blog blog) async {
    await blog.update(req.body);
    return blog;
  }

  /// DELETE /resource/{id}
  Future<dynamic> destroy(DoxRequest req, Blog blog) async {
    await blog.delete();
  }
}
```

`show`, `edit`, `update` and `destroy` take the model. [Route model binding](dependency-injection.md#route-model-binding) loads it by the `{id}`.

`create()` and `update()` take only the columns in the model's `fillable` list, so add your columns there first.

You can use `--api` and `--model` together. And `dox make:model Blog -r` makes the model and this controller in one step.

## Parameters

A controller method asks for what it needs by **type**, and Dox fills each parameter:

```dart
Route.put('/teams/{teamId}/users/{id}', (UserController c) => c.update);

@Inject()
class UserController {
  Future<User> update(int teamId, int id, UpdateUser body) async { ... }
}
```

These types work:

| Parameter type | Dox gives |
| --- | --- |
| `DoxRequest` | the request |
| a `@Dto` class | the checked body or query. See [Validation](validation.md). |
| `String`, `int`, `double`, `num`, `bool` | the path params, in the order of the route |
| the same types with `?` | an optional path param (`{id?}`). `null` when it is not in the URL. |
| a `@DoxModel` class | the model, loaded by the route param. See [route model binding](dependency-injection.md#route-model-binding). |
| an `@Inject()` class | the instance from the [container](dependency-injection.md#handler-parameters) |

You can put the parameters in any order. Path params are matched by position: the first path-param parameter gets the first `{...}` in the route. `DoxRequest` is not needed, so add it only when you use it.

There are a few rules:

- At most one `@Dto` parameter.
- Only positional parameters. Named and `[optional]` parameters are not supported.
- A catch-all `{path*}` param is a `String`.
- The same rules work for static methods and plain functions.

### Path param types

Dox converts the text from the URL to the type you ask for. If the text does not fit the type, the client gets `404 Not Found`:

- `int`: `"42"` is `42`. `"abc"` or `"4.5"` answers `404`.
- `double`, `num`: `"4.5"` is `4.5`.
- `bool`: `true` or `1` is `true`. `false` or `0` is `false`. Any other text answers `404`.

Path params are checked first. When one is wrong, the DTO is not checked.

## Returning a response

Return a `String`, a `Map`, a model, a `File` and more. See [Response](response.md).

## Details

- Dox reads the parameter types once, at start. It does not use `dart:mirrors`.
- The server does not start when a parameter type is not in the list above (did you run `dart run build_runner build`?), or when the method has more path-param parameters than the route has `{...}` params.

# Dependency injection

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/the-basic/dependency-injection/

# Dependency injection

The Dox container makes your classes and gives each constructor what it needs, so you never wire classes by hand.

Put `@Inject()` above a class, and `dox_builder` adds it to the container. Then any class can ask for it in its constructor. Dox does not use `dart:mirrors`: all the wiring is generated code.

## Setup

The builder writes `lib/generated/container.g.dart`. Give it to the app once:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
import 'package:my_app/generated/container.g.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  container: registerContainer,
  // ...
);
```

Run the builder again after you add a class:

```bash
dart run build_runner build
```

## A full example

A common setup has three layers. A repository reads the database. A service holds the business logic. A controller answers the route. Each one asks for the one below it in its constructor.

The repository needs nothing:

```dart title="lib/app/repositories/user.repository.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

@Inject()
class UserRepository {
  Future<User?> find(int id) => User().find(id);
}
```

The service asks for the repository:

```dart title="lib/app/services/user.service.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/repositories/user.repository.dart';

@Inject()
class UserService {
  UserService(this.users);

  final UserRepository users;

  Future<User> show(int id) async {
    User? user = await users.find(id);
    if (user == null) throw NotFoundHttpException();
    return user;
  }
}
```

The controller asks for the service:

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/user.controller.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/services/user.service.dart';

@Inject()
class UserController {
  UserController(this.service);

  final UserService service;

  Future<User> show(int id) => service.show(id);
}
```

And the route points to the controller:

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
class ApiRouter extends Router {
  @override
  String get prefix => 'api';

  @override
  void register() {
    Route.get('/users/{id}', (UserController c) => c.show);
  }
}
```

That is all. After `dart run build_runner build`, `GET /api/users/5` makes the repository, the service and the controller, and calls `show(5)`.

## Lifetime

By default, `@Inject()` makes one instance per isolate. It is made on first use, and every class that asks for it gets the same one.

If you want a new instance each time it is asked for, use `singleton: false`:

```dart
@Inject(singleton: false)
class ReportBuilder {}
```

Dox runs one server per isolate, and isolates do not share objects. So each isolate has its own instances. Do not keep state in a singleton that all isolates must see. Use the cache or the database for that.

## Constructor parameters

Each constructor parameter is found by its type. Positional and named parameters both work.

If the type is not in the container, an optional parameter keeps its default value, and a nullable parameter gets `null`. Any other parameter stops the build.

### Abstract types

A constructor parameter of an abstract type gets the one container class that implements it:

```dart
abstract class Mailer {}

@Inject()
class SmtpMailer implements Mailer {}

@Inject()
class SignupService {
  SignupService(this.mailer); // gets the SmtpMailer

  final Mailer mailer;
}
```

This works for constructor parameters only. `c.get<Mailer>()` and handler parameters still need the class itself.

## Routes to controller methods

Pass a function that picks the method. Dox finds the controller by the parameter type:

```dart
Route.get('/posts', (PostController c) => c.index);
Route.post('/posts', (PostController c) => c.store);
```

The controller comes from the container. Dox gets it once per isolate, at start, so a request does no extra work. `.name()`, groups and middleware lists work the same:

```dart
Route.get('/posts/{id}', (PostController c) => c.show).name('posts.show');
Route.get('/me', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(), (AuthController c) => c.me]);
```

For resource routes, pass the class:

```dart
Route.resource('posts', PostController);
```

The method still gets its parameters as usual: `DoxRequest`, a `@Dto`, path params and bound models. See [Controller: parameters](controller.md#parameters).

## Handler parameters

A controller method (or a plain route function) can ask for any class of the container:

```dart
Route.get('/stats', (StatsService stats) => stats.today());
```

A singleton is read once, at start. A `singleton: false` class is made on each request.

## Route model binding

Often a route gets the id of a model, and the controller loads the model first. Dox can do this for you. Every `@DoxModel` class gets a binder, so when a handler has a parameter of a model type, Dox loads the model by its primary key:

```dart
Route.get('/posts/{post}', (PostController c) => c.show);

@Inject()
class PostController {
  Post show(Post post) => post;
}
```

Dox uses the route param with the name of the model: `{post}` for `Post`, `{blogPost}` for `BlogPost`. When there is no such param, it uses the next route param in order, like `{id}`.

A missing row answers `404`. An `int` key that is not a number also answers `404`, with no database call.

A binder from `Route.bind` wins over this one. See [Routing: route model binding](routing.md#route-model-binding).

## Routers and providers

Routers and providers do not need `@Inject()`. Dox finds every class that extends `Router` and registers its routes at start. It finds every class that extends `DoxProvider` and runs its `setup()` at start, in every isolate. Their constructors get parameters from the container too.

They run in the order of their file path, then the order in the file. If you want to pick the order, list them in `AppConfig`:

```dart
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  container: registerContainer,
  providers: <DoxProvider>[ORMProvider()], // runs first
  routers: <Router>[ApiRouter()],       // registered first
);
```

A listed class comes first, and the others follow. No class runs twice. A listed provider is also the instance that the container gives.

A provider can add global middleware with `Dox().addGlobalMiddleware(...)` in `setup()`. See [Middleware](middleware.md#global-middleware).

## Using the container in code

Sometimes you need a class in code that the container does not build, like a script. `Dox().ioc` is the container of the current isolate. Use `get` to read a class:

```dart
UserService users = Dox().ioc.get<UserService>();
```

`get` throws when the class is not registered. Use `has` to check first:

```dart
if (Dox().ioc.has<UserService>()) {
  // ...
}
```

You can also add classes by hand. `singleton` makes one instance per isolate, on first use. `factory` makes a new instance on each `get`. `instance` uses the value you give, for example a config object:

```dart
Dox().ioc.singleton<Clock>((IocContainer c) => Clock());
Dox().ioc.factory<Report>((IocContainer c) => Report());
Dox().ioc.instance<MailConfig>(mailConfig);
```

## Testing

In a test you often want a fake in place of a real class. Use `override` before the app starts, and `clearOverrides` at the end:

```dart
setUpAll(() async {
  Dox().ioc.override<UserRepository>(FakeUserRepository());
  client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig);
});

tearDownAll(() async {
  await client.close();
  Dox().ioc.clearOverrides();
});
```

Call `override` before `DoxTestClient.start`, because controllers get their objects once, at start. An override stays when the app registers its classes again.

## Build errors

The build stops with a clear message, with the file and line, when:

- a required parameter has a type that is not in the container,
- a parameter has an abstract type, and two or more classes in the container implement it,
- classes need each other in a circle. The message shows the chain, like `A -> B -> C -> A`,
- `@Inject()` is on an abstract class or a generic class,
- a class has no unnamed constructor.

A private class (like `_AdminRouter`) is not put in the container. The build shows a warning for it. Remove the `_` to add it.

## Details

- Dox finds classes in `lib/` only.
- Two classes with the same name in two files both work. But use the typed route style (`Route.get<C>(...)`) for them. They can not be handler parameters, because Dox can not tell them apart by name.
- A route without a parameter of the model type does not load the model.

### The generated file

`lib/generated/container.g.dart` has one function. Each class gets a factory that calls its constructor. Do not edit it.

```dart title="lib/generated/container.g.dart"
// GENERATED CODE - DO NOT MODIFY BY HAND
// Made by dox_builder. Run `dart run build_runner build`.
// ignore_for_file: type=lint

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/user.controller.dart' as i1;
import 'package:my_app/app/repositories/user.repository.dart' as i2;
import 'package:my_app/app/services/user.service.dart' as i3;
import 'package:my_app/providers/orm_provider.dart' as i4;
import 'package:my_app/routes/api.dart' as i5;
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart' as i6;

/// Puts every class of the app into the container: the
/// `@Inject()` classes, routers, providers and model binders.
/// Use it in `AppConfig(container: registerContainer)`.
void registerContainer(IocContainer c) {
  c.singleton<i1.UserController>(
    (IocContainer c) => i1.UserController(c.get<i3.UserService>()),
  );
  c.singleton<i2.UserRepository>((IocContainer c) => i2.UserRepository());
  c.singleton<i3.UserService>(
    (IocContainer c) => i3.UserService(c.get<i2.UserRepository>()),
  );
  c.provider<i4.ORMProvider>((IocContainer c) => i4.ORMProvider());
  c.router<i5.ApiRouter>((IocContainer c) => i5.ApiRouter());
  c.bindModel<i6.User>((String id) {
    int? key = int.tryParse(id);
    if (key == null) return null;
    return i6.User().find(key);
  });
}
```

# Views

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/the-basic/views/

# Views

Views are HTML templates that Dox fills with your data and sends as the response.

Writing HTML in a controller gets messy fast. A view keeps the HTML in its own file, so the controller only gives the data. The `dox_view` package has the template engine. Templates are `.dox.html` files in `resources/views`.

## Install

Add the package with the CLI:

```bash
dox add view
```

It adds the package, the provider, the `resources/views` folder and a sample view. It never overwrites a file, so it is safe to run twice.

### Set it up by hand

If you do not use `dox add`, add the package yourself:

```bash
dart pub add dox_view
```

Add the provider in `lib/`, so every isolate sets up the engine:

```dart title="lib/providers/view_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_view/dox_view.dart';

class AppViewProvider extends ViewProvider {
  AppViewProvider() : super(const ViewConfig());
}
```

To make a view file, run `dox make:view emails/welcome`. It writes `resources/views/emails/welcome.dox.html`. See [`dox make:view`](../reference/cli.md#dox-makeview).

## Rendering views

`view()` renders a template and sends it as HTML. Leave out the `.dox.html` extension:

```dart
DoxResponse show(DoxRequest req) {
  return view(req, 'users/show', <String, dynamic>{
    'user': user,
    'posts': posts,
  });
}
```

This renders `resources/views/users/show.dox.html`:

```html
<h1>{{ user.name }}</h1>
```

If you need the HTML as a string, for example for an email, use `View.render()`:

```dart
String html = View.render('emails/welcome', <String, dynamic>{'name': 'Ann'});
```

## Displaying data

`{{ }}` prints a value. It escapes HTML, so a user can not add a `<script>` tag to your page:

```html
<p>Hello {{ user.name }}</p>
```

`{{{ }}}` prints a value with no escape. Use it only for HTML you trust:

```html
<article>{{{ post.html }}}</article>
```

`null` prints nothing, and a variable that does not exist prints nothing too. `true` prints `true`, `false` prints `false`, and `10.0` prints `10.0`. The `bladeOutput` and `strictVariables` options change this. See [Strict options](#strict-options).

### Comments

A comment is not in the output:

```html
{{-- only you see this --}}
```

To print `{{` or a tag as text, put `@` before it: `@{{ name }}` prints `{{ name }}`, and `@@if` prints `@if`.

### Stay safe

`{{ }}` escapes HTML, but it does not make every place in a page safe. Follow these three rules:

- **Always quote attributes.** Write `href="{{ url }}"`, not `href={{ url }}`.
  Without quotes, a space in the value starts a new attribute, like `onclick=...`.
- **Check URLs from users.** `href="{{ url }}"` does not block a `javascript:` URL.
  A click on `javascript:alert(1)` runs the code.
  Allow only `http://` and `https://` URLs (or your own paths) before you print them.
- **`<script>` and `<style>` are not safe for `{{ }}`.** Inside them, `{{ }}` only escapes HTML.
  It does not make a value safe for JavaScript or CSS.
  Do not print user data there with `{{ }}`. In a `<script>`, use `@json`. See [JSON for JavaScript](#json-for-javascript).
  Or put the value in a quoted `data-` attribute, and read it in your script.

```html
<a href="{{ profile.website }}">Website</a>  {{-- only after you check it is http or https --}}

<div id="app" data-user-name="{{ user.name }}"></div>
<script>
  const name = document.getElementById('app').dataset.userName;
</script>
```

## Expressions

Inside `{{ }}` and tags, you can use these expressions:

| What | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Values | `'text'`, `"text"`, `42`, `1.5`, `true`, `false`, `null` |
| Lists and maps | `[1, 2]`, `{ name: 'Ann', 'full name': 'Ann Lee' }` |
| Fields | `user.name`, `user?.name`, `items[0]`, `map['key']` |
| Math | `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%`, `~/` |
| Compare | `==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` (`===` and `!==` work too) |
| Logic | `&&`, `\|\|`, `!`, `a ?? b`, `a ? b : c` |
| Functions | `route('users.show', { id: 5 })`, `name.toUpperCase()` |

`+` joins text: `{{ 'Hi ' + name }}`. Fields work on maps, and on objects with a `toJson()` method, like Dox models.

Some methods work too:

- Lists, maps and text have `length`, `isEmpty` and `isNotEmpty`.
- Lists also have `first`, `last`, `contains()`, `join()` and `indexOf()`.
- Text has `toUpperCase()`, `toLowerCase()`, `trim()`, `contains()`, `startsWith()`, `endsWith()`, `split()`, `replaceAll()`, `substring()` and `indexOf()`.
- Numbers have `toStringAsFixed()`, `round()`, `floor()`, `ceil()` and `abs()`.

In `@if` and `?:`, these values are false: `null`, `false`, `0`, `''`, an empty list and an empty map. With the `stringZeroIsFalse` option, the text `'0'` is false too. See [Strict options](#strict-options).

## Conditions

Use `@if`, `@elseif` and `@else` to show a part only in some cases. Close it with `@end`:

```html
@if(user.isAdmin)
  <a href="/admin">Admin</a>
@elseif(user.isEditor)
  <a href="/posts">Posts</a>
@else
  <p>Welcome</p>
@end
```

`@unless(x)` is `@if(!x)`. A tag alone on its line leaves no empty line in the output.

A tag can not come right after a letter or a digit, so `me@mail.com` stays text. Put a space before the tag, or use `{{ on ? 'active' : '' }}`.

## Loops

Use `@each` to print a list. The `@else` part shows when the list is empty:

```html
<ul>
  @each(user in users)
    <li>{{ user.name }}</li>
  @else
    <li>No users yet</li>
  @end
</ul>
```

If you need the index too, or the key of a map, use two names:

```html
@each((user, index) in users)
  {{ index + 1 }}. {{ user.name }}
@end

@each((value, key) in settings)
  {{ key }}: {{ value }}
@end
```

### The loop variable

`$loop` tells you where the loop is. For example, to put a comma after every item but the last:

```html
@each(tag in tags)
  {{ tag }}{{ $loop.last ? '' : ', ' }}
@end
```

| Field | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `$loop.index` | the round, from 0 |
| `$loop.iteration` | the round, from 1 |
| `$loop.first` | true in the first round |
| `$loop.last` | true in the last round |
| `$loop.count` | the number of items. `$loop.length` is the same. |
| `$loop.remaining` | the rounds left after this one |
| `$loop.even` | true when `iteration` is even: the 2nd, 4th, ... round |
| `$loop.odd` | true when `iteration` is odd: the 1st, 3rd, ... round |
| `$loop.depth` | 1 for a loop, 2 for a loop inside a loop |
| `$loop.parent` | the `$loop` of the loop around this one. `null` when there is none. |

In a loop inside a loop, `$loop.parent` reads the outer loop:

```html
@each(row in rows)
  @each(cell in row)
    <td class="{{ $loop.parent.odd ? 'light' : 'dark' }}">{{ cell }}</td>
  @end
@end
```

## Variables

`@let` makes a variable, and `@assign` changes it:

```html
@let(total = 0)
@each(item in cart)
  @assign(total = total + item.price)
@end
Total: {{ total }}
```

## Partials

Some parts are the same on many pages, like a nav bar. `@include` puts another template in this one, and it sees the same variables:

```html
@include('partials/nav')
```

To give it more variables, pass a map as the second argument:

```html
@include('partials/card', { title: 'Profile', user: post.author })
```

On the same name, the map wins. The map is only for this include, so the page does not see it after the include.

To include a template only when a condition is true, use `@includeIf` or `@includeWhen`. The two tags do the same. The condition is the first argument, the template name is the second, and the map is the third:

```html
@includeIf(user, 'partials/account')
@includeWhen(user.isAdmin, 'partials/admin', { level: 2 })
```

## More tags

Dox has more tags for common cases. Close a block tag with `@end`. `@else` works in all of them, but not in `@once` and `@verbatim`.

| Tag | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `@isset(user.phone) ... @end` | shows when the value is not `null`. A field of `null` is not an error here. |
| `@empty(items) ... @end` | shows when the value is false: `null`, `false`, `0`, `''`, an empty list or map. With `stringZeroIsFalse`, `'0'` too. |
| `@auth ... @end` | shows when the user is logged in (`req.auth`) |
| `@guest ... @end` | shows when the user is not logged in |
| `@env('local') ... @end` | shows when `APP_ENV` is this value. A list works too: `@env(['local', 'staging'])`. Case does not matter. |
| `@production ... @end` | shows when `APP_ENV` is `production` |
| `@once ... @end` | shows only the first time in one render, for example a `<script>` in a component |
| `@verbatim ... @end` | prints the text as it is: no `{{ }}` and no tags run inside it |
| `@extends('layouts/app')` | the layout of the page. See [Layouts with sections](#layouts-with-sections). |
| `@section('name') ... @end` | fills a section. Short form: `@section('title', 'Home')`. |
| `@yield('name')` | prints a section. `@yield('title', 'My app')` has a default. |
| `@stack('scripts')` | prints every push of the stack. See [Stacks](#stacks). |
| `@push('scripts') ... @end` | adds to the end of a stack |
| `@prepend('scripts') ... @end` | adds to the start of a stack |
| `@csrf` | the hidden `_token` field. See [Forms](#forms). |
| `@method('PUT')` | the hidden `_method` field |
| `@error('email') ... @end` | shows when the field has a validation error. See [Forms](#forms). |
| `@json(value)` | the value as JSON. See [JSON for JavaScript](#json-for-javascript). |
| `@includeWhen(condition, 'name')` | includes a template when the condition is true. See [Partials](#partials). |
| `@datetime(...)` | a tag of your app. See [Your own tags](#your-own-tags). |

Put `@auth`, `@guest`, `@production`, `@once` and `@verbatim` alone on their line. In the middle of text, like `@once upon a time`, they stay text.

### Auth

`@auth` shows its body when the user is logged in, and `@guest` when not:

```html
@auth
  <a href="/logout">Log out</a>
@else
  <a href="/login">Log in</a>
@end
```

They use the `req.auth` that `view()` gets. In `View.render` there is no request, so `@guest` shows.

### Verbatim

Some JavaScript frameworks also use `{{ }}`. `@verbatim` prints its text as it is, so Dox does not run it. It ends at the first `@end`, so the text inside can not have `@end`:

```html
@verbatim
  <div id="app">{{ message }}</div>
@end
```

### Attributes from conditions

These tags print an HTML attribute when a condition is true:

```html
<a @class(['link', { active: isActive, muted: !isActive }])>Home</a>
<input type="checkbox" name="news" @checked(user.news)>
<option value="en" @selected(lang == 'en')>English</option>
<button @disabled(saving)>Save</button>
```

`@class` takes text, a map of class name to a condition, or a list of these. It prints `class="..."` with the names whose condition is true. `@checked`, `@selected` and `@disabled` print the attribute name when the value is true.

## Layouts and components

A component is a template with its own props and slots. You can use one for the page layout, so every page has the same head and header:

```html title="resources/views/layouts/main.dox.html"
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
  <head>
    <title>{{ title ?? 'My app' }}</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <header>{{ $slots.header }}</header>
    <main>{{ $slots.main }}</main>
  </body>
</html>
```

A page then puts its content in the component:

```html title="resources/views/home.dox.html"
@component('layouts/main', { title: 'Home' })
  @slot('header')
    <h1>Welcome</h1>
  @end

  <p>Hello {{ user.name }}</p>
@end
```

- The second argument is the props. In the component they are variables (`title`), and also `$props.title`.
- `@slot('name') ... @end` fills a named slot. Everything else goes into `$slots.main`. `$slot` is the same as `$slots.main`.
- A slot is HTML, so `{{ }}` does not escape it again.
- A component does not see the variables of the page. It only sees its props, `$props`, `$slots`, `$slot`, `$attributes`, the globals and the request helpers of `view()` (see [Forms](#forms)).

`@!component(...)` is a component with no body and no `@end`.

### Components as tags

A template in `resources/views/components/` is also a tag with its name. A `.` in the tag is a folder:

```html title="resources/views/components/button.dox.html"
<button class="btn btn-{{ type ?? 'primary' }}">{{ $slots.main }}</button>
```

Then use the tag:

```html
@button({ type: 'danger' })
  Delete
@end

@!form.input({ name: 'email' })   {{-- components/form/input.dox.html --}}
```

### Attributes

Often a component should pass its props on as HTML attributes, like `id` or `type`. `$attributes` has the props as HTML attributes, and `{{ $attributes }}` prints them, like `id="save" title="Save"`. The values are escaped.

`$attributes.merge({ ... })` adds default attributes. A prop wins over a default, but `class` is joined:

```html
<button {{ $attributes.merge({ class: 'btn', type: 'button' }) }}>{{ $slot }}</button>
```

```html
@button({ class: 'btn-big', type: 'submit' })
  Save
@end
```

This prints `<button class="btn btn-big" type="submit">`.

Only text, numbers and `true` are attributes. `true` prints the name alone, like `hidden`. `null`, `false`, lists, maps and objects are left out. You can still read any prop, like `$attributes.type`.

`$attributes` keeps any attribute name, like `onclick`. So do not pass a map from the user as the props of a component.

## Layouts with sections

A page can also name its layout with `@extends`. The page fills sections, and the layout prints them with `@yield`:

```html title="resources/views/layouts/app.dox.html"
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
  <head>
    <title>@yield('title', 'My app')</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <main>@yield('content')</main>
  </body>
</html>
```

```html title="resources/views/home.dox.html"
@extends('layouts/app')

@section('title', 'Home')

@section('content')
  <p>Hello {{ user.name }}</p>
@end
```

- `@extends` must be the first thing in the template. A template can have only one.
- `@section('name') ... @end` fills a section. The short form `@section('title', 'Home')` takes a value, which is escaped like `{{ }}`.
- `@yield('title', 'My app')` prints the second value when the page has no such section.
- Only the sections reach the layout. Text outside a section is not printed.
- A section and the layout both see the variables of the page.
- A layout can extend another layout. When a page and its layout fill the same section, the page wins.

Use `@extends` for the page layout. Use a component when you need props or more than one copy on a page.

## Stacks

Sometimes a page or a component needs its own script or style in the layout's `<head>`. A stack collects HTML from many templates and prints it in one place. The layout prints the stack with `@stack`:

```html
<head>
  @stack('styles')
</head>
<body>
  @yield('content')
  @stack('scripts')
</body>
```

A page or a component adds to it with `@push`:

```html
@push('scripts')
  <script src="/js/chart.js"></script>
@end
```

`@push` adds to the end of the stack, and `@prepend` adds to the start. A push works from the page, its layout, an `@include` and a component. `@stack` can come before the `@push`, and it still prints every push.

Put `@once` inside `@push` in a component, so the script is added one time only.

## Forms

Forms need a CSRF token, the old input and the validation errors. With `SessionMiddleware`, `view()` adds these to every template:

| Name | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `csrfField()` | the hidden `_token` field for `CsrfMiddleware`. `@csrf` prints the same. |
| `csrfToken()` | the CSRF token |
| `errors` | the flashed validation errors, like `errors.email` |
| `old('email')` | the input of the request before |
| `session('key')` | a value from the session |

```html
<form method="POST" action="/register">
  {{ csrfField() }}
  <input name="email" value="{{ old('email') }}">
  @error('email')
    <p class="error">{{ message }}</p>
  @end
  <button>Register</button>
</form>
```

### Validation errors

`@error('field') ... @end` shows its body when `errors` has a message for the field. Inside the body, `message` is that message. With no error for the field, the `@else` part is printed instead, if there is one.

A name with dots, like `@error('user.email')`, works for nested fields. The name can also be a variable, like `@error(name)` in an input component.

### CSRF and method fields

`@csrf` prints the same hidden field as `csrfField()`. Put it alone on its line.

A browser form can only send GET and POST. For a PUT, PATCH or DELETE route, send a POST and add `@method`. It prints the hidden `_method` field that the [`MethodOverride`](routing.md#forms-with-put-patch-and-delete) middleware reads:

```html
<form method="POST" action="/posts/{{ post.id }}">
  @csrf
  @method('PUT')
  <input name="title" value="{{ post.title }}">
  <button>Save</button>
</form>
```

This prints `<input type="hidden" name="_token" value="...">` and `<input type="hidden" name="_method" value="PUT">`.

Every template from `view()` also has `request.path`, `request.method` and `request.query`. Components and layouts see all of these too, so a layout can use `request.path` and a form component can use `csrfField()`.

## Globals

Some values are needed in every template, like the app name. Globals are variables and functions that every template can use. `route()` is there by default:

```dart
const ViewConfig(globals: <String, Object?>{'appName': 'My app'});

View.global('year', DateTime.now().year);
View.global('money', (num cents) => (cents / 100).toStringAsFixed(2));
```

Then use them in any template:

```html
<footer>{{ appName }} {{ year }}</footer>
<a href="{{ route('users.show', { id: user.id }) }}">Profile</a>
<p>{{ money(order.total) }}</p>
```

Each isolate has its own engine. So add globals in your provider, after `super.setup()`. Then every isolate gets them:

```dart title="lib/providers/view_provider.dart"
class AppViewProvider extends ViewProvider {
  AppViewProvider() : super(const ViewConfig());

  @override
  void setup() {
    super.setup();
    View.global('year', DateTime.now().year);
  }
}
```

If a global holds HTML, make it a `SafeString`. It is printed with no escape:

```dart
View.global('logo', const SafeString('<img src="/logo.svg" alt="Logo">'));
```

## JSON for JavaScript

Sometimes your JavaScript needs data from the server. `@json(value)` prints a value as JSON:

```html
<script>
  const user = @json(user);
</script>

<div data-tags='@json(tags)'></div>
```

Maps, lists, text, numbers, `true`, `false` and `null` work. An object with a `toJson()` method works too, like a Dox model.

The output is safe in two places: inside a `<script>` block, and inside an attribute in single quotes. Do not put it in an attribute in double quotes, because JSON has `"` in it, and that ends the attribute.

`json(value)` does the same as a function. Use it where you need an expression:

```html
@!chart({ points: json(points) })
```

In Dart, `SafeString.json(value)` gives the same text.

## Your own tags

If you print the same thing in many places, like a date format, you can add your own tag. A directive is a tag that your app adds. Write a class with a `render` method. It gets the values between `(` and `)`, and gives the text to print:

```dart
class DateTimeDirective implements ViewDirective {
  @override
  Object? render(List<Object?> args, Scope scope) {
    Object? value = args[0];
    DateTime time = value is DateTime ? value : DateTime.parse('$value');
    return '${time.day}/${time.month}/${time.year}';
  }
}

View.directive('datetime', DateTimeDirective());
```

Then use it in a template:

```html
<time>@datetime(post.createdAt)</time>
```

The text is escaped, like `{{ }}`. Give a `SafeString` to print HTML as it is. `scope.lookup('name')` reads a variable of the template. A directive has no body and no `@end`.

Each isolate has its own engine. So add directives in your provider, after `super.setup()`, like globals. You can also give them in the config: `ViewConfig(directives: <String, ViewDirective>{'datetime': DateTimeDirective()})`.

## Config

Set the options in `ViewConfig`:

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `path` | `resources/views` | the folder of the templates |
| `extension` | `.dox.html` | the file extension |
| `cache` | on, but off when `APP_ENV` is `development` or `local` | keep parsed templates in memory |
| `globals` | `{}` | variables for every template |
| `directives` | `{}` | your own tags, by name |
| `strictVariables` | `false` | a variable that does not exist throws a `ViewException`. See [Strict options](#strict-options). |
| `stringZeroIsFalse` | `false` | the text `'0'` is false in a condition |
| `bladeOutput` | `false` | print `true` as `1`, `false` as nothing and `10.0` as `10` |
| `bladeWarnings` | `true` | warn about tag names from other template engines that are not Dox tags. See [Unknown tag warnings](#unknown-tag-warnings). |

With the cache off, a changed template shows on the next request, with no restart.

## Strict options

These three options are off by default. Turn each one on in `ViewConfig`:

```dart
const ViewConfig(
  strictVariables: true,
  stringZeroIsFalse: true,
  bladeOutput: true,
);
```
