**`strictVariables`**: a variable that does not exist throws a `ViewException`. The message has the name of the variable, the template and the line. So a typo like `{{ titel }}` shows as an error, not as an empty spot on the page. When it is off, a variable that does not exist prints nothing.

A variable that is there with the value `null` is fine. These ways to read a variable that may not exist never throw:

| Code | What it gives when `user` does not exist |
| --- | --- |
| `@isset(user) ... @end` | the body is not printed |
| `@empty(user) ... @end` | the body is printed |
| `{{ user ?? 'Guest' }}` | `Guest` |
| `{{ user?.name }}` | nothing |

The rule covers the variable on the left of `??` and `?.`. In `{{ a ?? b ?? 'x' }}`, both `a` and `b` can be missing. `{{ user.name ?? 'Guest' }}` still throws when `user` does not exist: write `{{ user?.name ?? 'Guest' }}`.

**`stringZeroIsFalse`**: the text `'0'` is false in `@if`, `@unless`, `@empty`, `?:`, `&&`, `||`, `!`, `@class`, `@checked`, `@selected`, `@disabled`, `@includeIf` and `@includeWhen`. Other text, like `'0.0'` or `'00'`, is still true. When it is off, `'0'` is true, like any text that is not empty.

**`bladeOutput`**: `{{ }}` and `{{{ }}}` print `true` as `1`, `false` as nothing, and a number with no fraction, like `10.0`, as `10`. The values of `@yield`, `@section` and `@method`, and the numbers in `$attributes`, are printed the same way. Joining text with `+` does not change: `{{ 'a' + true }}` is still `atrue`. When it is off, `true` prints `true`, `false` prints `false`, and `10.0` prints `10.0`.

## Unknown tag warnings

Some tag names from other template engines, like `@foreach`, are not Dox tags. Dox prints them as plain text. To help you find them, Dox writes a warning to `stderr` when it reads a template that has one:

```
dox_view: warning: posts/index:12 "@foreach" is not a Dox tag. Use "@each(item in items) ... @end".
```

| Other name | Dox |
| --- | --- |
| `{!! html !!}` | `{{{ html }}}` |
| `@foreach`, `@forelse`, `@for` | `@each(item in items) ... @else ... @end` |
| `@endif`, `@endforeach`, `@endsection` and the other `@end...` names, `@stop` | `@end` |
| `@switch` | `@if ... @elseif ... @else ... @end` |
| `@php`, `@endphp` | `@let(name = value)` |
| `@show` | `@end`, then `@yield('name')` |
| `@parent` | not there. Use `@stack` and `@push` to add content. |

The output of the template does not change. The warning is only a hint, and each one is written one time. `ViewConfig(bladeWarnings: false)` turns the warnings off.

## Errors

A syntax error, or an error in an expression, throws a `ViewException`. The message has the template name and the line:

```
ViewException: expected ")" but found the end (in "users/show", line 12)
```

## Prettier

Prettier formats `.html` files, and it does not know the `@` tags. Add this line to `.prettierignore`:

```
*.dox.html
```

## Details

This section is for special cases. Most apps do not need it.

### When a tag is text

- A tag can not come right after a letter or a digit. Write `on @else off`, not `on@else off`. `L@yield('s')` also stays text.
- `@extends`, `@section`, `@yield`, `@stack`, `@push`, `@prepend`, `@method`, `@error`, `@json`, `@includeWhen` and your own directives need `( )`. With no `( )`, like `@section` in a sentence, they stay text.
- With no space before the `(`, like `@empty(items)` or `@json(user)`, a tag is always a tag.
- With a space before the `(`, in the middle of a line, it is a tag only when its args are one valid expression (one or two for `@section` and `@yield`). So `see @class (see docs)` stays text.
- With a space, alone on its line, it is a tag even when its args are not valid, unless a rule below says it stays text. Then the args give an error.
- A tag with a body, like `@isset`, `@empty`, `@env`, `@section` and `@push`, also needs its own `@end` after it. The `@end` of a block around it does not count. So `@empty (none)` stays text, also alone on its line.
- `@extends`, `@section`, `@yield`, `@stack`, `@push`, `@prepend`, `@method` and `@error` with a space also need text in quotes as the first argument. So `git @push (force)` stays text, but `@yield ('title')` is a tag. If such a tag stays text, its `@end` gives the error "@end has no matching tag before it".
- `@json` and `@includeWhen` are never tags with a space. So `the @json (format)` stays text.
- When `resources/views/components/` has a template with the same name as a tag or a directive, like `class.dox.html`, the component wins.

### Partials, loops and components

- `@include` with a second argument that is not a map throws a `ViewException`.
- A loop in an `@include` counts the loop around the `@include` as its parent. A loop in a component starts at depth 1.
- `$slot` and `$slots.main` are always there. They are empty when the component has no body.
- In `$attributes`, a number prints like `{{ }}`: `1.0` is `title="1.0"`, or `title="1"` with `bladeOutput`.

### Sections and stacks

- In a page with `@extends`, `@let` and `@push` outside a section still work. The `@yield` default value is escaped too.
- The names of sections and stacks must be plain text in quotes, like `'title'`.
- The first `@section` with a name wins. So a `@section` inside `@each` keeps only the first round.
- A `@yield('s')` that comes before the `@section('s')` in the same file prints nothing.
- An `@include` or a component with its own `@extends` prints its layout in place. It shares the section names with the page.
- The pushes are printed in the order they run. A page with `@extends` runs before its layout.

### Forms

- If your app has a global named `errors`, the global shows when the request has no validation errors. When there are validation errors, they win over the global.
- When the value in `errors` is a list, `message` is its first item.
- With no session, and in `View.render`, there are no errors, so the `@error` body is not printed. It does not throw. With no session, `@csrf` throws a `ViewException`.
- `@error('user.email')` reads the key `'user.email'` of `errors` first. That is how the validator names a nested field. When there is no such key, it reads `email` inside `user`.
- `message` is only there inside the `@error` body. After `@end`, a `message` variable of your page has its own value again.

### Globals, JSON and directives

- You can add globals before or after `View.configure()`. The engine keeps them. When a name is in both, the value in `ViewConfig.globals` wins.
- `@json` writes `<`, `>`, `&`, `'` and the line separators U+2028 and U+2029 as `\uXXXX`, so a value can not close the `<script>` block or the attribute. A value that can not be JSON, like a `DateTime` or an object with no `toJson()`, throws a `ViewException`. `{{ json(value) }}` does not escape the text again.
- A directive that returns `null` prints nothing. Its name can have letters, digits and `_`. The name of a built-in tag, like `if`, `section` or `json`, throws a `ViewException`.

### Which names warn

- `@end...` names warn anywhere in a line. The other names warn only with the `(` right after the name, like `@foreach(...)`, or alone on their line. So a sentence like `the @foreach loop` does not warn.
- Text in a `{{-- --}}` comment, in `@verbatim`, and a name with `@@` before it, do not warn. A name in an HTML comment, like `<!-- @endif -->`, does warn.


---

# Inertia

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/the-basic/inertia/

# Inertia

Inertia lets you build a single page app with React, Vue or Svelte, and keep routes and controllers in Dox.

You do not write an API. A controller gives a page name and its props, and Inertia shows the page in the browser. The first visit gets a full HTML page. After that, links and forms get only JSON, and the page changes without a reload.

The `dox_inertia` package is the server side of Inertia. Use it with Vite and the Inertia 3 client for your front-end (`@inertiajs/react`, `@inertiajs/vue3` or `@inertiajs/svelte`, version 3).

## Install

Add the package with the CLI:

```bash
dox add inertia
```

It does steps 1 to 3 of [Set it up by hand](#set-it-up-by-hand): the root view, the config and the provider. Then do steps 4 to 6 (Vite, the built files and the middleware) yourself. The command prints a short list of them. It never overwrites a file, so it is safe to run twice.

## Set it up by hand

If you do not use `dox add`, add the package yourself:

```bash
dart pub add dox_inertia
```

### 1. Root view

The root view is the HTML page of the first visit. Dox puts the script and style tags in place of `@vite`, and the page in place of `@inertia`. It is plain HTML, with no template engine. It can hold `{{ key }}` marks for values like the title. See [Root view data](#root-view-data).

```html title="resources/views/app.html"
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
    <title>My app</title>
    @vite
  </head>
  <body>
    @inertia
  </body>
</html>
```

### 2. Config

The config tells Dox where your Vite files are:

```dart title="lib/config/inertia.dart"
import 'package:dox_inertia/dox_inertia.dart';

InertiaConfig inertiaConfig = InertiaConfig(
  /// the Vite entry files
  entryPoints: <String>['resources/js/app.jsx'],

  /// load the scripts from the Vite dev server. null in production.
  devServerUrl: 'http://localhost:5173',

  /// add the React Fast Refresh code in dev mode
  reactRefresh: true,
);
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `rootView` | `resources/views/app.html` | the HTML page of the first visit. One request can use another file with `Inertia.setRootView` |
| `entryPoints` | `['resources/js/app.js']` | the Vite entry files |
| `publicPath` | `public` | the folder of public files |
| `buildDirectory` | `build` | the folder in `publicPath` where `vite build` writes its files |
| `devServerUrl` | `null` | the url of the Vite dev server, see [Vite](#vite) |
| `reactRefresh` | `false` | add the React Fast Refresh code in dev mode |
| `version` | hash of the manifest | the asset version, see [Asset version](#asset-version) |
| `encryptHistory` | `false` | encrypt the browser history of every page, see [History encryption](#history-encryption) |
| `ssr` | `null` | server side rendering, see [SSR](#server-side-rendering-ssr) |

Paths are from the project root, where the app runs.

### 3. Provider

The provider sets up Inertia in every isolate. Put it in `lib/`, so the generated container finds it:

```dart title="lib/providers/inertia_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_inertia/dox_inertia.dart';

import '../config/inertia.dart';

class AppInertiaProvider extends InertiaProvider {
  AppInertiaProvider() : super(inertiaConfig);
}
```

With no provider, Dox uses the defaults of `InertiaConfig`.

### 4. Vite

Set up Vite so it writes a manifest into `public/build`:

```js title="vite.config.js"
import { defineConfig } from 'vite'
import react from '@vitejs/plugin-react'

export default defineConfig(({ command }) => ({
  plugins: [react()],
  // public/ holds the Dox public files. The build goes into public/build,
  // so do not let Vite copy public/ into the build.
  publicDir: false,
  // the built files are served from /build/
  base: command === 'build' ? '/build/' : '/',
  server: { origin: 'http://localhost:5173' },
  build: {
    manifest: true,
    outDir: 'public/build',
    rollupOptions: { input: 'resources/js/app.jsx' },
  },
}))
```

Then start the Inertia app in your entry file:

```jsx title="resources/js/app.jsx"
import { createInertiaApp } from '@inertiajs/react'
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client'

createInertiaApp({
  resolve: (name) => {
    const pages = import.meta.glob('./Pages/**/*.jsx', { eager: true })
    return pages[`./Pages/${name}.jsx`]
  },
  setup({ el, App, props }) {
    createRoot(el).render(<App {...props} />)
  },
})
```

### 5. Serve the built files

In production the browser loads `/build/assets/...`. Add a route for them, or let your proxy (nginx, Caddy) serve `public/build`:

```dart title="lib/routes/web.dart"
Route.get('/build/{path*}', (String path) {
  if (path.contains('..')) throw NotFoundHttpException();
  // the file names have a hash, so the browser can keep them for a year
  return response(File('public/build/$path')).cache(const Duration(days: 365));
});
```

### 6. Middleware

Add three middleware to `globalMiddleware`, in this order:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[
    const SessionMiddleware(),
    const CsrfMiddleware(),
    HandleInertiaRequests(),
  ],
  // ...
);
```

- `SessionMiddleware` gives each request a session. Inertia uses it for validation errors and flash data.
- `CsrfMiddleware` stops cross site form posts. It sets the `XSRF-TOKEN` cookie. The Inertia client reads it and sends it back in the `X-XSRF-TOKEN` header. You do not write any code for this.
- `HandleInertiaRequests` is your `InertiaMiddleware`, see [Shared props](#shared-props). With no props to share, use `const InertiaMiddleware()`.

If only some routes are Inertia pages, you can add them to a router instead, in the same order.

## Rendering pages

Call `inertia` with the request, the page name and the props. The page name is the file in `resources/js/Pages`, without the extension:

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/user.controller.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_inertia/dox_inertia.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

@Inject()
class UserController {
  Future<DoxResponse> index(DoxRequest req) {
    return inertia(req, 'Users/Index', <String, dynamic>{
      'title': 'Users',
      'users': () => User().query().all(),
    });
  }
}
```

A normal request gets the root view as HTML. An Inertia request (a link or a form) gets the page as JSON.

A prop can be a function, like `users` above. It runs only when the prop is sent, and it can give a `Future`. Props become JSON, so a model or any object with `toJson()` works. A `DateTime` becomes ISO text.

`Inertia.render(req, 'Users/Index', {...})` does the same as `inertia(...)`.

## Shared props

Some props are needed on every page, like the signed in user or the app name. Extend `InertiaMiddleware` and return them from `share`. Then add it to `globalMiddleware` (see [Middleware](#6-middleware)):

```dart title="lib/app/http/middleware/handle_inertia_requests.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_inertia/dox_inertia.dart';

class HandleInertiaRequests extends InertiaMiddleware {
  @override
  Map<String, dynamic> share(DoxRequest req) {
    return <String, dynamic>{
      'appName': 'My app',
      'auth': () => req.auth?.toJson(),
    };
  }
}
```

A page prop with the same name wins over a shared prop. `share` can be `async`. You can also share from any middleware or controller with `Inertia.share(req, {...})`.

### Global values

For a value that is the same for the whole app, use `Inertia.shareGlobal(key, value)`. Call it once in the `setup()` of your `InertiaProvider`, so it runs in every isolate:

```dart
class AppInertiaProvider extends InertiaProvider {
  AppInertiaProvider() : super(inertiaConfig);

  @override
  void setup() {
    super.setup();
    Inertia.shareGlobal('appName', 'Dox');
  }
}
```

A global value is kept for all users and all requests. So use it only for a constant, or a function that does not read a request. Data of one user, like the signed in user, must go in `InertiaMiddleware.share`.

## Partial reloads

Sometimes a page only needs new data for one prop. The client can ask for some props only, with `router.reload({ only: ['users'] })`. Dox then sends only those props, and function props that are not sent do not run.

These helpers change when a prop is sent.

### Optional props

`Inertia.optional` sends the prop only when a partial reload asks for it:

```dart
'stats': Inertia.optional(() => Stats.load()),
```

### Always props

`Inertia.always` sends the prop on every request, also on a partial reload that does not ask for it:

```dart
'notices': Inertia.always(notices),
```

### Deferred props

A slow prop can make the first visit slow. `Inertia.defer` leaves it out of the first visit, and the page loads it right after:

```dart
'comments': Inertia.defer(() => Comment().query().all()),
```

Deferred props of the same `group` load in one request. The default group is `default`:

```dart
'likes': Inertia.defer(() => Like().query().count(), group: 'side'),
```

### Merging props

For infinite scroll, the page should add the new items to the old ones, not replace them. Use `Inertia.merge` for this:

```dart
'posts': Inertia.merge(posts),
```

A deferred prop can merge too:

```dart
'feed': Inertia.defer(() => Post().query().all()).merge(),
```

This table shows when each prop is sent:

| Helper | First visit | Partial reload |
| --- | --- | --- |
| plain value or function | sent | sent when asked |
| `Inertia.optional` | not sent | sent when asked |
| `Inertia.always` | sent | always sent |
| `Inertia.defer` | not sent, listed in `deferredProps` | sent when asked |
| `Inertia.merge` | sent, listed in `mergeProps` | sent when asked |

## Forms and validation errors

A form post needs no extra code for errors. This is how it works:

1. The page posts the form: `router.post('/users', data)` or `useForm`.
2. The controller validates. The validation fails.
3. Dox flashes the errors and the old input to the session, and redirects back.
4. The page loads again. It gets the errors in the `errors` prop.

```dart
Future<DoxResponse> store(DoxRequest req) async {
  await req.validateSchema(
    v.object(<String, Schema<Object?>>{
      'name': v.string().min(2),
      'email': v.string().email(),
    }),
  );
  // ... save the user
  return redirect('/users');
}
```

The page reads the errors from the form:

```jsx
const { data, setData, post, errors } = useForm({ name: '', email: '' })
// errors.email holds the message, or is undefined
```

Every page gets `errors`, also on a partial reload. It is `{}` when there are no errors. The old input is in `req.session.old('email')`. Password fields are not kept.

### Error bags

If one page has two forms, the errors of one form should not show on the other. Pass `errorBag` in the post, like `router.post(url, data, { errorBag: 'login' })` or `form.post(url, { errorBag: 'login' })`. Then the errors are under the bag name: `errors.login.email`.

## Redirects

After a form, redirect with `redirect(url)` or `back(req)` from Dox:

```dart
Future<DoxResponse> update(DoxRequest req, int id) async {
  // ... save the user
  return redirect('/users'); // 303 for an Inertia PUT
}
```

After `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE`, the browser must follow the redirect with `GET`, not with the same method. So `InertiaMiddleware` turns a `302` into `303` for these requests. You do not need to do anything.

If a controller returns nothing to an Inertia request, `InertiaMiddleware` sends the browser back to the page it came from, like `back(req)`.

### External redirects

To go to an outside site, or any page that is not an Inertia page, use `Inertia.location`. The client then loads the url with a full page load:

```dart
return Inertia.location(req, 'https://checkout.example.com/pay/1');
```

## Flash data

Flash data is a short message for the next page, like "User saved". Use `Inertia.flash`, and the next page gets it in `page.flash`, once:

```dart
Future<DoxResponse> store(DoxRequest req) async {
  // ... save the user
  Inertia.flash(req, 'message', 'User saved');
  return redirect('/users');
}
```

Read it on the page:

```jsx
import { usePage } from '@inertiajs/react'

const { flash } = usePage()
// flash.message is 'User saved'
```

The client also fires a `flash` event, and calls the `onFlash` callback of the visit. `Inertia.flash` needs `SessionMiddleware`.

## Vite

In dev mode, `@vite` loads the entry files from the Vite dev server, so you get hot reload. In production, Dox reads `public/build/.vite/manifest.json` and gives the `<link>` and `<script>` tags of the built files.

Dox is in dev mode when `devServerUrl` is set, or when the file `public/hot` exists. So set `devServerUrl` from the env, and production does not use it:

```dart title="lib/config/inertia.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_inertia/dox_inertia.dart';

InertiaConfig inertiaConfig = InertiaConfig(
  entryPoints: <String>['resources/js/app.jsx'],
  devServerUrl: Env.get<String>('APP_ENV') == 'development'
      ? 'http://localhost:5173'
      : null,
  reactRefresh: true,
);
```

## Asset version

When you deploy new JavaScript, a browser that is still open has the old files. The asset version fixes this. When the version changes, the next link click loads the whole page again, with the new files.

The default version is a hash of the Vite manifest. Dox reads it once per isolate, so restart the server after `vite build` (a deploy does this). To set your own, use `version` in the config, for example the git commit.

## Root view data

Page props go to the JavaScript page. Sometimes the root view itself needs a value, like the `<title>` or a CSRF meta tag. Use `Inertia.withViewData` for that.

Write `{{ key }}` in the root view:

```html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <meta name="csrf-token" content="{{ csrfToken }}">
    <title>{{ title }}</title>
    @vite
  </head>
  <body>
    @inertia
  </body>
</html>
```

Set the values in the controller:

```dart
Future<DoxResponse> index(DoxRequest req) {
  Inertia.withViewData(req, <String, Object?>{'title': 'Users'});
  return inertia(req, 'Users/Index', <String, dynamic>{
    'users': () => User().query().all(),
  });
}
```

The values are for the root view only. They are not page props, so an Inertia request (a link or a form) does not get them. You can call `withViewData` many times, also in a middleware, and the data is merged.

Each value is HTML escaped. Put a value in text or in a quoted attribute only. It is not safe inside a `<script>` block, an unquoted attribute or a link address.

`{{ csrfToken }}` is filled for you with the CSRF token of the session. It needs `SessionMiddleware`.

A `{{ key }}` that you did not set stays as it is, so set every key that the root view uses.

A title set this way is for the first page load only, because later visits do not load the root view again. There, the `<Head>` component of the Inertia client changes the title. So set the title in `<Head>` too.

### Another root view for some pages

Sometimes a part of the app needs another HTML page, like an admin area. `Inertia.setRootView` uses another file for one request:

```dart
Future<DoxResponse> dashboard(DoxRequest req) {
  Inertia.setRootView(req, 'resources/views/admin.html');
  return inertia(req, 'Admin/Dashboard');
}
```

`RootViewMiddleware` does the same for every page of a router:

```dart
class AdminRouter extends Router {
  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[
    const RootViewMiddleware('resources/views/admin.html'),
  ];

  // ...
}
```

The path is from the project root, like `rootView` in the config. Use a fixed path. Never pass a value from the request, because it could show any file of the server as the page.

## History encryption

The browser keeps the props of each page in its history, so the back button is fast. After a logout, the back button can still show a page with private data. History encryption stops this.

With it, the browser encrypts the page data before it goes into the history. When you clear the history, the old pages can not be read any more, and the back button asks the server for the page again. The browser can only encrypt on HTTPS, and on `localhost`.

Turn it on for all pages in the config:

```dart title="lib/config/inertia.dart"
InertiaConfig inertiaConfig = InertiaConfig(
  encryptHistory: true,
);
```

Or for one page, in the controller. `false` turns it off for one page when the config turns it on:

```dart
Future<DoxResponse> show(DoxRequest req) {
  Inertia.encryptHistory(req);
  // Inertia.encryptHistory(req, false);
  return inertia(req, 'Account/Show', props);
}
```

Or for all pages of a router, with `EncryptHistoryMiddleware`:

```dart
class AccountRouter extends Router {
  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[const EncryptHistoryMiddleware()];

  // ...
}
```

Call `Inertia.clearHistory(req)` to clear the history, for example on logout:

```dart
Future<DoxResponse> logout(DoxRequest req) async {
  // ... sign the user out
  Inertia.clearHistory(req);
  return redirect('/login');
}
```

The next Inertia page tells the browser to clear its history, once. The mark is kept in the session, so it works with a redirect. It needs `SessionMiddleware`.

## Server side rendering (SSR)

By default, the first visit gets an empty page, and the browser renders it. With SSR, the first visit gets the full HTML of the page. Search engines can read it, and the visitor sees the page sooner.

The page is rendered by the Inertia SSR server. It is a JavaScript process (Bun or Node) that you build with Vite and run next to your Dox app. On a first visit, Dox sends the page to it and puts the answer in the root view. Inertia requests (links and forms) never use it.

### 1. The SSR entry file

`dox inertia:install --ssr` writes this file for you, and adds a `build:ssr` script to `package.json`. It never overwrites a file. With no `package.json` (or one it cannot change safely), it prints a hint instead.

```json title="package.json"
{
  "scripts": {
    "build:ssr": "vite build && vite build --ssr resources/js/ssr.jsx --outDir bootstrap/ssr"
  }
}
```

Without `--ssr`, add the `build:ssr` line to `scripts` yourself, and write the entry file like this:

```jsx title="resources/js/ssr.jsx"
import { createInertiaApp } from '@inertiajs/react'
import createServer from '@inertiajs/react/server'
import ReactDOMServer from 'react-dom/server'

createServer(
  (page) =>
    createInertiaApp({
      page,
      render: ReactDOMServer.renderToString,
      resolve: (name) => {
        const pages = import.meta.glob('./Pages/**/*.jsx', { eager: true })
        return pages[`./Pages/${name}.jsx`]
      },
      setup: ({ App, props }) => <App {...props} />,
    }),
  { host: '127.0.0.1' },
)
```

Vue and Svelte have the same `createServer`, in `@inertiajs/vue3/server` and `@inertiajs/svelte/server`.

The SSR server listens on port `13714`. Set `host` to `127.0.0.1`, so only your own machine can reach it.

### 2. Hydrate in the browser

The browser must reuse the HTML from the server, and not render the page again. Change `setup` in your app file:

```jsx title="resources/js/app.jsx"
import { createInertiaApp } from '@inertiajs/react'
import { createRoot, hydrateRoot } from 'react-dom/client'

createInertiaApp({
  resolve: (name) => {
    const pages = import.meta.glob('./Pages/**/*.jsx', { eager: true })
    return pages[`./Pages/${name}.jsx`]
  },
  setup({ el, App, props }) {
    if (el.hasAttribute('data-server-rendered')) {
      hydrateRoot(el, <App {...props} />)
    } else {
      createRoot(el).render(<App {...props} />)
    }
  },
})
```

The `else` part is for a page that was sent without SSR.

### 3. Build and run

Build the browser files and the SSR file, then start the SSR server:

```bash
bun run build:ssr
dox inertia:start-ssr
```

`dox inertia:start-ssr` runs `bootstrap/ssr/ssr.js` (or `ssr.mjs`) with Bun, in the foreground. When both files exist, it starts the newer one and prints which. It stops with an error when the file is not built yet. A stop signal (Ctrl+C, `docker stop`) is sent on to the SSR process.

With Node, use `npm run build:ssr` and `dox inertia:start-ssr --node`.

The file is `ssr.js` when your `package.json` has `"type": "module"`. Else it is `ssr.mjs`. The SSR file loads your packages from `node_modules`, so keep that folder on the server.

The command does not run in the background. Run it under Docker, pm2 or systemd, like the Dox app. Build and start it again on each deploy.

### 4. Turn it on

Set `ssr` in the config:

```dart title="lib/config/inertia.dart"
InertiaConfig inertiaConfig = InertiaConfig(
  entryPoints: <String>['resources/js/app.jsx'],
  ssr: InertiaSsr(),
);
```

With no `ssr`, SSR is off. `InertiaSsr` has two options:

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `url` | `http://127.0.0.1:13714/render` | the render url of the SSR server |
| `timeout` | 2 seconds | how long Dox waits for the answer. Then it stops the request. |

The `url` must be a full `http` or `https` url. A wrong url gives an error when the app starts.

To use SSR only in production, set it from the env:

```dart
ssr: Env.get<String>('APP_ENV') == 'production' ? InertiaSsr() : null,
```

### The root view with SSR

The root view needs no change. The HTML from the SSR server goes in place of `@inertia`. The head tags of the page (from the `<Head>` component, like `<title>`) go right before `</head>`.

When your pages set a title with `<Head>`, remove the `<title>` from the root view, so the page does not have two.

### When the SSR server fails

If the SSR server is down, is too slow, or gives a bad answer, the visitor gets the normal page and the browser renders it. No error is shown. Dox prints one warning for the first failure, and no more until the SSR server works again.

## Not included

- The Inertia 1 and 2 clients. They read the page from `<div id="app" data-page="...">`. Use the Inertia 3 client.
- Once props, scroll props (infinite scroll), `prependProps`, `deepMergeProps` and `matchPropsOn`.
- Partial reloads of nested props with dots, like `only: ['auth.user']`. Ask for the top level prop (`auth`).

Inertia needs [sessions](session.md) for the errors, flash data and redirects. The client sends the CSRF token by itself, see [CSRF](../security/csrf.md#axios-and-inertia).

## Details

This section is for special cases. Most apps do not need it.

- `@inertia` becomes `<script data-page="app" type="application/json">{"component":"Home",...}</script><div id="app"></div>`. In the JSON, `<`, `>` and `&` are written as `\u003c`, `\u003e` and `\u0026`, so a prop can not end the script tag.
- An Inertia request has `X-Inertia: true`. Its answer has `X-Inertia: true` and `Vary: X-Inertia`.
- A Dart `int` above 2^53 in a prop loses precision, because JavaScript reads the page JSON. Send such a number as a string.
- The page lists the names of the shared props in `sharedProps`. The client keeps them on an instant visit. A prop shared for the request wins over a global one.
- `Inertia.lazy` is the same as `Inertia.optional`. A deferred prop with `.merge()` (or `merge: true`) is also listed in `mergeProps` when it is sent.
- With an error bag, the client sends the `X-Inertia-Error-Bag` header. You do not need to pass `errors` yourself, but a page prop named `errors` still wins.
- An empty `200` answer to an Inertia request goes back only to a `Referer` of the same site. Any other `Referer` goes to `/`. A request without `X-Inertia` gets the empty answer as it is.
- `Inertia.location` gives an Inertia request `409` with `X-Inertia-Location`. Other requests get `302`. An old asset version on an Inertia `GET` also gets `409` with `X-Inertia-Location`.
- In dev mode, `@vite` loads `@vite/client` too. With `reactRefresh: true` it adds the React Fast Refresh code first. In production, `@vite` gives a `<link>` tag for the css of each entry and of the chunks it imports, and a `<script type="module">` tag for each entry.
- `public/hot` holds the dev server url. Some Vite plugins write it while `vite` runs. Dox ignores it only when `APP_ENV` is `production` (in any case), and prints a warning. Other values, like `staging` or an empty value, still use it.
- Root view data: the escaped characters are `&`, `<`, `>`, `"` and `'`. A `null` value gives empty text. For the same key, the last call wins. A key has letters, digits and `_`, and the spaces are optional: `{{title}}` works too. With no session, `{{ csrfToken }}` stays as it is. Your own `csrfToken` value wins. Only `{{ key }}` in the root view file is replaced, not the same text in a prop or in the SSR HTML.
- With SSR, the `<Head>` title is also added to the first page, so use only one of `withViewData` and `<Head>` for the title.
- Another root view works like the default one, with `@vite`, `@inertia` and `{{ key }}`.
- History encryption keeps its key in the browser, in session storage. With no session, `clearHistory` only works when the same request renders a page with `inertia(...)`.
- With SSR, head tags need a `</head>` tag (`</HEAD>` works too). A root view with no `</head>` gets no head tags. The SSR HTML holds the page data and the rendered `<div id="app">`.


---

# Serializer

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/the-basic/serializer/

# Serializer

A serializer sets the JSON shape of a response: which keys the client gets, their names and their values.

You often do not want to send a model as it is. Maybe the client needs other key names, a formatted date, or a field made from two columns. A serializer does this in one place. It works with any Dart type: a model, a plain class, or a map.

!!! tip
    You do not always need a serializer.
    A controller can return a model, a `Map` or a `List` as it is. See [Response](response.md#return-a-value).
    To only hide some model fields, use [`hidden`](../database/model/index.md#hide-fields).

## Create a serializer

Make a serializer with the CLI:

```bash
dox make:serializer Blog
```

This makes `lib/app/serializers/blog.serializer.dart`. The file is for a model with the same name. Change the type to use it for something else.

## Writing a serializer

Extend `Serializer<T>` and write `convert`. `convert` gets one value of type `T` and gives back one JSON object:

```dart title="lib/app/serializers/blog.serializer.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

import 'package:my_app/app/models/blog/blog.model.dart';

class BlogSerializer extends Serializer<Blog> {
  BlogSerializer(super.data);

  @override
  Map<String, dynamic> convert(Blog m) {
    return <String, dynamic>{
      'uid': m.id,
      'title_en': m.title,
    };
  }
}
```

Return the serializer from a controller, and Dox sends its `toJson()`. You can give it one model or a list:

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/blog.controller.dart"
class BlogController {
  Future<BlogSerializer> index(DoxRequest req) async {
    List<Blog> blogs = await Blog().all();
    return BlogSerializer(blogs); // a list
  }

  Future<BlogSerializer> show(DoxRequest req, String id) async {
    Blog? blog = await Blog().find(id);
    return BlogSerializer(blog); // one model
  }
}
```

The response of `show`:

```json
{
  "uid": 1,
  "title_en": "This is title"
}
```

This is what the client gets for each input:

| You give | The client gets |
| --- | --- |
| one value of type `T` | one JSON object |
| a `List<T>` | a JSON list (`[]` when the list is empty) |
| `null` (for example, `find` found nothing) | `null` |
| any other type | `null` |

!!! warning "The list type must be `List<T>`"
    A `List<dynamic>` is not a `List<T>`, so the response is `null`.
    This happens with a list from `jsonDecode`. Call `.cast<T>()` first.
    See [JSON from another API](#json-from-another-api).

## Examples with models

### Change values

`convert` is plain Dart, so you can format dates, join fields and add new keys:

```dart title="lib/app/serializers/user.serializer.dart"
class UserSerializer extends Serializer<User> {
  UserSerializer(super.data);

  @override
  Map<String, dynamic> convert(User m) {
    return <String, dynamic>{
      'id': m.id,
      'name': '${m.firstName} ${m.lastName}',
      'is_active': m.status == 'active',
      'joined_at': m.createdAt?.toIso8601String(),
    };
  }
}
```

### A serializer inside a serializer

If a model has a relation, use its serializer inside the other one. Load the relation first, for example with [`preload`](../database/model/relationship/belongs-to.md#loading-the-relation):

```dart title="lib/app/serializers/comment.serializer.dart"
class CommentSerializer extends Serializer<Comment> {
  CommentSerializer(super.data);

  @override
  Map<String, dynamic> convert(Comment m) {
    return <String, dynamic>{
      'id': m.id,
      'content': m.content,
      'user': UserSerializer(m.user).toJson(), // null when there is no user
    };
  }
}
```

Then preload the relation in the controller:

```dart
Future<CommentSerializer> index(DoxRequest req) async {
  List<Comment> comments = await Comment().preload('user').all();
  return CommentSerializer(comments);
}
```

### With pagination

A paginated result has its own keys, like the page number. `page.data` is a `List<User>`, so put the serializer output in place of `data`:

```dart
Future<Map<String, dynamic>> index(ListUsers query) async {
  Pagination<User> page = await User()
      .orderBy('id', 'desc')
      .paginate(currentPage: query.page, perPage: query.perPage);
  return <String, dynamic>{
    ...page.toJson(),
    'data': UserSerializer(page.data).toJson(),
  };
}
```

See [Pagination](../guides/pagination.md) for the full example.

## Examples without models

`T` can be any type, so you do not need the ORM.

### A plain Dart class

A serializer for a plain class works the same way:

```dart title="lib/app/serializers/weather.serializer.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

class Weather {
  final String city;
  final double celsius;

  Weather(this.city, this.celsius);
}

class WeatherSerializer extends Serializer<Weather> {
  WeatherSerializer(super.data);

  @override
  Map<String, dynamic> convert(Weather m) {
    return <String, dynamic>{
      'city': m.city,
      'celsius': m.celsius,
      'fahrenheit': m.celsius * 9 / 5 + 32,
    };
  }
}
```

```dart
WeatherSerializer today(DoxRequest req) {
  return WeatherSerializer(<Weather>[Weather('Yangon', 30)]);
}
```

### Rows from the query builder

`QueryBuilder.table(...)` gives rows as maps, not models. Use `Serializer<Map<String, dynamic>>` to pick and rename the keys:

```dart title="lib/app/serializers/sales_report.serializer.dart"
class SalesReportSerializer extends Serializer<Map<String, dynamic>> {
  SalesReportSerializer(super.data);

  @override
  Map<String, dynamic> convert(Map<String, dynamic> m) {
    return <String, dynamic>{
      'product': m['name'],
      'sold': m['total'],
    };
  }
}
```

```dart
Future<SalesReportSerializer> report(DoxRequest req) async {
  List<Map<String, dynamic>> rows = await QueryBuilder.table('orders')
      .selectRaw('name, count(*) as total')
      .groupBy('name')
      .get();
  return SalesReportSerializer(rows);
}
```

### JSON from another API

`jsonDecode` gives a `List<dynamic>`, so cast it to the type of the serializer first:

```dart
Future<SalesReportSerializer> remote(DoxRequest req) async {
  String body = await fetchReport(); // your HTTP call
  List<dynamic> rows = jsonDecode(body);
  return SalesReportSerializer(rows.cast<Map<String, dynamic>>());
}
```

## See also

- [CLI: `dox make:serializer`](../reference/cli.md#dox-makeserializer)


---

# Response

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/the-basic/response/

# Response

A controller returns a value, and Dox turns it into the response for the client.

Most of the time you just return a string, a map or a model. When you need to set the status, headers or cookies, use the `response()` helper.

## Return a value

Return the value from your controller. Dox sends a `String` as text, and a `Map` or a model as JSON:

```dart
// JSON
Map<String, String> hello(DoxRequest req) {
  return <String, String>{'message': 'hello world!'};
}

// a model
Future<Blog?> show(int id) async {
  return Blog().find(id);
}
```

This is what the client gets for each type:

| You return | The client gets |
| --- | --- |
| a `String` | the text |
| a `Map` or a `List` | JSON |
| a model, a list of models, a [serializer](serializer.md) | JSON (from `toJson()`) |
| a `DateTime` | the ISO 8601 text |
| an `IHttpException`, like `NotFoundHttpException()` | its status code and JSON: `{"code": ..., "message": ...}`, or a `Map` message as it is |
| a `File` (from `dart:io`) | the file, streamed |
| a `Stream<List<int>>` | the bytes, streamed |
| `StreamFile`, `DownloadableFile` (also from `Storage()` of `dox_storage`) | the file, streamed |
| `response(...)` | full control: status, headers, cookies |

## Errors

To answer with an error, throw or return an exception:

```dart
throw NotFoundHttpException(message: 'Blog not found');
```

The client gets `404` with `{"code":"not_found","message":"Blog not found"}`. Each exception takes `message:`, `errorCode:` and `code:`. `code` in the JSON is the `errorCode`. A `Map` message is sent as it is.

Dox has these exceptions:

| Exception | Status |
| --- | --- |
| `BadRequestException()` | `400` |
| `NotFoundHttpException()` | `404` |
| `PayloadTooLargeException()` | `413` |
| `UnsupportedMediaTypeException()` | `415` |
| `TokenMismatchException()` | `419` |
| `ValidationException()` | `422` |
| `TooManyRequestsException()` | `429` |
| `InternalErrorException()` | `500` |

If you need another status, extend `IHttpException`:

```dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

class ForbiddenException extends IHttpException {
  ForbiddenException({String message = 'Forbidden'}) {
    super.code = HttpStatus.forbidden;
    super.errorCode = 'forbidden';
    super.message = message;
  }
}
```

Any other error gets `500`. It is also passed to the [exception handler](errors.md).

## Files and big responses

Return a `File` or a `Stream<List<int>>` to send a file. Dox sends it in chunks, so it does not load it all into memory:

```dart
import 'dart:io';

// a file from disk
Route.get('/video', (DoxRequest req) => File('storage/video.mp4'));
```

A `File` gets the right `Content-Type`, `Content-Length` and `Accept-Ranges`. It also answers `Range` requests with `206 Partial Content`, so video players can seek and downloads can resume.

### Files from storage

If you use [File Storage](../digging-deeper/file-storage.md), return `Storage().download()` to make the browser save the file. It sends `Content-Disposition`:

```dart
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';

// a download from Storage
Future<DownloadableFile> download(DoxRequest req) async {
  // sends Content-Disposition, so the browser saves the file
  return Storage().download('report.pdf');
}
```

To show the file in the browser instead, return `Storage().stream()`:

```dart
// a stream from Storage
Future<StreamFile> show(DoxRequest req) async {
  return Storage().stream('photo.jpg');
}
```

## The `response()` helper

Use `response(content)` when you need to set the status, headers or cookies. All methods return the response, so you can chain them:

```dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

DoxResponse store(DoxRequest req) {
  return response(<String, String>{'status': 'created'})
      .statusCode(201)
      .header('X-Request-Id', 'abc')
      .contentType(ContentType.json);
}
```

### Setting the status

`statusCode` sets the status code. The default is `200`:

```dart
response(data).statusCode(201);
```

### Setting headers

`header` sets one header. If a middleware already put the same header on the response, the old value stays and this one is added. Pass `replace: true` to replace it:

```dart
response(data).header('X-Key', 'value');

response(data).header('X-Key', 'value', replace: true);
```

`withHeaders` adds many headers. A key replaces the header with the same name, in any case. Other headers stay:

```dart
response(data).withHeaders(<String, String>{'X-One': '1', 'X-Two': '2'});
```

`contentType` sets `Content-Type`. `ContentType` is from `dart:io`:

```dart
response(html).contentType(ContentType.html);
```

### Caching

`cache` sets `Cache-Control`. For example, `Duration(minutes: 5)` sends `Cache-Control: max-age=300`:

```dart
response(data).cache(Duration(minutes: 5));
```

### Changing the body

`content` changes the body, and `stream` sends a `Stream<List<int>>` as the body:

```dart
response('').content(value);

response('').stream(byteStream);
```

## Redirect

Use `redirect` to send the browser to another page. The status is `302`, unless you pass another one:

```dart
// 302 to a path
return redirect('/login');

// another status
return redirect('/posts', status: 301);
```

`back` sends the browser back to the page the request came from (the `Referer` header). When there is no `Referer`, or it points to another host, it goes to `/`. This is useful after a form post:

```dart
return back(req);
```

See [Session](session.md#flash-data) for flash messages and errors with a redirect.

## Cookie

To set a cookie, make a `DoxCookie` and add it with `cookie`:

```dart
DoxCookie cookie = DoxCookie('theme', 'dark');
return response('ok').cookie(cookie);
```

You can set the cookie options too:

```dart
DoxCookie token = DoxCookie(
  'token',
  'value',
  maxAge: Duration(days: 7), // sent as Max-Age in seconds. default 1 hour
  httpOnly: true, // default true: page scripts can not read it
  secure: true,   // default: Secure only when the request came over https
  path: '/',
  sameSite: SameSite.lax, // from dart:io. default: none sent
);
return response('ok').cookie(token);
```

To delete a cookie, pass `setExpire: true`:

```dart
return response('ok').cookie(DoxCookie('token', ''), setExpire: true);
```

Dox encrypts the cookie value with `APP_KEY`, and decrypts it when you read it. If the browser or another app must read the value, turn this off with `DoxCookie(key, value, encrypt: false)`. Then read it with `req.cookie(key, decrypt: false)`.

To read a cookie, see [Request: cookies](request.md#cookies).

## Send the response yourself

Some handlers write the raw response, for example a stream with trailers. Call `req.takeOverResponse()` first. Then Dox sends nothing more for the request: not the value you return, not a change of a middleware after `next` (like `ETag`), and not the `responseHandler`:

```dart
Future<void> handle(DoxRequest req) async {
  req.takeOverResponse();
  HttpResponse res = req.httpRequest.response;
  res.write('done');
  await res.close();
}
```

Your code must end the response. An error after this call is still reported, but Dox does not send an error answer.

## Change every response

Sometimes you want to change every response in one place, for example to add a header. Set a `responseHandler` in `AppConfig` for this:

```dart title="lib/app/http/handler.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

class ResponseHandler extends ResponseHandlerInterface {
  @override
  DoxResponse handle(DoxResponse res) {
    return res.header('X-Powered-By', 'Dox');
  }
}
```

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  responseHandler: ResponseHandler(),
  // ...
);
```

## Details

- Some flags change this page: `htmlStrings` sends a string as `text/html`, `replaceHeaders` makes `header()` replace, and `cookieDefaults` sends `Path=/` and `SameSite=Lax` when you set no `path` or `sameSite`. See [Core flags](../reference/app-config.md#core-flags).
- `Storage().stream()` and `Storage().download()` on the local disk also stream the file.


---

# Error handling

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/the-basic/errors/

# Error handling

Every error that a route throws goes to one exception handler, which logs it and sends an answer to the client.

The handler has two methods:

- `report(error, stackTrace)` logs the error.
- `render(error, req)` decides what the client gets.

You do not need to set anything up. The default handler already gives good answers. You only write your own handler when you want to change them.

## The default answer

This is what the client gets with the default handler:

| Error | Status | Body |
| --- | --- | --- |
| an `IHttpException`, like `NotFoundHttpException` | its `code` | `{"code": "not_found", "message": "Not Found"}` |
| a `ValidationException` (bad input) | `422` | the field errors, like `{"name": "The name is required"}` |
| a `ValidationException` on a request with a [session](session.md#validation-errors-and-old-input) that does not want JSON, like a form post | `302` | a redirect back. The errors and the old input are in the session. |
| a URL with no route | `404` | `{"code": "not_found", "message": "GET /x not found"}` |
| any other error | `500` | `{"code": "server_error", "message": "Server Error"}` |

For a `500`, the error text is sent only when `APP_ENV` is `development` or `local`. In production the client never sees it, because it can hold SQL, file paths or hosts.

See [HTTP exceptions](../reference/http-exceptions.md) for the built-in exception classes.

### Which errors are logged

`report` is called for every error, except an `IHttpException` with a `4xx` code. A `4xx` exception (like `404`) is a normal answer, so it is not logged. A `5xx` exception, like `InternalErrorException`, is logged. The default `report` prints the error and the stack with the logger.

## An HTML error page

By default an error is sent as JSON, so a browser that opens a bad URL sees JSON, not a page. In `development` or `local`, a `500` is plain text with the error text.

If you want browsers to get an HTML page, turn on `htmlErrors`:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  htmlErrors: true,
  // ...
);
```

The page shows the status and its title, like `404 Not Found`. It loads no files from outside. When `APP_ENV` is `development` or `local`, the page also shows the error text and the stack trace.

Only a request that does not want JSON gets the page. A JSON client, a validation error and an answer from your own `render` stay the same.

### Your own error page

To make your own page, set `errorPage`. It gets the status, the error, the stack trace and a `debug` flag. `debug` is `true` when `APP_ENV` is `development` or `local`. Escape every value you put in the page.

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  htmlErrors: true,
  errorPage: (int status, Object error, StackTrace stack, bool debug) =>
      '<h1>Sorry, error $status</h1>',
  // ...
);
```

The default page is `defaultErrorPage`. You can call it from your own function, for example for the statuses you do not handle.

## Your own handler

Sometimes you want to send errors to an error tracker, or give your own exception a special answer. For this, extend `ExceptionHandler` and override one method or both:

```dart title="lib/app/exception_handler.dart"
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

class PaymentRequiredException implements Exception {}

class AppExceptionHandler extends ExceptionHandler {
  const AppExceptionHandler();

  @override
  void report(Object error, StackTrace stackTrace) {
    // send it to your error tracker
    print('ERROR $error\n$stackTrace');
  }

  @override
  dynamic render(Object error, HttpRequest req) {
    if (error is PaymentRequiredException) {
      return response(<String, String>{'message': 'Please pay'})
          .statusCode(402);
    }
    // everything else: the default answer
    return super.render(error, req);
  }
}
```

Then set it in `AppConfig`:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  exceptionHandler: const AppExceptionHandler(),
  // ...
);
```

### What render can return

`render` can return anything a controller can return: a `DoxResponse`, a map or a string. If you return the error itself, the client gets the default answer. This is what `super.render` does.

`req` is the raw `HttpRequest`. It is there even when the error came before Dox read the body. Use it to read headers, like `req.headers.value('accept')`.

See [Custom errors](../guides/custom-errors.md) for a full example with your own exception classes.

## Errors of one route

Some routes answer in their own format, like gRPC. A JSON error makes no sense to their clients. `.renderErrorsWith` gives the errors of one route to your own function. It covers the errors of the middleware too, and a body that fails to read (for example a broken multipart body):

```dart
DoxResponse? rpcError(Object error, DoxRequest req) {
  return response(<String, String>{'error': 'failed'}).statusCode(500);
}

Route.post('/rpc', (RpcController c) => c.call).renderErrorsWith(rpcError);
```

The error is still reported. Return `null` to get the normal answer from your `ExceptionHandler`.

Dox sends routes to every isolate. So the function must be a top-level or static function, or one that captures nothing. A request with a `_method` override (`MethodOverride`) is not covered for a body error, because its route is not known before the body is read.

## Show error text only in development

Your code may send an error answer itself. Then use `showErrors()` to decide if the client may see the error text. It is `true` when `APP_ENV` is `development` or `local`, the same rule as the Dox error answers:

```dart
String message = showErrors() ? '$error' : 'Server Error';
```

## Details

- A request wants JSON (`DoxRequest.expectsJson()`) when it has an `Accept` header with json, a JSON body, or `X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest`. An Inertia request does not want JSON, so it gets the HTML page.
- If `render` itself throws, Dox logs that error and sends the default answer. The client always gets a response.
- Errors outside a request, like a future that nobody awaits or an error in the `shutdown()` of a provider, also go to `report`. The server keeps running.
- The `responseHandler` of `AppConfig` still runs after `render`, so it sees error responses too. Use `render` to change errors, and `responseHandler` to change all responses.


---

# Cache

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/cache/

# Cache

`Cache()` keeps data that is slow to make, so the next request can read it fast.

Some work takes a long time, like a big database query or a call to another service. If the result does not change often, you can keep it in the cache and read it from there. The cache runs on [`dox_cache`](../packages/cache.md), which is built into `dox_core`.

## Configuration

A new project already has `lib/config/cache.dart`, with a `file` store and a `memory` store. `CACHE_STORE` in `.env` picks the default store. It is `file` when it is not set.

### Install

A new app already has the cache. In an older app, run `dox add cache`:

```bash
dox add cache
```

It writes `lib/config/cache.dart`, adds it to `lib/config/app.dart` and adds the `CACHE_STORE` key. It never overwrites a file, so it is safe to run twice.

To pick another default store, add `--store=redis` (or `memory`, `database`). `redis` also adds the `REDIS_*` keys. `database` also adds `dox_cache_database`, its provider and the cache table migration, and it needs `dox add orm` first.

### Drivers

A store uses one driver. The driver decides where the data is kept:

| Driver | Where the data is | Shared between isolates |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `file` | files in a folder (default `storage/cache`) | yes, on the same machine |
| `memory` | a map inside the isolate | no |
| `redis` | a Redis server | yes, also between machines |
| `database` | a table in your database, from [`dox_cache_database`](../packages/cache.md#database-store) | yes, also between machines |
| `null` | nowhere. It stores nothing | - |

Dox runs one isolate per CPU core, and each isolate has its own `memory` store. So a value you put in one isolate is missing in the others. If all isolates and servers must see the same data, use `redis` or `database`.

Sessions on a `memory` store are the exception. They live in the main isolate, so every isolate sees them. See [Session](../the-basic/session.md).

### Adding a Redis store

To add a store, edit `lib/config/cache.dart`. This example adds a `redis` store:

```dart title="lib/config/cache.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

CacheConfig cache = CacheConfig(
  defaultStore: env.cacheStore,
  stores: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
    'file': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'file', 'path': 'storage/cache'},
    'memory': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'memory', 'max_size': 10000},
    'redis': <String, dynamic>{
      'driver': 'redis',
      'host': env.redisHost,
      'port': env.redisPort,
      'prefix': 'app_cache:',
    },
  },
);
```

Redis needs two env keys that a new project does not have yet. Add them to `lib/config/env.dart`, then run `dart run build_runner build`:

```dart title="lib/config/env.dart"
  String get redisHost => '127.0.0.1';

  int get redisPort => 6379;
```

`lib/config/app.dart` already passes the config to `AppConfig(cache: cache)`. All options of each driver are in [Store options](#store-options).

## Retrieving items

Use `get` to read a value. It gives `null` when the key is missing. The second argument is the default, which you get instead of `null`:

```dart
await Cache().get('foo');            // 'bar', or null when missing
await Cache().get('foo', 'default'); // 'default' when missing
```

### Checking if an item exists

The `has` method returns `true` when the key is in the cache:

```dart
if (await Cache().has('foo')) {
  // ...
}
```

### Retrieving many items

The `many` method reads many keys at once. A missing key gives `null`:

```dart
await Cache().many(<String>['a', 'b', 'c']); // {a: 1, b: 2, c: null}
```

### Retrieve and store

Often you want to read a value, and make it when it is missing. The `remember` method does this. If the key is missing, the function runs and its result is stored for the given time:

```dart
List<dynamic> posts = await Cache().remember(
  'posts',
  Duration(minutes: 5),
  () async => (await Post().all()).map((Post p) => p.toJson()).toList(),
);
```

The value is stored as JSON, so return maps, lists, strings and numbers, not models. To keep the value with no expiry, use `rememberForever(key, fn)`.

`remember` has two options:

- `decode:` turns the stored JSON back into your type on a hit, like `decode: (j) => (j as List).cast<String>()`. Without it, use JSON types like `List<dynamic>`.
- `lock: true` lets only one caller on all isolates and servers run the function. The others wait for its value. Use it when the function is slow and many requests could run it at once.

### Serving stale values

Sometimes an old value is fine for a while, but you do not want a user to wait while it is made again. The `flexible` method serves the value as it is for `fresh`. Then, until `stale` more has passed, it still serves the old value at once and runs the function once in the background:

```dart
Map<String, dynamic> stats = await Cache().flexible(
  'stats', Duration(minutes: 1), Duration(minutes: 5), loadStats,
);
```

After `fresh` + `stale`, the value is gone and the next call waits for the function.

If an old value is always better than no value, pass `null` as `stale`. Then the value stays until a refresh replaces it. This is good for data from a service that can be down: when the function fails, callers still get the last good value:

```dart
Map<String, dynamic> rates = await Cache().flexible(
  'rates', Duration(minutes: 10), null, fetchRates,
);
```

### Retrieve and delete

The `pull` method reads a value and removes it in one step:

```dart
dynamic code = await Cache().pull('login_code');
```

### Retrieving raw JSON

If you only send the cached value back as a response, you do not need to decode it and encode it again. `getRaw` gives the stored JSON text as it is:

```dart
String? json = await Cache().getRaw('posts');
if (json != null) {
  return response(json).contentType(ContentType.json);
}
```

A missing key gives `null`. A stored `String` comes back as JSON, with its quotes: `"bar"`.

## Storing items

Use `put` to store a value. Pass a `duration` to make it expire. With no duration, the value stays forever:

```dart
await Cache().put('foo', 'bar', duration: Duration(minutes: 10));

await Cache().put('foo', 'bar');
```

A value must be a JSON type: `Map`, `List`, `String`, `num`, `bool` or `null`. A `Map` comes back as `Map<String, dynamic>`, and a `List` comes back as `List<dynamic>`.

### Storing an item forever

The `forever` method stores a value with no expiry:

```dart
await Cache().forever('settings', <String, dynamic>{'theme': 'dark'});
```

### Storing if not present

The `add` method stores a value only when the key is missing. It returns `true` when the value was stored:

```dart
bool stored = await Cache().add('foo', 'bar', duration: Duration(minutes: 10));
```

### Storing many items

The `putMany` method stores many values at once:

```dart
await Cache().putMany(<String, Object?>{'a': 1, 'b': 2});
```

### Incrementing and decrementing

The `increment` and `decrement` methods change an integer. A missing key starts at 0:

```dart
await Cache().increment('visits');
await Cache().decrement('stock', 5);
```

### Changing the expiry

The `touch` method gives a key a new expiry. It returns `false` when the key is missing:

```dart
await Cache().touch('foo', duration: Duration(hours: 1));
```

## Removing items

The `forget` method removes one key. The `flush` method removes all items of the store:

```dart
await Cache().forget('foo');

await Cache().flush();
```

## Using another store

By default, `Cache()` uses the default store. If you want another store from the config, use `store`:

```dart
await Cache().store('redis').put('foo', 'bar');
```

`store()` changes the `Cache` it is called on. The flag `cacheCopies` makes `store()` and `tags()` give a new `Cache` instead. See [Core flags](../reference/app-config.md#core-flags).

## Cache tags

Tags let you group items, so you can remove only the items of one group. Put items under a tag with `tag`, then call `flush` on the tag:

```dart
await Cache().tag('users').put('u1', 'Ann');
await Cache().tag('users').flush(); // removes only the items of this tag
```

To use many tags, call `tags(['a', 'b'])`.

## Atomic locks

Sometimes only one request (or one server) may run some code at a time, like building a report. A lock does this. The `memory`, `file`, `redis` and `database` stores support locks:

```dart
CacheLock lock = Cache().store('redis').lock('report', Duration(seconds: 30));
if (await lock.get()) {
  try {
    await buildReport();
  } finally {
    await lock.release();
  }
}
```

`get()` tries once. It is `true` when you got the lock. The lock is freed after its time (`30` seconds here), even if you never call `release()`.

The `memory` lock works inside one isolate only, and the `file` lock works for all isolates on one machine. If many servers must share the lock, use `redis` or `database`.

### Waiting for a lock

`block` tries again and again until the time is over. It gives `false` when the time is over:

```dart
if (await lock.block(Duration(seconds: 5))) {
  // ...
}
```

If you pass a callback, `block` runs it while it holds the lock, then frees the lock. It returns the result of the callback, and throws a `LockTimeoutException` when it could not get the lock in time:

```dart
await lock.block(Duration(seconds: 5), buildReport);
```

With the flag `CacheFlags(lockThrows: true)`, `block` with no callback throws a `LockTimeoutException` instead of giving `false`. See [CacheConfig](../reference/app-config.md#cacheconfig).

To free a lock, whoever holds it, use `forceRelease()`.

## Encrypting the cache

By default the cache keeps plain JSON. So anyone who can read the cache files or the Redis database can read the values. To hide them, add `'encrypt': true` to a `file` or `redis` store:

```dart
'file': {'driver': 'file', 'path': 'storage/cache', 'encrypt': true},
```

The values are encrypted with your `APP_KEY`. When the key changes, old entries count as a miss and the cache fills again. Old keys in `previousKeys` can still read old entries.

Encryption only stops people from reading values. Cache keys and tag names are not encrypted. On Redis, a plain `int` stays plain text, so `increment` still works. To keep a secret number encrypted, store it as a `String`.

## Testing

To use a memory store in tests, see [Testing](testing.md#test-the-cache).

## Details

### Store options

| Driver | Options |
| --- | --- |
| `file` | `path` (default `storage/cache`), `prefix`, `encrypt` |
| `memory` | `max_size`: the most items. When it is full, the item used least recently is removed. No limit by default. Also `prefix`. |
| `redis` | `host` (default `127.0.0.1`), `port` (default `6379`), `username`, `password`, `db` (default `0`), `tls` (`true`/`false`), `pool_size` (default 10), `max_value_bytes` (no limit by default), `prefix`, `encrypt` |

- A `redis` store with no `prefix` gets `<app name>_cache:` from `APP_NAME`, like `my_shop_cache:`. So two apps on one Redis do not share keys. The other drivers use `dox_cache:`.
- To set any other ioredis option, see [Redis options](#redis-options).
- You rarely need `pool_size`. The cache sends no blocking commands, so each isolate uses about one Redis connection.
- Each store is made once per isolate, the first time you use it.
- The `memory` driver removes expired items when they are read, and in a sweep after many writes (at least 1000). It also keeps JSON text, so `get` decodes on every hit.
- `repository` gives the `dox_cache` `CacheStore`. See [dox_cache](../packages/cache.md) for custom drivers.

### Redis options

To set an option that Store options does not have, like a command timeout, give the `redis` store a `RedisOptions`. It is used as it is. `prefix`, `max_value_bytes` and `encrypt` still work next to it.

Do not set `host`, `port`, `username`, `password`, `db`, `tls` or `pool_size` with it. That throws an `ArgumentError`.

The client uses the ioredis defaults, not the `pool_size` default of the store. For example, `commandTimeout` is 10 seconds.

```dart title="lib/config/cache.dart"
'redis': <String, dynamic>{
  'driver': 'redis',
  'options': RedisOptions(
    host: env.redisHost,
    port: env.redisPort,
    commandTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 2),
  ),
},
```

Sessions and the [rate limit](../security/rate-limiting.md) use the same store, so they get these options too.

`RedisOptions`, `RedisTimeoutError` and `RedisQueueFullError` come with `package:dox_core/dox_core.dart`. You need no `ioredis` import.

### Encryption

- `encrypt` must be `true` or `false`. Any other type, like `'true'`, throws an `ArgumentError`.
- A `CacheManager` you build yourself needs `encrypter:`, for example `const CryptCacheEncrypter()`. The normal `Dox().cache` has it set for you.
- A `memory` or `null` store does not encrypt, because its values never leave the process. The option still needs an encrypter, or building the store throws.
- On a `file` store, the whole file is encrypted, also the expiry time. Lock files are not encrypted, because they hold no values. `prune` deletes files that can not be decrypted.
- Tag counters are `int` values, so on Redis they stay plain too.
- Old plain values read as a miss after you turn the option on. Only an `int` on Redis still reads as a value.
- A value is not tied to its key. So someone who can write to Redis or the cache folder can copy an encrypted value to another key.
- `max_value_bytes` is checked on the plain JSON size. The encrypted text is about a third bigger.


---

# Queue

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/queue/

# Queue

A queue runs slow work in the background, so the request can answer at once.

Some tasks take too long to do during a request, like sending an email, calling a slow API, making a report or resizing an image. You put these tasks on a queue as jobs. A worker process then takes each job and runs it.

The `dox_queue` package gives you jobs, retries, delays and a worker. It has a `redis` driver and a `sync` driver. The `database` driver is in the `dox_queue_database` package.

## Setup

A new app from `dox create` already has the queue. In other apps, run:

```bash
dox add queue
```

The default driver is `database`. Add `--driver=redis` or `--driver=sync` to pick another one. The command adds the package and writes the config, the provider, `bin/queue.dart` and a sample job. It never overwrites a file, so it is safe to run twice.

With `database`, it also adds `dox_queue_database` and the migration for the jobs tables, so run `dox add orm` first. With `redis`, it adds the `REDIS_*` keys.

The sections below show the files it writes. Check them, and change the driver if you want. To set it up by hand, run `dart pub add dox_queue` and write the same files.

### Configuration

The queue config picks the driver and lists your jobs:

```dart title="lib/config/queue.dart"
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';

import '../generated/jobs.g.dart';

QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  /// sync, database or redis
  driver: 'database',

  /// every @Job class, from lib/generated/jobs.g.dart
  jobs: jobRegistry,
);
```

`jobRegistry` holds every job class of your app. `dart run build_runner build` writes it, because the job builder is in `dox_builder`, which your app already runs. See [All options](#all-options) for the other settings.

Dox has three drivers:

- `sync`: `dispatch()` runs the job at once and waits for it. There is no worker, no retry and no delay. Use it for tests and local work.
- `database`: jobs are rows in the `jobs` table. It needs `dox_queue_database`, and Postgres, MySQL 8+, MariaDB 10.6+ or SQLite.
- `redis`: jobs are kept in Redis.

!!! warning "Keep `retryAfter` bigger than your longest job"
    `retryAfter` (default 90 seconds) is how Dox finds the job of a crashed worker.
    A job that runs longer than `retryAfter` looks crashed, so a second worker runs it again.

### The provider

The provider sets up the queue in every isolate. Put it in `lib/providers/`, so the generated container finds it:

```dart title="lib/providers/queue_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';

import '../config/queue.dart';

/// Sets up the queue. Dox finds every DoxProvider class,
/// see lib/generated/container.g.dart.
class AppQueueProvider extends QueueProvider {
  AppQueueProvider() : super(queueConfig);
}
```

### The worker file

The worker runs from `bin/queue.dart`. It starts the providers of your app (database, cache, queue), but not the HTTP server:

```dart title="bin/queue.dart"
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';

/// run queued jobs: `dart run bin/queue.dart [work] [flags]`.
/// the `dox` CLI runs this file for its queue commands.
Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  exitCode = await QueueWorker(app: appConfig).run(args);
}
```

### Database driver

The `database` driver, [job batches](#job-batching) and [dispatching after the commit](#dispatching-after-the-commit) are in the `dox_queue_database` package. If you use only Redis or sync and none of these, skip this step.

```bash
dart pub add dox_queue_database
```

Then make your queue provider extend `DatabaseQueueProvider` in place of `QueueProvider`. This turns the package on. Without it, `QueueConfig(driver: 'database')` throws an `ArgumentError` that names the package.

```dart title="lib/providers/queue_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_queue_database/dox_queue_database.dart';

import '../config/queue.dart';

class AppQueueProvider extends DatabaseQueueProvider {
  AppQueueProvider() : super(queueConfig);
}
```

The database driver needs the `jobs` and `failed_jobs` tables. Batches need the `job_batches` table, with every driver. `dox queue:table` writes a migration in `db/migration` that makes all three:

```bash
dox queue:table
dox migrate
```

The migration looks like this, so you can also write it by hand:

```dart title="db/migration/2026_10_25_000000_create_queue_tables.dart"
// ignore_for_file: file_names
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:dox_queue_database/dox_queue_database.dart';

/// The jobs, failed_jobs and job_batches tables of dox_queue_database.
class CreateQueueTables extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await QueueTables.up(schema);
    await QueueTables.upBatches(schema);
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {
    await QueueTables.downBatches(schema);
    await QueueTables.down(schema);
  }
}
```

To keep the jobs in another database connection of `config/database.dart`, use `QueueConfig(connection: 'postgres')`.

#### Adding the pop indexes to an old table

A new `jobs` table has the indexes a worker needs to find the next job fast. A table you made earlier works too, but a poll can read every waiting job. To add the indexes, write a new migration. It adds only the indexes the table does not have, so you can run it more than once:

```dart title="db/migration/2026_11_20_000000_add_queue_pop_index.dart"
// ignore_for_file: file_names
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:dox_queue_database/dox_queue_database.dart';

class AddQueuePopIndex extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await QueueTables.popIndex(schema);
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {}
}
```

On MySQL and MariaDB it does nothing, because the index on `queue` is enough.

### Redis driver

Set the driver to `redis` and give the Redis server:

```dart
QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  driver: 'redis',
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  redis: RedisOptions(host: env.redisHost, port: 6379),
);
```

A Redis command that gets no reply in 10 seconds fails with `RedisTimeoutError`, and the client reconnects. This stops a Redis outage from hanging every request. Change it with `commandTimeout`. `null` turns it off. Blocking commands and subscriber connections never time out.

To cap the commands that wait for a connection, set `maxQueuedCommands`. One more fails at once with `RedisQueueFullError`. It is off by default:

```dart
QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  driver: 'redis',
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  redis: RedisOptions(
    host: env.redisHost,
    port: 6379,
    commandTimeout: Duration(seconds: 5),
    maxQueuedCommands: 1000,
  ),
);
```

You can also read the Redis server from the env with `QueueConfig.redisFromEnv()`:

```dart
QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  driver: 'redis',
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  redis: QueueConfig.redisFromEnv(),
);
```

It reads `REDIS_URL`, like `rediss://user:password@host:6380/0`, where `rediss` turns on TLS. If `REDIS_URL` is not set, it reads `REDIS_HOST`, `REDIS_PORT`, `REDIS_USERNAME`, `REDIS_PASSWORD` and `REDIS_TLS`. A key that is not set keeps the default of `RedisOptions`.

## Creating jobs

### Generating job classes

`dox make:job` makes a new job file in `lib/app/jobs/`:

```bash
dox make:job SendWelcomeEmail
```

### Class structure

A job is a class with `@Job()` that extends `DoxJob`. The worker calls its `handle()` method:

```dart title="lib/app/jobs/send_welcome_email.job.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';

@Job()
class SendWelcomeEmail extends DoxJob {
  SendWelcomeEmail({required this.userId});

  final int userId;

  @override
  Future<void> handle() async {
    MailService mail = Dox().ioc.get<MailService>();
    await mail.sendWelcome(userId);
  }
}
```

Run `dart run build_runner build` after you add or change a job. It writes `lib/generated/jobs.g.dart`, which knows how to save and load each job.

### Job data

The parameters of the unnamed constructor are saved with the job. Each parameter needs a field or getter with the same name. These types work:

- `int`, `double`, `num`, `String`, `bool`
- `DateTime`
- enums (saved by name)
- `List` and `Map<String, ...>` of these, also nested
- `dynamic` and `Object` (the value must be JSON)
- nullable versions of all of them

Any other type stops the build with a clear message.

!!! tip "Save an id, not an object"
    Do not save a `User`. Save the `userId`, and load the user in `handle()`.
    The user may change between dispatch and run, so the id gives you fresh data.

### Using services in a job

A job is made again from its saved data, so it can not get services in its constructor. Get them in `handle()` from the Dox container:

```dart
UserService users = Dox().ioc.get<UserService>();
```

The worker runs `registerContainer`, so every `@Inject()` class of your app is there.

### Setting the number of tries

By default a job runs once. If you want the worker to try again when `handle()` throws, set `tries`. Use `backoff` to wait between the tries:

```dart
/// run up to 3 times
@override
int get tries => 3;

/// wait 10 seconds before the 2nd try, 60 seconds before the 3rd
@override
List<Duration> get backoff => const <Duration>[
  Duration(seconds: 10),
  Duration(seconds: 60),
];
```

The last `backoff` entry is used for all later tries. With no `backoff`, the retry happens at once.

There are three more settings for retries:

- `retryUntil` retries until a time, in place of a number of tries. It is read once, when the job is dispatched.
- `maxExceptions` fails the job after this many tries that threw an error. A timeout does not count.
- `failOnTimeout` fails the job at once when a try times out, with no retry.

### Setting a timeout

`timeout` is the max run time of one try. The default is the worker `--timeout`, which is 60 seconds:

```dart
/// stop a try after 30 seconds
@override
Duration? get timeout => const Duration(seconds: 30);
```

### Choosing the queue

Jobs go on the `default` queue. You can give a job its own queue, so a worker can run it first or apart:

```dart
/// the queue of this job
@override
String get queue => 'emails';
```

### Handling failed jobs

`failed()` runs once, after the last try failed. Use it to tell someone, or to clean up:

```dart
/// runs once, after the last try failed
@override
Future<void> failed(Object error, StackTrace stack) async {
  // tell someone, or clean up
}
```

### Encrypting job data

If a job holds private data, add the `ShouldBeEncrypted` mixin. Then a person who can read Redis or the `jobs` table can not read the data:

```dart
@Job()
class ChargeCard extends DoxJob with ShouldBeEncrypted {
  // ...
}
```

The data is encrypted with the app key (`AppConfig.appKey`), so the worker needs the same key, or one of `AppConfig.previousKeys`. The job name, the queue and the id stay plain text.

### Renaming a job class

The class name is saved with each job. So when you rename a class, queued jobs with the old name can not be found. Keep the old name with `name`:

```dart
@Job(name: 'SendWelcomeEmail')
```

## Dispatching jobs

Call `dispatch()` to put a job on the queue. It returns the job id:

```dart
await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: user.id).dispatch();
```

`Queue.dispatch()` does the same:

```dart
await Queue.dispatch(SendWelcomeEmail(userId: user.id));
```

### Delayed dispatching

Sometimes a job should wait before it runs. Use `delay`. You can also pick another queue here:

```dart
await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatch(
  delay: Duration(minutes: 10),
  queue: 'emails',
);
```

To wait until a fixed time, use `delayUntil`. Give `delay` or `delayUntil`, not both:

```dart
await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatch(
  delayUntil: DateTime.utc(2030, 1, 1, 9),
);
```

### Conditional dispatching

`dispatchIf` dispatches only when the condition is true, and `dispatchUnless` only when it is false. They return null when the job was not dispatched:

```dart
await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatchIf(user.wantsEmail);
```
