```dart
await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatchUnless(user.isBlocked);
```

### Synchronous dispatching

`dispatchSync` runs the job now, in this process, with no queue:

```dart
await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatchSync();
```

### Dispatching after the response

Sometimes a job is short, but the client should not wait for it. `dispatchAfterResponse` runs the job in this process after the answer is sent:

```dart
SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatchAfterResponse();
```

Do not `await` it, because it returns nothing. The job does not go on the queue, so it has no job id and no retry. If the job throws, its `failed()` runs and the error goes to the exception handler, never to the client. If the server stops before the job runs, the job is lost.

### Dispatching after the commit

If you dispatch a job inside a database transaction, it is pushed at once. Then a worker can run it before the transaction commits, or after it rolls back. So the job reads data that is not saved yet, or is never saved.

Use `afterCommit: true` to wait for the commit. This needs [`dox_queue_database`](#database-driver):

```dart
await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  User user = await User().create(<String, dynamic>{'email': email});
  await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: user.id).dispatch(afterCommit: true);
});
```

- The job is pushed after the outermost transaction commits.
- If the transaction rolls back, the job is not pushed.
- Outside a transaction, the job is pushed at once.
- `dispatch()` still returns the job id at once.

To do this for every dispatch, set `QueueConfig(afterCommit: true)`. Then `afterCommit: false` on one dispatch pushes that job at once. Chains and batches take `afterCommit` too. See [Dispatch after the commit details](#dispatch-after-the-commit-details) for special cases.

### Queueing an email

You do not need a job class to send an email later. With [dox_mailer](mail.md#queue-an-email), call `Mail.queue()`:

```dart
await Mail.queue(message);
await Mail.later(Duration(minutes: 10), message, queue: 'emails');
```

The mail jobs are part of dox_mailer, so the queue provider and a worker run them.

## Running the worker

Start a worker to run the jobs:

```bash
dart run bin/queue.dart
```

Use `--queue` to pick the queues. The first one goes first. Use `--concurrency` to run more jobs at once:

```bash
dart run bin/queue.dart work --queue=emails,default --concurrency=4
```

`--concurrency` runs jobs as async tasks on one thread. It helps for jobs that wait, like email, HTTP or database calls. For CPU heavy jobs, run more worker processes. See [Worker flags](#worker-flags) for all flags.

The `dox` CLI runs the same file, with the same flags: `dox queue:work`, `dox queue:failed`, `dox queue:retry <id|all>`, `dox queue:forget <id>`, `dox queue:flush`, `dox queue:clear [queue]`, `dox queue:restart` and `dox queue:prune-failed`.

### Stopping the worker

Press Ctrl+C, or send SIGTERM (`docker stop` does it). The worker takes no new job, waits for the running jobs, then stops. A second signal stops it at once.

### Restarting after a deploy

The worker keeps your code in memory. So restart it after each deploy, or it runs the old code:

```bash
dart run bin/queue.dart restart
```

This tells every running worker to stop after its current jobs, and your process manager starts them again with the new code. It works through the app cache, so the workers and the command must use the same cache store, like `file` on one machine, or `redis`. The `memory` store does not work for it.

### Running the worker in production

In production, run the binary, not `dart run`. `dox build` makes `build/bundle/bin/queue`, next to the server. It takes the same commands and flags:

```bash
cd build/bundle
./bin/queue work --concurrency=4
```

Run the worker as its own process, next to the web server. For example, with Docker Compose and the image of the project `Dockerfile`:

```yaml
services:
  web:
    build: .
    command: /app/bin/server
  worker:
    build: .
    command: /app/bin/queue work --concurrency=4
```

You can also use systemd, Supervisor or a second Fly.io process. Set it to restart when it stops.

### Running jobs in the web server

A small app can skip the worker process. Set `inProcess: true`, and the first isolate of the web server runs jobs too:

```dart
QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  driver: 'database',
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  inProcess: true,
);
```

When the server stops, it waits for the running jobs. Only the web server runs this worker, not the scheduler process (`bin/schedule.dart`).

!!! warning "Heavy jobs slow down your API"
    The jobs share the isolate with web requests, so a long or CPU heavy job makes requests on that isolate slow.
    Use a worker process when your jobs are heavy or many.

## Dealing with failed jobs

When `handle()` throws, the worker waits the `backoff` time and tries again, up to `tries` times. After the last try, the job goes to the failed jobs, and `failed()` runs. A timeout counts as a failed try.

!!! info "A timeout does not stop the code"
    Dart can not stop a running `Future`. After a timeout the try counts as failed, but `handle()` keeps running in the background until it ends.
    So write jobs that are safe to run twice.

If you want the worker to wait for the old run, start it with `--timeout-grace=SECONDS` (or set `workerTimeoutGrace` for the in-process worker). Keep `timeout` plus the grace time below `retryAfter`.

When a worker crashes, its job stays reserved. After `retryAfter`, another worker takes it, and this counts as a try.

### Retrying failed jobs

Failed jobs are kept until you retry or delete them. List them with `failed`, and put one or all of them back on their queue with `retry`:

```bash
dart run bin/queue.dart failed
dart run bin/queue.dart retry 6f1c0e...
dart run bin/queue.dart retry all
```

### Deleting failed jobs

`forget` deletes one failed job, and `flush` deletes all of them:

```bash
dart run bin/queue.dart forget 6f1c0e...
dart run bin/queue.dart flush
```

`prune-failed` deletes failed jobs older than `--hours=N` (default 24):

```bash
dart run bin/queue.dart prune-failed --hours=48
```

### Controlling the job from handle()

Sometimes the job itself knows what should happen next. For example, an API is busy, so the job should try again later. Add the `InteractsWithQueue` mixin, then call one of these in `handle()`:

| Call | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `attempts()` | how many times a worker took the job. The first run gives 1 |
| `release(delay)` | put the job back on its queue. It runs again after `delay` |
| `fail(error)` | fail the job now, with no retry. `failed()` runs |
| `delete()` | delete the job, with no retry and no `failed()` |

```dart
@Job()
class SendReport extends DoxJob with InteractsWithQueue {
  SendReport({required this.reportId});

  final int reportId;

  @override
  int get tries => 5;

  @override
  Future<void> handle() async {
    ReportApi api = Dox().ioc.get<ReportApi>();
    if (await api.isBusy()) {
      release(Duration(seconds: 30));
      return;
    }
    if (!await api.hasReport(reportId)) {
      delete();
      return;
    }
    await api.send(reportId);
  }
}
```

`release()` counts as a try. Because the default `tries` is 1, set `tries` above 1 (or `retryUntil`) when a job calls `release()`. If not, the job fails on its next pickup.

### Clearing jobs from a queue

`clear` deletes all jobs of a queue, also the running ones. The default queue is `default`:

```bash
dart run bin/queue.dart clear emails
```

## Job middleware

Job middleware wraps `handle()` of a job. Use it for rules that many jobs share, like a rate limit. Add the `HasMiddleware` mixin and list the middleware. The first one runs first:

```dart
@Job()
class SendReport extends DoxJob with HasMiddleware {
  SendReport({required this.reportId});

  final int reportId;

  @override
  int get tries => 5;

  @override
  List<JobMiddleware> get middleware => <JobMiddleware>[
    RateLimited('report-api', 10, Duration(minutes: 1)),
  ];

  // ...
}
```

The built-in middleware keeps its counts and locks in the default cache store. So all workers must use the same store: `file` on one machine, or `redis` for several servers. The `memory` store is per process, so the limit would not work.

A middleware that puts the job back counts as a try. So give these jobs `tries` above 1, or a `retryUntil`.

### Rate limiting

`RateLimited(key, max, per)` runs at most `max` jobs of `key` in each `per` window. The other jobs go back on the queue until the window ends:

```dart
RateLimited('report-api', 10, Duration(minutes: 1)),
```

### Preventing job overlaps

`WithoutOverlapping(key)` runs only one job of `key` at a time:

```dart
WithoutOverlapping(
  'report-$reportId',
  releaseAfter: Duration(seconds: 30),
  expireAfter: Duration(minutes: 10), // longer than the longest report run
),
```

- `releaseAfter` is when the other jobs go back on the queue. The default is zero, so at once. With `releaseAfter: null`, they are dropped.
- `expireAfter` frees the lock after this time, also while a job still runs. The default is no expiry. Set it longer than the longest run of the job, so a crash can not hold the lock forever.
- The key has no class name in it, so job classes with the same key share one lock. Put the class name in the key if they should not.

### Throttling exceptions

`ThrottlesExceptions(key, maxAttempts:, decay:, retryAfter:)` is for jobs that call a service that is down. After `maxAttempts` errors (default 10), jobs of `key` wait until `decay` is over (default 10 minutes). A job that threw goes back after `retryAfter` (default zero).

### Writing your own middleware

Extend `JobMiddleware`. Call `next()` to go on. If you do not call it, the job is skipped and counts as done. Call `release(job, delay)` to put the job back on the queue:

```dart
class SkipAtNight extends JobMiddleware {
  @override
  Future<void> handle(DoxJob job, JobNext next) async {
    if (DateTime.now().hour < 6) {
      release(job, Duration(hours: 1));
      return;
    }
    await next();
  }
}
```

## Unique jobs

Some jobs should wait in the queue only once, like "rebuild the search index of product 5". Add the `ShouldBeUnique` mixin. While a job with the same class and `uniqueId` waits or runs, `dispatch()` pushes nothing and returns `''`:

```dart
@Job()
class UpdateSearchIndex extends DoxJob with ShouldBeUnique {
  UpdateSearchIndex({required this.productId});

  final int productId;

  @override
  String get uniqueId => '$productId';

  @override
  Duration? get uniqueFor => Duration(hours: 1);

  // ...
}
```

- `uniqueId` is the key next to the class. The default is empty, so only one job of the class at a time.
- `uniqueFor` ends the lock after a time, also when the job never ran. You should set it, because the lock of a crashed worker never ends without it.
- The worker frees the lock when the job is done, deleted or failed for good. A release or a retry keeps it.
- The lock is in the default cache store, so the web app and the workers must use the same store, like `redis`.

If a new job may be queued while the old one runs, use `ShouldBeUniqueUntilProcessing` in place of `ShouldBeUnique`. It frees the lock when a worker starts the job.

## Job chaining

A chain runs jobs one after the other. The next job is pushed only when the job before it is done. If a job fails for good, the rest of the chain is dropped and the catch job runs:

```dart
await Queue.chain(<DoxJob>[
  ResizeImage(imageId: 1),
  UploadImage(imageId: 1),
  TellUser(imageId: 1),
]).catchError(TellAdmin(imageId: 1)).dispatch(queue: 'images');
```

The rest of the chain is saved in the job that runs now, so the chain works across worker processes and restarts. `dispatch()` returns the id of the first job. `queue` and `connection` count for every job, but `delay` counts for the first job only.

Each job carries the data of the jobs after it. So keep chains short, and save ids in the jobs, not big data. Give chain jobs more than one try, and make them safe to run twice.

### Handling chain failures

A function can not be saved in the queue. So the catch handler is a job too, of a class in `jobRegistry`. Add the `CatchesError` mixin to read the error:

```dart
@Job()
class TellAdmin extends DoxJob with CatchesError {
  TellAdmin({required this.imageId});

  final int imageId;

  @override
  Future<void> handle() async {
    await alertAdmin('image $imageId failed: $caughtError');
  }
}
```

The catch job runs once, in the worker where the job failed, with no queue and no retry. An error in it is logged. For slow work, dispatch a new job from it.

`queue:retry` of the failed job brings the chain back. When the job is then done, the chain goes on.

## Job batching

A batch runs many jobs and acts when they are all done. Batches need [`dox_queue_database`](#database-driver) and the `job_batches` table, with every driver. Without the package, `Queue.batch()` throws a `StateError`.

```dart
Batch batch = await Queue.batch(<DoxJob>[
  ImportRows(from: 0),
  ImportRows(from: 1000),
  ImportRows(from: 2000),
])
    .name('import')
    .then(ImportDone())
    .catchError(ImportFailed())
    .whenComplete(CleanUpImport())
    .dispatch(queue: 'imports');

print(batch.id);
```

The batch is saved in the `job_batches` table of the `QueueConfig.connection` database, also with the Redis and `sync` drivers.

### Batch callbacks

These callbacks run at the steps of a batch:

| Callback | Runs |
| --- | --- |
| `before(job)` | once, at `dispatch()`, before the jobs are pushed |
| `progress(job)` | each time a job is done. With `allowFailures()`, also when one fails |
| `then(job)` | once, when every job is done |
| `catchError(job)` | once, when the first job fails for good |
| `whenComplete(job)` | once, when every job ran, done or failed |

A function can not be saved in the queue, so each callback is a job of a class in `jobRegistry`. It runs once, with no queue and no retry. An error in a callback is logged. Add `Batchable` to read the batch, and `CatchesError` to read the error:

```dart
@Job()
class ImportFailed extends DoxJob with Batchable, CatchesError {
  @override
  Future<void> handle() async {
    Batch? batch = await this.batch();
    await alertAdmin('import ${batch?.name} failed: $caughtError');
  }
}
```

### Defining batchable jobs

Add the `Batchable` mixin to a job to read its batch. `batchId` is the id, and `batch()` reads the batch as it is now. For example, a job can skip its work when the batch was cancelled:

```dart
@Job()
class ImportRows extends DoxJob with Batchable {
  ImportRows({required this.from});

  final int from;

  @override
  Future<void> handle() async {
    Batch? batch = await this.batch();
    if (batch?.cancelled ?? false) return;
    await importRows(from);
  }
}
```

### Inspecting batches

A `Batch` has these fields:

| Field | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `id`, `name` | the id and the name |
| `totalJobs` | how many jobs the batch has |
| `pendingJobs` | how many jobs are not done. It also counts failed jobs, because they can be retried |
| `failedJobs` | how many jobs failed |
| `processedJobs` | how many jobs are done. Failed jobs are not counted |
| `progress` | the percent of done jobs, from 0 to 100 |
| `finished` | `true` when every job ran, or the batch was cancelled |
| `cancelled` | `true` after `cancel()`, or after a first failure |

A `Batch` shows the state at the time it was read. To read it again, use `Queue.findBatch(id)`. It gives `null` when there is no such batch.

### Cancelling batches

The first job that fails for good cancels the batch. If you want the batch to go on, add `allowFailures()`. You can also cancel a batch yourself with `cancel()`. This does not stop the jobs: they still run and count, so a `Batchable` job should read `cancelled` to skip its work.

### Adding jobs to a batch

`add(jobs)` adds jobs to a batch, for example from a job of the batch. They go on the queue and connection of the batch. It throws a `StateError` when the batch is finished, cancelled or deleted.

### Chains in a batch

Use `chain(jobs)` to put a chain in a batch. Its jobs run one after the other, and the batch counts the chain as one job:

```dart
await Queue.batch(<DoxJob>[ImportUsers()])
    .chain(<DoxJob>[ImportOrders(), SumOrders()])
    .dispatch();
```

When a job of the chain fails for good, the rest of the chain is dropped, and the batch counts one failed job.

### Pruning batches

Old batch rows stay in the table until you delete them. `prune-batches` deletes batches that finished, or were cancelled, more than `--hours` ago (default 24). Add `--unfinished` to also delete batches that never finished and were made more than that many hours ago:

```bash
dart run bin/queue.dart prune-batches --hours=48
dart run bin/queue.dart prune-batches --hours=48 --unfinished=168
```

In code, use `Queue.pruneBatches(before, unfinishedBefore:)`.

## Queue events

Sometimes you want to log or count jobs. Listen to the steps of a job:

```dart
Queue.before((QueueEvent event) => print('start ${event.name} ${event.id}'));
Queue.after((QueueEvent event) => print('done ${event.name}'));
Queue.failing((QueueEvent event) => alert(event.name, event.error));
```

| Hook | When |
| --- | --- |
| `Queue.queued` | `dispatch()` pushed a job |
| `Queue.before` | a worker starts a job |
| `Queue.after` | a worker finished a job and deleted it |
| `Queue.released` | a worker put a job back (`release()` or a retry) |
| `Queue.exceptionOccurred` | `handle()` threw and the job will be tried again |
| `Queue.failing` | a job failed for good |
| `Queue.looping` | a worker is about to take the next job |
| `Queue.stopping` | a worker stops |

Listeners are per isolate. So register them where the app starts, like in a provider. Then the web app and each worker have them. A listener can be async, and a listener that throws is only logged. See [Event details](#event-details) for the fields of `QueueEvent`.

### Batch events

A batch has its own events. In them, `event.batch` is the batch after the step:

```dart
Queue.batchProgress((QueueEvent event) {
  Batch batch = event.batch!;
  print('${batch.name}: ${batch.progress}%');
});
Queue.batchFailed((QueueEvent event) => alert(event.batch!.id, event.error));
```

| Hook | When | Where it fires |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Queue.batchDispatched` | the batch was saved, before its jobs are pushed | the process that called `dispatch()` |
| `Queue.batchProgress` | a job (or a chain) of the batch is done. With `allowFailures()`, also when one failed | the worker that counted it |
| `Queue.batchFailed` | the first job failed for good. `event.error` is its error | the worker that counted it |
| `Queue.batchCancelled` | the batch was cancelled: `cancel()`, the first failure without `allowFailures()`, or a push that threw | the process that cancelled it |
| `Queue.batchFinished` | every job ran, done or failed | the worker that counted the last job |

Each event fires once per step, also with many workers. When one failure cancels the batch, `batchFailed` fires first, then `batchCancelled`.

## Queue connections

Sometimes one app needs more than one queue store. The config is the main connection. Add more in `connections`, by name:

```dart
QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  driver: 'redis',
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  connections: <String, QueueConfig>{
    'database': QueueConfig(driver: 'database'),
  },
);
```

Pick a connection when you dispatch. With no `connection`, the job goes to the main connection. An unknown name throws an `ArgumentError`:

```dart
await SendReport(reportId: 1).dispatch(connection: 'database');
```

Run a worker for each connection. Every command of `bin/queue.dart` takes `--connection`:

```bash
dart run bin/queue.dart work
dart run bin/queue.dart work --connection=database
dart run bin/queue.dart failed --connection=database
```

- An entry uses only `driver`, `redis`, `prefix`, `connection` (the dox_orm one), `retryAfter`, `serializeSync` and `failedAtTimestamp`. The `jobs` of the main config count for all connections.
- The in-process worker (`inProcess`) runs the jobs of the main connection only.
- Two `database` connections on the same dox_orm connection share the `jobs` and `failed_jobs` tables. So give each one its own dox_orm connection.

## Using the queue without Dox

`dox_queue` also works in a plain Dart app. Add `build_runner` and `dox_builder`, so it writes `lib/generated/jobs.g.dart`:

```bash
dart pub add dox_queue dox_core
dart pub add dev:build_runner dev:dox_builder
```

Write your jobs as in [Creating jobs](#creating-jobs), and run `dart run build_runner build`. Then set up the queue and run a worker yourself:

```dart
import 'dart:async';
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';
import 'package:my_app/generated/jobs.g.dart';
import 'package:my_app/jobs/resize_image.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  // the worker logs with the Dox logger, so it needs an AppConfig
  Dox().initialize(AppConfig(appKey: 'not-used'));

  Queue.configure(QueueConfig(
    driver: 'redis',
    jobs: jobRegistry,
    redis: RedisOptions(host: '127.0.0.1', port: 6379),
  ));

  await ResizeImage(path: 'photo.png').dispatch();

  Worker worker = Worker(
    driver: Queue.driver,
    jobs: jobRegistry,
    options: WorkerOptions(queues: <String>['default'], concurrency: 4),
  );

  // Ctrl+C: finish the running jobs, then stop
  StreamSubscription<ProcessSignal> signal =
      ProcessSignal.sigint.watch().listen((_) => worker.stop());
  await worker.run();
  await signal.cancel();
  await Queue.close();
}
```

- `WorkerOptions` takes the same settings as the flags of `work`: `queues`, `concurrency`, `once`, `tries`, `timeout`, `sleep` and `stopWhenEmpty`.
- The `database` driver needs `dox_queue_database`. There are no providers here, so call `QueueDatabase.register()` before `Queue.configure()`. It uses the default `dox_orm` connection, so set that up first with `SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(...)`.
- No services are in the Dox container, so make the services of a job in `handle()`.

## Testing

### Running jobs in tests

Use the `sync` driver. `dispatch()` then runs the job at once, so you can check the result right after:

```dart
import 'package:dox_queue/dox_queue.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/jobs/send_welcome_email.job.dart';
import 'package:my_app/generated/jobs.g.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

void main() {
  setUp(() {
    Queue.configure(QueueConfig(driver: 'sync', jobs: jobRegistry));
  });

  test('sends the welcome email', () async {
    await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).dispatch();
    // check the email was sent
  });
}
```

A job that uses `Dox()` (for example `Dox().ioc` or `Logger`) needs the app config. Call `Dox().initialize(appConfig)` in `setUpAll`.

The sync driver runs the job object as it is. So a job that is not in `jobRegistry`, or a field that is not JSON, works here and fails later in the worker. Set `serializeSync: true` to save the job and read it back before it runs, the way a worker gets it. Then `dispatch()` throws for such a job:

```dart
Queue.configure(
  QueueConfig(driver: 'sync', jobs: jobRegistry, serializeSync: true),
);
```

To test a job alone, call `handle()`:

```dart
await SendWelcomeEmail(userId: 1).handle();
```

### Faking the queue

If you only want to check that your code dispatched a job, without running it, use `Queue.fake()`. It records every `dispatch()` in a list, and needs no `Queue.configure()`:

```dart
late QueueFake queue;

setUp(() {
  queue = Queue.fake();
});

tearDown(Queue.restore);

test('signing up queues the welcome email', () async {
  await signUp(userId: 1);

  queue.assertPushed<SendWelcomeEmail>();
  queue.assertPushed<SendWelcomeEmail>(
    (SendWelcomeEmail job) => job.userId == 1,
  );
  queue.assertPushedTimes<SendWelcomeEmail>(1);
  queue.assertNotPushed<SendInvoice>();
});
```

| Method | Checks |
|---|---|
| `assertPushed<T>([test])` | a `T` job was pushed. With `test`, one of them passes it |
| `assertPushedTimes<T>(n)` | exactly `n` `T` jobs were pushed |
| `assertNotPushed<T>()` | no `T` job was pushed |
| `assertNothingPushed()` | no job was pushed at all |
| `assertChained(<Type>[A, B])` | a chain of exactly these job classes, in this order, was dispatched |
| `assertBatched([test])` | a batch was dispatched. With `test`, one of them passes it. `test` gets a `PendingBatch` |
| `assertBatchedChain(<Type>[A, B])` | a batch has a chain of exactly these job classes, in this order |
| `assertBatchCount(n)` | exactly `n` batches were dispatched |

To read the jobs, use `queue.pushed`. Each item has the `job`, the `queue` name and the `delay`. `queue.jobsOf<T>()` gives the `T` jobs, `queue.clear()` forgets them, and `Queue.restore()` stops the fake.

The fake does not encode the job. So a job that is missing from `QueueConfig.jobs`, or has data that is not JSON, passes a faked test but fails for real.

### Testing the queue itself

To test the real queue, use the `database` driver of `dox_queue_database` with SQLite `:memory:`. Then run a worker that stops when the queue is empty:

```dart
await Worker(
  driver: Queue.driver,
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  options: WorkerOptions(stopWhenEmpty: true),
).run();
```

## Details

This section is for special cases. Most apps do not need it.

### All options

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `driver` | `sync` | `sync`, `database` (needs `dox_queue_database`) or `redis` |
| `jobs` | empty | `jobRegistry` from `lib/generated/jobs.g.dart` |
| `redis` | 127.0.0.1:6379 | `RedisOptions(host: ..., port: ..., password: ...)` for the `redis` driver. `QueueConfig.redisFromEnv()` reads it from the env |
| `prefix` | `dox_queue:` | the start of every Redis key |
| `connection` | default | the dox_orm connection name, for `dox_queue_database` |
| `retryAfter` | 90 seconds | when a worker does not finish a job in this time, another worker can take it |
| `inProcess` | `false` | run a worker inside the web server, see [Running jobs in the web server](#running-jobs-in-the-web-server) |
| `workerQueues` | `['default']` | the queues of the in-process worker |
| `workerConcurrency` | `1` | jobs at once in the in-process worker |
| `workerTimeoutGrace` | none | the `--timeout-grace` wait of the in-process worker |
| `serializeSync` | `false` | the `sync` driver saves the job and reads it back before it runs |
| `connections` | none | more queue connections by name, see [Queue connections](#queue-connections) |
| `afterCommit` | `false` | push jobs that are dispatched inside a transaction only after it commits (needs `dox_queue_database`) |
| `failedAtTimestamp` | `false` | the `failed_at` column is a timestamp, not a number, see [The failed_at column](#the-failed_at-column) |

### Worker flags

| Flag | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--queue=high,default` | `default` | the queues to work. The first one goes first |
| `--concurrency=4` | `1` | jobs at once in this process |
| `--once` | off | run one job, then stop |
| `--tries=3` | `1` | tries of a job that does not set `tries` |
| `--timeout=60` | `60` | max run time in seconds of a job that does not set `timeout` |
| `--sleep=3` | `3` | seconds to wait when the queues are empty |
| `--max-sleep=30` | off | when the queues stay empty, double the sleep on each empty poll, up to this many seconds. A job sets it back to `--sleep` |
| `--stop-when-empty` | off | stop when the queues are empty |
| `--timeout-grace=10` | none | after a timeout, wait up to this many seconds for the old run to end before the next try |
| `--backoff=1,5,10` | none | seconds to wait before each retry of a job that does not set `backoff` |
| `--max-jobs=1000` | off | stop after this many jobs |
| `--max-time=3600` | off | stop after this many seconds |
| `--memory=256` | off | stop when the process uses more than this many MB |
| `--connection=name` | main | the [queue connection](#queue-connections) to use |

With `--max-jobs`, `--max-time` and `--memory`, the worker stops after its running jobs, so let your process manager start it again.

### Worker details

- The worker logs one warning when a job may run longer than `retryAfter` (the `--timeout`, the `timeout` of a job class, and the grace time all count). Then a second worker can take the job while the first one still runs it. Raise `retryAfter` or lower the timeout.
- While the worker waits for `--timeout-grace`, it takes no other job. If `timeout` plus the grace time is above `retryAfter`, another worker can take the job while this one waits.
- When a crashed worker's job has no tries left, it fails with a message that the worker did not finish.
- `restart` writes a time to the app cache, and each worker reads it every 3 seconds.
- With `InteractsWithQueue`, the worker does the call when `handle()` ends. When you call more than one, the last one wins. A call also wins over an error that `handle()` throws after it. When `handle()` times out, the call is dropped.
- With `dispatchSync()`, `dispatchAfterResponse()` and the `sync` driver there is no queue. There `attempts()` is 1, `release()` and `delete()` do nothing, and `fail()` only runs `failed()`.
- In a test file, `package:test` has its own `fail()`. Inside a job class with `InteractsWithQueue`, write `this.fail(...)` to make it clear which one you call.
- Job middleware also runs with the `sync` driver, `dispatchSync()` and `dispatchAfterResponse()`. There is no queue there, so a release logs a warning and `handle()` does not run.
- `dispatchAfterResponse()` works because `QueueProvider` turns on `AfterResponse`. Outside a request, the job runs soon.

### Dispatch after the commit details

- `afterCommit` needs `dox_queue_database`. Without it, a dispatch with `afterCommit` on throws a `StateError`.
- A job that is not in the registry, or data that is not JSON, throws at `dispatch()`, not at the commit.
- When the push fails after the commit, the `QueryBuilder.transaction()` call throws that error. The data stays saved.
- It waits only for a transaction on the default dox_orm connection, opened with no `connection:` name. A transaction opened by name pushes the job at once.
- The `sync` driver runs the job after the commit. A `sync` chain runs as a whole after the commit, and gets a new id.
- A batch saves its `job_batches` row and pushes its jobs after the commit. A rollback drops it all. Before the commit, the returned `Batch` is not saved yet.
- `dispatchSync()` and `dispatchAfterResponse()` do not wait for a commit.
- `Queue.fake()` keeps the job when you call `dispatch()`, also when the transaction later rolls back.
- It works through [`QueryBuilder.afterCommit()`](../database/transactions.md#run-code-after-the-commit) of dox_orm.

### Unique job details

- `clear` frees the locks of the jobs it deletes. `retry` of a failed job does not take the lock.
- `dispatchSync()` ignores uniqueness.
- With `afterCommit` inside a transaction, the lock is taken at the commit. `dispatch()` returns the id at once, also when the job is then skipped.
- `Queue.fake()` keeps its own locks and needs no cache.

### Chain details

- A job that is released or retried keeps the chain. A job that ends with `delete()`, or that a middleware skips, counts as done, so the chain goes on.
- The `sync` driver runs the jobs now, one after the other. When one throws, the catch job runs and `dispatch()` throws the error.
- A `ShouldBeEncrypted` job stays encrypted inside the job before it.
- A skipped [unique job](#unique-jobs) stops the chain, and the catch job runs with a `StateError`. When the first job is skipped, `dispatch()` returns `''` and nothing runs.
- A next job that can not be read, for example because its class was removed, stops the chain. The catch job runs with the error.
- The worker pushes the next job before it deletes the job that is done. So a crash between the two can run the next job twice.
- When the push of the next job fails, the try of the current job counts as failed, and the job is tried again.
- The unique lock of a job is freed before the next job is pushed. So a next job with the same unique id is not skipped.

### Batch details

- A failed job that you retry with `queue:retry` is not counted again when it fails again. When it is done, `pendingJobs` and `failedJobs` both go down by one, so `catchError` can run again on a later failure.
- An empty batch throws an `ArgumentError`, because it would never finish.
- `then` and `whenComplete` run once, also with many workers, because each count changes in one atomic step.
- A skipped [unique job](#unique-jobs) is taken out of the counts. When it was the last open job, `then` and `whenComplete` run. In a chain of a batch, a skipped first job takes the chain out of the counts, and a skipped later job fails the chain.
- When a push fails in `dispatch()` or `add()`, the jobs that were not pushed are taken out of the counts. The batch is cancelled and the error is thrown. The jobs that were pushed still run.
- A job that runs twice, for example when it runs longer than `retryAfter`, can be counted twice. `failedJobs` never goes below 0.
- The batch is marked finished before `then` and `whenComplete` run, so `add()` from a callback throws a `StateError`. `add()` takes jobs only, not chains.
- When a worker crashes after a job is done and before it counted the job, the batch keeps that job as pending, and `then` never runs. Delete such batches with `prune-batches --unfinished`.
- The `sync` driver runs the jobs at `dispatch()` and counts them. A job that throws counts as failed, and `dispatch()` does not throw.
- In `Queue.fake()`, chains are in `queue.chains` and batches in `queue.batches`, and the chains of a batch in `PendingBatch.chains`. Nothing is saved or run. In a faked batch, `add()` adds to the batch, `cancel()` does nothing and `Queue.findBatch()` gives `null`.

### Event details

A listener gets a `QueueEvent`:

| Field | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| `type` | the kind of event |
| `job` | the job. `null` for `looping` and `stopping`, and when the worker can not read the job |
| `name` | the job name of the registry |
| `id` | the job id |
| `queue` | the queue name |
| `attempts` | the try number. `0` for `queued`, `looping` and `stopping` |
| `error`, `stack` | the error and its stack trace, for `exceptionOccurred` and `failing`. `batchFailed` has `error` only |
| `delay` | the wait, for `queued` and `released` |
| `batch` | the `Batch`, for the [batch events](#batch-events). `null` for other events |

- The `sync` driver, `dispatchSync()` and `dispatchAfterResponse()` fire no job events. The `sync` driver does fire the batch events, all in the process that called `dispatch()`.
- `Queue.fake()` fires no events.
- `Queue.forgetListeners()` removes all listeners, for example between tests.

### Fake details

- `dispatchSync()` and `dispatchAfterResponse()` still run the job under the fake. Their jobs are in `queue.dispatchedSync` and `queue.dispatchedAfterResponse`, not in `queue.pushed`.
- `Queue.fake()` keeps the connection name in `PushedJob.connection`.
- The fake also catches `Mail.queue()` on the default queue, but only when `Mail.fake()` is off. It does not catch a custom queue set with `Mail.useQueue()`. See [Mail](mail.md#testing).

### How the drivers store jobs

- Database: jobs are rows in `jobs`, failed jobs are rows in `failed_jobs`. On Postgres, MySQL and MariaDB a worker takes a job with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, so many workers do not wait on each other. On SQLite a worker takes a job with one `UPDATE ... RETURNING`. SQLite runs one write at a time, so this is safe for small apps.
- Redis: each queue has a list of ready jobs, a sorted set of delayed jobs and a sorted set of reserved jobs. A Lua script takes a job, so two workers never get the same one. Failed jobs are in the hash `dox_queue:failed`.
- `failed_jobs.connection` has the name of the [queue connection](#queue-connections), or NULL for the main one. A table without this column works too, but then the name is not saved, and `failed --connection=X` lists all failed jobs of the table. A worker checks for the column once, so restart the workers after you add it:

```dart
await schema.table('failed_jobs', (Table table) {
  table.string('connection').nullable();
});
```

### The failed_at column

`failed_jobs.failed_at` is the time the job failed. By default it is a big integer with unix time in milliseconds. If you want a UTC timestamp, pass `failedAtTimestamp: true` to `QueueTables.up` in the migration, and set it in the queue config too:

```dart
await QueueTables.up(schema, failedAtTimestamp: true);
```

```dart
QueueConfig queueConfig = QueueConfig(
  driver: 'database',
  jobs: jobRegistry,
  failedAtTimestamp: true,
);
```

`FailedJob.failedAt` is the same `DateTime` with both types. Each entry of `connections` has its own `failedAtTimestamp`.

!!! warning "The setting and the column must match"
    A worker reads the column type once, when it first uses `failed_jobs`. If the setting does not match the column, `fail`, `failed`, `retry`, `forget` and `prune-failed` throw a `StateError`, and nothing is written. A job that fails all its tries is NOT moved to `failed_jobs`, and its `failed()` does not run. It stays in `jobs` and runs again after `retryAfter`, until the setting matches.

If the type can not be read (for example, the connection dropped), the worker tries again on the next call. With the setting off, it logs a warning and goes on. With the setting on, the call throws.

| Database | Column | How the time is kept |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SQLite | `TIMESTAMP` | ISO text in UTC, with milliseconds |
| Postgres | `TIMESTAMP` (without time zone) | the UTC time, with milliseconds |
| MySQL, MariaDB | `TIMESTAMP` | whole seconds, in UTC. The queue writes it with `FROM_UNIXTIME()` and reads it with `UNIX_TIMESTAMP()`, so the session time zone does not change the time. A MySQL and MariaDB `TIMESTAMP` can not hold a time after 2038-01-19 |

To change an existing integer column to a timestamp:

1. Stop all workers, on every server. Stop the app too when it has `inProcess: true`. A worker that still runs writes numbers into the timestamp column, and on SQLite this gives no error.
2. Run the SQL for your database below, in a new migration (`await schema.driver.execute('...');` for each line) or in a database client.
3. Set `failedAtTimestamp: true` in the queue config.
4. Start the workers again.

SQLite (3.35 or newer). The new column allows NULL, because SQLite can not add a NOT NULL column without a default. The queue never writes NULL there:

```sql
ALTER TABLE failed_jobs ADD COLUMN failed_at_utc TIMESTAMP;
UPDATE failed_jobs SET failed_at_utc = strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%fZ', failed_at / 1000.0, 'unixepoch');
ALTER TABLE failed_jobs DROP COLUMN failed_at;
ALTER TABLE failed_jobs RENAME COLUMN failed_at_utc TO failed_at;
```

Postgres:

```sql
ALTER TABLE failed_jobs ALTER COLUMN failed_at TYPE TIMESTAMP USING to_timestamp(failed_at / 1000.0) AT TIME ZONE 'UTC';
```

MySQL and MariaDB:

```sql
ALTER TABLE failed_jobs ADD COLUMN failed_at_utc TIMESTAMP NULL;
UPDATE failed_jobs SET failed_at_utc = FROM_UNIXTIME(failed_at DIV 1000);
ALTER TABLE failed_jobs DROP COLUMN failed_at;
ALTER TABLE failed_jobs CHANGE failed_at_utc failed_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL;
```


---

# Mail

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/mail/

# Mail

The `dox_mailer` package sends email from your app with SMTP, Amazon SES, Azure, Resend, Mailgun, Postmark or sendmail.

You write a `Message` and call `Mail.send()`, and a transport sends it. You pick the transport in a config file, so you can change providers with no code change. Slow emails can go through the [queue](queue.md), so the request does not wait.

## Install

Add the package with the `dox` CLI. Add `--transport=smtp` (or `resend`, `mailgun`, `postmark`, `ses`) to pick a transport. `log` is the default:

```bash
dox add mailer
```

It adds the package, writes the mail config and the provider, and adds `MAIL_MAILER`, `MAIL_FROM` and the keys of the transport to `.env`. If the app has `dox_view`, it also makes the `resources/views/emails` folder. It never overwrites a file, so it is safe to run twice.

If you want to set it up by hand, add the package and write the two files below yourself:

```bash
dart pub add dox_mailer
```

## Setup

### Configuration

A mailer is a name and a transport. `defaultMailer` is the one that `Mail.send()` uses:

```dart title="lib/config/mail.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';

MailConfig mailConfig = MailConfig(
  /// the mailer of Mail.send()
  defaultMailer: Env.get('MAIL_MAILER', 'log'),

  /// for messages with no from address
  from: Address(Env.get('MAIL_FROM', 'hello@example.com'), 'My app'),

  mailers: <String, Transport>{
    'smtp': SmtpTransport(
      host: Env.get('MAIL_HOST', 'localhost'),
      port: Env.get<int>('MAIL_PORT', 587),
      username: Env.get<String?>('MAIL_USERNAME'),
      password: Env.get<String?>('MAIL_PASSWORD'),
    ),

    /// prints emails, sends nothing
    'log': LogTransport(),
  },
);
```

`Env.get()` reads the `.env` file and the real environment. You can also add the keys to the `AppEnv` class of your app and use `env.mailHost`.

```bash title=".env"
MAIL_MAILER=smtp
MAIL_FROM=hello@example.com
MAIL_HOST=smtp.example.com
MAIL_PORT=587
MAIL_USERNAME=me
MAIL_PASSWORD=secret
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `defaultMailer` | `log` | the mailer of `Mail.send()` |
| `mailers` | a `log` mailer | each mailer name and its transport |
| `from` | none | the from address of a message that has none |
| `replyTo` | none | the reply-to addresses of a message that has none |

### The mail provider

The provider sets up the mailers in every isolate. Put it in `lib/providers/`, so the generated container finds it:

```dart title="lib/providers/mail_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';

import '../config/mail.dart';

/// Sets up the mailers. Dox finds every DoxProvider class,
/// see lib/generated/container.g.dart.
class AppMailProvider extends MailProvider {
  AppMailProvider() : super(mailConfig);
}
```

When the server stops, the provider closes open SMTP connections and HTTP clients.

## Sending mail

Make a `Message` and pass it to `Mail.send()`:

```dart
import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';

await Mail.send(
  Message(
    to: <Address>[Address('ann@example.com', 'Ann Lee')],
    subject: 'Welcome',
    text: 'Hello Ann, welcome!',
    html: '<p>Hello Ann, <b>welcome</b>!</p>',
  ),
);
```

A message needs a from address, at least one recipient, and a text or HTML body. If the message can not be sent, `send()` throws a `MailException`. It has the `statusCode` and the `body` of the server's answer.

### Using another mailer

If you want to send with a mailer that is not the default, use `Mail.mailer()`:

```dart
await Mail.mailer('ses').send(message);
```

### Short ways to send

For a quick plain text email, use `Mail.raw()`:

```dart
await Mail.raw('Your code is 1234', to: 'ann@example.com', subject: 'Your code');
```

`Mail.to()` starts an email with chained calls. `to()`, `cc()` and `bcc()` take an `Address`, an email text, or a list of these. `send()` takes a [mailable](#mailables), and the recipients are added to the ones of the mailable:

```dart
await Mail.to('ann@example.com')
    .cc('Bob Lee <bob@example.com>')
    .bcc(<String>['audit@example.com'])
    .send(WelcomeMail(user));
```

`queue()` and `later()` work here too, like `Mail.to(email).queue(WelcomeMail(user))`.

### The message

| Field | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `from` | an `Address`. Null: `MailConfig.from` |
| `to`, `cc`, `bcc` | lists of `Address` |
| `replyTo` | a list of `Address` |
| `subject` | text |
| `text` | the plain text body |
| `html` | the HTML body |
| `attachments` | a list of `Attachment` |
| `headers` | extra headers, like `{'X-Campaign': 'fall'}` |
| `tags` | tags for the reports of the provider |
| `metadata` | key and value data for the provider, like `{'user_id': '42'}` |

An `Address` is an email and an optional name. You can also read one from text:

```dart
Address('ann@example.com', 'Ann');
Address.parse('Ann <ann@example.com>');
```

`Address.list()` reads many addresses. One text is one address, so pass a list for more:

```dart
Message(to: Address.list(<String>['ann@example.com', 'bob@example.com']), ...)
```

### Attachments

Add files with `attachments`. The content type comes from the file extension, or you can pass `contentType`:

```dart
Message(
  to: <Address>[Address('ann@example.com')],
  subject: 'Your invoice',
  text: 'The invoice is attached.',
  attachments: <Attachment>[
    Attachment(pdfBytes, 'invoice.pdf'),
    Attachment.fromFile('storage/terms.pdf'),
  ],
);
```

To attach a file from a storage disk, like S3, read its bytes first. This works with every disk:

```dart
Uint8List? pdf = await Storage().disk('s3').get('invoices/42.pdf');
Attachment(pdf!, 'invoice.pdf');
```

### Inline images

To show an image inside the HTML, give the file a `cid` and use it with `cid:`:

```dart
Message(
  to: <Address>[Address('ann@example.com')],
  subject: 'Hello',
  html: '<img src="cid:logo.png"> Hello!',
  attachments: <Attachment>[
    Attachment.fromFile('assets/logo.png', cid: 'logo.png'),
  ],
);
```

Mailgun uses the file name as the cid. So for Mailgun, use a cid with the file extension, like `logo.png`.

### HTML from a view

With [views](../the-basic/views.md), you can render a template to HTML:

```dart
String html = View.render('emails/welcome', <String, dynamic>{'name': 'Ann'});
await Mail.send(Message(to: to, subject: 'Welcome', html: html));
```

## Mailables

A mailable is one kind of email in its own class, for example the welcome email. It keeps the address, the subject, the template and the data in one place.

To make one, run `dox make:mail`. It writes `lib/app/mail/welcome_mail.dart` and the view `resources/views/emails/welcome.dox.html`. Add `--no-view` for a mail with a plain text body. See [`dox make:mail`](../reference/cli.md#dox-makemail).

```bash
dox make:mail Welcome
```

Override the getters you need:

```dart
class WelcomeMail extends Mailable {
  WelcomeMail(this.user);

  final User user;

  @override
  List<Address> get to => <Address>[Address(user.email, user.name)];

  @override
  String get subject => 'Welcome';

  @override
  String? get view => 'emails/welcome';

  @override
  Map<String, Object?> get data => <String, Object?>{'name': user.name};
}
```

| Getter | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `to`, `cc`, `bcc`, `replyTo` | the addresses |
| `from` | the sender. Null: the `from` of the mail config |
| `subject` | the subject |
| `html`, `text` | the body as text, when there is no template |
| `view` | a [dox_view](../the-basic/views.md) template for the HTML body |
| `textView` | a dox_view template for the plain text body |
| `markdown` | a dox_view template with Markdown, see [Markdown mail](#markdown-mail) |
| `data` | the variables of the templates |
| `attachments` | the files |
| `mailer` | the mailer name, eg. `ses`. Null: the default mailer |

### Sending a mailable

Call `send()` on the mailable, or put it on the queue with `queue()` or `later()`:

```dart
await WelcomeMail(user).send();
await WelcomeMail(user).queue();
await WelcomeMail(user).later(Duration(minutes: 10));
```

`queue()` and `later()` render the templates at once, so the worker sends the finished email. They take the same options as [`Mail.queue()`](#queue-an-email).

### Changing the message

`toMessage()` gives the email as a `Message`. If you want to set more, like headers or tags, override it:

```dart
@override
Message toMessage() {
  return super.toMessage().copyWith(tags: <String>['welcome']);
}
```

### Markdown mail

You can write the email in Markdown. From one template you get a simple HTML email with a layout (a white card on a grey page) and a plain text part. The Markdown is CommonMark with tables.

```markdown title="resources/views/emails/welcome.dox.html"
# Hi {{ name }}

Thanks for joining. Here is what you can do next:

- Fill in your profile
- Invite your team

[Open your profile]({{ profileUrl }})

<a href="https://example.com/dashboard" class="button">Open the app</a>
```

Then point the `markdown` getter to it:

```dart
@override
String? get markdown => 'emails/welcome';
```

`<a class="button">` shows as a button. In the text body it stays an `<a>` tag, so the link is still there.

Do not indent the Markdown inside `@if` or `@each`, because Markdown makes a line that starts with 4 spaces into a code block.

`{{ }}` escapes HTML and Markdown, so a user's name like `[click](https://evil.example)` shows as text and does not become a link. Links with an unsafe URL, like `javascript:`, lose their URL. Raw HTML in the template, like `<a href="{{ url }}">`, is not checked, so only put full URLs that your app builds there. For links, write `[text]({{ url }})` instead. To put Markdown from a value into the email, pass a `SafeString`.

### Custom layout

To use your own look, override `layout()`. It gets the HTML of the Markdown and returns the full page. Put it in a base class to use it for all your mailables:

```dart
import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';
import 'package:dox_view/dox_view.dart'; // View, SafeString

abstract class AppMail extends Mailable {
  @override
  String layout(String body) {
    return View.render('emails/layout', <String, Object?>{'body': SafeString(body)});
  }
}
```

### A simple email with no template

Sometimes you only need a few lines and a button. `MailMessage` is a mailable for this. It needs no template and uses the Markdown layout:

```dart
await (MailMessage(subject: 'Invoice paid', to: <Address>[Address('ann@example.com')])
      ..line('We got your payment.')
      ..action('View invoice', 'https://example.com/invoices/1')
      ..line('Thank you!'))
    .send();
```

- `cc:` in the constructor adds cc addresses.
- `attach(Attachment(...))` adds a file.
- `error()` makes the buttons red, for a message about a problem.
- The email starts with `greeting` (default `Hello!`) and ends with `salutation` (default none). Set them to null to leave them out.

Lines can use Markdown, like `**bold**`. HTML in a line shows as text. `action()` throws an `ArgumentError` for an unsafe URL.

To send one email on more than one channel, see [Notifications](notifications.md).

## Queue an email

Sending an email can take a second or more. With a queue, the request does not wait, because a queue worker sends the email later:

```dart
await Mail.queue(message);
```

To send it later, use `Mail.later()`. Both methods return the job id:

```dart
await Mail.later(Duration(minutes: 10), message);
```

You can pick another mailer and another queue:

```dart
await Mail.mailer('ses').queue(message, queue: 'emails');
```

This uses [dox_queue](queue.md), so you need its `QueueProvider` and a worker. The mail jobs come with dox_mailer, and `build_runner` adds them to `lib/generated/jobs.g.dart`. The worker (`bin/queue.dart`) must run your `MailProvider` too, because the job sends with your mail config. Without it, the job fails with "Mail is not set up".

The message is checked at once, so a bad message fails in the request and not in the worker. The worker sends with the same mailer you picked.

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `queue` | `default` | the queue name |
| `encrypt` | `false` | save the job data encrypted with the app key. The worker needs the same key |

The whole email, with every attachment, is saved in Redis or in the `jobs` table. So keep attachments small, a few MB at most. For a big file, write your own job that saves the file path, and build the email in `handle()`.

An email has personal data. If other people can read Redis or the `jobs` table, use `encrypt: true`.

## Transports

### SMTP

```dart
'smtp': SmtpTransport(
  host: 'smtp.example.com',
  port: 587,
  username: Env.get('MAIL_USERNAME'),
  password: Env.get('MAIL_PASSWORD'),
  encryption: SmtpEncryption.starttls,
),
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `host` | required | the server |
| `port` | 465 for `tls`, 587 for `starttls`, 25 for `none` | the port |
| `username`, `password` | none | the login. No username: no login |
| `encryption` | `starttls` | `none`, `starttls` (switch to TLS after connect) or `tls` (TLS from the start) |
| `allowInsecure` | `false` | accept a self-signed TLS certificate. Only for test servers |
| `auth` | PLAIN, or LOGIN when the server has no PLAIN | `SmtpAuth.plain`, `SmtpAuth.login` or `SmtpAuth.xoauth2` |
| `localDomain` | `localhost` | the name of this machine, for `EHLO` |
| `timeout` | 30 seconds | the time to connect, and to wait for each reply |
| `keepAlive` | `false` | keep the connection open for the next message |

With `starttls`, the send fails if the server does not offer STARTTLS, so your password is never sent in plain text by mistake.

For Gmail or Outlook with OAuth 2, use `auth: SmtpAuth.xoauth2`. The `username` is the email and the `password` is the access token.

If you send many emails, use `keepAlive: true`, so one connection sends them one by one.

For local work, [Mailpit](https://mailpit.axllent.org) catches all emails:

```dart
'mailpit': SmtpTransport(
  host: 'localhost',
  port: 1025,
  encryption: SmtpEncryption.none,
),
```

### Amazon SES

There are two classes, and both send the same MIME message with attachments and inline images. `SesTransport` uses SES API v1 (`SendRawEmail`), and `SesV2Transport` uses SES API v2 (`SendEmail` with raw content):

```dart
'ses': SesV2Transport(
  key: Env.get('AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID'),
  secret: Env.get('AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY'),
  region: Env.get('AWS_REGION', 'us-east-1'),
),
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `key` | required | the AWS access key id |
| `secret` | required | the AWS secret access key |
| `sessionToken` | none | for temporary keys, eg. from a role |
| `region` | `us-east-1` | the AWS region of SES |
| `configurationSet` | none | the SES configuration set, to track events |
| `endpoint` | `https://email.<region>.amazonaws.com/` | another API address |

No AWS SDK is needed.

### Azure Communication Services

```dart
'azure': AzureTransport(
  endpoint: 'https://my-app.europe.communication.azure.com',
  accessKey: Env.get('AZURE_EMAIL_KEY'),
),
```

Or use the connection string of the Azure portal:

```dart
'azure': AzureTransport.fromConnectionString(
  Env.get('AZURE_EMAIL_CONNECTION_STRING'),
),
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `endpoint` | required | the address of your resource |
| `accessKey` | required | the access key of the resource |
| `apiVersion` | `2023-03-31` | the API version |
| `disableTracking` | `false` | turn off open and click tracking |

Inline images need a newer `apiVersion` that supports them.

### Resend

```dart
'resend': ResendTransport(apiKey: Env.get('RESEND_API_KEY')),
```

### Mailgun

```dart
'mailgun': MailgunTransport(
  apiKey: Env.get('MAILGUN_API_KEY'),
  domain: 'mg.example.com',
  region: MailgunRegion.eu,
),
```

`region` is `MailgunRegion.us` (the default) or `MailgunRegion.eu`. Use the region of your Mailgun domain.

### Postmark

```dart
'postmark': PostmarkTransport(
  serverToken: Env.get('POSTMARK_TOKEN'),
  messageStream: 'outbound',
),
```

`messageStream` is optional. Without it, Postmark uses the default stream of the server.

### sendmail

This sends with the `sendmail` program of the server (Postfix, Exim, msmtp and others):

```dart
'sendmail': SendmailTransport(
  path: '/usr/sbin/sendmail',
  mode: SendmailMode.smtp,
),
```

| Mode | Command | How it works |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `SendmailMode.smtp` (default) | `sendmail -bs` | speaks SMTP on stdin and stdout |
| `SendmailMode.pipe` | `sendmail -t -i` | pipes the message in. sendmail reads the recipients from the headers |

### Log

The log transport prints each email and sends nothing, so it is good for local work:

```dart
'log': LogTransport(),
```

Pass `output` to print somewhere else, eg. `LogTransport(output: stderr.writeln)` (from `dart:io`). To show both the text and the HTML body, set `bothBodies: true`. When it is off, only the text body is shown:

```dart
'log': LogTransport(bothBodies: true),
```

### Array

The array transport keeps each email in a list and sends nothing. See [Testing](#testing).

```dart
'array': ArrayTransport(),
```

### Failover

If one provider is down, you may want to try another. `FailoverTransport` tries each transport in order, until one sends the email. If every transport fails, it throws the error of the last one:

```dart
SesV2Transport ses = SesV2Transport(key: '...', secret: '...');
SmtpTransport smtp = SmtpTransport(host: 'smtp.example.com');

MailConfig mailConfig = MailConfig(
  defaultMailer: 'main',
  mailers: <String, Transport>{
    'main': FailoverTransport(<Transport>[ses, smtp]),
  },
);
```

To see why the first ones failed, pass `onError`. It gets the error of each transport that fails.

## Tags and metadata

Each provider has its own way to group and mark emails. This is what each transport does with `tags` and `metadata`:

| Transport | `tags` | `metadata` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SES | not used | message tags |
| Resend | tags with the value `true` | tags |
| Mailgun | `o:tag` | variables (`v:name`) |
| Postmark | the first tag | metadata |
| Azure, SMTP, sendmail | not used | not used |

For SMTP and sendmail, use `headers` instead.

## Hooks

Sometimes you want to run code before or after each email is sent, for example to log it. Use `Mail.onSending` and `Mail.onSent`.

Each isolate has its own hooks, also the queue worker. So add them in `setup()` of your mail provider, after `super.setup()`. A hook added in `main()` does not reach queued emails.

```dart
class AppMailProvider extends MailProvider {
  AppMailProvider() : super(mailConfig);

  @override
  void setup() {
    super.setup();
    Mail.clearHooks(); // a second setup() does not add each hook twice
    Mail.onSending((Message message) {
      print('sending "${message.subject}" to ${message.to}');
    });
    Mail.onSent((SentMessage sent) {
      print('sent ${sent.messageId}');
    });
  }
}
```

Hooks run for every mailer, for queued emails and with `Mail.fake()`. If an `onSending` hook throws, the email is not sent and `send()` throws that error. If an `onSent` hook throws, the error is only logged, because the email is already sent.

## Sending all mail to one address

On a staging server, you want every email to go to your own inbox, so real users get nothing. Use `Mail.alwaysTo()`. Like hooks, call it in `setup()` of your mail provider, so every isolate gets it:

```dart
class AppMailProvider extends MailProvider {
  AppMailProvider() : super(mailConfig);

  @override
  void setup() {
    super.setup();
    if (Env.get<String>('APP_ENV') == 'staging') {
      Mail.alwaysTo('qa@example.com');
    }
  }
}
```

The `to` of each email becomes that address, and `cc` and `bcc` are cleared. This counts for queued emails too. `Mail.alwaysTo(null)` turns it off.

## Custom transports

If your provider is not in the list, extend `Transport` and add it to `mailers`:

```dart
class MyApiTransport extends Transport {
  @override
  Future<SentMessage> send(Message message) async {
    // call your API here
    return SentMessage(message, messageId: 'id from the API');
  }
}
```

The message is already checked, and has a from address, when it gets to `send()`. For a provider that takes raw MIME, `MimeBuilder().build(message)` gives the MIME text.

## Without Dox

`dox_mailer` also works on its own. Call `Mail.configure()` once at start, and `Mail.close()` at the end. The rest of this page works the same way:

```dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  Map<String, String> env = Platform.environment;

  Mail.configure(MailConfig(
    defaultMailer: 'smtp',
    from: Address('hello@example.com', 'My app'),
    mailers: <String, Transport>{
      'smtp': SmtpTransport(
        host: env['MAIL_HOST'] ?? 'localhost',
        username: env['MAIL_USERNAME'],
        password: env['MAIL_PASSWORD'],
      ),
    },
  ));

  await Mail.send(Message(
    to: <Address>[Address('ann@example.com')],
    subject: 'Hello',
    text: 'Hello Ann!',
  ));

  // closes open SMTP connections and HTTP clients
  await Mail.close();
}
```

## Testing

`Mail.fake()` sends every mailer to one `ArrayTransport`, so nothing goes out. Then you check what was sent:

```dart
import 'package:dox_mailer/dox_mailer.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

void main() {
  late ArrayTransport mail;

  setUp(() {
    mail = Mail.fake();
  });

  tearDown(() {
    Mail.restore();
  });

  test('sign up sends a welcome email', () async {
    await signUp('ann@example.com');

    expect(mail.messages, hasLength(1));
    Message message = mail.messages.single;
    expect(message.to.single.email, 'ann@example.com');
    expect(message.subject, 'Welcome');
  });
}
```

The fake works with or without a config, and it stays on when `MailProvider` sets up the config again.

### Testing queued mail

The fake also catches queued emails: `Mail.queue()`, `Mail.later()`, the `queue()` and `later()` of a mailable, and notifications with `shouldQueue`. They go to `mail.queued`, not to the job queue, so you need no queue setup:

```dart
await Mail.queue(message);

mail.assertQueued((Message m) => m.subject == 'Welcome');
mail.assertNothingSent();
```

Each item in `mail.queued` is a `QueuedMessage` with `mailer`, `message`, `id`, `delay`, `queue` and `encrypt`.

### Assertions

| Method | Checks |
|---|---|
| `assertSent([test])` | an email was sent. With `test`, one of them passes it |
| `assertSentCount(count, [test])` | exactly `count` emails were sent. With `test`, `count` emails pass it |
| `assertNotSent(test)` | no sent email passes `test` |
| `assertNothingSent()` | no email was sent |
| `assertQueued([test])` | an email was queued. With `test`, one of them passes it |
| `assertNotQueued(test)` | no queued email passes `test` |
| `assertNothingQueued()` | no email was queued |

`test` is a `bool Function(Message)`. A failed check throws a `StateError`. `mail.clear()` forgets the sent and the queued emails, and `Mail.restore()` stops the fake.

## Details

This section is for special cases. Most apps do not need it.

### Sending

- `send()` gives a `SentMessage`. Its `messageId` is the id of the provider, or the `Message-ID` header for SMTP and sendmail.
- A subject or header with a line break is an error, so user input can not add headers. `FailoverTransport` throws this `MailException` at once, and no transport tries it.
- In `FailoverTransport`, an error thrown by `onError` is ignored and the next transport is still tried. An `async` `onError` is not awaited.
- `{{ }}` in a template escapes HTML. In the plain text body of `textView` and `markdown`, the escape is undone, so `Tom & Jerry` stays `Tom & Jerry`.
- With `keepAlive: true`, if the server closed the connection, the next send opens a new one.
- SES requests are signed with AWS Signature Version 4. Azure requests are signed with the access key (HMAC-SHA256).
- The package has its own SMTP client, AWS signer and MIME builder.

### Markdown safety

- The escaped characters are backslash, backtick, `*`, `[`, `]`, `#` and `|`. A `_` is not changed, so `_word_` can still be italic. In `@if`, a value with one of these characters is not equal to the same text written in the template.
- Escaping covers text values in `data`, in its maps, lists and sets, and in objects with `toJson()`. Values from `View.global()` and from functions are not changed.
- Only `http`, `https`, `mailto`, `tel`, `cid` and relative URLs are kept. The same check runs on the lines of `MailMessage`. Email apps can not open a relative link like `/dashboard`, so use full URLs.
- `[text]({{ url }})` and `<{{ url }}>` keep the URL as it is, with `&` and `%XX`. Entity text inside a URL is decoded, so `?q=&lt;b&gt;` reaches the browser as `?q=<b>`.
- A bare URL does not become a link, but most email apps make it a link anyway.

### Queue

- The default from and reply-to addresses are added when the email is queued.
- The worker flags `--tries` and `--timeout` work for queued emails, like for other jobs.
- With the `sync` queue driver, the email is sent at once, and `later()` does not wait.
- Attachments are saved as base64, so they take about 4/3 of their size. MySQL and MariaDB refuse a job bigger than `max_allowed_packet` (by default 64 MB in MySQL 8, 16 MB in MariaDB). Redis keeps every job in memory.
- With `encrypt: true`, a send error is encrypted too. The plain text of the error is only its type and code, like `RedactedMailError: MailException (code 550). Details are encrypted: ...`. The encrypted part holds at most the first 64K characters (UTF-16 code units). To read it, take a `FailedJob` from `Queue.driver.failed()` and call `RedactedMailError.decrypt(job.error)`. It works with the app key or any key in `AppConfig.previousKeys`.
- To use another queue than dox_queue, call `Mail.useQueue(queue)`. `null` goes back to the dox_queue queue.

### Hooks

- If an `onSent` hook throws, a queue worker does not try the job again, so the email is not sent twice. The other `onSent` hooks still run.
- `Mail.clearHooks()` removes all hooks. Call it first in `setup()`, and in tests.


---

# Notifications

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/notifications/

# Notifications

A notification tells a user about something, like "your invoice is paid", by email or by any channel you write.

One notification can go out on more than one channel, like email, a database table or SMS. Each notification is a class, so the text and the channels live in one place.

Notifications are in the `dox_mailer` package. Set up [mail](mail.md) first.

## Creating notifications

A notification extends `Notification`. The `via` method picks the channels, and `toMail` builds the email:

```dart
class InvoicePaid extends Notification {
  InvoicePaid(this.invoiceId);

  final int invoiceId;

  @override
  List<NotificationChannel> via(Object notifiable) {
    return <NotificationChannel>[const MailChannel()];
  }

  @override
  Mailable toMail(Object notifiable) {
    return MailMessage(subject: 'Invoice paid')
      ..line('We got your payment.')
      ..action('View invoice', 'https://example.com/invoices/$invoiceId');
  }
}
```

`toMail()` can return any mailable, so a `WelcomeMail` with a template works too.

## Sending notifications

### Making a model notifiable

The class that gets notifications, usually the user model, needs the `Notifiable` mixin. Its `routeNotificationFor` method tells each channel where to send. For the `mail` channel, it returns the email address:

```dart
class User extends Model<User> with Notifiable {
  @override
  Object? routeNotificationFor(String channel) {
    return channel == 'mail' ? Address(email!, name) : null;
  }
}
```

The mail route can be an `Address`, an email text like `Ann <ann@example.com>`, or a list of these. If the mailable has its own `to` address, that address is used and the route is not.

### Sending to one user

Call `notify` on the model:

```dart
await user.notify(InvoicePaid(1));
```

### Sending to many users

Use `Notification.send` with a list:

```dart
await Notification.send(users, InvoicePaid(1));
```

### Sending to an address with no user

Sometimes the person has no user row, like a guest. Pass an `Address`:

```dart
await Notification.send(<Object>[Address('ann@example.com')], InvoicePaid(1));
```

## Handling errors

If one channel throws, the other channels and the other notifiables still get the notification. At the end, `Notification.send()` throws a `NotificationException`. Its `errors` list says which notifiable and channel failed, and why.

The error text of a `NotificationException` has no email addresses and no error messages, so it is safe for logs. Read `errors` for the details.

With one notifiable and one error, like in `user.notify()`, the error is thrown as it is. So `on MailException catch (e)` still works there.

## Queueing notifications

Sending an email can be slow, so you may want to send it in the background. Override `shouldQueue`. The mail channel then puts the email on the job queue, like `Mail.queue()`. This needs [a queue](queue.md):

```dart
@override
bool get shouldQueue => true;
```

The email is rendered at once, and the worker sends the finished email.

You can set the queue options with these getters. They work like the options of `Mail.queue()`:

| Getter | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `queue` | null (`default`) | the queue name |
| `delay` | null | the worker sends the email after this wait |
| `encrypt` | `false` | save the job data encrypted with the app key |

`shouldQueue` and these options only change the mail channel. Your own channels still run at once. To queue them, dispatch a job in the channel.

## Custom channels

If you want to send a notification another way, like to a database table, write your own channel. A channel implements `NotificationChannel`. It gets the data of the notification from `toArray()`:

```dart
import 'dart:convert';

class DatabaseChannel implements NotificationChannel {
  @override
  Future<void> send(Object notifiable, Notification notification) async {
    // only a user has a row. An Address or an email text has none.
    if (notifiable is! User) return;
    AppNotification row = AppNotification()
      ..userId = notifiable.id
      ..data = jsonEncode(notification.toArray(notifiable));
    await row.save();
  }
}
```

Then add the channel to `via()`, and give the data in `toArray()`:

```dart
class InvoicePaid extends Notification {
  @override
  List<NotificationChannel> via(Object notifiable) {
    return <NotificationChannel>[const MailChannel(), DatabaseChannel()];
  }

  @override
  Map<String, Object?> toArray(Object notifiable) {
    return <String, Object?>{'type': 'invoice_paid', 'invoice_id': invoiceId};
  }

  // ...
}
```

`dox_mailer` has no database channel of its own, so it does not need the ORM.

## Testing

`Mail.fake()` also catches the emails of the mail channel:

```dart
ArrayTransport mail = Mail.fake();
await user.notify(InvoicePaid(1));
expect(mail.messages.single.subject, 'Invoice paid');
```

With `shouldQueue`, the email goes to `mail.queued`, not to `mail.messages`, and it does not reach the job queue. Check it with `mail.assertQueued()`. See [Mail](mail.md#testing).

## Details

- Each item of `NotificationException.errors` has the notifiable and the channel. When `via()` throws, the channel is null. The error text has one line per failure: the place and the type of the notifiable, the channel, and the error type.
- When `shouldQueue` is false, the queue options do nothing.


---

# Broadcasting

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/broadcasting/

# Broadcasting

Broadcasting sends server events to browsers and apps over Socket.IO, on public, private and presence channels.

Many apps need live pages: an order status that changes, a chat, or a list of who is online. With broadcasting, a client subscribes to a channel, your code sends an event to the channel, and every client in it gets the event. You do not need to poll the server.

Broadcasting is part of the `dox_socketio` package. It is off by default.

## Setup

Do the [Socket.IO setup](../packages/socketio.md#in-a-dox-app) first. Then turn on broadcasting in the config:

```dart title="lib/config/socketio.dart"
SocketIoConfig socketIoConfig = SocketIoConfig(
  broadcasting: true,
  namespaces: <NamespaceHandler>[ChatNamespace()],
);
```

### Channel rules

Private and presence channels need a rule that says who may join. Rules are kept per isolate, so add them where every isolate runs them. A provider is a good place:

```dart title="lib/providers/broadcast_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_socketio/dox_socketio.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

class BroadcastProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Broadcast.channel('orders.{id}', (Object? user, String id) {
      return (user as User).id.toString() == id;
    });
  }
}
```

Run `dart run build_runner build`, so the generated container finds the provider. Without it, no rule is added, and every private subscribe gets `Forbidden`. See [Authorizing channels](#authorizing-channels) for how rules work.

### The auth route

A client that has not logged in its socket gets a token from the auth route. Add the route with your own auth middleware:

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
@override
void register() {
  Broadcast.routes(middleware: <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware()]); // POST /api/broadcasting/auth
}
```

The router prefix is added to the path. This router has the prefix `api`, so the path is `/api/broadcasting/auth`. Pass `path:` to use another path.

The route runs the channel rule with `req.auth`, and answers `{"auth": "<token>"}` or `403`. The token is signed with a key made from `APP_KEY`, so broadcasting needs `APP_KEY`. A token works for one socket, one channel and one minute.

## Channel types

There are three kinds of channels:

| Channel | Name | Who can subscribe |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Channel('news')` | `news` | any client |
| `PrivateChannel('orders.5')` | `private-orders.5` | a client that passes the rule |
| `PresenceChannel('chat.lobby')` | `presence-chat.lobby` | a client that passes the rule. Members see each other |

## Defining broadcast events

An event is a class with the `ShouldBroadcast` mixin:

```dart
class OrderShipped with ShouldBroadcast {
  OrderShipped(this.order);
  final Order order;

  @override
  List<Channel> broadcastOn() => <Channel>[PrivateChannel('orders.${order.id}')];

  @override
  String broadcastAs() => 'order.shipped'; // default: the class name

  @override
  Map<String, Object?> broadcastWith() => <String, Object?>{'id': order.id};
}
```

- `broadcastOn` gives the channels. It is required.
- `broadcastAs` gives the event name. The default is the class name.
- `broadcastWith` gives the payload. It must be JSON. The default is an empty map.

Do not give an event a name that starts with `client-`, because that prefix is for [client events](#client-events).

## Authorizing channels

`Broadcast.channel(pattern, rule)` adds a rule for private and presence channels. The pattern has no `private-` or `presence-` prefix. A `{name}` part matches any text with no dot.

The rule gets the user, then one string for each `{name}` part. It can be async.

- A private rule returns `true` to allow. Anything else refuses.
- A presence rule returns a map with the member info, with an `id`. Anything else refuses.
- A rule that throws refuses, and the error goes to stderr.

This presence rule lets any logged in user join a chat room:

```dart
Broadcast.channel('chat.{room}', (Object? user, String room) {
  User u = user as User;
  return <String, Object?>{'id': u.id, 'name': u.name};
});
```

One rule serves both kinds, so `orders.{id}` checks `private-orders.1` and `presence-orders.1`. When more than one pattern matches, the first one added wins.

## Broadcasting events

Use `broadcast` to send an event. `Broadcast.event` does the same:

```dart
await broadcast(OrderShipped(order));
await Broadcast.event(OrderShipped(order)); // the same
```

### Only to others

Sometimes the user who made a change should not get the event again, because their page already shows it. Use `toOthers` to skip their socket. The client sends its socket id in the `X-Socket-ID` header, and `Broadcast.socketId(req)` reads it:

```dart
await Broadcast.event(OrderShipped(order), toOthers: Broadcast.socketId(req));
```

## Receiving broadcasts

On the client, use `socket.io-client`. A public channel needs no token.

Subscribe inside the `connect` handler. A subscription belongs to one socket, and after a reconnect the client has a new socket with no channels. The `connect` handler runs again after each reconnect, so it subscribes again:

```js
import { io } from 'socket.io-client';

const socket = io('https://app.example.com', { transports: ['websocket'] });

socket.on('order.shipped', (channel, payload) => console.log(channel, payload));
socket.on('connect', () => {
  socket.emit('subscribe', { channel: 'news' }, (ack) => console.log(ack));
});
```

Events arrive as `(channel, payload)`, under the name from `broadcastAs`.

### Private and presence channels

For a private or presence channel, get a token from the auth route first, then send it in `subscribe`. A token works for one socket id only, so ask for a new one in the `connect` handler:

```js
socket.on('connect', async () => {
  const res = await fetch('/api/broadcasting/auth', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json', authorization: `Bearer ${apiToken}` },
    body: JSON.stringify({ socket_id: socket.id, channel_name: 'private-orders.5' }),
  });
  const { auth } = await res.json();
  socket.emit('subscribe', { channel: 'private-orders.5', auth }, (ack) => console.log(ack));
});
```

Send the token as a string in `auth`, like above.

A socket that is already logged in with [`SocketAuth`](../packages/socketio.md#log-in-a-socket) needs no token. The server runs the rule with `socket.user`.

### Leaving a channel

Use `socket.emit('unsubscribe', { channel }, ack)` to leave a channel.

### Subscribe errors

The ack of `subscribe` and `unsubscribe` is `{ok: true}` or `{ok: false, error}`:

| `error` | Why |
| --- | --- |
| `channel is missing` | no channel name |
| `channel name is too long` | over `Broadcast.maxChannelLength` |
| `too many channels` | over `Broadcast.maxChannelsPerSocket` |
| `already subscribing` | the same channel is still being checked |
| `Forbidden` | the rule refused, or the token is missing, wrong or old |
| `unsubscribed` | an `unsubscribe` came while it was subscribing |
| `presence is not available` | another server did not answer in time |

## Presence channels

A presence channel tells its members who else is in it. The client gets three events:

| Event | Arguments | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `presence:subscribed` | `(channel, members)` | to the new socket, with all members |
| `presence:joining` | `(channel, member)` | to the others, when a member joins |
| `presence:leaving` | `(channel, member)` | to the others, when a member leaves |

A member is `{user_id, user_info}`. `user_info` is the map from the rule.

```js
socket.on('presence:subscribed', (channel, members) => console.log(members));
socket.on('presence:joining', (channel, member) => console.log(member.user_info.name));
socket.on('presence:leaving', (channel, member) => console.log(member.user_id));
```

A user with two sockets is one member. `presence:joining` is sent for the first socket, and `presence:leaving` for the last one. The member list covers all isolates and servers that share the adapter.

## Queued broadcasting

Sometimes you do not want the request to wait while the event is sent. A queued broadcast goes through your [queue](queue.md) instead.

`dox_socketio` does not depend on `dox_queue`, so you connect them with a hook and a small job. Follow these steps.

### 1. Mark the event

Use `ShouldBroadcastQueued` in place of `ShouldBroadcast`:
