# Scheduler

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/scheduler/

# Scheduler

`dox_scheduler` runs your tasks on a schedule, so you do not need a cron line for each task.

You write the whole schedule in Dart, in one file, and each task is a plain function. One small process runs the schedule. A task runs only once per tick, even when many isolates or servers run the schedule.

## Install

Add the package with the `dox` CLI. A new app from `dox create` already has it:

```bash
dox add scheduler
```

It adds the package and writes three files. It never overwrites a file, so it is safe to run twice.

- `lib/config/schedule.dart`: your tasks and the `ScheduleConfig`. See [Defining tasks](#defining-tasks).
- `bin/schedule.dart`: the program that runs the schedule. See [Running the scheduler](#running-the-scheduler).
- `lib/providers/schedule_provider.dart` (optional): runs the schedule inside the server. See [Run inside the server](#run-inside-the-server).

If you want to set it up by hand, add the package and write these files yourself:

```bash
dart pub add dox_scheduler
```

## Defining tasks

Put your tasks in the `schedule` function in `lib/config/schedule.dart`. Use `s.call(name, function)` to add a task, then chain a frequency:

```dart title="lib/config/schedule.dart"
import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';

ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig = const ScheduleConfig();

void schedule(Schedule s) {
  s.call('cleanup', cleanup).dailyAt('02:00');
  s.call('report', sendReport).hourly();
  s.call('ping', ping).cron('*/5 * * * *').timezone('Asia/Yangon');
}

Future<void> cleanup() async {
  // delete old rows, files, ...
}
```

The name must be unique, because it is used in the logs and in the lock keys. A task with no frequency runs every minute.

### Scheduling queued jobs

If a task is slow, you can put a [queue](queue.md) job on the queue instead. Wrap the dispatch in a function, so the task only adds the job and a queue worker runs it:

```dart
s.call('report', () => SendReport().dispatch()).hourly();
```

To use another [queue connection](queue.md#queue-connections), pass `connection:` to `dispatch()`:

```dart
s.call('prune', () => PruneFiles().dispatch(connection: 'redis')).hourly();
```

### Scheduling shell commands

Use `exec` to run a program. A non-zero exit code fails the task:

```dart
s.exec('pg_dump', args: <String>['-f', 'backup.sql', 'mydb']).daily();
```

No shell is used, so `|`, `>` and `*` are plain text. If you need a shell, run it yourself:

```dart
s.exec('sh', args: <String>['-c', 'pg_dump mydb | gzip > backup.sql.gz']).daily();
```

### Scheduling dox commands

Use `command` to run a `dox` command of your app. It runs as the process `dox <command> <args>`:

```dart
s.command('queue:prune', args: <String>['--hours=48']).hourly();
```

The task name is the command line, like `dox queue:prune --hours=48`, and it shows in the logs and in `list`. So if `args` holds a secret, give the task your own name:

```dart
s.command('sync', args: <String>['--token=$token'], name: 'sync');
```

The output of `exec` and `command` tasks is dropped. Use the [output hooks](#task-output) to keep it.

## Frequency options

Chain one of these methods to say how often a task runs:

| Method | Runs |
| --- | --- |
| `everySecond()` | every second. Also `everyTwoSeconds`, `everyFiveSeconds`, `everyTenSeconds`, `everyFifteenSeconds`, `everyTwentySeconds`, `everyThirtySeconds` |
| `everyMinute()` | every minute (the default) |
| `everyTwoMinutes()` | every 2 minutes |
| `everyThreeMinutes()` | every 3 minutes |
| `everyFourMinutes()` | every 4 minutes |
| `everyFiveMinutes()` | every 5 minutes |
| `everyTenMinutes()` | every 10 minutes |
| `everyFifteenMinutes()` | every 15 minutes |
| `everyThirtyMinutes()` | at minute 0 and 30 |
| `hourly()` | at minute 0 of every hour |
| `hourlyAt(17)` | at minute 17 of every hour |
| `everyTwoHours()` | every 2 hours at minute 0. Also `everyThreeHours`, `everyFourHours`, `everySixHours`. Pass a minute: `everyTwoHours(15)` |
| `everyOddHour()` | at 01:00, 03:00 ... 23:00. Pass a minute: `everyOddHour(30)` |
| `daily()` | every day at 00:00 |
| `dailyAt('13:00')` | every day at 13:00 |
| `twiceDaily(1, 13)` | every day at 01:00 and 13:00 |
| `twiceDailyAt(1, 13, 15)` | every day at 01:15 and 13:15 |
| `at('13:00')` | same as `dailyAt('13:00')` |
| `weekly()` | every Sunday at 00:00 |
| `weeklyOn(DateTime.monday, '08:00')` | every Monday at 08:00 |
| `monthly()` | the 1st of every month at 00:00 |
| `monthlyOn(15, '12:00')` | the 15th of every month at 12:00 |
| `twiceMonthly(1, 16, '13:00')` | the 1st and 16th of every month at 13:00 |
| `lastDayOfMonth('15:00')` | the last day of every month at 15:00 |
| `quarterly()` | January, April, July and October 1st at 00:00 |
| `quarterlyOn(4, '14:00')` | January, April, July and October 4th at 14:00 |
| `yearly()` | January 1st at 00:00 |
| `yearlyOn(6, 1, '17:00')` | June 1st at 17:00 |
| `cron('*/5 9-17 * * 1-5')` | any 5 field cron expression |

### Day constraints

If a task should run only on some days, add a day method:

| Method | Runs |
| --- | --- |
| `weekdays()` | Monday to Friday |
| `weekends()` | Saturday and Sunday |
| `mondays()` ... `sundays()` | only on that day of the week |
| `days(<int>[DateTime.monday, DateTime.friday])` | only on these days |

```dart
s.call('standup', remind).weekdays().dailyAt('09:00');
```

A day method and a time method like `dailyAt()` can come in any order.

### Sub-minute tasks

A task with a seconds method, like `everyFiveSeconds()`, repeats inside each due minute. You can still limit the minutes with a frequency, days or filters. Call the seconds method first, because it also sets the task to every minute:

```dart
s.call('poll', poll).everyFiveSeconds().between('09:00', '17:00');
```

### Cron expressions

`cron()` takes the standard 5 fields: `minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week`.

| Field | Values |
| --- | --- |
| minute | 0-59 |
| hour | 0-23 |
| day of month | 1-31 |
| month | 1-12 or `JAN`-`DEC` |
| day of week | 0-7 or `SUN`-`SAT` (0 and 7 are Sunday) |

Each field takes `*`, a number `5`, a range `1-5`, a list `1,15`, and a step `*/15` or `0-30/10`.

## Time zones

The schedule uses UTC by default. Use `timezone()` to read the time of a task in another zone:

```dart
s.call('report', sendReport).dailyAt('08:00').timezone('Asia/Yangon');
```

The name is an IANA name, like `Europe/London` or `America/New_York`. An unknown name throws an `ArgumentError` when the schedule starts.

To use one zone for every task, set it in the config. A task's own `timezone()` still wins:

```dart
ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig = const ScheduleConfig(timezone: 'Asia/Yangon');
```

## Limiting when a task runs

### Between times

Use `between` to run a task only in one time of day. Use `unlessBetween` to skip a time of day. Both ends are included, and a range can cross midnight:

```dart
s.call('sync', sync).everyFiveMinutes().between('09:00', '17:00');
s.call('night', night).hourly().between('22:00', '06:00');
s.call('quiet', quiet).hourly().unlessBetween('23:00', '04:00');
```

### Truth tests

Sometimes a task should run only when a condition is true. `when` runs the task when the function gives `true`, and `skip` skips it when the function gives `true`. The function can give a `bool` or a `Future<bool>`:

```dart
s.call('promo', promo).daily().when(isPromoOn);
s.call('backup', backup).daily().skip(isHoliday);
```

### Environments

Use `environments` to run a task only when `APP_ENV` is one of the names. When `APP_ENV` is not set, the task does not run:

```dart
s.call('emails', sendEmails).daily().environments(<String>['production']);
```

## Preventing task overlaps

A slow task may still run when its next minute comes. If it must not run twice at the same time, use `withoutOverlapping`. The task is then skipped while the last run still runs:

```dart
s.call('report', sendReport).everyFiveMinutes().withoutOverlapping();
```

The lock expires after 24 hours, in case the process dies. You can pass another expiry: `withoutOverlapping(Duration(hours: 1))`. After a crash, remove the lock at once with [`clear-cache`](#clearing-overlap-locks).

## Running tasks on one server

A task runs only once per tick across all isolates and servers. This is on by default (`onOneServer()`). Before a task runs, the scheduler takes a lock named after the task and the minute. The first process to get it runs the task, and the others skip it.

The locks live in a [cache](cache.md) store. If many servers run the schedule, use a shared store like Redis, because a `memory` or `file` store is not shared between servers:

```dart
ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig = const ScheduleConfig(store: 'redis');
```

If a task should run on every process instead, use `onEveryServer()`:

```dart
s.call('clear-tmp', clearTmp).hourly().onEveryServer();
```

## Background tasks

Tasks of the same minute run one after another. If a long task should not hold back the next one, use `runInBackground`:

```dart
s.call('export', export).daily().runInBackground();
```

## Timeouts

Use `timeout` to count a run as failed when it takes too long. The failure hooks then run:

```dart
s.exec('pg_dump', args: <String>['mydb']).daily().timeout(Duration(minutes: 5));
```

For an `exec()` or `command()` task, the process is killed at the timeout. A Dart function can not be stopped, so its work may go on after the timeout.

## Running the scheduler

`bin/schedule.dart` runs your schedule. With `app`, the runner starts your app providers first (like the database), and it stops them at the end:

```dart title="bin/schedule.dart"
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/schedule.dart';
import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';

Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  exitCode = await SchedulerRunner(
    schedule: schedule,
    app: appConfig,
    config: scheduleConfig,
  ).run(args);
}
```

The `dox` CLI runs the same file. For example, `dox schedule:work` is the same as `dart run bin/schedule.dart work`.

### Running the worker

`work` is a long running process. It wakes at each full minute and runs the due tasks. Run it next to your server, with the same deploy tool (systemd, Docker, Kubernetes):

```bash
dox schedule:work
```

On Ctrl+C or SIGTERM it starts no new task and waits for the running ones. A second signal stops it at once.

### Running from cron

If you would rather use the system cron, `run` runs the tasks of this minute once, waits for them, and exits. Add one line to the crontab:

```bash
* * * * * cd /path/to/app/build/bundle && ./bin/schedule run
```

`./bin/schedule` is the binary that `dox build` makes in `build/bundle`. It starts fast and needs no Dart SDK. Do not use `dart compile exe`, because it can not build apps with native libraries like SQLite. The exit code is 1 when a task failed.

### Listing tasks

`list` shows each task, its schedule and its next run time:

```bash
dox schedule:list
```

```
Task     Schedule                   Next run
cleanup  0 2 * * *                  2026-10-26 02:00 UTC
report   0 * * * *                  2026-10-25 14:00 UTC
ping     */5 * * * * Asia/Yangon    2026-10-25 20:35 Asia/Yangon
```

### Running one task now

`test` runs one task now, with its hooks. It does not check the schedule, the filters or the locks:

```bash
dox schedule:test cleanup
```

### Clearing overlap locks

If the process crashed while a task ran, its `withoutOverlapping()` lock stays in the store, so the task is skipped until the lock expires. `clear-cache` removes these locks:

```bash
dox schedule:clear-cache
```

Only run it when the task does not really run on another process or server. Otherwise that task could start a second time.

## Run inside the server

For a small app, you can run the schedule inside your Dox server instead of a `work` process. Add a provider that extends `SchedulerProvider`:

```dart title="lib/providers/schedule_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/schedule.dart';

class ScheduleProvider extends SchedulerProvider {
  ScheduleProvider() : super(schedule: schedule, config: scheduleConfig);
}
```

Then turn it on in the config, and run `dart run build_runner build` so the generated container finds the provider:

```dart title="lib/config/schedule.dart"
ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig = const ScheduleConfig(inProcess: true);
```

Only the first isolate of the web server runs the tasks, and the other isolates only serve requests. A `bin/queue.dart` worker, a test or the `work` process does not start this in-process schedule. The `work` process runs the tasks on its own. In a test of the in-process schedule, set `Dox().isWebServer = true;` first. With many servers, each server runs the loop, and the once-per-tick lock makes each task run once. Use a Redis store for this. When the server stops, it waits for the running tasks.

The tasks use the CPU of the server, so they can slow down requests on the first isolate. A separate `work` process can be deployed, scaled and restarted on its own. So use `work` for heavy tasks.

## Logging the schedule

By default the scheduler prints its own plain `[schedule]` lines. To send them through the app `Logger` instead, turn on `loggerLines`:

```dart title="lib/config/schedule.dart"
ScheduleConfig scheduleConfig = const ScheduleConfig(
  flags: SchedulerFlags(loggerLines: true),
);
```

The lines get the tag `[scheduler]`, for example `[scheduler] ran cleanup in 12ms`. They follow `LoggerConfig.enabled`, `level` and `prettyPrint`. `SchedulerFlags.all()` turns on every flag.

## Task output

These hooks keep the output (stdout and stderr) of an `exec()` or `command()` task. They do nothing on a function task.

Use `sendOutputTo` to write the output to a file. It replaces the file each run:

```dart
s.exec('pg_dump', args: <String>['mydb']).daily().sendOutputTo('storage/logs/backup.log');
```

Use `appendOutputTo` to add the output to the end of the file:

```dart
s.exec('pg_dump', args: <String>['mydb']).daily().appendOutputTo('storage/logs/backup.log');
```

Use `onOutput` to get the output in code after the process ends. It holds the whole output in memory, so do not use it for a very large output:

```dart
s.exec('pg_dump', args: <String>['mydb']).daily().onOutput((String output) {...});
```

## Task hooks

Hooks run code around a task, for example to log it or to alert your team when it fails:

```dart
s
    .call('report', sendReport)
    .daily()
    .before(logStart)
    .onSuccess(logDone)
    .onFailure(alertTeam)
    .after(cleanUp);

Future<void> alertTeam(Object error, StackTrace stack) async {
  await notifyTeam('report failed: $error');
}
```

| Hook | Runs |
| --- | --- |
| `before` | before the task. If it throws, the task does not run and counts as failed |
| `onSuccess` | after the task worked |
| `onFailure` | after the task threw or timed out. It gets the error and the stack trace |
| `after` | after the task, always |

An error in a task is logged, and the next task still runs.

### Pinging URLs

You can send a GET request to a URL around a task, for example to a health check service:

```dart
s
    .call('backup', backup)
    .daily()
    .pingBefore('https://health.example.com/backup/start')
    .pingOnSuccess('https://health.example.com/backup')
    .pingOnFailure('https://health.example.com/backup/fail');
```

`thenPing(url)` pings after the task, always. Each ping method also has an `If` form that takes a bool first, like `pingOnFailureIf(isProduction, url)`. A failed ping is logged, but it never fails the task.

## Without Dox

`dox_scheduler` also works in a plain Dart app. Leave out `app`:

```dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';

void schedule(Schedule s) {
  s.call('cleanup', cleanup).dailyAt('02:00');
}

Future<void> cleanup() async {
  // delete old files, ...
}

Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  exitCode = await SchedulerRunner(schedule: schedule).run(args);
}
```

With no `app`, no providers start, and the locks use a memory store. For many servers, pass a shared `CacheStore` from `dox_cache`, like `SchedulerRunner(schedule: schedule, store: myRedisStore)`. The commands are the same.

## Testing

`Scheduler` runs the tasks. Give it a fake clock, so you can test a schedule with no waiting:

```dart
import 'package:dox_cache/dox_cache.dart';
import 'package:dox_scheduler/dox_scheduler.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/schedule.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

class FakeClock extends ScheduleClock {
  FakeClock(this.time);

  DateTime time;

  @override
  DateTime now() {
    return time;
  }
}

test('cleanup runs at 02:00', () async {
  Schedule s = Schedule(timezone: scheduleConfig.timezone);
  schedule(s);
  Scheduler scheduler = Scheduler(
    tasks: s.tasks,
    store: CacheStore(MemoryDriver()),
    clock: FakeClock(DateTime.utc(2026, 10, 25, 2)),
  );
  Map<String, TaskOutcome> outcomes = await scheduler.runDue();
  expect(outcomes['cleanup'], TaskOutcome.ran);
});
```

To check a schedule without running anything, use `ScheduledTask.isDue(time)` and `ScheduledTask.nextRun(time)`. To replace the ping request in tests, set `ScheduledTask.sendPing = (Uri url) async {...};`.

## Details

This section is for special cases. Most apps do not need it.

### Frequencies

- The day methods, `weekly()`, `weeklyOn()` and `cron()` all set the day of the week. The last call wins: `.mondays().weekly()` runs on Sundays.
- `weekly()` and `weeklyOn()` also set the time (00:00 unless you pass one). So `.dailyAt('09:00').weekly()` runs at 00:00, but `.weekly().dailyAt('09:00')` runs at 09:00.
- A day of the month and a day of the week join with OR, like standard cron: `monthlyOn(15).fridays()` and `0 0 1 * MON` run on that date and on every such weekday. When one day field of a cron expression starts with `*`, both must match.
- `lastDayOfMonth()` runs only on the last day of the month, whatever day methods you add. `list` shows it as `28-31`, but the next run time is right.
- `yearlyOn()` with a day the month never has, like `yearlyOn(2, 30)`, throws.
- A seconds method called last undoes the frequency before it: `.everyFiveSeconds().hourly()` repeats in minute 0 of each hour, but `.hourly().everyFiveSeconds()` repeats in every minute.
- With a sub-minute task, `when()` and `skip()` are checked before each repeat. A run that takes longer than its step skips the steps it missed. `run` from cron then stays until the end of the minute, and `work` also wakes inside the minute.
- With summer time (DST), a time that does not exist that day does not run, and a time that happens twice runs once. `hourly()` and other "every" frequencies keep running every real hour.
- The zone data comes from the `timezone` package.

### Filters and locks

- `environments()` ignores case and spaces around the names. It is read at run time. An empty list or a blank name throws.
- With `loggerLines` on, the plain `[schedule]` line is left out on stdout and stderr when the Logger printed it. So the lock store warning goes to stdout, not to stderr. Other sinks (like a `StringBuffer`) still get every plain line.
- The once-per-tick lock is not released, so a late server can not run the same minute again. It expires after 10 minutes. When the store is `null`, the scheduler uses a memory store.
- At start, the scheduler prints one warning to stderr when a task uses `onOneServer()` and the lock store is `memory`, `file` or `null`. It does not print when `APP_ENV` is `development` or `local`. With one server you can ignore it.
- `clear-cache` removes only the `withoutOverlapping()` lock of each task, by its exact name. Other cache keys and the once-per-tick locks stay. It exits with 0, also when there was no lock. A `memory` store loses its locks with the process, so `clear-cache` is for `file` and Redis stores.

### Processes

- The stdin of an `exec()` or `command()` process is closed, so a program that waits for input ends at once.
- At a timeout the process gets SIGTERM, and SIGKILL 5 seconds later (`Schedule.processGrace`). Only the process itself is killed, so the children of a shell (`sh -c 'a | b'`) may live on.
- A stop of `work` waits for the processes to end.
- If `dox` is not on PATH, set its full path: `Schedule.doxExecutable = '/usr/local/bin/dox';`.
- A `name:` also lets you add the same command line twice.

### Output and pings

- The file gets the output as it comes. Two runs at the same time write to the same file, so use `withoutOverlapping()` or `appendOutputTo()`.
- A file that can not be written fails the task, and so does a throwing `onOutput` hook. `onOutput` still gets the output first. When more than one thing fails, the error is the first of: a non-zero exit code, an `onOutput` error, a file error.
- After a timeout, the file and `onOutput` finish a bit later, after the failure hooks ran. An error there is lost.
- A ping fails after 10 seconds (`ScheduledTask.pingTimeout`), or on a status of 400 or more. A URL that is not `http` or `https` throws an `ArgumentError` when the schedule is made.
- The next run time in `list` checks the frequency, `between()` and `unlessBetween()`. It does not check `when()`, `skip()` and `environments()`.


---

# File Storage

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/file-storage/

# File Storage

`Storage()` saves and reads files on a disk: a local folder, AWS S3 (and R2, MinIO, Spaces), or memory.

You use the same methods for every disk. So you can keep files in a local folder in development and on S3 in production, and your code stays the same.

It is in the [`dox_storage`](../packages/storage.md) package. A new project already has it.

```dart
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';

Route.post('/avatar', (DoxRequest req) async {
  RequestFile file = req.input('avatar');
  String path = await Storage().putFile('avatars', file);
  return <String, String>{'path': path}; // /avatars/<uuid>.png
});
```

## Setup

If your project does not have storage yet, add it with the CLI:

```bash
dox add storage
```

It writes `lib/config/storage.dart`, the provider, the `storage` folder and the `STORAGE_DISK=local` key. It never overwrites a file, so it is safe to run twice.

Add `--disk=s3` to also add an `s3` disk and the `AWS_*` keys. `STORAGE_DISK` stays `local`, so the app starts before you fill in the keys. Fill them in, then set `STORAGE_DISK=s3`.

### Configuration

The disks are in `lib/config/storage.dart`. A new project has one `local` disk in the `storage` folder. `STORAGE_DISK` in `.env` picks the default disk.

To add disks, edit the file. This example adds a `url` to the local disk, an `s3` disk and a `memory` disk:

```dart title="lib/config/storage.dart"
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

StorageConfig storageConfig = StorageConfig(
  defaultDisk: env.storageDisk,
  disks: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
    'local': <String, dynamic>{
      'driver': 'local',
      'root': 'storage',
      'url': 'https://app.test/files', // for signedUrl(); url() gives /storage/<path> without it
    },

    /// only when AWS_BUCKET is set
    if (env.awsBucket != null)
      's3': <String, dynamic>{
        'driver': 's3',
        'bucket': env.awsBucket,
        'region': env.awsDefaultRegion,
        'key': env.awsAccessKeyId,
        'secret': env.awsSecretAccessKey,
        'endpoint': env.awsEndpoint, // R2, MinIO, Spaces
      },
    'memory': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'memory'},
  },
);
```

Each driver takes these options:

| Driver | Options |
| --- | --- |
| `local` | `root` (default `storage`), `url`, `app_key` (default: your APP_KEY), `visibility`, `atomic_writes`, `permissions` |
| `s3` | `bucket`, `region`, `key`, `secret`, `token`, `endpoint`, `path_style` (MinIO), `url` (CDN), `visibility`, `acl`, `batch_delete`, `unsigned_payload` |
| `memory` | none. For tests |

The provider of a new project sets up these disks in every isolate. It is in `lib/providers/`, so the generated container finds it:

```dart title="lib/providers/storage_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/storage.dart';

class AppStorageProvider extends StorageProvider {
  AppStorageProvider() : super(storageConfig);
}
```

### The S3 disk

The `s3` disk reads five keys that a new project does not have yet. Add them to `lib/config/env.dart` and run `dart run build_runner build`. They are nullable, and the `s3` disk is only added when `AWS_BUCKET` is set, so the app starts without them:

```dart title="lib/config/env.dart"
  String? get awsBucket;

  String get awsDefaultRegion => 'us-east-1';

  String? get awsAccessKeyId;

  String? get awsSecretAccessKey;

  /// R2, MinIO or Spaces. Null for AWS.
  String? get awsEndpoint;
```

The `s3` disk needs `bucket`, `key` and `secret`. If one is missing, the app stops at start with an `ArgumentError` that names the setting.

### Skipping the body hash

To save CPU on big uploads, add `unsigned_payload` to the `s3` disk. The upload then skips the hash of the body. Only use it over HTTPS:

```dart
's3': <String, dynamic>{
  'driver': 's3',
  'bucket': env.awsBucket,
  // ... region, key, secret, endpoint
  'unsigned_payload': true,
},
```

## Using another disk

`Storage()` uses the default disk. Use `disk` to pick another one:

```dart
await Storage().disk('s3').put('reports/2026.pdf', bytes, exact: true);
```

## Storing files

The `putFile` method saves a file in a folder with a new uuid name, and returns the path. It takes a `RequestFile` or bytes. For bytes, Dox finds the extension from the bytes, or you pass `extension:`:

```dart
// save with a new uuid file name, returns '/images/<uuid>.png'
String path = await Storage().putFile('images', file);  // a RequestFile
Uint8List bytes = Uint8List.fromList(<int>[1, 2, 3]);
String path2 = await Storage().putFile('images', bytes, extension: 'png');
String path3 = await Storage().put('images', bytes, extension: 'png'); // like putFile
```

### Storing with your own name

If you want to pick the file name, use `putFileAs`. It replaces an old file with the same name:

```dart
String path4 = await Storage().putFileAs('avatars', file, 'user-1.png'); // your own name
```

Do not use the file name from the client here, because the name is used as it is. Make your own name, like `user-1.png`.

### Storing at an exact path

Use `put` with `exact: true` to write to an exact path. It replaces an old file there and returns the path. It takes a `String`, a `List<int>` or a `Stream<List<int>>`:

```dart
// save to this exact path. String, List<int> or Stream<List<int>>
await Storage().put('notes/a.txt', 'hello', exact: true);
```

### Storing uploaded files

An uploaded file can store itself. `store` gives it a new uuid name, like `putFile`. `storeAs` uses your name, like `putFileAs`. Both take `disk:`:

```dart
RequestFile file = req.input('image');
String path = await file.store('images');
String onS3 = await file.store('images', disk: 's3');
String avatar = await file.storeAs('avatars', 'user-1.png');
```

`putFile` and `store` take the extension from the file name. But if the bytes are a known format (png, jpg, pdf, zip, ...) that does not match the name, the extension of the bytes is used. So a png sent as `a.html` is saved as `.png`, and it is never served as a web page.

### Prepending and appending

Use `append` and `prepend` to add text to the end or the start of a file. A missing file is made:

```dart
await Storage().append('logs/app.log', 'new line');    // a missing file is made
await Storage().prepend('logs/app.log', 'first line');
```

They add a new line between the old and the new text, if the file is not empty. Change it with `separator`.

## Retrieving files

The `get` method returns the bytes of a file, or `null` when the file is missing:

```dart
Uint8List? found = await Storage().get(path);  // null when missing
```

### Checking if a file exists

`exists` checks for a file. `missing` is the opposite:

```dart
bool exists = await Storage().exists(path);           // files only
bool gone = await Storage().missing(path);            // not exists()
```

### File metadata

`size` gives the size in bytes, and `lastModified` gives the time of the last change. Both throw `FileNotFoundException` when the file is missing:

```dart
int size = await Storage().size(path);                 // throws when missing
DateTime changed = await Storage().lastModified(path); // throws when missing
```

## Downloading files

Sometimes you want to send a stored file to the browser. `stream` shows it in the browser, and `download` makes the browser save it as a file:

```dart
Route.get('/photo', (DoxRequest req) {
  return Storage().stream(req.input('path'));    // shown in the browser
});

Route.get('/report', (DoxRequest req) {
  return Storage().disk('s3').download('reports/2024.pdf'); // saved as a file
});
```

Both read the file as a stream, so a big file is never loaded into memory. A missing file answers `404`.

`download` names the file after the last part of the path. Pass `name:` to pick another name:

```dart
Route.get('/invoice', (DoxRequest req) {
  return Storage().download('invoices/42.pdf', name: 'Invoice 42.pdf');
});
```

If you want to add headers, put the download in a `response()`:

```dart
Route.get('/invoice', (DoxRequest req) async {
  DownloadableFile file = await Storage().download('invoices/42.pdf');
  return response(file).header('Cache-Control', 'no-store');
});
```

## File URLs

The `url` method gives the URL of a file. On a local disk with no `url` option, it gives `/storage/<path>`:

```dart
String url = await Storage().url(path);         // /storage/<path> when the disk has no `url`
```

Dox only serves that URL when you add `Storage.route('storage', signed: false)`. See [Serving local files](#serving-local-files).

### Signed URLs

Sometimes a file should only be open for a short time, like a private invoice. Use `signedUrl` for this. `temporaryUrl` is the same method:

```dart
String signed = await Storage().signedUrl(path, expiresIn: Duration(minutes: 10));
String same = await Storage().temporaryUrl(path); // the same as signedUrl()
```

On a local disk, `signedUrl` needs the disk `url` option. Set it to the full URL of the route, like `https://app.test/files`.

### Serving local files

A local disk needs a route, so the browser can open its files. `Storage.route` adds one:

```dart
// lib/routes/web.dart
Storage.route('files');                    // GET /files/{key*}, signed URLs only
Storage.route('public', signed: false);    // any file of the disk
Storage.route('docs', disk: 'memory', signed: false); // another disk than the default
Storage.route('uploads', download: true);  // every file is a download
```

With a signed route, the URL looks like this:

```dart
String url = await Storage().signedUrl('invoices/1.pdf'); // https://app.test/files/invoices/1.pdf?expires=...&signature=...
```

- A missing, wrong or expired signature answers `403`.
- Signed URLs work only on a `local` disk, and only on the route of their own disk. For another disk, use `signed: false`.
- An html, svg, xml or javascript file is always sent as a download in a sandbox, so its script does not run on your site.
- Every file has `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`.

## Copying and moving files

`copy` and `move` replace an old file at the new path:

```dart
await Storage().copy('notes/a.txt', 'backup/a.txt');
await Storage().move('backup/a.txt', 'old/a.txt');
```

On S3 the copy runs inside S3, so the bytes do not pass through your app. A missing source file answers `404`.

## Deleting files

```dart
await Storage().delete(path);
```

## Directories

`files` gives the files in a folder. `allFiles` also gives the files in sub-folders. `directories` gives the sub-folders. All paths start with `/`, like the paths from `putFile`:

```dart
List<String> files = await Storage().files('images');         // direct files only
List<String> all = await Storage().allFiles('images');        // in sub-folders too
List<String> folders = await Storage().directories('images'); // direct sub-folders
```

Use `directoryExists` to check for a folder. On S3 and memory disks, a folder exists when a file is under it:

```dart
bool folder = await Storage().directoryExists('images');
```

`makeDirectory` makes a folder. It only works on a local disk. On other disks it does nothing:

```dart
await Storage().makeDirectory('reports');              // local disk only
```

`deleteDirectory` deletes a folder and every file in it. A missing folder is not an error:

```dart
await Storage().deleteDirectory('old');                       // the folder and its files
```

It refuses the root (`''` or `/`) with `InvalidKeyException`, so a wrong path can not empty the disk. To empty a whole disk on purpose, use `Storage().use().deleteAll()`.

## File visibility

A file can be `public` or `private`. Use `setVisibility` and `getVisibility`:

```dart
await Storage().setVisibility(path, Visibility.private);
Visibility visibility = await Storage().getVisibility(path);
```

- On S3, `setVisibility` sets the ACL, because `acl` is on by default. With `'acl': false` (R2 and similar), it does nothing, and `getVisibility` gives the disk `visibility`.
- On a local disk, `setVisibility` does nothing by default, and `getVisibility` gives the disk `visibility`. Turn on `permissions` to use file modes.

### Visibility on a local disk

If you want visibility to be the file mode on a local disk, add `'permissions': true` to the disk. Then `setVisibility` runs `chmod`, and `getVisibility` reads the mode of the file:

```dart
'local': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'local', 'root': 'storage', 'permissions': true},
```

The modes are: public file `0644`, private file `0600`, public folder `0755`, private folder `0700`. To change them, see [Custom file modes](#custom-file-modes). On Windows, `permissions` does nothing, because there is no `chmod`.

## Full disk API

`Storage().use('s3')` returns the `dox_storage` `Disk`. It has more methods, like `listAll` with pages, `getMetaData`, `putStream`, `deleteAll` and write options. See [dox_storage](../packages/storage.md).

## Custom drivers

Implement `DriverContract` from `package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart`. Register it in a [provider](providers.md), so every isolate has it:

```dart
Storage.manager.register('dropbox', DropboxDriver());
await Storage().disk('dropbox').put('notes/a.txt', 'hello', exact: true);
```

## Testing

To swap a disk with a memory disk in tests, see [Testing](testing.md#test-file-storage).

## Details

This section is for special cases. Most apps do not need it.

### Signature and the body

`unsigned_payload` is off by default. The signature then does not cover the body, so only use it over HTTPS.

### S3 part size

`multipartPartSize` is the size of one part of a big upload. It is a field of `S3DriverConfig`, not a key of the disk map. The default is 8 MiB. See [Storage](../packages/storage.md). S3 needs 5 MiB to 5 GiB. With another size, Dox prints one warning to stderr. It does not throw.

### Atomic writes

A local disk writes a file in place by default. Add `'atomic_writes': true` to write to a temp file and rename it when the write is done. Then a failed upload never leaves a partial file, and the old file stays:

```dart
'local': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'local', 'root': 'storage', 'atomic_writes': true},
```

The rename makes a new file. So the folder must be writable, the file gets the default mode and owner, a hard link keeps the old content, and a symlink is replaced.

### Custom file modes

Give `permissions` a map with a `file` and a `dir` key. Each has a `public` and a `private` mode. A mode you leave out keeps its default. Dart has no octal numbers, so write the modes in hex: `0x1a0` is `0640`, `0x1e8` is `0750`:

```dart
'private': <String, dynamic>{
  'driver': 'local',
  'root': 'storage-private',
  'visibility': 'private',
  'permissions': <String, dynamic>{
    'file': <String, int>{'public': 0x1a4, 'private': 0x1a0},
    'dir': <String, int>{'public': 0x1ed, 'private': 0x1e8},
  },
},
```

Each mode must be an int from 0 to 0x1ff (0777). Anything else, like the string `'0644'`, throws `ArgumentError` when the disk is made. Other keys are ignored.

### How file modes work

- The mode is set before the content is written, so a private file is never readable by others, not even for a moment.
- A new file gets the visibility of the write, or the disk `visibility`.
- An overwrite, `append`, `prepend` and `move` keep the mode of the file, unless the call gives a visibility.
- A `copy` gets the visibility of the call, or else the mode of the source.
- Folders that a write creates get the folder mode. Folders that were there before, and the disk root, keep their mode.
- `getVisibility` reads the real mode. The private mode is private. Any other mode is public.
- `getVisibility` and `setVisibility` of a symlink throw `UnsupportedOperationException`.
- If the `chmod` fails, a file that the write created is removed.

### Other cases

- `append` and `prepend` read the file and write it back, so two writers at the same time can lose a write. They keep the visibility and content type of the file.
- `putFile` with a `RequestFile` on a local disk moves the upload temp file, so it does not read the file into memory.
- `directoryExists('')` is always true: the empty path is the root.
- `getVisibility` and `setVisibility` of a missing file answer `404`. With `'acl': false` on S3, `getVisibility` gives the disk `visibility`, also for a missing file.
- On a local disk, a `copy` or `move` of a missing file makes no folders. A local `copy` writes a temp file and renames it. Listings hide that temp file.
- Any `download` name is safe in the header. Quotes are escaped, a new line becomes `_`, and a name like `résumé.pdf` is also sent as `filename*=UTF-8''r%C3%A9sum%C3%A9.pdf`.


---

# Environment Variables

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/env/

# Environment Variables

Declare your env keys once, in a typed class, and read them as normal Dart values.

Your app needs different settings on each machine. For example, the database password on your laptop is not the one in production. You keep these values in environment variables or in a `.env` file, not in your code.

Dox reads them through a typed class. So `env.appPort` is an `int`, your IDE suggests every key, and a missing key stops the app at startup, not in the middle of a request.

## Defining env keys

A new project already has `lib/config/env.dart`. Its keys are listed in the [Env reference](../reference/env.md#read-by-a-new-project). Each getter in the class is one env key. This example shows the kinds of getters you can write:

```dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'env.g.dart';

enum LogLevel { debug, info, error }

@DoxEnv()
abstract class AppEnv {
  static AppEnv load([EnvReader? reader]) {
    return _$AppEnv.load(reader);
  }

  String get appName;                       // APP_NAME, required
  String get appKey;                        // APP_KEY, required
  int get dbPort => 5432;                   // DB_PORT, default 5432
  bool get appDebug => false;               // APP_DEBUG, default false
  LogLevel get logLevel => LogLevel.info;   // LOG_LEVEL=debug
  Duration get cacheTtl => const Duration(minutes: 5); // CACHE_TTL=5m
  List<String> get corsOrigins => <String>[];          // CORS_ORIGINS=a.com,b.com

  @EnvKey('AWS_BUCKET')
  String? get s3Bucket;                     // optional, null when not set
}

/// The env of the app. Read and checked once, on first use.
final AppEnv env = AppEnv.load();
```

Run `dart run build_runner build` after each change to the class. It writes `env.g.dart`.

### Key names

The key is the getter name in UPPER_SNAKE case. `appName` reads `APP_NAME`. A run of capitals is one word, so `dbURL` reads `DB_URL`. If you want another name, use `@EnvKey('X')`.

### Default values

The getter body is the default. It runs only when the key is missing. It can be any expression, like `Platform.numberOfProcessors`.

A default can use another env getter, and it gets the loaded value. Write the getter directly (`appPort`), not `env.appPort`, because the global `env` is not ready while it loads:

```dart
String get appUrl => 'http://localhost:$appPort';
```

This getter is still a key: it reads `APP_URL`, and when `APP_URL` is set, it wins over the body.

### Required and optional keys

- A getter with no body is required. A missing key stops the app.
- A nullable getter with no body, like `String? get s3Bucket;`, is optional. It is `null` when the key is missing.
- An empty value (or the text `null`) counts as missing.

### Types

| Type | Value in `.env` |
|------|-----------------|
| `String` | any text |
| `int`, `double`, `num` | `3000`, `0.5` |
| `bool` | `true`/`false`, `1`/`0`, `yes`/`no`, `on`/`off` (any case) |
| `Uri` | `https://dox.dev` |
| `Duration` | a number and a unit: `500ms`, `30s`, `5m`, `2h`, `1d`. A plain number is seconds: `300` is 5 minutes. |
| an enum | the name of a value, any case: `debug` |
| `List<String>` | comma separated: `a, b, c`. Empty items are dropped. |

Any other type is a build error.

### Missing or bad keys

When the app starts, `AppEnv.load()` reads and checks every key. If something is wrong, it throws one `EnvException` that lists every missing or bad key:

```
EnvException: the env is not valid
  - APP_KEY is missing
  - DB_PORT must be an int
```

The error names the key, never the value, because a value may be a secret and this text goes to logs and CI output.

## Reading env values

Import the config file and use `env` anywhere:

```dart
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  connection: 'postgres',
  connections: <String, ConnectionConfig>{
    'postgres': ConnectionConfig(port: env.dbPort /* int */, ...),
  },
);
```

Keep only plain keys in the env class. A computed value, like "is this development", does not go there. Use `appConfig.isDevelopment` from the app config instead. It is `true` when `APP_ENV` is `development`.

## Where values come from

Dox reads values from these places. The first one that has the key wins:

1. Real environment variables (set in the shell, Docker or systemd).
2. In tests only: the `.env.testing` file. See [Testing: a test database](testing.md#use-a-test-database-with-envtesting).
3. The `.env` file in the folder where you start the app. It is optional.

So you can keep a `.env` file for development and use real environment variables in production.

### The `.env` file

The `.env` file has one `KEY=value` per line:

```ini title=".env"
APP_NAME=dox
APP_KEY=<output of dox key:generate>
DB_PORT=5432
```

- Quotes around a value are removed, so `APP_NAME="My app"` gives `My app`. Use `"`, `'` or `` ` ``.
- A line that starts with `#` is a comment. A `#` after a space also starts a comment: `APP_PORT=3000 # dev` gives `3000`.
- A `#` with no space before it, or inside quotes, is kept: `COLOR=#fff` gives `#fff`.
- `KEY=` (empty) gives the default value, the same as a missing key.
- `export KEY=value` works too.
- A value can not go over more lines. For a multi-line PEM key, keep the key in a file and put the file path in the env. Or turn on `envExpand` (below) and write it on one line with `\n`.

## Use one value in another

Sometimes you want to build a value from other values, like `APP_URL` from `HOST` and `PORT`. Turn on `CoreFlags.envExpand` for this. It is off by default.

```ini title=".env"
HOST=localhost
PORT=3000
APP_URL=http://${HOST}:${PORT}
GREETING="Hello\nWorld"
```

- `${OTHER}` works in an unquoted value and in a `"..."` value. It does not work in `'...'`.
- Dox looks for a real environment variable first, then for a key above this line. A name it does not find stays as `${OTHER}`.
- In a `"..."` value, `\n`, `\t`, `\"`, `\\` and `\$` become a new line, a tab, `"`, `\` and `$`.

### Turning on envExpand

The `.env` file is read before `AppConfig` exists. So you set the flags in two places: in `AppConfig`, and in `Env.flags` at the very top of `main()`, before any env value is read:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

const CoreFlags flags = CoreFlags(envExpand: true);

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  appKey: Env.get('APP_KEY', ''),
  flags: flags,
  // ...
);
```

```dart title="bin/server.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';

void main() async {
  Env.flags = flags;
  Dox().initialize(appConfig);
  await Dox().startServer();
}
```

`my_app` is the `name` in your `pubspec.yaml`.

A test does not run `bin/server.dart`. So set `Env.flags = flags;` at the top of `main()` in each test file too:

```dart title="test/http_test.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/testing.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

void main() {
  Env.flags = flags;
  late DoxTestClient client;

  setUpAll(() async {
    client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig);
  });
  // ...
}
```

If you forget it, `${OTHER}` stays as written, and Dox prints a warning.

## Generating the env class

If you have a `.env.example`, `dox env:generate` makes `lib/config/env.dart` from it:

```bash
dox env:generate   # make lib/config/env.dart from .env.example
```

- Digits become an `int` with that default: `APP_PORT=3000` gives `int get appPort => 3000;`.
- `true`/`false` become a `bool` with that default.
- An empty value becomes an optional `String?`.
- Any other value becomes a required `String`. The example value is never a default, so a secret in the example can not leak into the code.
- `#` comment lines above a key become its doc comment.

It does not overwrite an existing `lib/config/env.dart`. Run `dox build_runner:build` after it.

## Checking the env

`dox env:check` loads the env and prints every missing or bad key. It exits with code 1 when a key is wrong, so you can use it in CI or before a deploy:

```bash
dox env:check      # load the env and print every missing or bad key
```

## The app key

Dox needs `APP_KEY` to encrypt and sign data. Make one with `dox key:generate`.

When `APP_KEY` is missing, not 32 characters, or a public sample key, `Dox().startServer()` stops with an error. When `APP_ENV` is `development`, `local`, `test` or `testing`, it only logs a warning.

## Reading a key by name

Sometimes you only know the key name at run time. Use `Env.get()` for this. For normal config, use the typed class.

```dart
Env.get<String>('APP_KEY');             // '' when missing
Env.get('APP_KEY', 'default_value');
Env.get<int>('APP_PORT', 3000);
Env.get<bool>('SOCKETIO_ENABLED', false); // true, 1, yes, on
Env.get<String?>('AWS_BUCKET');          // null when it is not set
```

A missing or empty key gives the default. With no default:

- `String` gives `''`.
- `String?` and `dynamic` give `null`. `Env.get('KEY')` with no type is `dynamic`.
- `int`, `num`, `double` and `bool` throw an `ArgumentError` with the key name. A value that is not a number throws too.

`Env.get()` looks up and converts the value on every call, so do not call it on a hot path.

## Testing

To pass your own values in a test, see [Testing](testing.md#test-the-env).

## Details

- The builder only reads getters of the `@DoxEnv()` class itself. Getters from a superclass or a mixin are not read from the env. A field (`final String x = ...;`) is a build error.
- If a default reads the global `env`, the app stops at startup with a `StateError`: "A default of AppEnv reads the global `env`. Use the getter directly".
- After startup, `env.dbPort` is a plain field read.
- A `=` inside a value is kept: `TOKEN=a=b` gives `a=b`.
- With `envExpand`, `.env.testing` also sees the keys of `.env`.
- The first env read (like `Env.get()` or `env.appName`) loads `.env` with the flags of that moment. The file is not read again. If `Env.flags` was not set yet, `Dox().initialize` prints a warning.
- The server isolates follow the main isolate, so you set nothing for them. When the flag is on in `AppConfig` but `.env` was read without it, Dox prints a warning at start, once in each isolate.


---

# Isolate

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/isolate/

# Isolate

Dox runs your app on many isolates (threads) at once, so it can use every CPU core.

Each isolate runs its own [native server](native-server.md) on the same port, and the operating system spreads the connections between them. You write your app once, and Dox starts a copy of it in every isolate.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    OS["Port 3000<br>the OS spreads the connections"] --> A1["Rust acceptor"]
    OS --> A2["Rust acceptor"]
    OS --> A3["Rust acceptor"]
    A1 --> I1["Isolate 1, main<br>own memory cache"]
    A2 --> I2["Isolate 2<br>own memory cache"]
    A3 --> I3["Isolate N<br>own memory cache"]
    I2 -. "crash: started again after 1 second" .-> I2
    I1 -. "crash: the process exits" .-> S["Supervisor restarts the process<br>Docker, systemd"]
```

With the Postgres and MySQL drivers, all isolates share one database pool in Rust. See [How Dox works](../concepts/how-dox-works.md#where-the-database-pools-live).

## Setting the number of isolates

By default Dox starts one isolate per CPU the process may use. In a container, this respects the cpuset and the CPU quota (`--cpuset-cpus`, `--cpus`, Kubernetes limits). A quota rounds up: 1.5 CPUs gives 2 isolates. You may want fewer when the same machine also runs the database or other heavy work.

Set `totalIsolate` in the app config. A new app reads it from `APP_TOTAL_ISOLATE`:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  // ...
  totalIsolate: env.appTotalIsolate,
);
```

You can also set it in code, before `startServer()`. This wins over the config:

```dart title="bin/server.dart"
Dox().initialize(appConfig);
Dox().totalIsolate(2);
await Dox().startServer();
```

## Each isolate has its own memory

Isolates do not share memory. This matters when you keep state in your code:

- A static value or a singleton exists once **per isolate**. If you change it in one isolate, the others do not see it.
- The `memory` cache store is per isolate. See [Cache](cache.md).
- To share data between isolates or servers, use a database, Redis or files.

If you need to know which isolate runs your code, use `Dox().isolateId`. The first isolate is `1`:

```dart
int id = Dox().isolateId;
```

## Sending a message to the other isolates

Sometimes one isolate needs to tell the others that something changed, for example "forget this cache key". Use `IsolateBus` for this. It sends a message from one isolate to all the others in the same process.

Listen on a channel in a provider's `setup()`, and publish from anywhere:

```dart
IsolateBus.instance.on('users').listen(onMessage); // in a provider's setup()
IsolateBus.instance.publish('users', <Object>['changed', 42]);
```

A listener only gets the messages of its own channel, and an isolate never gets its own message. A message must be something a `SendPort` can send: null, bool, num, String, typed data, and lists and maps of those.

The bus works inside one process only. For many servers, use Redis. Socket.IO uses the bus to share broadcasts, see [Socket.IO](../packages/socketio.md#many-isolates).

## What each isolate does at start

Dox copies the `AppConfig`, the providers and the routes you added before `startServer()` to each new isolate. Then every isolate:

1. runs `setup()` of each provider (for example, it opens the database pool),
2. registers the routes of your routers,
3. reads the parameter types of each controller once,
4. runs `boot()` of each provider,
5. starts its HTTP server.

Because the config and providers are copied, they must not hold open sockets or database pools. Open these in `setup()`. See [Providers](providers.md).

## When an isolate crashes

Dox keeps your app running when code fails:

- An error in a request is caught. Dox sends a `500` and keeps going.
- An async error outside a request (for example a future that nobody awaits) is passed to the `report` method of the [exception handler](../the-basic/errors.md). The isolate keeps running.
- If a worker isolate still dies, Dox prints `[server] isolate N exited, restarting` to stderr and starts a new isolate after 1 second.

If the first (main) isolate dies, the process exits with a non-zero code. So let a supervisor start it again, like Docker `restart:` or systemd `Restart=always`. See [Deployment](deployment.md#keep-it-running).

## Details

- Linux gives each isolate its own socket (`SO_REUSEPORT`). On macOS the isolates share one socket. On Windows only one isolate serves HTTP.
- `Dox().isolateCount` is the number of running isolates. `IsolateBus.instance.size` is the number of isolates that listen on the bus, this one included. `size` can be old for a short time after an isolate joins or leaves.
- `publish` throws an `ArgumentError` for a value a `SendPort` can not send, and then no isolate gets the message. In the main isolate it only throws when another isolate listens.
- `publish` never waits. A slow listener keeps the messages in a queue in its memory.
- A message only reaches the isolates that listen at that moment. An isolate that calls `on()` later does not get older messages.


---

# Providers

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/providers/

# Providers

A provider is a class that sets up one part of your app when it starts, for example the database, auth or a Redis connection.

Dox runs your app on many [isolates](isolate.md), and they do not share memory. So code that you run once in `bin/server.dart` only sets up the first isolate, and the others have, for example, no database connection. A provider fixes this, because each isolate runs it itself.

## Writing providers

To make a provider, run `dox make:provider`. It writes `lib/providers/cache_provider.dart` with an empty `setup()`:

```bash
dox make:provider Cache
```

See [`dox make:provider`](../reference/cli.md#dox-makeprovider).

### The setup method

A provider extends `DoxProvider`. Put your code in `setup()`. It runs when the app starts, and it can be `async`, because Dox waits for it:

```dart title="lib/providers/orm_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';

class ORMProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  Future<void> setup() async {
    SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(databaseConfig);
  }

  /// Close the database connections when the server stops.
  @override
  Future<void> shutdown() async {
    await SqlQueryBuilder.close();
  }
}
```

Open connections in `setup()`, not in the constructor. A provider listed in `AppConfig` is copied to each isolate. An open socket or database pool can not be copied, so the isolate fails to start.

Keep `setup()` short, because it runs once per isolate. Data you load in it is also kept once per isolate, so 8 isolates keep 8 copies.

A package that does not use `dox_core` imports `DoxProvider` from `package:dox_annotation/provider.dart`.

### The boot method

Sometimes a provider needs other providers to be ready, for example to start a background worker. Use `boot()` for this. It runs after `setup()` of every provider is done:

```dart
class ReportProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {}

  @override
  Future<void> boot() async {
    // every provider has run setup() here
  }
}
```

The boots run one by one, in the provider order. `boot()` is optional.

The web server and the queue worker (`bin/queue.dart`) run `boot()`. The scheduler (`bin/schedule.dart`) and `dox openapi:generate` do not. They run only `setup()`.

### Clean up on shutdown

When the app stops, you often want to close connections or flush data. Use `shutdown()` for this. On `SIGTERM` or `SIGINT`, Dox stops the server gracefully (see [Deployment](deployment.md#graceful-shutdown)). After the open requests are done, it runs `shutdown()` of every provider, in every isolate:

```dart title="lib/providers/redis_provider.dart"
class RedisProvider extends DoxProvider {
  late RedisConnection redis;

  @override
  Future<void> setup() async {
    redis = await RedisConnection.open();
  }

  @override
  Future<void> shutdown() async {
    await redis.close();
  }
}
```

`shutdown()` is optional. The `ORMProvider` of a new project already closes the database here. Dox closes the cache stores (like Redis) by itself, after the providers.

An error in `shutdown()` goes to the `report` method of the [exception handler](../the-basic/errors.md). The other providers still run.

## Registering providers

You do not need to register a provider. Dox finds every class that extends `DoxProvider`. Run `dart run build_runner build`, and the provider is then in `lib/generated/container.g.dart`.

Each isolate makes its own instance from the container, so its constructor can ask for other classes of the container. See [Dependency injection](../the-basic/dependency-injection.md#routers-and-providers).

### Choosing the order

Providers run in the order of their file path. If one provider must run first, list it in `AppConfig`:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  container: registerContainer,
  providers: <DoxProvider>[ORMProvider()], // runs before the others
);
```

A listed provider runs first, then the others run. No provider runs twice.

### Adding a provider in code

You can also add a provider in `bin/server.dart`, before `startServer()`:

```dart title="bin/server.dart"
Dox().initialize(appConfig);
Dox().addProvider(MyProvider());
await Dox().startServer();
```

## Example: auth

This provider sets up [authentication](../security/authentication.md):

```dart title="lib/providers/auth_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

class AppAuthProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Auth.initialize(AuthConfig(
      defaultGuard: 'web',
      guards: <String, AuthGuard>{
        'web': AuthGuard(
          driver: JwtAuthDriver(secret: SecretKey(env.appKey)),
          provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
        ),
      },
    ));
  }
}
```

The class is named `AppAuthProvider`, because `dox_auth` already has a class named `AuthProvider` (it finds the user model).

## Details

- In each isolate, Dox runs `setup()` of each provider one after the other: the listed ones first, then the ones of the container. Then it registers the routes and starts the server, so routes can use what a provider set up. See [What each isolate does at start](isolate.md#what-each-isolate-does-at-start).
- `dox openapi:generate` also runs `setup()` of every provider, because it needs the routes.
- The queue `inProcess` worker starts in `boot()`, so it does not run in the scheduler process.

# Dox CLI

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/dox-cli/

# Dox CLI

The `dox` CLI creates projects and files, runs the dev server, builds for production and runs migrations.

Run `dox help` to see all commands, or `dox help <command>` for one command. Many `make:*` commands also answer to a `create:*` name. Every command is in the [table at the end](#all-commands).

## Installation

Install the CLI with `dart pub`:

```bash
dart pub global activate dox
```

If your shell can not find `dox`, add the pub bin folder to your `PATH`. Put this line in `~/.bashrc` or `~/.zshrc`, then open a new terminal:

```bash
export PATH="$PATH":"$HOME/.pub-cache/bin"
```

### Updating the CLI

`dox update` installs the newest version with the same major version as your CLI. To pick the version yourself, run the install command again.

```bash
dox update
```

To remove the CLI, run `dart pub global deactivate dox`.

## Creating a project

Use `dox create` to start a new project:

```bash
dox create new_blog
```

It copies the [dox-sample](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-sample) template from GitHub and makes `.env` from `.env.example`, with a new `APP_KEY`. The folder name is the project name in snake case, so `NewBlog` makes `new_blog`.

Then run `cd new_blog`, `dart pub get` and `dox serve`.

By default it uses the newest template release with the same major version as the CLI. To pick a release, pass `--version`:

```bash
dox create new_blog --version <release tag>
```

## Running the dev server

`dox serve` (or `dox s`) starts your app for development:

```bash
dox serve
```

When a file in `lib/app/` changes, it hot reloads the new code into the running server. This takes about 0.1 to 0.2 seconds. When routes, providers, config, `bin/`, `db/` or generated files change, it restarts the server instead. It also runs `build_runner watch`, so generated files stay up to date.

Hot reload does not run code again that already ran once. So a changed static or global value keeps its old value until a restart.

The server prints the VM service link. Open it in a browser to get DevTools, the debugger and the profiler.

If you do not want hot reload, or you run `build_runner` yourself, use these options:

```bash
dox s --no-reload             # restart on every change, no hot reload
dox s --ignore-build-runner   # do not run build_runner watch
```

See [dox serve](../reference/cli.md#dox-serve) for all details.

## Building for production

`dox build` builds a native (AOT) bundle into `build/bundle`. Run the server from there:

```bash
dox build
cd build/bundle
./bin/server
```

See [Deployment](deployment.md#build).

## Creating files

The `make:*` commands write new files with the right names and folders. Names keep their word breaks, so `BlogPost` makes `blog_post.controller.dart` with the class `BlogPostController`.

After `make:controller` or `make:dto`, run `dox build_runner:build`, or keep `dox serve` running. See [Validation](../the-basic/validation.md).

### Controllers

`make:controller` writes a controller in `lib/app/http/controllers`:

```bash
dox make:controller Blog        # lib/app/http/controllers/blog.controller.dart
```

If you want a controller for all actions of a resource, add `-r` (or `--resource`). It adds the methods `index`, `create`, `store`, `show`, `edit`, `update` and `destroy`. For an API, `--api` adds the same methods without `create` and `edit`. To use a model in it, add `--model`:

```bash
dox make:controller Blog -r
dox make:controller Blog --api
dox make:controller Blog --model=Post
```

### Models

`make:model` writes a model. The options also make the files that belong to it:

```bash
dox make:model Blog -m          # model and a create_blogs_table migration
dox make:model Blog -mcr        # model, migration and a resource controller
dox make:model Blog -a          # model, migration, factory, seeder and a resource controller
```

The options are `-m` migration, `-c` controller, `-r` resource controller, `--api` resource controller without `create` and `edit`, `-f` factory, `-s` seeder and `-a` for all of them. You can join them, like `-mfs`. See [CLI reference](../reference/cli.md#dox-makemodel).

The table of a model is its name in plural snake case. So `BlogPost` gets `@DoxModel(table: 'blog_posts')`.

### Migrations

`make:migration` writes a Dart migration. Add `--sql` for a `.sql` file:

```bash
dox make:migration create_blogs_table
dox make:migration create_blogs_table --sql
```

### Mail and views

`make:mail` writes a mailable in `lib/app/mail` and its view. If you want a plain text body, add `--no-view`. `make:view` writes a `.dox.html` view:

```bash
dox make:mail Welcome           # lib/app/mail/welcome_mail.dart and resources/views/emails/welcome.dox.html
dox make:mail Invoice --no-view # the mail only, with a plain text body
dox make:view pages/about       # resources/views/pages/about.dox.html
```

### Tests

`make:test` writes a test that starts the app with `DoxTestClient`. Add `--unit` for a plain test:

```bash
dox make:test Ping              # test/ping_test.dart
dox make:test Math --unit       # test/math_test.dart
```

### Other files

```bash
dox make:middleware Auth        # lib/app/http/middleware/auth.middleware.dart
dox make:dto CreateBlog         # lib/app/dtos/create_blog/create_blog.dto.dart
dox make:serializer Blog        # lib/app/serializers/blog.serializer.dart
dox make:provider Cache         # lib/providers/cache_provider.dart
dox make:command send_report    # lib/app/commands/send_report_command.dart, run it with dox app:send-report
```

## Listing routes

`dox route:list` prints every route of the app, without starting the server. Add `--json` for JSON output:

```bash
dox route:list
```

See [`dox route:list`](../reference/cli.md#dox-routelist).

## Running migrations

The migration commands read the database settings from `.env` and the real environment. A real environment variable wins over `.env`:

```ini title=".env"
# postgres, mysql or sqlite
DB_CONNECTION=postgres
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=5432
# for sqlite: the file path
DB_NAME=postgres
DB_USERNAME=admin
DB_PASSWORD=password
```

`DB_CONNECTION` defaults to `sqlite`. If `DATABASE_URL` is set, it wins over all the `DB_*` keys. All keys are in the [Env reference](../reference/env.md#read-by-the-framework).

Use `migration:run` (or `migrate`) to run new migrations, and `migration:status` to see which ones ran:

```bash
dox migration:run
dox migration:status
```

A failed migration stops the run, and the CLI exits with code 1. On MySQL, statements like `CREATE`, `ALTER` and `DROP` save right away. So when a migration fails half way, these changes are not undone.

### Rolling back migrations

`migration:rollback` undoes the last batch. Use `--step` to undo the last N migrations, or `--batch` to undo only one batch:

```bash
dox migration:rollback
dox migration:rollback --step=2
dox migration:rollback --batch=3
```

### Resetting the database

`migration:reset` undoes all migrations. `migration:refresh` undoes all, then runs them again. `migration:fresh` drops all tables, then runs all migrations:

```bash
dox migration:reset
dox migration:refresh
dox migration:fresh
```

If you also want to run the seeders, add `--seed` to `migration:run`, `migration:refresh` or `migration:fresh`.

The `migrate:*` names also work, like `migrate:rollback` and `migrate:fresh`.

## All commands

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `dox create <name> [--version <v>]` | create a new project |
| `dox serve` (or `dox s`) | start the dev server with hot reload and build_runner watch |
| `dox build` | build the native (AOT) bundle into `build/bundle` |
| `dox build_runner:watch` / `dox build_runner:build` | run the code generator |
| `dox make:controller <name> [-r] [--api] [--model=<model>]` | create a controller |
| `dox make:middleware <name>` | create a middleware |
| `dox make:dto <name>` | create a DTO (typed, checked input) |
| `dox make:serializer <name>` | create a serializer |
| `dox make:provider <name>` | create a provider in `lib/providers` |
| `dox make:command <name>` | create a command in `lib/app/commands` and add it to the commands list |
| `dox make:mail <name> [--no-view]` | create a mailable in `lib/app/mail`, and its view unless you pass `--no-view` |
| `dox make:view <name>` | create a `.dox.html` view in `resources/views` |
| `dox make:test <name> [--unit]` | create a test in `test/` that uses `DoxTestClient`, or a plain one with `--unit` |
| `dox route:list [--json]` | list every route of the app, without starting the server |
| `dox make:model <name> [-m] [-c] [-r] [--api] [-f] [-s] [-a]` | create a model, and with the options its migration, controller, factory and seeder |
| `dox make:migration <name> [--sql]` | create a Dart migration, or a `.sql` one with `--sql` |
| `dox migration:run` (or `dox migrate`) | run new migrations |
| `dox migration:rollback [--step=N] [--batch=N]` | undo the last batch, the last N migrations, or only batch N |
| `dox migration:reset` | undo all migrations |
| `dox migration:refresh` | undo all, then run all again |
| `dox migration:fresh` (or `migrate:fresh`) | drop all tables, then run all migrations |
| `dox migration:status` | show which migrations ran, and their batch |
| `dox make:factory <model>` | create a model factory in `db/factories`, see [Factories](../database/factories.md) |
| `dox make:seeder <name>` | create a seeder in `db/seeders` (and `bin/seed.dart`), see [Seeders](../database/seeders.md) |
| `dox db:seed [--class=<name>]` | run `DatabaseSeeder`, or another seeder |
| `dox make:job <name>` | create a queue job in `lib/app/jobs` (and `bin/queue.dart`) |
| `dox queue:work [--queue=a,b] [--concurrency=N] [--once] [--tries=N] [--timeout=S] [--sleep=S] [--stop-when-empty] [--timeout-grace=S]` | run the queue worker |
| `dox queue:failed` | list the failed jobs |
| `dox queue:retry <id\|all>` | put a failed job (or all) back on the queue |
| `dox queue:forget <id>` | delete one failed job |
| `dox queue:flush` | delete all failed jobs |
| `dox queue:clear [queue]` | delete the jobs of a queue |
| `dox queue:restart` | stop the running workers after their current jobs |
| `dox queue:prune-failed [--hours=N]` | delete failed jobs older than N hours (default 24) |
| `dox queue:table` | create a migration for the `jobs`, `failed_jobs` and `job_batches` tables (from the `dox_queue_database` package) |
| `dox auth:tokens-table` | create a migration for the `auth_access_tokens` table (from the `dox_auth` package) |
| `dox schedule:work` | run the scheduler and keep it running |
| `dox schedule:run` | run the tasks that are due now, once |
| `dox schedule:list` | list the scheduled tasks |
| `dox schedule:test <name>` | run one scheduled task now |
| `dox schedule:clear-cache` | remove the `withoutOverlapping()` locks left by a crash |
| `dox key:generate [--show] [--force]` | make a new `APP_KEY`. `--show` prints a key and writes nothing. In production it asks first, `--force` skips |
| `dox env:generate` | make `lib/config/env.dart` (the typed env class) from `.env.example`, see [Environment Variables](env.md) |
| `dox env:check` | check the env against `lib/config/env.dart`. Prints every missing or bad key (exit code 1) |
| `dox openapi:generate [dir]` | run `bin/openapi.dart` to write `openapi.json` and `openapi.yaml` (default `storage/openapi`). A new project has no `bin/openapi.dart` yet, see [OpenAPI](../packages/openapi.md#write-the-files) |
| `dox update` | update the CLI |
| `dox version` (or `dox -v`) | show the CLI version |
| `dox help [command]` | show help |

## Details

- `DB_CONNECTION` must be `sqlite`, `postgres` or `mysql`. Any other value is an error. The default port is `5432` for postgres and `3306` for mysql.
- `DB_DATABASE` works too, in place of `DB_NAME`.
- In `.env`, a `#` after a space starts a comment, the same as in the app. The migration commands do not expand `${VAR}` and do not read `.env.testing`.
- `dox serve` runs `dart run bin/server.dart`. A failed hot reload restarts the server. One save gives one restart.
