# Package commands

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/package-commands/

# Package commands

A package can add its own `dox` commands.

Your app can add its own commands too. You do not write a `bin` file, and you do not register anything, because the `dox` CLI finds the commands by itself. For example, `dox queue:table` comes from the `dox_queue_database` package, and `dox auth:tokens-table` comes from the `dox_auth` package.

## Using a package command

Add the package and run `dart pub get`. Then run the command:

```bash
dart pub add dox_queue_database
dox queue:table
```

`dox help` lists the commands of each package, under the package name.

## Add a command to your package

A package command needs three things: the command class, a list of commands, and a key in `pubspec.yaml`.

### 1. Write the command

A command extends `Command` from `package:dox_core/command.dart`. The `run` method gets the words after the command name as `args`:

```dart title="lib/src/commands/hello_command.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/command.dart';

class HelloCommand extends Command {
  @override
  String get name => 'hello:say';

  @override
  String get description => 'Say hello';

  /// optional, shown by `dox help`. The default is the name.
  @override
  String get usage => 'hello:say <name>';

  @override
  Future<void> run(List<String> args) async {
    print('Hello ${args.join(' ')}');
  }
}
```

So `dox hello:say Ann` calls `run(['Ann'])`.

A package that does not use `dox_core` imports `package:dox_annotation/command.dart` instead.

### 2. List the commands

Make one library with a top-level `commands` list:

```dart title="lib/commands.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/command.dart';

import 'src/commands/hello_command.dart';

final List<Command> commands = <Command>[HelloCommand()];
```

### 3. Name the library in pubspec.yaml

Add the `dox: commands:` key. Its value must be a library of the package itself:

```yaml title="pubspec.yaml"
dox:
  commands: package:my_package/commands.dart
```

That is all. An app that depends on your package now has `dox hello:say`.

## Add a command to your app

It works the same way. The easy way is `dox make:command`:

```bash
dox make:command send_report
```

It writes `lib/app/commands/send_report_command.dart`, adds the command to `lib/app/commands/commands.dart`, and sets the `dox: commands:` key in your `pubspec.yaml`. The command name is `app:send-report`. See [`dox make:command`](../reference/cli.md#dox-makecommand).

If you write it by hand, put the command in `lib/` of your app and add the key to the app's own `pubspec.yaml`:

```yaml title="pubspec.yaml"
dox:
  commands: package:my_app/commands.dart
```

## Failing a command

When `run` ends, `dox` exits with code 0. If something went wrong, set `exitCode` from `dart:io`, or throw:

```dart
exitCode = 1;
```

A thrown error is printed with its stack trace, and the exit code is 1. The exit code of the command is the exit code of `dox`, so scripts and CI see it.

## Writing a migration

Some packages need a table, so their command adds a migration file. Use `MigrationFile` for this. The file gets the same name as `dox make:migration` makes, like `2026_10_21_120000_create_queue_tables.dart`:

```dart
String? path = MigrationFile().create('create_queue_tables', source);
if (path == null) {
  print('A create_queue_tables migration is already in db/migration.');
  exitCode = 1;
}
```

`create` returns `null` and writes nothing when a migration with this name is already there. The next `dox migrate` runs the new file.

## Ship an install command

`dox add <x>` adds the package `dox_x`, then runs its `<x>:install` command. So if your package needs setup (config files, `.env` keys, a provider), ship an `<x>:install` command.

Use `Installer` from `package:dox_annotation/install.dart`. Each step is safe to run twice, because it never overwrites a file and never adds a key twice:

```dart title="lib/src/commands/hello_install_command.dart"
import 'package:dox_annotation/command.dart';
import 'package:dox_annotation/install.dart';

class HelloInstallCommand extends Command {
  @override
  String get name => 'hello:install';

  @override
  String get description => 'Set up dox_hello in this app';

  @override
  Future<void> run(List<String> args) async {
    Installer installer = Installer();
    String app = installer.appName;
    installer.writeFile(
      'lib/config/hello.dart',
      "import 'package:$app/config/env.dart';\n",
    );
    installer.addEnvGetter("String get helloName => 'world';");
    installer.addEnv('HELLO_NAME', 'world');
    await installer.buildRunner();
    installer.printSummary(<String>['Restart the server.']);
  }
}
```

| Method | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `writeFile(path, content)` | Writes the file only when it is not there. |
| `makeFolder(path)` | Makes the folder when it is not there. |
| `addEnv(key, value)` | Adds `KEY=value` to `.env.example` and `.env` when the key is missing. A key that is there is never changed. |
| `addEnvGetter(getter)` | Adds a getter to `AppEnv` in `lib/config/env.dart` when the class has no member with that name. When it can not find the class, it changes nothing and prints a hint. |
| `addDependency(package, dev: false)` | Runs `dart pub add` when the app does not have the package. |
| `buildRunner()` | Runs `dart run build_runner build`. |
| `note(line)` | Adds your own line to the summary, like `added    hooks to pubspec.yaml`. |
| `printSummary(nextSteps)` | Prints what was done and the next steps. Sets exit code 1 when a step failed. |

Some tips for a good install command:

- Read the options from `args`, like `--driver=postgres`. Give a good default, so `dox add <x>` with no options works.
- Test it on an app made without your package. Run it twice and check that nothing changes the second time.
- Add `dox add <x>` to the skill of your package (`skills/<name>/SKILL.md`), so AI agents set it up the same way.

`dox_orm` has an example: `orm:install`.

## Details

### Name clashes and errors

- A built-in command always wins. If a package has a command with the same name as a built-in one, `dox` runs the built-in one, and `dox help` marks the package command as not used.
- If two packages have a command with the same name, `dox <name>` prints an error with both package names and exits with code 1.
- A bad `dox: commands:` key (not a library of the package, or a missing file) prints a warning with the package name. The commands of the other packages still work.
- The key path may use only letters, digits, `_`, `-`, `.` and `/`, and no `..`.
- An unknown command prints `Could not find a command named "<name>"`, with a hint about the `dox: commands:` key.

### How it works

- `dox <name>` first looks for a built-in command. Then it reads `.dart_tool/package_config.json` and the `dox: commands:` key of each package and of the app.
- It writes `.dart_tool/dox/commands.dart`, which imports each commands library, and runs it with `dart run`. So the command code is always the newest.
- It writes that file again only when `.dart_tool/package_config.json` or a `pubspec.yaml` changes. If a package had a warning, `dox` looks again on the next run.
- `dox help` keeps the list in `.dart_tool/dox/commands.json`. If you change only a file that the commands library imports, `dox help` can show an old description. The command itself always runs the new code.
- `MigrationFile().create` finds a migration with the same name and any time in its name. `dox migrate` writes `db/migration/migrations.dart` again before it runs, and makes `bin/migrate.dart` when it is missing.
- An app inside a pub workspace works too, also when the `workspace:` list uses a glob like `apps/*`. `dox` finds the workspace root from `.dart_tool/pub/workspace_ref.json`.


---

# Deployment

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/deployment/

# Deployment

This page shows how to build a Dox app for production and run it safely.

When your app is ready, you build it into a native binary, copy the binary to a server or a Docker image, and put a proxy in front of it for HTTPS.

!!! danger "Never run production with `dart run`"
    `dart run` (and `dox serve`) uses the JIT compiler, which is made for
    development. It uses about 25x more memory at start (around 390 MB
    instead of 16 MB) and starts slower. Always build an AOT binary for
    production.

## Build

Run `dox build` to build your app for production:

```bash
dox build
```

It makes a `build/bundle/` folder:

| File                        | What it is                                       |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------ |
| `build/bundle/bin/server`   | the native binary. No Dart SDK needed to run it  |
| `build/bundle/bin/queue`    | the queue worker, when `bin/queue.dart` exists   |
| `build/bundle/bin/schedule` | the scheduler, when `bin/schedule.dart` exists   |
| `build/bundle/lib/`         | native libraries from build hooks (eg. SQLite)   |
| `build/bundle/db/`          | your `db/` folder (migrations, seeders). SQLite database files are left out |
| `build/bundle/.env.example` | copy it to `build/bundle/.env`, or use env variables |

Keep `bin/` and `lib/` together, because the binary loads the native libraries from `../lib`.

`dox build` exits with code 1 when a step fails, so CI can stop.

### Starting the server

Start the binary from the bundle folder:

```bash
cd build/bundle
./bin/server
```

The binary reads `.env` and `db/` from the folder you start it in. A real environment variable wins over the `.env` file.

A new Dox app runs the migrations in `bin/server.dart`, before the server starts. So the database is up to date when the first request comes in.

## Docker

A new Dox app has this multi-stage `Dockerfile`. The final image is `FROM scratch`: only the Dart AOT runtime, the bundle, `db/`, `libgcc_s` and an empty `/tmp`.

```dockerfile
FROM dart:stable AS build

# Resolve dependencies first, so this layer is cached.
WORKDIR /app
COPY pubspec.* ./
RUN dart pub get

COPY . .
RUN dart pub get --offline

# The dox CLI. `dox build` runs build_runner, then AOT-compiles
# bin/server.dart, bin/queue.dart and bin/schedule.dart with
# `dart build cli`. It puts all of them in build/bundle/bin, the native
# libraries in build/bundle/lib and the migrations in build/bundle/db.
# The queue worker and the scheduler run as their own processes:
# `/app/bin/queue work` and `/app/bin/schedule work`.
ARG DOX_VERSION=^3.2.0
RUN dart pub global activate dox "$DOX_VERSION"
RUN /root/.pub-cache/bin/dox build

# Lay out the final file tree:
# /app/bin/server, /app/bin/queue, /app/bin/schedule, /app/lib (native
# libraries), /app/db/migration, /app/storage and a writable /tmp
# (uploads bigger than 1 MB are streamed to a temp file).
RUN mkdir -p /out/app/storage /out/tmp \
  && chmod 1777 /out/tmp \
  && cp -r build/bundle/. /out/app/ \
  # the native HTTP server (Rust) needs libgcc_s, which /runtime/ does not have
  && LIBGCC=$(find / -name libgcc_s.so.1 -path '*lib*' | head -n 1) \
  && mkdir -p /out$(dirname $LIBGCC) && cp $LIBGCC /out$LIBGCC

# Minimal serving image: the AOT runtime files from the dart image
# (`/runtime/`) plus our bundle. No Dart SDK, no source code.
FROM scratch
COPY --from=build /runtime/ /
COPY --from=build /out/ /
WORKDIR /app

# Config comes from env variables. The image has no .env file,
# so secrets stay out of it.
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["/app/bin/server"]
```

The image has no `.env` file, so secrets stay out of it. Pass config as environment variables:

```bash
docker build -t my-app .
docker run -p 3000:3000 --env-file .env -e DB_HOST=... my-app
```

### Docker compose

A new app also has a `docker-compose.yml`. It runs the app, a queue worker and Postgres, and reads `.env` with `env_file: .env`:

```bash
docker compose up -d --build
```

- A new `.env` uses SQLite. The compose services set `DB_CONNECTION=postgres` and `DB_NAME=dox` themselves. To use the compose Postgres with `dox s`, set the same two values in `.env`.
- A new app skips the Postgres driver in `pubspec.yaml`, because it uses SQLite. Remove the `dox_postgres_native` skip lines before you run the compose app. See [Skip unused drivers](../database/index.md#skip-unused-drivers).
- The database port listens on `127.0.0.1` only.

See [Docker](../guides/docker.md) for a health check in the image.

## Running the queue worker and scheduler

One build has three binaries. Run each one as its own process:

| Process | Command |
| --- | --- |
| web server | `/app/bin/server` (the default `CMD`) |
| queue worker | `/app/bin/queue work` |
| scheduler | `/app/bin/schedule work` |

The image is `FROM scratch`, so it has no shell. Start the other binaries with `--entrypoint`:

```bash
docker run -d -p 3000:3000 --env-file .env my-app
docker run -d --env-file .env --entrypoint /app/bin/queue my-app work
docker run -d --env-file .env --entrypoint /app/bin/schedule my-app work
```

In compose, use `command: ["/app/bin/queue", "work"]`. The `worker` service of a new app does this.

Without Docker, run `./bin/queue work` and `./bin/schedule work` in `build/bundle`, for example as two more systemd services.

Only the server runs the migrations when it starts, so start the server first.

For a small app, you can skip the extra processes. `QueueConfig(inProcess: true)` runs the jobs inside the server, and `ScheduleConfig(inProcess: true)` runs the schedule there. But heavy jobs then slow down requests. See [Running jobs in the web server](queue.md#running-jobs-in-the-web-server).

## HTTPS: put a proxy in front

Dox serves plain HTTP only, because its [native server](native-server.md) has no TLS. So run Dox on a private port, and put [Caddy](https://caddyserver.com) or nginx in front of it. The proxy does TLS, HTTP/2 and gzip.

By default Dox listens on all network interfaces. When the proxy runs on the same machine, set `APP_HOST=127.0.0.1`, so the app port can not be reached from outside.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    C["Client"] -->|HTTPS| X["Caddy or nginx"]
    X -->|HTTP| D["Dox"]
    D --> DB[("Database")]
```

Dox runs one isolate per core, and they share one database pool. The migrations run once, before the server starts.

### Trusting the proxy

Behind a proxy, every request comes from the proxy. Tell Dox to trust the proxy, so `req.ip()` and `req.scheme()` show the real client:

```dart
AppConfig(
  /// the proxy's IP, or a range like '10.0.0.0/8', or '172.16.0.0/12' for docker
  trustedProxies: <String>['127.0.0.1', '::1'],
);
```

- `req.ip()` reads `X-Forwarded-For`. Dox walks the list from the right and skips your proxies, so a fake value from the client is ignored.
- `req.scheme()` reads `X-Forwarded-Proto` (`http` or `https`). `req.isSecure()` is true for `https`.
- `trustedProxies` is empty by default. Then Dox ignores those headers, because any client can send them.
- `['*']` trusts any direct client. Only use it when the app port can not be reached from outside. If you have two proxies in a row, list their IPs or ranges instead.

### Caddy

Caddy gets a certificate for you and sets `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto`. Websockets work with no extra config.

```
example.com {
  encode gzip
  reverse_proxy 127.0.0.1:3000
}
```

### Nginx

```nginx
upstream dox {
  server 127.0.0.1:3000;
  keepalive 64;
}

map $http_upgrade $connection_upgrade {
  default upgrade;
  ''      '';
}

server {
  listen 443 ssl http2;
  server_name example.com;

  ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/fullchain.pem;
  ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/privkey.pem;

  # match maxMultipartSize in AppConfig
  client_max_body_size 100m;

  gzip on;
  gzip_types application/json text/plain text/css application/javascript;

  location / {
    proxy_pass http://dox;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;

    # websocket upgrade
    proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header Connection $connection_upgrade;

    proxy_set_header Host $host;
    proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
    proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;

    # stream uploads to Dox, do not buffer them in nginx first
    proxy_request_buffering off;
  }
}

server {
  listen 80;
  server_name example.com;
  return 301 https://$host$request_uri;
}
```

### HTTP/2 and gRPC

Dox can speak HTTP/2 to your proxy. This is needed for gRPC. It is opt-in: set `http2: true` in `AppConfig` (see [HTTP/2](http2.md)). Dox speaks h2c only, which is HTTP/2 without TLS. The proxy keeps the TLS. HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 use the same port, so the same upstream address works for both.

With Caddy, `h2c://` tells it to use HTTP/2 without TLS to the app:

```
example.com {
  reverse_proxy h2c://127.0.0.1:3000
}
```

With nginx, gRPC calls need `grpc_pass`, and normal routes need `proxy_pass`. Use a separate location for each. The `grpc://` scheme is used because the app has no TLS:

```nginx
server {
  listen 443 ssl;
  http2 on;
  server_name example.com;

  ssl_certificate     /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/fullchain.pem;
  ssl_certificate_key /etc/letsencrypt/live/example.com/privkey.pem;

  # Normal routes: HTTP/1.1 to the app
  location / {
    proxy_pass http://127.0.0.1:3000;
    proxy_set_header Host $host;
  }

  # gRPC service paths only
  location /greeter.Greeter/ {
    grpc_pass grpc://127.0.0.1:3000;
  }
}
```

nginx can not send normal `proxy_pass` requests to an upstream over HTTP/2. It always uses HTTP/1.1 there, and that works fine because Dox accepts it on the same port. Use `grpc_pass` only for gRPC routes, and keep `proxy_pass` for the rest.

nginx `grpc_read_timeout` and `grpc_send_timeout` are 60 seconds by default. A long stream is cut when it is quiet for that long, so raise them for long streams.

### Pass the real `Host` header

The proxy must pass the real `Host` header to Dox, like `proxy_set_header Host $host;` above. Some checks compare the request with this header:

- the WebSocket origin check (`allowedOrigins` on `Route.websocket`, or `AppConfig.webSocketAllowedOrigins`)
- `back()`, which only goes back to a page of the same host
- `allowedOrigins` of socket.io

If the proxy sends its own host (like `localhost:3000`) instead, your own pages look like another site. Then their sockets get `403`, and `back()` goes to the fallback.

## Behind a load balancer

A load balancer keeps idle connections to Dox open and sends new requests on them. Dox closes a connection after 30 seconds with no request. If the balancer keeps it longer, it may send a request on a connection Dox just closed, and the client gets `502`.

To fix this, set `idleTimeout` longer than the idle timeout of the balancer. AWS ALB keeps idle connections for 60 seconds, so use 65 seconds:

```dart
AppConfig(
  // ...
  idleTimeout: Duration(seconds: 65),
)
```

## Keep it running

When a worker isolate dies, Dox starts it again. But when the main isolate dies, the process exits with a non-zero code (see [Isolate](isolate.md#when-an-isolate-crashes)). So let a supervisor restart it: `restart: unless-stopped` in Docker compose, or `Restart=always` in systemd.

```ini
# /etc/systemd/system/dox.service
[Service]
WorkingDirectory=/srv/app/build/bundle
ExecStart=/srv/app/build/bundle/bin/server
EnvironmentFile=/srv/app/build/bundle/.env
Restart=always

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

## Graceful shutdown

When the platform stops your app, you want open requests to finish first. Dox does this on `SIGTERM` (docker stop, Kubernetes, Cloud Run, Fly, systemd) and on `SIGINT` (Ctrl+C), in every isolate:

1. It stops taking new connections at once.
2. Open requests can finish. Each keep-alive connection closes after its current answer.
3. After `shutdownTimeout` (default 8 seconds), it closes the connections that are still open.
4. It runs `shutdown()` of every provider (see [Providers](providers.md#clean-up-on-shutdown)). The `ORMProvider` of a new project closes the database connections here.
5. It closes the cache stores of `Cache()`, eg. the Redis connections.
6. The process exits with code `0`.

A second `SIGINT` or `SIGTERM` stops the process at once.

Set the timeout in `lib/config/app.dart`:

```dart
AppConfig(
  shutdownTimeout: Duration(seconds: 20),
  ...
)
```

Keep it shorter than the time your platform waits before it kills the process:

| Platform | Waits | Change it with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `docker stop` | 10 seconds | `docker stop -t 30`, or `stop_grace_period` in compose |
| Kubernetes | 30 seconds | `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` |
| Cloud Run | 10 seconds | can not be changed |
| Fly.io | 5 seconds | `kill_timeout` in `fly.toml` |
| systemd | 90 seconds | `TimeoutStopSec` |

In code, `await Dox().stop()` does steps 1 to 5 and does not exit.

## Many processes or machines

One Dox process already uses every core. You only need more processes to run on more machines, or to restart one process without downtime. Run each one on its own port (or machine), and list them in the proxy:

```nginx
upstream dox {
  server 10.0.0.11:3000;
  server 10.0.0.12:3000;
  keepalive 64;
}
```

Socket.IO rooms then need a shared adapter (like Redis), because each process has its own memory.

## Details

- `dox build` runs `build_runner` (when your app uses it), then `dart build cli --target bin/server.dart --output build`. It builds `bin/queue.dart` and `bin/schedule.dart` the same way, when they exist.
- Do not use `dart compile exe`. `dox_orm` bundles SQLite with a build hook, and `dart compile exe` does not run build hooks, so it stops with an error. `dart build cli` is the same AOT compiler and runs the hooks.
- With `trustedProxies: ['*']`, `req.ip()` is the right-most `X-Forwarded-For` hop, the one your proxy added.

# Native server

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/native-server/

# Native server

Dox runs on a native HTTP server from the package `dox_http_native`.

You do not need to set anything. Every app uses it, also an app with WebSocket or Socket.IO routes. Rust owns the sockets and parses HTTP, but all your code stays in Dart: routes, controllers, DTOs, middleware and the ORM. It gets about 5 times more requests than the `dart:io` server on one or two cores. See [Performance](performance.md).

You do not need Rust. The package downloads a ready-built library for your system when you build the app.

## Using it without Dox

`dox_http_native` also works on its own, in any Dart app. Add the package:

```bash
dart pub add dox_http_native
```

Then bind a server and listen for requests. The API is the same as the `dart:io` `HttpServer`:

```dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_http_native/dox_http_native.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  NativeHttpServer server = await NativeHttpServer.bind(3000);
  server.listen((HttpRequest req) async {
    req.response.write('Hello World');
    await req.response.close();
  });
}
```

With no address, the server listens on all interfaces. To listen on one host, pass `address`:

```dart
NativeHttpServer.bind(3000, address: '127.0.0.1');
```

If the port is open to the internet, set `maxConnections`. At the limit, the server stops accepting new connections until one closes. There is no limit by default:

```dart
NativeHttpServer.bind(3000, maxConnections: 10000);
```

`close()` waits for open requests. `close(force: true)` closes every connection at once.

The rest of this page is the same with or without Dox.

## Writing handlers

Because the server has the same API as `dart:io`, `req.httpRequest`, `HttpResponse` and code written for `dart:io` keep working.

Each isolate runs the server on its own thread. So a slow synchronous handler holds all the sockets of its isolate until it is done. `await` is fine, because it gives the isolate back.

## When the library does not load

If the native library can not load, Dox stops at start, before any isolate runs. The error says why and how to fix it:

```
Unsupported operation: dox_http_native did not load: <reason>.
Fix: install Rust (cargo, see https://rustup.rs), then run the app again ...
```

`<reason>` is for example `native library ABI 8, expected 9`. This means the library on disk is from another version of the package. See [Troubleshooting](../reference/troubleshooting.md#the-native-http-library-did-not-load).

You must build with `dox build` or `dart build cli`, because `dart compile exe` does not run build hooks, so it has no library. See [Deployment](deployment.md).

## HTTP/2

The native server also speaks HTTP/2 (h2c) on the same port, when you turn it on with `http2: true`. See [HTTP/2](http2.md).

## WebSocket

Rust also does the WebSocket upgrade and the WebSocket protocol. Your route, middleware and the `Origin` check run first, like for any request. If they give a normal answer (like `403`), the upgrade is refused.

In your own code, use `NativeWebSocket.upgrade(request)`. It gives a `dart:io` `WebSocket`:

```dart
WebSocket socket = await NativeWebSocket.upgrade(request);
```

A message over the size limit closes the socket with code `1009`. Set the limit with `maxMessageSize` of `NativeWebSocket.upgrade`. Socket.IO uses `maxHttpBufferSize`.

To find clients that vanished with no close (like a phone that lost its network), set `pingInterval`. When the client sent nothing for that long, the server sends a ping. When it still sends nothing for one more interval, the socket closes with `1001`. It is off by default:

```dart
socket.pingInterval = Duration(seconds: 30);
```

On a graceful stop (SIGTERM), every open WebSocket gets close code `1001`.

## Streaming a response

To send a body in parts, like server-sent events, write with `add()` and call `flush()`. The first `flush()` sends the status, the headers and the bytes so far. Later writes go out at once:

```dart
import 'dart:convert';
import 'dart:io';

server.listen((HttpRequest req) async {
  req.response.headers.contentType = ContentType('text', 'event-stream');
  req.response.add(utf8.encode('data: hello\n\n'));
  await req.response.flush();
});
```

`NativeResponse.headSent` is `true` once the status and headers went out. After that, an error page can not be sent any more. The response can only end. `req.response` is an `HttpResponse`, so cast it to read the flag:

```dart
bool sent = (req.response as NativeResponse).headSent;
```

## Security notes

- On the internet, run it behind a reverse proxy like Caddy or nginx. The proxy does HTTPS, buffers slow clients and caps connections.
- Set `maxConnections` when the app port is open to the internet.
- Another process of the same OS user can bind the same port. So do not run untrusted code as the user of the app.
- `req.uri` resolves `..` in the path. Never build a file path from the raw path. Use the storage helpers.

## Where the library comes from

The build hook of `dox_http_native` (`hook/build.dart`) picks the first one that works:

1. A path you give in the root `pubspec.yaml` of your app:

    ```yaml
    hooks:
      user_defines:
        dox_http_native:
          lib_path: /path/to/libdox_http_native.so
    ```

2. A local build in `native/target/release` of the package (for work on the package itself).
3. The ready-built library from the GitHub release, checked with sha256. There are builds for macOS (arm64, x64), Linux (x64, arm64) and Windows (x64).
4. A build from source with `cargo`, when Rust is installed.

For a git or path dependency, step 4 comes before step 3, because the source can be newer than the release.

When none works, the app still builds, but it stops at start with the error above. Install Rust and run it again, so step 4 works.

## Working on the native code

`dox_http_native` lives in its own repo: [dartondox/dox-http-native](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-http-native). The Rust code is in its `native` folder:

```bash
cd dox-http-native/native
cargo build --release   # the hook uses this build from now on
cargo test
cd .. && dart test --concurrency=1
```

To use your local copy in the Dox repo, or to release the package, see [Contribute](../community/contribute.md#native-packages).

## Details

### How it works

The server runs on the thread of the isolate, in a loop:

1. Dart calls Rust (one FFI call).
2. Rust writes the answers of the last batch, reads the sockets and parses the new requests. It gives them back to Dart as one batch.
3. Dart runs your handlers and calls Rust again with their answers.

- Under load there is no other thread, so a request never waits for a thread to wake up. When the isolate has nothing to do, a small helper thread watches the sockets and wakes the isolate once when a request comes.
- A second helper thread does gzip, only with `compress: true`. Under load both helper threads sleep.
- The loop gives the event loop a turn after a few batches, so timers and database answers still run on time.
- Each isolate runs its own server on the same port. See [Isolate](isolate.md). The OS spreads connections, not requests, so a keep-alive connection stays on one isolate. A few busy connections (like from one proxy) can keep some isolates idle, so use more connections than isolates.
- WebSocket: Rust sends the `101` answer, answers pings, does the close handshake, checks that text is UTF-8 and checks the size of each frame. Dart gets whole messages in the same batches as requests.
- Compression (permessage-deflate) is never agreed, because a small compressed message could grow very big in memory.

### Limits

- The request line plus headers can be at most 16 KB. Bigger gets `431`. A bad request gets `400`.
- A multipart form over `maxMultipartSize`, or any other body over `maxBodySize`, gets `413` from Rust. With `Expect: 100-continue`, the `413` comes before the body is sent. Else Rust reads and drops the body first, so the client sees the `413`.
- A client that sends no body bytes for 120 seconds gets `408`. A slow but steady upload is fine.
- Accepted sockets get TCP keep-alive. After 60 seconds with no traffic, the OS checks the client every 10 seconds, and a client that misses 6 checks (about 2 minutes) is closed. A live client always answers.
- A client that closed its side while the handler has not answered is closed when nothing was written for `idleTimeout` (30 seconds by default). Set it with the `idleTimeout` argument of `NativeHttpServer.bind`. In a Dox app, set `AppConfig.idleTimeout`.
- A request head must arrive within 30 seconds. A keep-alive connection with no request for 30 seconds is closed. A client that does not read its answer for 30 seconds is cut off.
- A request with both `Content-Length` and `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` gets `400`. A transfer encoding other than `chunked` gets `501`.
- At most 64 requests of one connection wait for an answer, and at most 1 MB of answers waits to be sent. Then the server stops reading that connection until the answers go out.
- A streamed response with a `contentLength` must send exactly that many bytes. `add()` throws when the body passes it, and `close()` fails when it is shorter.
- A streamed response over 64 KB goes out in parts, and at most 1 MB of it waits in memory. Dart reads more of a file only when the client has read what was sent, and stops when the client leaves.
- A request body of 64 KB or more goes to Dart without a copy.
- `compress: true` in `AppConfig` gzips on a helper thread. A streamed response is not compressed.
- WebSocket: one turn reads at most 256 KB of one socket, so one busy client can not hold the isolate. While more than 256 KB waits to be sent to a client, the server stops reading its frames.

# Performance

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/performance/

# Performance

This page shows how fast Dox is, and how to keep your app fast in production.

Dox is fast by default, so most apps only need to follow a few rules in production:

1. Build with `dox build` and run the AOT binary. Never use `dart run` in production. See [Deployment](deployment.md#build).
2. Put Caddy or nginx in front, for HTTPS and gzip.
3. Keep the default isolates, one per CPU core.
4. Keep the body limits on. Uploads stream to disk.

For the code mistakes that slow an app down, see [Performance mistakes](performance-mistakes.md).

## Bodies, uploads and big responses

Big requests and responses can fill the memory of your server. Dox protects you from this by default, so you only need to keep these settings:

- A body over `maxBodySize` or `maxMultipartSize` gets `413` from the native server, before Dart reads it. Set the same limit in the proxy. See [Size limits](../the-basic/request.md#size-limits).
- An upload over 1 MB streams to a temp file. See [Request](../the-basic/request.md#requestfile).
- A `File` or `Stream` response is streamed, not loaded into memory. See [Files and big responses](../the-basic/response.md#files-and-big-responses).

## gzip

gzip saves bandwidth, but it costs CPU on every response. A proxy like Caddy or nginx does it better. So gzip in Dart is off by default. If there is no proxy, turn it on:

```dart
AppConfig(compress: true);
```

Only a body over 256 bytes is gzipped, and only when the client accepts gzip. Streamed responses are not compressed.

## Logging

`LogMiddleware` logs one line per request. If a proxy already writes access logs, turn `LogMiddleware` off, because writing logs costs time. A new project does this for you: `enabled` is `false` when `APP_ENV` is `production` or not set.

## Response handler

Leave `responseHandler` unset if you do not need it. With no handler, a plain value (text, map, list) is sent without building a `DoxResponse`.

## Benchmark

This benchmark uses the rules of [the-benchmarker/web-frameworks](https://github.com/the-benchmarker/web-frameworks):
each server answers `GET /` (empty body), `GET /user/:id` (the id) and
`POST /user` (empty body). Dox is a full Dox app with these three routes.
"Dox server only" is `dox_http_native` with no framework, to show what the
framework costs.

This only measures the HTTP stack. A real app spends most of its time on
the database, JSON and your own code, so the gaps are smaller there. See
[App benchmark](#app-benchmark).

### Why it is fast

The server runs on the isolate's own thread. One FFI call writes the
answers, reads the sockets and parses the new requests. Dart runs the
handlers and calls again. A request never waits for another thread to
wake up. A small helper thread only watches the sockets while the isolate
has nothing to do. See [Native server](native-server.md#how-it-works).

A profile with `perf` (4 server cores, 64 connections) shows the effect:

| | Dox | Bun |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| CPU time per request | 4.85 µs | 5.5 µs |
| Context switches per request | 0.08 | 0.035 |

### How it was run

- Docker on an Apple M2 (8 CPUs in the Docker VM), `linux/arm64`.
- One server at a time. The server and wrk run in two containers on
  different CPUs: the server on 2 CPUs, wrk on the other 6. Host
  network, keep-alive.
- wrk 4.1, 64, 256 and 512 connections, 5 seconds warm-up, then 15 seconds
  per route.
- 3 rounds on 2026-11-22. In each round, every server runs one time. The
  tables show the median of the 3 rounds.
- Every server has as many workers as server CPUs.
- Peak memory is the peak of the container (all workers).
- Dart 3.13.7, AOT build with `dart build cli` (this is what `dox build`
  does). `dox_core` and `dox_http_native` are the releases of 2026-11-22. Node 26.13, Bun 1.4.5, Go 1.26, Rust 1.99 with hyper 1.
- Relic is `relic` 2.0.0 with `relic_native` 2.0.0, started with `serveNative()`.

## Database drivers

One find-by-id query, AOT build (`dart build cli`), database on the same machine (Apple M-series), one isolate:

| Database | One query at a time | Many queries in flight | App CPU time per query |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Postgres 14 (4 connections) | 60 µs | 12.5 µs each (64 in flight) | |
| MySQL 8.4 (10 connections) | 67 µs | 11 µs each (32 in flight) | 13.5 µs |
| MariaDB 11 (10 connections) | 63 µs | 9.7 µs each (32 in flight) | 12.4 µs |

- The CPU time counts the Dart thread and the Rust thread. For MySQL, it is about 75,000 queries per second on one core.
- Dart sends many queries to Rust in one call. Rust sends many results back in one message.
- One query alone spends most of its time on the trip to the database. Many requests at the same time, like in a web server, get the most out of the driver.

## Details

### Dart VM flags

A bigger young generation (`DART_VM_OPTIONS=--new_gen_semi_max_size=64` or `128`) did not give a better p99. Over 5 runs the change was inside the noise, and memory did not move. So there is no flag to set, and Dox never sets VM flags for you. `DART_VM_OPTIONS` is read by the AOT binary from `dox build`, so you can try your own.

### How logs are written

- `Logger` collects log lines and writes them every 20 ms (or every 64 KB) in one write, because writing to stdout blocks the isolate.
- A `warn`, `warning`, `danger` or `error` line is written right away, with the waiting lines before it, so the order stays.
- The buffer is also written when the app stops. If the process is killed hard, the last 20 ms of logs can be lost.

### What Dox does for you

- Routes are grouped by method. The regex of each route is built once, not on every request.
- The argument types of each controller are read once at start, not on every request.
- JSON and text responses are encoded once, straight to bytes, with `Content-Length` set.
- The native server gzips on a Rust thread, and the gzipped body still gets a `Content-Length`.

# Performance mistakes

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/performance-mistakes/

# Performance mistakes

These are the mistakes that make a Dox app slow, with the fix for each one, and a strict mode that warns you about the worst of them while you develop.

Dart runs one thing at a time in each isolate. When one request does slow work without an `await`, every other request on that isolate waits. Most of the mistakes below come from this, or from using too much memory or too many connections. For server settings, see [Performance](performance.md).

## Heavy CPU work in a request

Hashing, building a PDF, resizing an image or parsing a huge JSON file keeps the CPU busy. Run it on a worker isolate with `Dox().compute`, so the server can answer other requests meanwhile:

```dart title="Wrong"
Future<List<int>> invoice(DoxRequest req) async {
  Order order = await Order().findOrFail(req.param['id']);
  return buildPdf(order.toJson()); // blocks the isolate
}
```

```dart title="Right"
Future<List<int>> invoice(DoxRequest req) async {
  Order order = await Order().findOrFail(req.param['id']);
  return renderPdf(order.toJson());
}

Future<List<int>> renderPdf(Map<String, dynamic> data) {
  return Dox().compute(() => buildPdf(data));
}
```

The task runs in another isolate. So make it in a small top-level or static function, and pass only plain values (numbers, strings, lists, maps). Do not use a database connection, the container or a cache store inside it. To change the number of workers, set `computeWorkers` in `AppConfig`.

## Sync password hashing

`Hash.make` and `Hash.verify` run bcrypt on the isolate, and bcrypt is slow on purpose. In a handler, use the async methods. They run bcrypt on a worker:

```dart title="Wrong"
bool ok = Hash.verify(password, user.password);
```

```dart title="Right"
bool ok = await Hash.verifyAsync(password, user.password);
String hashed = await Hash.makeAsync(password);
```

## Sync file calls

A sync file call stops the isolate until the disk answers. Use the async call:

```dart title="Wrong"
String text = File('data/terms.txt').readAsStringSync();
```

```dart title="Right"
String text = await File('data/terms.txt').readAsString();
```

## Loading a whole table

`all()` and `get()` read every row into memory. On a big table, this is slow and can use all your memory. Read one page, or read the rows in parts:

```dart title="Wrong"
List<Order> orders = await Order().all();
```

```dart title="Right"
Pagination<Order> page = await Order().orderBy('id').paginate(currentPage: 1, perPage: 50);
```

To work on all rows, use `chunk()`, `lazy()` or `cursor()`. They keep only a few rows in memory:

```dart
await for (Order order in Order().orderBy('id').cursor(chunkSize: 500)) {
  // one row at a time
}
```

See [Paginating results](../database/query-builder.md#paginating-results), [Chunking results](../database/query-builder.md#chunking-results) and [Streaming results](../database/query-builder.md#streaming-results).

## A query inside a loop

This is the N+1 problem. One query loads the rows, then one more query runs for each row. 100 posts make 101 queries. Use `preload()` to load the relation for all rows in one extra query:

```dart title="Wrong"
List<Post> posts = await Post().all();
for (Post post in posts) {
  await post.$getRelation('author'); // one query per post
  User? author = post.author;
}
```

```dart title="Right"
List<Post> posts = await Post().preload('author').get();
for (Post post in posts) {
  User? author = post.author; // already loaded
}
```

## Awaiting independent work one by one

If two calls do not need each other, start both and wait for both. The total time is then the slowest call, not the sum:

```dart title="Wrong"
int users = await User().count();
int orders = await Order().count();
```

```dart title="Right"
(int, int) counts = await (User().count(), Order().count()).wait;
```

For a list of futures, use `Future.wait(futures)`.

## A static Map as a cache

A `static` Map that you fill and never clean grows until the memory is full. Also, each isolate has its own copy, so the isolates do not agree. Use the [cache](cache.md) with a time to live:

```dart title="Wrong"
static final Map<String, Object> _settings = <String, Object>{};
```

```dart title="Right"
Map<String, dynamic> settings = await Cache().remember(
  'settings',
  Duration(minutes: 10),
  loadSettings,
);
```

With the `redis` or `database` store, all isolates and servers share the same values.

## Forgetting await

If you call an async function without `await`, the work runs on its own. Its error is lost, and it can end after the response is sent. Await it:

```dart title="Wrong"
mailer.sendWelcome(user);
```

```dart title="Right"
await mailer.sendWelcome(user);
```

Turn on the `unawaited_futures` lint in `analysis_options.yaml` and the analyzer finds these for you. If you really want the client to answer first, use a [queue job with `dispatchAfterResponse`](queue.md).

## A new client for every request

An HTTP client or a Redis client opens connections. If you make one in each request, you open and close a connection every time. Make one client and share it:

```dart title="Wrong"
Future<String> rate(DoxRequest req) async {
  HttpClient client = HttpClient();
  // ...
}
```

```dart title="Right"
class RateService {
  RateService(this._client);

  final HttpClient _client;

  Future<String> rate() async {
    // use _client
  }
}
```

Register the client once in the [container](../the-basic/dependency-injection.md) and inject it. Each isolate makes its own copy, which is fine.

## A long transaction

A transaction holds one database connection until it ends. If you call an outside API inside it, the connection waits for that API. When many requests do this, the pool runs out of connections. Do the slow call before or after the transaction:

```dart title="Wrong"
await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  await order.save();
  await paymentApi.charge(order); // the connection waits here
});
```

```dart title="Right"
await paymentApi.charge(order);
await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  await order.save();
});
```

## Reading a big file into memory

`bytes` loads the whole upload into memory. A big download read into a variable does the same. Stream both. See [Request](../the-basic/request.md#requestfile) and [Files and big responses](../the-basic/response.md#files-and-big-responses):

```dart title="Wrong"
List<int> data = await file.bytes;
```

```dart title="Right"
Stream<List<int>> data = file.stream();
```

Keep `maxBodySize` and `maxMultipartSize` set, so a huge body gets `413` before Dart reads it. See [Size limits](../the-basic/request.md#size-limits).

## Timers and listeners that never stop

On a long connection, like server-sent events or a WebSocket, a `Timer.periodic` or a stream listener keeps running after the client leaves. Keep it and cancel it when the connection closes:

```dart
StreamSubscription<Event> subscription = events.listen(send);
// when the client disconnects
await subscription.cancel();
```

## Let Dox warn you

Strict mode finds the worst mistakes while you develop. It writes a warning, and it never throws or changes the response. It is off by default, and when it is off it costs nothing.

### Strict mode in Dox

Set `strict` in `AppConfig`. Turn it on only in development:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  strict: StrictConfig(enabled: Env.appEnv == 'development'),
  // ...
);
```

Warnings go to stderr with a `[strict]` tag. `blockLimit` is how long code may block the isolate, 50 ms by default. To change it, use `StrictConfig(enabled: true, blockLimit: Duration(milliseconds: 100))`.

A route that blocks the isolate for too long warns once:

```text
[strict] GET /invoices/{id} blocked the isolate for 180 ms (limit 50 ms). Other requests on this isolate had to wait. Move heavy CPU work (like bcrypt, PDF or image work) to await Dox().compute(...), and use Hash.makeAsync or Hash.verifyAsync for passwords.
```

Code that blocks the event loop, also after an `await`, warns at most once in 10 seconds. It cannot tell you which code did it:

```text
[strict] The event loop of isolate 1 was blocked for about 120 ms (limit 50 ms). Some code ran that long without an await, so other requests had to wait. Move heavy CPU work to await Dox().compute(...).
```

`Hash.make`, `Hash.verify` and `Hash.check` in the web server warn once for each place in your code:

```text
[strict] Hash.make ran in the web server at AuthController.register (package:my_app/app/http/controllers/auth_controller.dart:21:18). It blocks the isolate while bcrypt runs, so other requests wait. Use await Hash.makeAsync(...) instead.
```

### Strict mode in the ORM

Set `strict` in `DatabaseConfig`:

```dart title="lib/config/database.dart"
DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  // ...
  strict: OrmStrict(enabled: appConfig.isDevelopment),
);
```

`nPlusOneCount` (default 5) is how many row by row loads of one relation in about one second make a warning. `maxRows` (default 1000) is how many rows `get()` or `all()` may read. The warnings are printed with a `[db]` tag:

```text
[db] Strict mode: possible N+1 query. The relation "author" of Post was loaded row by row 5 times in a short time. Load it for all rows in one query with preload('author').
```

```text
[db] Strict mode: table "orders" read 25000 rows into memory (the limit is 1000). Use paginate(), chunk(), lazy() or cursor() for big results.
```


---

# Testing

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/testing/

# Testing

This page shows how to test a Dox app with the `test` package: HTTP routes, cache, storage, env and the database.

Dox starts your real app inside the test, so you can send requests to it and check the answers. Helpers for the cache, storage and the database let each test start from a clean state.

## Setup

A new app from `dox create` already has the `test` package. In another app, add it as a dev dependency:

```bash
dart pub add dev:test
```

Put your tests in the `test/` folder and run them with `dart test`:

```bash
dart test
```

### Creating a test

Use `dox make:test` to make a test file. It writes `test/ping_test.dart`, which already starts the app with a `DoxTestClient`:

```bash
dox make:test Ping
```

If the test does not need the app, add `--unit` to get a plain test. See [`dox make:test`](../reference/cli.md#dox-maketest).

## Test HTTP routes

`DoxTestClient` from `package:dox_core/testing.dart` starts your app inside the test and sends requests to it. Start it once in `setUpAll` and close it in `tearDownAll`:

```dart title="test/http_test.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/testing.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

void main() {
  late DoxTestClient client;

  setUpAll(() async {
    client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig);
  });

  tearDownAll(() async {
    await client.close();
  });

  test('GET /api/ping', () async {
    TestResponse res = await client.get('/api/ping');
    res.expectStatus(200).expectBody('pong');
  });

  test('POST /api/posts', () async {
    TestResponse res = await client.post(
      '/api/posts',
      body: <String, dynamic>{'title': 'Hello', 'body': 'My first post.'},
    );
    res.expectStatus(201).expectJson(containsPair('title', 'Hello'));
  });
}
```

`DoxTestClient.start(appConfig)` runs your providers and adds your routes, the same as a real start. `client.close()` stops the server and runs `shutdown()` of every provider, so for example the database is closed.

### Making requests

The client has `get`, `post`, `put`, `patch` and `delete`. The path can have a query, like `'/api/users?page=2'`. For any other method, use `send`:

```dart
await client.get('/api/users?page=2');
await client.send('OPTIONS', '/api/users');
```

A `Map` or `List` body is sent as JSON. A `String` or `List<int>` body is sent as it is.

Redirects are not followed, so you can check a `302` and its `Location` header.

### Sending headers

To send extra headers with one request, pass `headers:`. If every request needs them, use `withHeaders`. It gives a copy of the client that sends these headers each time:

```dart
await client.get('/api/me', headers: <String, String>{'Accept-Language': 'de'});

DoxTestClient german = client.withHeaders(<String, String>{'Accept-Language': 'de'});
```

### Log in as a user

If your API uses tokens, log in first, then use `withToken`. It gives a copy of the client that sends `Authorization: Bearer <token>`:

```dart
TestResponse login = await client.post(
  '/api/auth/login',
  body: <String, dynamic>{'email': 'ann@example.com', 'password': 'secret123'},
);
DoxTestClient ann = client.withToken(login.json['token'] as String);
(await ann.get('/api/auth/me')).expectStatus(200);
```

### Keep a session (cookies and CSRF)

Web pages with forms use a session cookie and a CSRF token. `client.withSession()` gives a client that works like a browser. It keeps the cookies of every response and sends them back. On `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` and `DELETE` it sends the `XSRF-TOKEN` cookie in the `X-XSRF-TOKEN` header, so `CsrfMiddleware` lets the request in:

```dart
test('log in with a form', () async {
  DoxTestClient browser = client.withSession();

  // the first page gives the session and XSRF-TOKEN cookies
  (await browser.get('/login')).expectStatus(200);

  (await browser.post(
    '/login',
    body: <String, dynamic>{'email': 'ann@example.com', 'password': 'secret123'},
  )).expectStatus(303).expectHeader('location', '/dashboard');

  (await browser.get('/dashboard')).expectStatus(200);
});
```

Each `withSession()` call gives a new browser with no cookies. You can read and change the kept cookies in `browser.cookies` (name to raw value).

The normal client keeps no cookies. To send the cookies of one response once, use `withCookies(res.cookies)`.

## Checking the response

A `TestResponse` has the status, body and headers:

```dart
int status = res.status;
String body = res.body;
dynamic json = res.json; // the body read as JSON
String? type = res.header('content-type'); // any case
```

`res.headers` has all headers, with lower case names.

The `expect` methods fail the test when the response is not right. They return the response, so you can chain them:

```dart
res
    .expectStatus(422)
    .expectHeader('content-type', contains('application/json'))
    .expectJson(<String, dynamic>{'title': 'The title is required'});
```

### Checking the status

`expectStatus` fails when the status is another one. The message shows the body, so you can see what went wrong:

```dart
res.expectStatus(200);
```

### Checking JSON

`expectJson` takes a value or a matcher. Use a `Map` for the whole body, or a matcher to check only one part:

```dart
res.expectJson(containsPair('id', 1));
```

### Checking the body

`expectBody` checks the body as text:

```dart
res.expectBody('pong');
```

### Checking a header

`expectHeader` takes a header name and a value or matcher. Use `isNull` to check that a header is not there:

```dart
res.expectHeader('location', '/dashboard');
res.expectHeader('set-cookie', isNull);
```

## Test the cache

Tests should not write cache files or need Redis. So replace `Dox().cache` with a memory store. `Cache()` uses `Dox().cache`, so your code then uses the memory store:

```dart
setUp(() {
  Dox().cache = CacheManager(CacheConfig(
    defaultStore: 'memory',
    stores: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
      'memory': <String, dynamic>{'driver': 'memory'},
    },
  ));
});

test('caches the posts', () async {
  await Cache().put('posts', <String>['a', 'b']);
  expect(await Cache().get('posts'), <dynamic>['a', 'b']);
});
```

Because the new `CacheManager` is made in `setUp`, each test starts with an empty cache. See [Cache](cache.md).

## Test file storage

If your code saves files, you do not want the test to write to S3 or your disk. `Storage.manager.fake(name)` from `dox_storage` swaps one disk with an empty memory disk. `restore(name)` puts the real disk back:

```dart
setUpAll(() {
  Dox().initialize(appConfig);
});

test('saves the report', () async {
  Disk fake = Storage.manager.fake('s3');

  String path = await Storage()
      .disk('s3')
      .putFile('reports', <int>[1, 2, 3], extension: 'pdf'); // '/reports/<uuid>.pdf'

  expect(await fake.exists(path.substring(1)), isTrue);
  Storage.manager.restore('s3');
});
```

Call `Dox().initialize()` first. Without the `StorageProvider`, `Storage.manager` has only the `local` disk.

`Storage()` paths start with `/`, but a `Disk` key does not. So remove the first `/` when you ask the `Disk` directly.

A disk also has `assertExists(key)` and `assertMissing(key)`. They throw a `StateError` when the check fails:

```dart
await fake.assertExists('reports/a.pdf');
```

See [File Storage](file-storage.md).

## Use a test database with `.env.testing`

Your tests should never use the database with your real data. Put the values for tests in a `.env.testing` file, next to `.env`:

```ini title=".env.testing"
DB_NAME=my_app_test
CACHE_STORE=memory
```

When the app runs its tests (`dart test`, or `APP_ENV=testing`), Dox reads `.env` first and then `.env.testing`. A key in `.env.testing` wins over the same key in `.env`. Keys that are only in `.env` stay.

A real environment variable still wins over both files. So CI can run `DB_NAME=ci_test dart test`. Outside tests, `.env.testing` is never read.

## Test the database

A test that uses models needs a real database. Run the migrations once in `setUpAll`. Then empty the tables before each test with `refreshDatabase()` from `package:dox_orm/testing.dart`:

```dart title="test/user_test.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/testing.dart';
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/testing.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

import '../db/migration/migrations.dart';

void main() {
  late DoxTestClient client;

  setUpAll(() async {
    await Migrator(
      migrations: migrations,
      config: databaseConfig.getConnectionConfig(),
    ).migrate();
    client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig); // runs the ORM provider
  });

  // every test starts with empty tables
  setUp(refreshDatabase);

  tearDownAll(() async {
    await client.close();
  });

  test('register makes a user', () async {
    TestResponse res = await client.post(
      '/api/auth/register',
      body: <String, dynamic>{
        'name': 'Ann',
        'email': 'ann@example.com',
        'password': 'secret123',
      },
    );
    res.expectStatus(201);
  });
}
```

`refreshDatabase()` empties every table and starts the ids at 1 again. The tables stay, and the rows of the migrations table (`dox_db_migration`) are kept. It works on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite.

Use a separate test database, set in [`.env.testing`](#use-a-test-database-with-envtesting). Never run `refreshDatabase()` on a database with real data.

### Keeping some tables

If a table holds data that every test needs, like a list of countries, pass it in `keep`:

```dart
refreshDatabase(keep: <String>['dox_db_migration', 'countries']);
```

See [Testing with a database](../guides/testing-with-database.md) for a full example with SQLite.

### Running test files one by one

`dart test` runs test files at the same time. When two files use the same tables, they can break each other. So run them one by one:

```bash
dart test --concurrency=1
```

## Test the env

Sometimes you want to test code that reads the env, or test that the app stops on a bad env. Pass your own values to `AppEnv.load()`. Then nothing is read from the shell or the `.env` file:

```dart
AppEnv env = AppEnv.load(
  EnvReader(
    environment: <String, String>{'APP_KEY': 'test'},
    dotEnv: <String, String>{'DB_PORT': '5433'},
  ),
);
expect(env.dbPort, 5433);
```

A missing or bad key throws an `EnvException`. See [Environment Variables](env.md).

Only the getters read through the `EnvReader`. A getter default that calls `Env.get()` or `Platform.environment` reads the real env. So in a default, use other getters, like `appEnv == 'development'`.

## Details

- The test server listens on `127.0.0.1` on a free port. So it does not clash with `dox serve`, and many test files can run at the same time.
- It runs on one isolate. `serverPort` and `totalIsolate` of the config are not used. Because of this, a `Route.get(...)` you add inside a test works right away.
- The session client removes a cookie when the response deletes it (an empty value, `Max-Age=0` or an old `Expires`). A copy made from it, for example with `withHeaders`, shares its cookies.
- Without the server, you can set the disks yourself with `Storage.manager = StorageDiskFactory().create(storageConfig);`, and start the ORM with `SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(databaseConfig)`.
- `refreshDatabase()` turns off foreign key checks while it empties the tables.
- `.env.testing` is also read by the typed `AppEnv.load()`, not only by `Env.get()`.

# Health check

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/digging-deeper/health-check/

# Health check

A health route tells a load balancer, Docker or Kubernetes if the app can serve requests.

The load balancer calls the route every few seconds. If the answer is not `200`, it stops sending traffic to this server, or it restarts it.

## Adding the route

Add `Route.health` in `register()` of a router:

```dart title="lib/routes/web.dart"
@override
void register() {
  Route.get('/ping', (WebController c) => c.pong);
  Route.health('/health');
}
```

`GET /health` answers `200` with:

```json
{"status": "ok"}
```

The route gets the middleware of its router and the global middleware. So put `Route.health` in a router with no auth middleware, or the health check gets `401`.

## Checking the database and the cache

The app may run, but its database may be down. To check this, give named checks. Each check is a function:

```dart title="lib/routes/web.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

Route.health(
  '/health',
  checks: <String, HealthCheckFunction>{
    'database': () => QueryBuilder.query('select 1'),
    'cache': HealthCheck.cache(),
  },
);
```

When all checks pass, the answer is `200`:

```json
{"status": "ok", "checks": {"database": "ok", "cache": "ok"}}
```

When one check fails, the answer is `503 Service Unavailable`:

```json
{"status": "fail", "checks": {"database": "fail", "cache": "ok"}}
```

A check fails when it throws an error, returns `false`, or takes longer than the timeout. The checks run at the same time.

`HealthCheck.cache()` writes a key to the default cache store and reads it back. `HealthCheck.cache('redis')` checks the store with that name. Any other check is your own function, like a call to another API.

## Changing the timeout

A check fails after 5 seconds by default. Use `timeout` to change it:

```dart
Route.health(
  '/health',
  timeout: Duration(seconds: 2),
  checks: <String, HealthCheckFunction>{
    'database': () => QueryBuilder.query('select 1'),
  },
);
```

## Seeing why a check failed

The error of a failed check goes to `exceptionHandler.report()`, so you see it in your logs.

The answer has the error text (in `errors`) only when `APP_ENV` is `development` or `local`. In other envs the text is left out, because it can show hosts or user names.

## See also

- [Docker](../guides/docker.md) for a health check in the image
- [Deployment](deployment.md)


---

# Database

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/database/

# Database

Connect Dox to Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB or SQLite with the `dox_orm` package.

Almost every web app keeps its data in a database. Dox gives you two ways to work with it:

- The [query builder](query-builder.md) builds SQL with methods, like `QueryBuilder.table('blog').where('id', 1).get()`.
- [Models](model/index.md) give you one class per table, with relations and events.

You can also run [transactions](transactions.md), and create and change tables with [migrations](migration.md) and the [schema builder](schema.md).

## Installation

A new app already has `dox_orm`. To add it to an app, run:

```bash
dox add orm --driver=sqlite
```

`--driver` is `sqlite` (the default), `postgres` or `mysql`. The command adds `dox_orm` and `dox_migration`, writes `lib/config/database.dart`, the ORM provider, `bin/migrate.dart` and `db/migration/`, and adds the `DB_*` keys to `.env`. It also turns off the build of the drivers you do not use (see [Skip unused drivers](#skip-unused-drivers)). It never overwrites a file, so it is safe to run twice. See [Add a package](../getting-started/add-a-package.md).

If you only want the package, run `dart pub add dox_orm` and import it:

```dart
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
```

## Supported databases

| Database | `Driver` | Driver | Pool | Good for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Postgres | `Driver.postgres` | [`dox_postgres_native`](postgres-native.md) | Yes | Production |
| MySQL 8+ and MariaDB | `Driver.mysql` | [`dox_mysql_native`](mysql-native.md) | Yes | Production |
| SQLite | `Driver.sqlite` | `sqlite3` | No, one connection per isolate | Development, tests, small apps |

Postgres and MySQL use a native (Rust) driver, and there is no other driver. If the native library can not load, the app stops with an error. See the [Postgres](postgres-native.md#when-the-library-does-not-load) and [MySQL](mysql-native.md#when-the-library-does-not-load) pages.

## Configuration

Put your connections in `lib/config/database.dart`. `connection` is the name of the default connection:

```dart title="lib/config/database.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  connection: env.dbConnection,
  connections: <String, ConnectionConfig>{
    'postgres': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.postgres,
      host: env.dbHost,
      port: env.dbPort ?? 5432,
      user: env.dbUsername,
      password: env.dbPassword,
      database: env.dbName,
      extra: <String, dynamic>{'maxConnectionCount': 10},
      debug: appConfig.isDevelopment,
    ),
    'mysql': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.mysql, // also for MariaDB
      host: env.dbHost,
      port: env.dbPort ?? 3306,
      user: env.dbUsername,
      password: env.dbPassword,
      database: env.dbName,
      extra: <String, dynamic>{'maxConnectionCount': 10},
      debug: appConfig.isDevelopment,
    ),
    'sqlite': ConnectionConfig(
      driver: Driver.sqlite,
      database: env.dbName, // file path, like db/dox.sqlite, or ':memory:'
      debug: appConfig.isDevelopment,
    ),
  },
);
```

`env` is the typed env of the app, in `lib/config/env.dart`. Change `my_app` to the name of your app in `pubspec.yaml`. SQLite does not use `user`, `password`, `host` or `port`.

`debug: true` prints each SQL query with its values put in, so you can copy it and run it in psql, mysql or the sqlite CLI. The app template turns it on only in development:

```
▌ [db:default] SELECT * FROM "users" WHERE "email" = 'a@b.com' LIMIT 1;
```

### Environment values

The app config and the [migration](migration.md) commands read these keys from `.env`:

```py title=".env"
DB_CONNECTION=postgres # postgres, mysql or sqlite
DB_HOST=localhost
DB_PORT=5432           # 3306 for mysql
DB_NAME=dox            # for sqlite: the file path, like db/dox.sqlite
DB_USERNAME=postgres
DB_PASSWORD=postgres
```

### Starting the ORM

The ORM starts in a provider. The app template already has this file:

```dart title="lib/providers/orm_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';

class ORMProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  Future<void> setup() async {
    SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig(databaseConfig);
  }

  /// Close the database connections when the server stops.
  @override
  Future<void> shutdown() async {
    await SqlQueryBuilder.close();
  }
}
```

Dox finds every `DoxProvider` class on its own. After you add a provider, run `dart run build_runner build`.

Each isolate runs the provider. Isolates with the same settings share one pool, so `maxConnectionCount` is for the whole process, not for one isolate.

### `DATABASE_URL`

Many hosts (Fly, Render, Heroku and others) give you one database url. Dox reads it from the `DATABASE_URL` key, in `.env` or in the shell. If both have it, the shell wins.

When `DATABASE_URL` is set, it wins over the config of the default connection. That config still gives `debug`, `printer`, `slowQueryMs` and `extra`. Other named connections do not change.

```bash
DATABASE_URL=postgres://app:s%40cret@db.example.com:5432/blog?sslmode=require
```

| Form | Database |
|---|---|
| `postgres://user:pass@host:5432/db` or `postgresql://...` | Postgres |
| `mysql://user:pass@host:3306/db` or `mariadb://...` | MySQL, MariaDB |
| `sqlite:///abs/path.db`, `sqlite://db/dox.sqlite`, `sqlite::memory:`, `file:db/dox.sqlite` | SQLite |

The app passes the url in through the env class, so the app and `dox migrate` use the same url:

```dart title="lib/config/env.dart"
String? get databaseUrl;
```

```dart title="lib/config/database.dart"
DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  url: env.databaseUrl,
  connection: env.dbConnection,
  connections: {...},
);
```

If your `lib/config/database.dart` has no `url: env.databaseUrl` line, Dox reads `DATABASE_URL` only from the shell, not from `.env`. An empty `url` (`url: ''`) turns `DATABASE_URL` off.

Some rules for the url:

- The user, password and database name are url-decoded. Write `@` in a password as `%40`.
- With no port, Postgres uses `5432` and MySQL uses `3306`.
- For Postgres, `sslmode` works like libpq (`disable`, `prefer`, `require`, `verify-ca`, `verify-full`). `require` does not check the certificate, so use `verify-full` when your host supports it. See [Postgres TLS](postgres-native.md#tls).
- For MySQL, `ssl=true` (or `sslmode=require`) turns TLS on and checks the certificate. Add `verifyCertificate=false` to skip the check, only for a self-signed certificate in development.
- `host=/path` (or `socket=/path`) connects to a Unix socket. See [Unix socket](#unix-socket).
- Any other option goes to `extra`, like `?maxConnectionCount=20`. A number becomes an `int`, and `true` and `false` become a `bool`. This works for SQLite too, like `sqlite://db/dox.sqlite?background=true`.

To make one `ConnectionConfig` from a url, use `ConnectionConfig.fromUrl(url)`.

### Unix socket

Some hosts, like Google Cloud SQL on Cloud Run, give you a Unix socket instead of a network host. A host that starts with `/` is a Unix socket:

```bash
DB_HOST=/cloudsql/my-project:europe-west1:blog
# or
DATABASE_URL=postgres://blog:secret@/blog?host=/cloudsql/my-project:europe-west1:blog
```

For Postgres, the host is the socket folder, like in libpq. The driver uses the socket file `<folder>/.s.PGSQL.<port>`. A host that already ends with `/.s.PGSQL.5432` works too.

For MySQL and MariaDB, the host is the socket file itself, and the port is not used. On Cloud SQL the socket file is `/cloudsql/PROJECT:REGION:INSTANCE`. A local server often uses `/var/run/mysqld/mysqld.sock` or `/tmp/mysql.sock`:

```bash
DB_CONNECTION=mysql
DB_HOST=/var/run/mysqld/mysqld.sock
# or
DATABASE_URL=mysql://app:secret@/app?socket=/var/run/mysqld/mysqld.sock
```

In the url, `?socket=` and `?host=` do the same thing.

### Pool settings

Postgres and MySQL keep a pool of connections. You can set how long the pool waits and how long it keeps a connection, in the `extra` map. A time is a `Duration` or a number of seconds, so `?requestTimeout=30` in `DATABASE_URL` works too:

```dart
extra: <String, dynamic>{
  'maxConnectionCount': 10,
  'requestTimeout': const Duration(seconds: 30),
  'maxConnectionAge': const Duration(minutes: 30),
  'idleTimeout': const Duration(minutes: 5),
  'serverKill': false, // MySQL only
},
```

- `maxConnectionCount` (default `10`): the most connections in the pool.
- `requestTimeout` (default 300 s): the longest wait for one request. A request is getting a free connection, connecting and running the query. If it takes longer, it fails and its connection is closed. A transaction with no request for this long is rolled back.
- `maxConnectionAge` (default: no limit on Postgres, 12 hours on MySQL): a connection older than this is closed and opened again. It is never closed while it runs a query or a transaction. This helps behind a load balancer, or after a database failover.
- `idleTimeout` (default: no limit on Postgres, 12 hours on MySQL): a free connection that is not used for this long is closed.
- `serverKill` (MySQL, default `true`): the server stops a cancelled or timed out query with `KILL QUERY`. Set it to `false` behind a proxy like ProxySQL, because the `KILL` may reach another server. Then a cancelled query stops in Dart at once, but it runs to its end on the server.

To stop one query by hand, see [Cancel a query](query-builder.md#cancelling-a-query). All other `extra` keys are in [All `extra` options](#all-extra-options).

## Skip unused drivers

`dox_orm` brings all three drivers, and the build downloads a native library for each one. Your app needs only the driver of its database. To skip the others, add a `hooks: user_defines:` block to the `pubspec.yaml` of your app. In a pub workspace, put it in the root `pubspec.yaml`, because Dart reads `user_defines` only from the root package.

`skip: true` turns off the download of a driver. Only the bool `true` skips, any other value does nothing.

A new app uses SQLite, and its `pubspec.yaml` already has this block:

```yaml title="pubspec.yaml"
hooks:
  user_defines:
    dox_postgres_native:
      skip: true
    dox_mysql_native:
      skip: true
```

For a Postgres app:

```yaml title="pubspec.yaml"
hooks:
  user_defines:
    dox_mysql_native:
      skip: true
    sqlite3:
      source: system
```

For a MySQL app:

```yaml title="pubspec.yaml"
hooks:
  user_defines:
    dox_postgres_native:
      skip: true
    sqlite3:
      source: system
```

`sqlite3: source: system` comes from the `sqlite3` package. The build does not download SQLite, and the app loads the `libsqlite3` library of the system when it opens SQLite. So if your app does open SQLite, remove these lines: a system without `libsqlite3`, like the `FROM scratch` Docker image, fails then.

When you switch to another database, remove the `skip` line of the driver you now use, and run `dart pub get`. A driver that is still skipped stops the app when it opens a pool. The error tells you to remove `skip`.

## Running raw queries

Sometimes the query builder can not build the SQL you need. `QueryBuilder.query()` runs your own SQL on the default connection. Use `@name` for values, so they are sent as bound parameters and are safe from SQL injection:

```dart
List<Map<String, dynamic>> rows = await QueryBuilder.query(
  'select * from blog where id = @id',
  substitutionValues: <String, dynamic>{'id': 1},
);
```

Pass `connection` to run it on another connection:

```dart
await QueryBuilder.query('select 1', connection: 'mysql');
```

## Using other connections

If your app has more than one connection, use `withConnection()` with a connection name from the config:

```dart
List<Map<String, dynamic>> rows = await QueryBuilder.table('blog')
    .withConnection('mysql')
    .get();
```

A model keeps its connection, so `save()` and `delete()` use it. Models that a query returns use the connection of the query:

```dart
Blog blog = Blog()..withConnection('mysql');
blog.title = 'Hello';
await blog.save(); // saved on 'mysql'
```

## Listen to queries

If you want metrics or your own query log, `SqlQueryBuilder().listen()` runs your function after each query. It works on every connection and inside transactions:

```dart
void onQuery(QueryEvent e) {
  print('${e.connection} ${e.time.inMilliseconds} ms: ${e.sql}');
}

SqlQueryBuilder().listen(onQuery);
```

A `QueryEvent` has:

- `sql`: the SQL text, with `@name` for each value.
- `bindings`: the values. A value named in `logRedact` shows as `***`.
- `time`: how long the query took, a `Duration`.
- `connection`: the name of the connection.

The function runs only after a query that worked, because the error of a failed query goes to your code. If the function throws, Dox logs the error and the query still returns its rows. `SqlQueryBuilder().removeListener(onQuery)` stops it.

### Slow query log

To find slow queries in production, set `slowQueryMs` on a connection. Dox then logs each query that takes longer than that many milliseconds. It is off by default, and it works with `debug` off:

```dart
'postgres': ConnectionConfig(
  driver: Driver.postgres,
  // ...
  debug: appConfig.isDevelopment,
  slowQueryMs: 500,
),
```

The line goes to the query `printer`, with the connection name, the time and the SQL:

```
▌ [db:postgres SLOW 812ms] SELECT * FROM "orders" WHERE "user_id" = 42;
```

Set `slowQueryMs` to `0` to log every query. A failed query is not logged here.

## ORM flags

`OrmFlags` turns on opt-in ORM behaviors. Each flag is off by default, and with all flags off the ORM works as the database pages say. Pass the flags as `flags:` in `DatabaseConfig`. A new app can start with `OrmFlags.all()`, which turns on every flag:

```dart title="lib/config/database.dart"
DatabaseConfig databaseConfig = DatabaseConfig(
  connection: env.dbConnection,
  connections: <String, ConnectionConfig>{ /* ... */ },
  flags: OrmFlags.all(), // every flag on
);
```

To turn on only some flags, name them:

```dart
flags: const OrmFlags(pluralTableNames: true, sumReturnsZero: true),
```

| Flag | Off (default) | On |
|---|---|---|
| `skipCleanUpdateEvents` | `save()` with no changes fires `saving`, `updating`, `updated` and `saved`. | It fires only `saving` and `saved`. A model with a `Map` or `List` field always counts as changed. A save with changes runs `beforeSave` two times, and a save with no changes runs it one time. |
| `belongsToKeyFromRelation` | The default `belongsTo` foreign key comes from the class name: `@BelongsTo(User) User? author` uses `user_id`. | It comes from the relation name: `author_id`. |
| `pluralTableNames` | The default table name is singular: `User` uses `user`. | It is plural, with English plural rules: `users`, `blog_posts`, `categories`. |
| `createWritesNull` | `create()` does not send a `null` key, so the column default is used. | It writes `NULL` for a key that is `null` in the map. |
| `sumReturnsZero` | `sum()` gives `null` when no row matches. | It gives `0`. |
| `selectRawAdds` | `selectRaw()` replaces the select list. | It adds to it, so `select('a').selectRaw('count(*) as c')` selects both. |
| `groupByAdds` | A second `groupBy()` replaces the first. | It adds to the first. `groupByRaw()` too. |
| `lastPageAtLeastOne` | `paginate()` gives `lastPage` `0` when there are no rows. | It gives `1`. |
| `updateSetsUpdatedAt` | A model query `update()`, like `Blog().where('id', 1).update({...})`, does not touch `updated_at`. | It sets `updated_at`, unless the data already has it. |
| `incrementFiresEvents` | `increment()` and `decrement()` on a model do not fire events or set `updated_at`. | They fire `saving`, `updating`, `updated` and `saved`, and set `updated_at`. A hook that cancels stops the write. |
| `preloadUnknownThrows` | `preload('typo')` loads nothing, with no error. | It throws an `ArgumentError`. With a dot path, each level is checked. |
| `toJsonLoadedRelations` | `toJson()` has only the relations named in `preload()`. | It also has the relations loaded with `$getRelation()`. |
| `laravelPostgresTypes` | On Postgres, `timestamps()` and `softDeletes()` make `TIMESTAMPTZ`, and `json()` makes `JSONB`. | A new table gets `TIMESTAMP` and `JSON`. |

`bin/migrate.dart` does not start the ORM, so give the flags to the migrator too: `Migrator(migrations: migrations, flags: databaseConfig.flags)`. See [Migration](migration.md#database-settings).

## SQLite

SQLite is good for development, tests and small apps. For a busy production app, use Postgres or MySQL.

You do not install SQLite on your system, because the `sqlite3` package bundles it with a build hook. For the AOT binary, use `dox build`. It puts the library in `build/bundle/lib/`, next to `build/bundle/bin/server`, so keep the two folders together. `dart compile exe` does not work with build hooks. See [Deployment](../digging-deeper/deployment.md).

SQLite has no bool, JSON or date type, so Dox converts them for you:

- `boolean()` is saved as `0`/`1` and read back as `bool`.
- `json()` is saved as text and read back as `Map` or `List`.
- Dates are saved as ISO text in UTC and read back as `DateTime`.

This works for tables made by `Schema`, or by SQL with the same type names (`BOOLEAN`, `JSON`, `TIMESTAMP`, `DATE`, `DATETIME`). A column with an alias (`active as is_active`) is not converted.

Schema limits, like `change()`, `dropColumn` and `NOT NULL` columns, are in [SQLite notes](schema.md#sqlite-notes).

### Run queries in a helper isolate

A SQLite query blocks the isolate while it runs, so one slow query stops every other request on that isolate. Set `background` to `true` to run the queries in a helper isolate instead. Your isolate only waits for the answer, so it keeps serving other requests:

```dart
'sqlite': ConnectionConfig(
  driver: Driver.sqlite,
  database: 'db/dox.sqlite',
  debug: false,
  extra: {'background': true},
),
```

With `DATABASE_URL`, add `?background=true`, like `sqlite://db/dox.sqlite?background=true`.

Each query costs one message to the helper isolate and one back. So turn it on when some queries are slow, like a big report or a search with no index. Leave it off when the app runs many tiny queries, because they get a little slower.

## MySQL and MariaDB

The driver is [`dox_mysql_native`](mysql-native.md). Its page lists how values are converted.
