Dox has no fake data generator, but the [faker](https://pub.dev/packages/faker) package works well with factories:

```bash
dart pub add faker
```

```dart title="db/factories/user.factory.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/factory.dart';
import 'package:faker/faker.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

class UserFactory extends Factory<User> {
  @override
  User definition() {
    return User()
      ..name = faker.person.name()
      ..email = faker.internet.email();
  }
}
```

## Creating models

### Saving models

Use `create` to make models and save them. `count` sets how many you get, and the default is 1:

```dart
List<User> users = await UserFactory().count(10).create();
```

If you want only one model, use `createOne`:

```dart
User user = await UserFactory().createOne();
```

The models are saved one by one with `save()`. So [model events](model/events.md) run, and each model gets its id.

### Making models without saving

Sometimes you need a model but not a row in the database. Use `make` for a list, or `makeOne` for one model:

```dart
User user = UserFactory().makeOne();

List<User> users = UserFactory().count(3).make();
```

## States

A state changes each model after `definition`. Use it when you need a different kind of model, like an admin user. The examples below use a `bool? isAdmin` and a `String? role` field on `User`:

```dart
User admin = await UserFactory()
    .state((User u) => u..isAdmin = true)
    .createOne();
```

You can add more than one state. They run in the order you add them.

If you use a state often, put it in a method on the factory:

```dart
class UserFactory extends Factory<User> {
  @override
  User definition() => User()..name = 'Jane';

  UserFactory admin() {
    state((User u) => u..isAdmin = true);
    return this;
  }
}

List<User> admins = await UserFactory().admin().count(3).create();
```

Call your own methods first, because `count()` and `state()` return a `Factory<User>`, not a `UserFactory`.

### Sequences

Sometimes each model needs a different value. `sequence` is a state that also gets the index of the model: 0, 1, 2 and so on:

```dart
List<User> users = await UserFactory()
    .count(3)
    .sequence((User u, int i) => u..email = 'user$i@example.com')
    .create();
// user0@example.com, user1@example.com, user2@example.com
```

To switch between a few values, use the index:

```dart
List<String> roles = <String>['admin', 'editor'];
await UserFactory()
    .count(4)
    .sequence((User u, int i) => u..role = roles[i % roles.length])
    .create();
```

## Relationships

### Belongs to relationships

To make models that belong to a parent, set the parent key with a state:

```dart
User user = await UserFactory().createOne();

await PostFactory()
    .count(3)
    .state((Post p) => p..userId = user.id)
    .create();
```

### Has many relationships

`has` creates child models for each saved model. The second argument sets the parent on each child:

```dart
List<User> users = await UserFactory()
    .count(2)
    .has(PostFactory().count(3), (Post p, User u) => p..userId = u.id)
    .create();
// 2 users, each with 3 posts
```

`has` only works with `create` and `createOne`. `make` saves nothing, so it makes no children.

## Testing

A factory needs the ORM, so set it up first, the same as in your app. Then create the data your test needs:

```dart
import 'package:test/test.dart';

import '../db/factories/user.factory.dart';

void main() {
  test('lists users', () async {
    await UserFactory().count(3).create();
    // call your route and check the result
  });
}
```

See [Testing with a database](../guides/testing-with-database.md).

## Details

- Each call like `count()` or `state()` changes the factory and returns it. So make a new factory for each set of models.


---

# Seeders

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/database/seeders/

# Seeders

A seeder puts data in your database, like sample data for development or a list of countries your app needs.

## Writing seeders

Use the `make:seeder` command to make a seeder:

```bash
dox make:seeder UserSeeder
```

This makes `db/seeders/user.seeder.dart`. It also writes `db/seeders/seeders.dart`, the list of all seeders, and `bin/seed.dart`, the script that runs them. Do not edit the list, because Dox writes it again on each `make:seeder` and `db:seed`.

A seeder has one method, `run`. Put your code there. You can use [factories](factories.md), models or the [query builder](query-builder.md):

```dart title="db/seeders/user.seeder.dart"
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

import '../factories/user.factory.dart';

class UserSeeder extends Seeder {
  @override
  Future<void> run() async {
    await UserFactory().count(10).create();
  }
}
```

### Calling other seeders

`dox db:seed` runs `DatabaseSeeder` by default. So you use `DatabaseSeeder` to call your other seeders, with the `call` method:

```bash
dox make:seeder DatabaseSeeder
```

```dart title="db/seeders/database.seeder.dart"
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

import 'post.seeder.dart';
import 'user.seeder.dart';

class DatabaseSeeder extends Seeder {
  @override
  Future<void> run() async {
    await call(<Seeder>[UserSeeder(), PostSeeder()]);
  }
}
```

`call` runs the seeders one after another, in the list order.

## Running seeders

Use the `db:seed` command to run `DatabaseSeeder`:

```bash
dox db:seed
```

If you want to run only one seeder, use `--class`:

```bash
dox db:seed --class=UserSeeder
```

You can also seed right after the migrations. Add `--seed` to `migration:run`, `migration:refresh` or `migration:fresh`:

```bash
dox migration:fresh --seed
```

`migration:fresh` drops every table of the database, also tables that no migration made. So do not run it on a production database.

The seeders use the same database as the migrations. See [Database settings](migration.md#database-settings).

### Transactions

A seed runs in one transaction. If a seeder throws an error, nothing is saved, and the command exits with code 1.

On MySQL and MariaDB, `CREATE`, `ALTER` and `DROP TABLE` save right away, and a rollback can not undo them. So keep schema changes in migrations.

A very large seed can turn the transaction off with `withinTransaction`. Only the seeder you run decides this. For `dox db:seed` it is `DatabaseSeeder`:

```dart
class BigSeeder extends Seeder {
  @override
  bool get withinTransaction => false;

  @override
  Future<void> run() async {
    // ...
  }
}
```

## Testing

A seeder is a normal class. In a test, call `run` after you set up the ORM:

```dart
await DatabaseSeeder().run();
```

## Details

### bin/seed.dart

`dox db:seed` runs `dart run bin/seed.dart`. You can run it yourself too, for example in a deploy script:

```bash
dart run bin/seed.dart
dart run bin/seed.dart --class=UserSeeder
```

`bin/seed.dart` is made only when it is missing. `SeederRunner` sets up the ORM, runs the seeder and closes the ORM:

```dart title="bin/seed.dart"
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

import '../db/seeders/seeders.dart';

Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  exitCode = await SeederRunner(seeders: seeders).run(args);
}
```

By default it reads the database from `.env`. Pass `config:` to use your app's database config instead:

```dart
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';

Future<void> main(List<String> args) async {
  exitCode = await SeederRunner(
    seeders: seeders,
    config: databaseConfig,
  ).run(args);
}
```

### Other cases

- `migrate:fresh` and `migrate:refresh` are short names, so `dox migrate:fresh --seed` works too.
- `migration:refresh --seed` undoes all migrations, runs them again, then runs `DatabaseSeeder`. `migration:run --seed` runs the new migrations, then `DatabaseSeeder`.


---

# Schema builder

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/database/schema/

# Schema builder

The schema builder creates, changes and drops tables with Dart code that works on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite.

You mostly use it inside a [migration](migration.md). There, `up` and `down` get a `Schema` that runs on the migration connection:

```dart
await schema.create('posts', (Table table) {
  table.id();
  table.foreignId('user_id').constrained().cascadeOnDelete();
  table.string('title');
  table.text('body').nullable();
  table.enumeration('status', <String>['draft', 'published']).defaultTo('draft');
  table.timestamps();
});
```

If you need a schema outside a migration, `Schema()` uses the query builder connection. You can also give a driver with `Schema(driver)`:

```dart
Schema schema = Schema();
await schema.dropIfExists('posts');
```

## Tables

### Creating tables

Use `create` to make a new table. The second argument is a function that adds the columns. It fails when the table already exists:

```dart
await schema.create('users', (Table table) {
  table.id();
  table.string('email');
});
```

### Updating tables

Use `table` to change a table that exists. You can add columns, change columns and add keys:

```dart
await schema.table('users', (Table table) {
  table.string('avatar').nullable();
});
```

### Renaming and dropping tables

Use `rename` to rename a table:

```dart
await schema.rename('posts', 'articles');
```

Use `drop` to drop a table. It fails when the table is missing, so use `dropIfExists` if the table may not be there:

```dart
await schema.drop('users');

await schema.dropIfExists('users');
```

### Checking tables and columns

Sometimes a migration must check what is already there. `hasTable`, `hasColumn` and `hasColumns` return `true` when the table or columns exist:

```dart
if (await schema.hasTable('users')) {
  // ...
}

if (await schema.hasColumn('users', 'email')) {
  // ...
}

await schema.hasColumns('users', <String>['name', 'email']);
```

`getColumnListing` returns the column names of a table, in order:

```dart
await schema.getColumnListing('users');
```

## Columns

### Available column types

Each column type is a method on `Table`. This table shows the SQL type that each database gets:

| Method | Postgres | MySQL / MariaDB | SQLite |
|---|---|---|---|
| `id()` / `bigIncrements('id')` | `BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY` | `BIGINT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY` | `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT` |
| `increments('id')` | `SERIAL PRIMARY KEY` | `INT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY` | `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT` |
| `string('c', [255])` | `VARCHAR(n)` | `VARCHAR(n)` | `VARCHAR(n)` |
| `char('c', [255])` | `CHAR(n)` | `CHAR(n)` | `CHAR(n)` |
| `text('c')` | `TEXT` | `TEXT` | `TEXT` |
| `mediumText('c')` | `TEXT` | `MEDIUMTEXT` | `TEXT` |
| `longText('c')` | `TEXT` | `LONGTEXT` | `TEXT` |
| `integer('c')` | `INTEGER` | `INT` | `INTEGER` |
| `bigInteger('c')` | `BIGINT` | `BIGINT` | `INTEGER` |
| `smallInteger('c')` | `SMALLINT` | `SMALLINT` | `INTEGER` |
| `tinyInteger('c')` | `SMALLINT` | `TINYINT` | `INTEGER` |
| `unsignedInteger('c')` (and `unsignedBigInteger`, `unsignedSmallInteger`, `unsignedTinyInteger`) | signed type | `... UNSIGNED` | `INTEGER` |
| `float('c')` | `REAL` | `FLOAT` | `FLOAT` |
| `double('c')` | `DOUBLE PRECISION` | `DOUBLE` | `DOUBLE` |
| `decimal('c', [8], [2])` | `DECIMAL(p, s)` | `DECIMAL(p, s)` | `DECIMAL(p, s)` |
| `boolean('c')` | `BOOLEAN` | `TINYINT(1)` | `BOOLEAN` |
| `date('c')` | `DATE` | `DATE` | `DATE` |
| `dateTime('c')` | `TIMESTAMP` | `DATETIME` | `DATETIME` |
| `dateTimeTz('c')` | `TIMESTAMPTZ` | `DATETIME` | `DATETIME` |
| `time('c')` | `TIME` | `TIME` | `TIME` |
| `timestamp('c')` | `TIMESTAMP` | `TIMESTAMP` | `TIMESTAMP` |
| `timestampTz('c')` | `TIMESTAMPTZ` | `TIMESTAMP` | `TIMESTAMP` |
| `json('c')` / `jsonb('c')` | `JSONB` | `JSON` | `JSON` |
| `uuid(['uuid'])` | `UUID` | `CHAR(36)` | `TEXT` |
| `binary('c')` | `BYTEA` | `BLOB` | `BLOB` |
| `enumeration('c', ['a', 'b'])` | `VARCHAR(255)` + `CHECK` | `ENUM('a', 'b')` | `VARCHAR(255)` + `CHECK` |
| `foreignId('user_id')` | `BIGINT` | `BIGINT UNSIGNED` | `INTEGER` |
| `foreignUuid('user_id')` | `UUID` | `CHAR(36)` | `TEXT` |
| `foreignIdFor(User())` | `BIGINT` | `BIGINT UNSIGNED` | `INTEGER` |
| `ulid(['ulid'])` / `foreignUlid('user_id')` | `CHAR(26)` | `CHAR(26)` | `CHAR(26)` |
| `year('c')` | `INTEGER` | `YEAR` | `INTEGER` |
| `ipAddress(['ip_address'])` | `VARCHAR(45)` | `VARCHAR(45)` | `VARCHAR(45)` |

SQLite has no JSON type. The column is declared as `JSON`, so the SQLite driver knows to decode it when you read it.

### Column helpers

Some columns are needed in many tables, so Dox has helpers for them.

`timestamps` adds nullable `created_at` and `updated_at` columns (`timestampTz`):

```dart
table.timestamps();
```

`softDeletes` adds a nullable `deleted_at` column (`timestampTz`). You need it for models with `softDelete: true`:

```dart
table.softDeletes();
```

`morphs` adds the columns for a [polymorphic relation](model/relationship/polymorphic.md): `owner_id` (unsigned big integer), `owner_type` (string), and one index on both. Use `nullableMorphs` if both columns can be `NULL`, or `uuidMorphs` for a uuid `owner_id`:

```dart
table.morphs('owner');
```

`rememberToken` adds a nullable `remember_token` `VARCHAR(100)` column:

```dart
table.rememberToken();
```

### Column modifiers

Modifiers come after the column type, and you can chain them:

```dart
table.string('email').nullable().unique();
```

| Modifier | What it does |
|---|---|
| `nullable()` | Allow `NULL`. Columns are `NOT NULL` by default. `nullable(false)` makes it `NOT NULL` again. |
| `defaultTo(value)` | Set a default value. Strings are escaped, so any text is safe. `bool`, numbers, `null`, `Map`/`List` (saved as JSON) and `DateTime` work too. `withDefault` does the same. |
| `defaultRaw('sql')` | Set the default as raw SQL. It is **not** escaped. Put expressions in `( )`, like `defaultRaw('(1 + 1)')`, because MySQL and SQLite need it. |
| `useCurrent()` | Default to the current time. The same as `defaultRaw('CURRENT_TIMESTAMP')`. |
| `useCurrentOnUpdate()` | Set the current time on each update. MySQL only, so on Postgres and SQLite set the time in your code. |
| `unique()` | Add a unique index `{table}_{column}_unique`. |
| `index()` | Add an index `{table}_{column}_index`. |
| `primary()` | Make the column the primary key. |
| `unsigned()` | `UNSIGNED`. MySQL only. |
| `comment('text')` | Add a column comment. Postgres and MySQL only. |
| `collation('utf8mb4_bin')` | Set the column collation, for example so `A` and `a` are two keys. MySQL and MariaDB only, and only on text columns. |
| `after('column')` | Put the new column after another one. MySQL only, and only in `schema.table`. |
| `change()` | Change a column that exists. See [Modifying columns](#modifying-columns). |

### Modifying columns

In `schema.table`, a column is **added** by default. To change a column that exists, add `.change()`:

```dart
await schema.table('posts', (Table table) {
  table.string('title', 500).nullable().defaultTo('x').change();
});
```

`change()` sets the full new column: type, null, default and comment. So give every modifier you want to keep. For example, if the column had a default and you leave out `defaultTo`, the default is gone.

### Renaming columns

Use `renameColumn` to rename a column:

```dart
await schema.table('users', (Table table) {
  table.renameColumn('bio', 'about');
});
```

### Dropping columns

Use `dropColumn` to drop one column, or `dropColumns` to drop many:

```dart
await schema.table('users', (Table table) {
  table.dropColumn('age');
  table.dropColumns(<String>['a', 'b']);
});
```

There are also helpers for the helper columns. `dropTimestamps` drops `created_at` and `updated_at`, and `dropSoftDeletes` drops `deleted_at`:

```dart
table.dropTimestamps();

table.dropSoftDeletes();
```

## Indexes

### Creating indexes

Indexes make lookups fast. You can add one with a modifier on the column:

```dart
table.string('slug').unique();
```

To make an index on more than one column, call the index method on the table. It takes a column name or a list of names:

```dart
table.index(<String>['state', 'created_at']); // posts_state_created_at_index
table.unique('slug');                         // posts_slug_unique
table.primary(<String>['post_id', 'tag_id']); // composite primary key
```

Index names are `{table}_{columns}_{index|unique|foreign}`. To use your own name, give it as the last argument:

```dart
table.unique('slug', 'my_name');
```

### Full text indexes

If you want to search text, use `fullText`. On MySQL it makes a `FULLTEXT` index. On Postgres it makes a `gin` index on `to_tsvector('english', ...)`:

```dart
table.fullText('body'); // posts_body_fulltext
```

### Renaming indexes

Use `renameIndex` with the old and the new name:

```dart
table.renameIndex('posts_slug_unique', 'posts_url_unique');
```

### Dropping indexes

`dropIndex` and `dropUnique` take the columns or the index name:

```dart
table.dropIndex(<String>['state', 'created_at']); // by columns
table.dropUnique('posts_slug_unique');            // or by name
```

Use `dropPrimary` to drop the primary key. On Postgres it takes the name, and the default is `{table}_pkey`. MySQL needs no name:

```dart
table.dropPrimary();
```

### Checking an index

`hasIndex` takes an index name, or a list of its columns:

```dart
await schema.hasIndex('posts', 'posts_slug_unique');             // by name
await schema.hasIndex('posts', <String>['state', 'created_at']); // by columns
```

The list must have all the columns of the index, in the same order.

### Foreign keys

A foreign key makes sure a row only points to a parent row that exists. `foreignId` with `constrained` is the short way to make one:

```dart
table.foreignId('user_id').constrained().cascadeOnDelete();
```

It does the same as this longer form:

```dart
table.foreignId('user_id');
table.foreign('user_id').references('id').on('users').onDelete('cascade');
```

`constrained` guesses the table from the column name: `user_id` becomes `users`, and `category_id` becomes `categories`. Dox models use singular table names by default (`User` is `user`), so if your table is singular, give the name:

```dart
table.foreignId('user_id').constrained('user');
```

If the column can be `NULL`, put `nullable()` before `constrained()`:

```dart
table.foreignId('editor_id').nullable().constrained('users');
```

`foreignIdFor` makes the foreign key column of a model, like `user_id`. Then `constrained` points to the table and primary key of that model. Give a name as the second argument to change the column name:

```dart
table.foreignIdFor(User()).constrained().cascadeOnDelete();
```

`foreignIdFor` is always a big integer. For a model with a text key, use `foreignUuid` or `foreignUlid`.

!!! warning "Same type on both sides"
    `id()` and `foreignId()` are both big integers, so they match. If the parent uses `increments()` (a normal integer), use `unsignedInteger()` for the child on MySQL.

#### Foreign key actions

You can say what happens to the child rows when the parent is deleted or updated. Use `onDelete` and `onUpdate` with `'cascade'`, `'set null'`, `'restrict'` or `'no action'`:

```dart
table.foreign('user_id').references('id').on('users').onDelete('set null');
```

There are also short methods: `cascadeOnDelete()`, `nullOnDelete()`, `restrictOnDelete()`, `cascadeOnUpdate()`, `nullOnUpdate()` and `restrictOnUpdate()`.

#### Dropping foreign keys

`dropForeign` takes the columns or the key name:

```dart
table.dropForeign(<String>['user_id']);

table.dropForeign('posts_user_id_foreign');
```

`dropConstrainedForeignId` drops the foreign key and then the column:

```dart
table.dropConstrainedForeignId('user_id');
```

#### Turning foreign key checks off

Sometimes you must write rows before their parent rows, for example when you copy data. Use `withoutForeignKeyConstraints` for that work. It turns the checks on again after the function, also when it throws:

```dart
await schema.withoutForeignKeyConstraints(() async {
  // the post first, its user later
  await QueryBuilder.table('posts').insert(<String, dynamic>{'user_id': 1, 'title': 'Hi'});
  await QueryBuilder.table('users').insert(<String, dynamic>{'id': 1, 'name': 'Ann'});
});
```

On SQLite, run it outside a transaction. Postgres only waits for keys made `DEFERRABLE`, and Dox keys are not, so on Postgres the keys are still checked. See [Foreign key checks per database](#foreign-key-checks-per-database).

## Details

This section is for special cases. Most apps do not need it.

### Other column notes

- `softDeletesTz` is the same as `softDeletes`, because it is already a time with a zone.
- With the [`laravelPostgresTypes` flag](index.md#orm-flags), a new Postgres table gets `TIMESTAMP` for `timestamps()` and `softDeletes()`, and `JSON` for `json()`.
- MySQL only allows a default on `TEXT`, `BLOB` and `JSON` as an expression. The schema builder writes it as `DEFAULT ('value')` for you.
- `collation` on a non-text column throws an `ArgumentError`. Postgres and SQLite ignore it. Give it again in `.change()`.
- `unsigned`, `comment`, `after` and `useCurrentOnUpdate` are ignored on databases that do not support them. `after` adds the column at the end there.
- `change()` with `unique()` or `index()` adds the index. It fails when the index already exists.
- `change()` runs one `ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE ... USING col::type` on Postgres (with `SET/DROP NOT NULL`, `SET/DROP DEFAULT` and the enum `CHECK` again), `MODIFY COLUMN` on MySQL, and a table rebuild on SQLite.

### Index name rules

- The primary key is named `primary` on MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite. On Postgres it has its real name, like `posts_pkey`.
- `hasIndex` compares names like the database does. MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite ignore the case. Postgres needs the exact case.
- The longest index name is 63 characters on Postgres and 64 on MySQL. SQLite has no limit.

### Foreign key checks per database

`disableForeignKeyConstraints()` and `enableForeignKeyConstraints()` do the same as `withoutForeignKeyConstraints`, in two steps:

```dart
await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  await schema.disableForeignKeyConstraints();
  // ...
  await schema.enableForeignKeyConstraints();
});
```

| Database | SQL | Limits |
|---|---|---|
| SQLite | `PRAGMA foreign_keys = OFF` | It is for the one connection of the isolate, so other code of that isolate is not checked either while it is off. Inside a transaction it does nothing. |
| MySQL, MariaDB | `SET FOREIGN_KEY_CHECKS = 0` | It is a setting of one pool connection, so `disable` and `enable` must run inside a transaction, else they throw a `StateError`. Turn the checks on again before the transaction ends. |
| Postgres | `SET CONSTRAINTS ALL DEFERRED` | Only keys made `DEFERRABLE` wait, and only until the checks are on again. It must run inside a transaction too. |

- On MySQL, MariaDB and Postgres, `withoutForeignKeyConstraints` runs in a transaction, so all its queries use the same connection. Inside another transaction it uses a savepoint.
- A migration runs in a transaction, so `disable` and `enable` work there on every database. On SQLite, a migration already runs with the checks off.

### SQLite notes

SQLite `ALTER TABLE` can only add, rename and drop columns. So for `change()`, for `foreign(...)` on an existing table and for `dropForeign(...)`, Dox makes the table again. It makes a new table with the change, copies the rows, drops the old table and renames the new one, all in one transaction. It keeps the columns, primary key, `AUTOINCREMENT`, foreign keys, indexes and enum checks. It fails on tables with other `CHECK` constraints or with generated columns.

Other SQLite limits:

- `primary(...)` on an existing table is not supported.
- `fullText` and `dropPrimary` throw an `UnsupportedError`.
- `renameIndex` drops the index and makes it again with the new name.
- A new `NOT NULL` column needs a default. A new column can not default to `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`.
- `dropColumn` fails when the column is in an index or a foreign key. Drop those first.
- On MySQL and MariaDB, schema changes save right away and are not part of a transaction. On Postgres and SQLite they are.

### See the SQL

Every change is a `Table` blueprint. A grammar turns it into SQL without a database. The grammars are `PostgresGrammar`, `MysqlGrammar` and `SqliteGrammar`:

```dart
Table table = Table('users', creating: true)
  ..id()
  ..string('email').unique();
print(table.toSql(PostgresGrammar()));
// [CREATE TABLE "users" ("id" BIGSERIAL NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY, "email" VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL),
//  CREATE UNIQUE INDEX "users_email_unique" ON "users" ("email")]
```

On SQLite, the changes that need a table rebuild (and `renameIndex`) only run on a database.

# Read replicas

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/database/replicas/

# Read replicas

A read replica is a copy of your database that only answers reads, and Dox can send reads to replicas and writes to the main database.

This spreads the load over more servers, which helps when your app reads much more than it writes. Postgres and MySQL support it. SQLite does not.

## Configuring replicas

Add `read` to the `ConnectionConfig`. The `host` of the config is the write host:

```dart title="lib/config/database.dart"
'postgres': ConnectionConfig(
  driver: Driver.postgres,
  host: env.dbHost, // the write host
  user: env.dbUsername,
  password: env.dbPassword,
  database: env.dbName,
  debug: _debug,
  read: <Map<String, dynamic>>[
    <String, dynamic>{'host': 'replica-1.db'},
    <String, dynamic>{'host': 'replica-2.db', 'user': 'reader'},
  ],
  sticky: true,
),
```

Each map in `read` can change `host`, `port`, `user`, `password`, `database` and `extra`. The other settings come from the config. Without `read`, nothing changes.

If the write host is not the host of the config, add `write`. It has the same keys as one `read` map:

```dart
write: <String, dynamic>{'host': 'primary.db', 'port': 6432},
```

## Where queries go

A plain `SELECT` goes to a read host. The read hosts take turns, in the order of the list. Everything else goes to the write host:

- `INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE`
- a raw query that is not a `SELECT`
- schema changes and migrations
- a `SELECT` with a lock (`lockForUpdate()`, `sharedLock()`) or with `INTO`
- every query in a transaction

### Reading from the write host

A replica may be a little behind, or a `SELECT` may change data. In these cases, use `onWriteConnection()` to read from the write host:

```dart
User? user = await User().onWriteConnection().find(id);
```

It also sends the queries of `preload()` to the write host. You do not need it after `insert()`, `create()` and `updateOrCreate()`, because they always read the new row back from the write host.

## Sticky reads

A replica can be a little behind the main database. So a user saves a post, the next page loads, and the post is not there yet.

`sticky: true` fixes this. After a write, the reads of the same request go to the write host, so a request always reads what it just wrote. Other requests still read from the replicas.

In a Dox app this works on its own. When a connection uses `sticky`, `dox_orm` adds the `stickyReads` middleware as a [global middleware](../the-basic/middleware.md).

Outside a request, like in a job or a script, wrap the work in `stickyScope()`:

```dart
await ReplicaDriver.stickyScope(() async {
  await Post().create(<String, dynamic>{'title': 'Hello'});
  List<Post> posts = await Post().get(); // read from the write host
});
```

If you forget it, `dox_orm` prints a warning on stderr, once, when a read from a replica follows a write outside `stickyScope()`.

## Details

- When [`DATABASE_URL`](index.md#database_url) is set, the url is the write host. The `read` hosts and `sticky` stay, and `write` is not used.

# Native Postgres driver

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/database/postgres-native/

# Native Postgres driver

`dox_postgres_native` is the Postgres driver of the Dox ORM, written in Rust.

You use it through your models and queries, and it needs no extra config. Rust ([tokio-postgres](https://docs.rs/tokio-postgres)) owns the connections and the pool, and each connection keeps its prepared statements.

## Installation

`dox_orm` already depends on `dox_postgres_native`, so you do not add it yourself. Add it only if you want to use `PgNativePool` without the ORM:

```bash
dart pub add dox_postgres_native
```

You do not need Rust, because the build hook downloads a ready-built library for your system. The package lives in its own repo: [dartondox/dox-postgres-native](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-postgres-native).

## When the library does not load

Postgres has no other driver in Dox. So if the native library does not load, `SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig` (and every other place that opens a Postgres connection) throws an `UnsupportedError` like this:

```text
dox_postgres_native did not load: <reason>.
Dox needs it to talk to Postgres. Fix: run the app with `dart run` or `dart build cli`. ...
```

The reason tells you what went wrong, for example that there is no library for your system. To fix it:

- Run the app with `dart run`, `dart test` or `dart build cli`, because they run the build hook. `dart compile exe` does not.
- Or install [Rust](https://rustup.rs). The build hook then builds the library from source.
- If you set `lib_path` in `pubspec.yaml`, check that the file is there and is built for your system.

## TLS

You should use TLS when the database is on another machine, so nobody on the network can read the data. Set the mode with `extra['sslMode']`, with `useSSL`, or with `sslmode` in `DATABASE_URL`:

```dart
ConnectionConfig(
  driver: Driver.postgres,
  // ... host, user, password, database as before
  extra: <String, dynamic>{'sslMode': 'verify-full'},
  debug: false,
),
```

| Mode | What it does |
|---|---|
| `disable` | No TLS. The default. |
| `prefer` | TLS when the server has it. No certificate check. |
| `require` | TLS. No certificate check, like libpq. `useSSL: true` gives this mode. |
| `verify-ca` | TLS. The certificate is checked, the host name is not. |
| `verify-full` | TLS. The certificate and the host name are checked. |

Use `verify-full` if your host supports it. In mode `require`, Dox prints a warning (once per isolate), because the server certificate is not checked. To hide it, set `extra['sslWarning']` to `false`, or add `sslWarning=false` to `DATABASE_URL`.

### Trusting your own CA

By default, `verify-ca` and `verify-full` trust the Mozilla roots and the roots of the system. If your database uses another CA (for example the CA bundle of your cloud database, or a self-signed CA in development), give the path of a PEM file in `extra['sslRootCert']`:

```dart
extra: <String, dynamic>{
  'sslMode': 'verify-full',
  'sslRootCert': '/etc/ssl/certs/db-ca.pem',
},
```

Or use `sslrootcert` in the url:

```bash
DATABASE_URL=postgres://app:secret@db.example.com/blog?sslmode=verify-full&sslrootcert=/etc/ssl/certs/db-ca.pem
```

Then `verify-ca` and `verify-full` trust only the certificates in that file. `prefer` and `require` do not use it. A missing file, or a file with no valid certificate, throws `PgException` when the pool opens.

## Options

The driver reads these keys from `extra` of the `ConnectionConfig`:

| Key | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `maxConnectionCount` | `10` | Most connections in the pool, for the whole process. |
| `requestTimeout` | 300 s | The longest wait for one request. |
| `maxConnectionAge` | no limit | A connection older than this is closed once it has no query. |
| `idleTimeout` | no limit | A free connection not used for this long is closed. |
| `sslMode` | `disable` | TLS mode, see [TLS](#tls). |
| `sslRootCert` | none | Path of a PEM file with the CA certificates to trust for `verify-ca` and `verify-full`, see [TLS](#tls). |
| `timeZone` | `UTC` | Time zone of the session. |
| `applicationName` | none | Name of the app in `pg_stat_activity`. |

The pool settings are explained in [Pool settings](index.md#pool-settings).

Isolates that open a pool with the same settings share one pool in Rust. So `maxConnectionCount` is for the whole process, not per isolate.

## Using the pool without the ORM

If you do not use the ORM, open a `PgNativePool` and run queries on it:

```dart
PgNativePool pool = PgNativePool.open(
  host: 'localhost',
  user: 'postgres',
  password: 'postgres',
  database: 'postgres',
);

PgNativeResult result = await pool.query(
  'SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE id = @id',
  parameters: <String, dynamic>{'id': 1},
);
print(result.rows); // [{id: 1, name: Ada}]
```

`parameters` is a map for `@name`, or a list for `$1, $2`. To make a pool from a url, use `PgNativePool.fromUrl('postgres://user:pass@host:5432/db?sslmode=require')`.

### Transactions

A transaction runs on one connection, and its queries run in the order you send them:

```dart
int tx = await pool.begin();
await pool.query('UPDATE users SET name = @n', parameters: <String, dynamic>{'n': 'Bob'}, transaction: tx);
await pool.commit(tx); // or pool.rollback(tx)
```

### Pool settings

All pool settings are optional. Pass them to `PgNativePool.open`. `fromUrl` takes the same three:

```dart
PgNativePool pool = PgNativePool.open(
  host: 'localhost',
  user: 'postgres',
  password: 'postgres',
  database: 'postgres',
  requestTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 30),
  maxConnectionAge: const Duration(minutes: 30),
  idleTimeout: const Duration(minutes: 5),
);
```

They work like the [ORM pool settings](index.md#pool-settings). When a request goes over `requestTimeout`, it fails with a `PgException` that says `timeout`, and a CancelRequest stops the query on the server.

### Cancelling a query

Sometimes a query takes too long and you want to stop it. Pass a `PgCancelToken` and call `cancel()`:

```dart
PgCancelToken token = PgCancelToken();
Future<PgNativeResult> slow = pool.query('SELECT pg_sleep(60)', cancelToken: token);
token.cancel();
try {
  await slow;
} on PgQueryCancelledException {
  print('stopped');
}
```

If the query has not started, it does not run. If it is running, the driver sends a Postgres CancelRequest and the future fails with `PgQueryCancelledException`. If it already ended, you keep the result.

In a transaction, a cancelled query is an error, so Postgres aborts the transaction. Roll it back then. In the ORM, use [`cancelWith()`](query-builder.md#cancelling-a-query).

### Streaming rows

For a big result, you do not want all rows in memory at once. `stream` gives the rows in chunks. Each chunk is a `PgNativeResult` with up to `chunkSize` rows (default 1000):

```dart
await for (PgNativeResult chunk in pool.stream(
  'SELECT * FROM events WHERE day = @day',
  parameters: <String, dynamic>{'day': '2026-01-01'},
  chunkSize: 500,
)) {
  for (Map<String, dynamic> row in chunk.rows) {
    // ...
  }
}
```

The driver asks for the next chunk only when your listener is ready, so only about two chunks are in memory, even for millions of rows. Stop listening (`break` in `await for`) to stop the query. In the ORM, use [`cursor()`](query-builder.md#streaming-results).

## Values and types

You send plain Dart values: `null`, `bool`, `int`, `double`, `String`, `DateTime`, `Duration` (an interval), `Uint8List` (bytea), `Map` (json) and `List` (an array, for example for `int4[]`). The server picks the type. If it can not, add a cast in the SQL, like `@id::int8`.

A `List` is an array, not json. On insert and update the ORM sends a `List` as json text, so a `List` in a json column works. With the pool alone, send `jsonEncode(list)` for a json column.

Rows come back with these Dart types:

| Postgres | Dart |
|---|---|
| `int2`, `int4`, `int8` | `int` |
| `float4`, `float8` | `double` |
| `numeric` | `String` |
| `text`, `varchar`, `char` | `String` |
| `bool` | `bool` |
| `timestamp`, `timestamptz`, `date` | `DateTime` in UTC |
| `infinity` dates | the text `'infinity'` or `'-infinity'` |
| `time` | `String`, like `'13:45:01.5'` |
| `interval` | `Duration` (a month is 30 days) |
| `json`, `jsonb` | the decoded JSON value |
| `uuid` | `String` |
| `bytea` | `Uint8List` |
| arrays of most types above | `List` |
| `NULL` | `null` |

Other types come back as `Uint8List`.

## Handling errors

A server error throws `PgServerException`. Its `code` is the SQLSTATE, like `23505` for a unique violation, so you can check for the error you expect:

```dart
try {
  await QueryBuilder.table('users').insert(<String, dynamic>{'email': email});
} on PgServerException catch (error) {
  if (error.code == '23505') print('taken: ${error.constraint}');
}
```

`PgServerException` also has `severity` and `message`, and `detail`, `hint`, `schema`, `table`, `column` and `constraint` when the server sends them.

Other errors, like the server is down, a TLS error or a timeout, throw `PgException`. A query stopped with a cancel token throws `PgQueryCancelledException`, which is a `PgException`. All of them come from `package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart`.

## Details

This section is for special cases. Most apps do not need it.

- A `driverFactory` on the connection wins over the native driver: the ORM uses your driver.
- The pool closes when the last isolate closes it. You can give `driver.pool.handle` (an `int`) to another isolate and use `PostgresNativeDriver(PgNativePool.fromHandle(handle))` there. `PostgresNativeDriver` comes from `package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart`.
- Isolates share one pool only when all settings are the same.
- Each connection keeps up to 512 prepared statements. When it is full, it drops the one used longest ago.
- A `CREATE`, `ALTER` or `DROP` makes every connection prepare its statements again. So run `CREATE TEMP TABLE` or `DROP` once at start up, not on every request.
- `maxConnectionAge` also helps to follow a DNS change after a failover. A connection is never closed while a query or a transaction uses it.
- A query with a cancel token gets a connection for itself, so the cancel can not stop another query. One token can stop many queries. Use it in the isolate that made it. The CancelRequest goes in plain text on a new connection, like libpq before Postgres 17.
- A stream runs on a server-side portal and starts when you listen. It holds one connection until it ends, and a paused listener that waits longer than `requestTimeout` fails with a timeout. `cancelToken` stops it too, and then the stream fails with `PgQueryCancelledException`. An error comes as a stream error, then the stream ends. It works in a transaction (`transaction: tx`), and other queries of that transaction wait until the stream ends.
- Speed: a find-by-id query takes about 60 µs alone, and about 12.5 µs each with 64 queries in flight (AOT build, local Postgres 14, Apple M-series). See [Performance: database drivers](../digging-deeper/performance.md#database-drivers).
- If you see a problem, please [open an issue](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-postgres-native/issues).


---

# Native MySQL driver

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/database/mysql-native/

# Native MySQL driver

`dox_mysql_native` is the MySQL and MariaDB driver of the Dox ORM, written in Rust.

You use it through your models and queries, and it needs no extra config. Rust ([mysql_async](https://docs.rs/mysql_async)) owns the connections and the pool, and each connection keeps its prepared statements. It works with MySQL 8.4 (with the default `caching_sha2_password` login) and MariaDB 11.

## Installation

`dox_orm` already depends on `dox_mysql_native`, so you do not add it yourself. Add it only if you want to use `MysqlNativePool` without the ORM:

```bash
dart pub add dox_mysql_native
```

You do not need Rust, because the build hook downloads a ready-built library for your system. The package lives in its own repo: [dartondox/dox-mysql-native](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-mysql-native).

## When the library does not load

MySQL has no other driver in Dox. So if the native library does not load, `SqlQueryBuilder.initializeWithDatabaseConfig` (and every other place that opens a MySQL connection) throws an `UnsupportedError` like this:

```text
dox_mysql_native did not load: <reason>.
Dox needs it to talk to MySQL. Fix: run the app with `dart run` or `dart build cli`. ...
```

To fix it:

- Run the app with `dart run`, `dart test` or `dart build cli`, because they run the build hook. `dart compile exe` does not.
- Or install [Rust](https://rustup.rs). The build hook then builds the library from source.
- If you set `lib_path` in `pubspec.yaml`, check that the file is there and is built for your system.

## Options

The driver reads the normal fields of the `ConnectionConfig` (`host`, `port`, `user`, `password`, `database`, `useSSL`) and these keys from `extra`:

| Key | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `maxConnectionCount` | `10` | Most connections in the pool. |
| `requestTimeout` | 300 s | The longest wait for one request. |
| `maxConnectionAge` | 12 hours | A connection older than this is closed once it has no query. |
| `idleTimeout` | 12 hours | A connection with no traffic for this long is closed. |
| `serverKill` | `true` | Stop a cancelled or timed out query on the server with `KILL`. |
| `preparedStatementCacheSize` | `100` | Prepared statements kept per connection. |
| `verifyCertificate` | `true` | With `useSSL`, TLS checks the server certificate. Set it to `false` only for a self-signed certificate in development. |

The pool settings are explained in [Pool settings](index.md#pool-settings).

Isolates that open a pool with the same settings share one pool in Rust. So `maxConnectionCount` is for the whole process, not per isolate.

### Behind a proxy

When a query is cancelled or times out, the driver sends `KILL QUERY` on a new connection, so the server stops it. Behind a proxy or a load balancer, like ProxySQL or a cloud endpoint over many servers, that new connection may reach another server.

The driver checks that both connections name the same server, and it sends no `KILL` (and prints a warning) if they do not. But behind a proxy with its own connection ids, like ProxySQL, you should set `serverKill` to `false`:

```dart
extra: <String, dynamic>{'serverKill': false},
```

Then a cancelled query fails in Dart at once, but it runs to its end on the server. A timed out query only has its socket closed.

## Using the pool without the ORM

If you do not use the ORM, open a `MysqlNativePool` and run queries on it:

```dart
MysqlNativePool pool = MysqlNativePool.open(
  host: 'localhost',
  user: 'root',
  password: 'password',
  database: 'app',
);

MysqlNativeResult result = await pool.query(
  'SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE id = ?',
  parameters: <Object?>[1],
);
print(result.rows); // [{id: 1, name: Ada}]
```

`parameters` is a list for `?`, or a map for `@name`. A write gives you the new id and the changed row count:

```dart
MysqlNativeResult insert = await pool.query(
  'INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES (@name)',
  parameters: <String, dynamic>{'name': 'Bob'},
);
print(insert.insertId); // the new AUTO_INCREMENT id
print(insert.affectedRows); // 1
```

### Transactions

A transaction runs on one connection, and its queries run in the order you send them. `execute` is like `query`, but the rows are not sent back to Dart:

```dart
int tx = await pool.begin();
await pool.execute('UPDATE users SET name = ?', parameters: <Object?>['Cy'], transaction: tx);
await pool.commit(tx); // or pool.rollback(tx)
```

### Pool settings

All pool settings are optional. Pass them to `MysqlNativePool.open`, with a `Duration` for each time:

```dart
MysqlNativePool pool = MysqlNativePool.open(
  host: 'localhost',
  user: 'root',
  password: 'password',
  database: 'app',
  requestTimeout: const Duration(seconds: 30),
  maxConnectionAge: const Duration(minutes: 30),
  idleTimeout: const Duration(minutes: 5),
  serverKill: true,
);
```

They work like the [ORM pool settings](index.md#pool-settings). In `MysqlNativePool.open`, `maxConnectionAge` has no limit by default. In the ORM config, the default is 12 hours.

### Cancelling a query

Sometimes a query takes too long and you want to stop it. Pass a `MysqlCancelToken` and call `cancel()`. `query`, `execute` and `stream` all take `cancelToken`:

```dart
MysqlCancelToken token = MysqlCancelToken();
Future<MysqlNativeResult> slow = pool.query('SELECT SLEEP(10)', cancelToken: token);
token.cancel(); // slow fails with MysqlQueryCancelledException
```

If the query has not started, it does not run. If it is running, the driver sends `KILL QUERY` so the server stops it (see `serverKill`). If it already ended, nothing changes. In the ORM, use [`cancelWith()`](query-builder.md#cancelling-a-query).

### Streaming rows

For a big result, you do not want all rows in memory at once. `stream` gives the rows in chunks of up to `chunkSize` rows:

```dart
await for (MysqlNativeResult chunk in pool.stream('SELECT * FROM logs', chunkSize: 1000)) {
  print(chunk.rows.length); // up to 1000
}
```

Rust reads at most 2 chunks ahead of your listener, so a big result does not fill the memory. Stop listening (`break` in `await for`) to stop the query. Do not pause a stream for longer than the server's `net_write_timeout` (60 s by default), because the server then stops the connection. In the ORM, use [`cursor()`](query-builder.md#streaming-results).

## Types

Rows come back with these Dart types:

| MySQL / MariaDB | Dart |
|---|---|
| `TINYINT(1)` (`boolean()`) | `bool` |
| `TINYINT`, `SMALLINT`, `INT`, `BIGINT`, `YEAR` | `int` |
| `FLOAT`, `DOUBLE`, `DECIMAL` | `double` |
| `CHAR`, `VARCHAR`, `TEXT`, `ENUM` | `String` |
| `DATE`, `DATETIME`, `TIMESTAMP` | `DateTime` in UTC |
| `TIME` | `String`, like `12:34:56` |
| `JSON` | the decoded JSON value |
| `BLOB`, `BINARY`, `VARBINARY` | `Uint8List` |
| `NULL` | `null` |

MariaDB keeps `JSON` columns as `LONGTEXT`. So on MariaDB, `TEXT` that holds a JSON object or array comes back decoded.

## Handling errors

Every error throws `MysqlException`. For an error from the server, `code` is the MySQL error number, like `1062` for a duplicate key, so you can check for the error you expect:

```dart
try {
  await QueryBuilder.table('users').insert(<String, dynamic>{'email': email});
} on MysqlException catch (error) {
  if (error.code == 1062) print('taken');
}
```

`sqlState` is the 5 letter SQLSTATE. For other errors, like the server is down, both `code` and `sqlState` are null. `MysqlException` comes from `package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart`.

## Details

This section is for special cases. Most apps do not need it.

### Limits

- The `timeZone`, `collation`, `serverPublicKey` and `timeoutMs` keys are not read. The connection uses `utf8mb4`.
- A login with `sha256_password` (not the default) does not work. The default `caching_sha2_password` and `mysql_native_password` work.

### Other cases

- A `driverFactory` on the connection wins over the native driver: the ORM uses your driver.
- You can give `driver.pool.handle` (an `int`) to another isolate and use `MysqlNativeDriver(MysqlNativePool.fromHandle(handle))` there. `MysqlNativeDriver` comes from `package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart`.
- A `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `RENAME` or `DROP` makes every connection prepare its statements again. So run `CREATE TEMP TABLE` or `DROP` once at start up, not on every request.
- `maxConnectionAge` is a real age, also for a busy connection. `idleTimeout` and `maxConnectionAge` never close a connection that runs a query.
- In the url of `MysqlNativePool.fromUrl`, the option is `server_kill`. In `DATABASE_URL` of the ORM, use `?serverKill=false`.
- With `serverKill` on, each connection reads the server name once after login (`@@server_uuid`, on MariaDB the hostname, port and `server_id`). This small query shows in the general log and the audit log of the server. Two servers with the same `server_uuid` (for example a copied data folder) still look like one server.
- The `KILL` connection counts for `max_user_connections`. A `KILL` that fails prints a warning on stderr.
- In a transaction, the next queries wait until the `KILL` has its answer, so it can only stop the cancelled query. When more queries wait on the same connection, the cancelled one runs to its end instead, and its rows are dropped. A connection that got a `KILL QUERY` closes once it has no query. Inside a transaction it stays, and the transaction goes on.
- A stream reads rows as they come, and a paused listener stops the reading. Stopping a stream sends `KILL QUERY` and closes the connection. Outside a transaction, a stream gets a connection of its own. Pass `transaction:` to stream inside a transaction.
- Speed: a find-by-id query takes about 65 µs alone, and about 10 µs each with 32 queries in flight (AOT build, local MySQL 8.4 or MariaDB 11, Apple M-series). See [Performance: database drivers](../digging-deeper/performance.md#database-drivers).
- If you see a problem, please [open an issue](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-mysql-native/issues).


---

# Model

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/database/model/

# Model

A model is a Dart class for one database table, used to read, create, change and delete its rows.

Each model maps to one table, and each object of the model is one row. A model also has all the [query builder](../query-builder.md) methods, so you can query the table through it.

## Generating models

Use `make:model` to make a new model. The `-m` option also makes a migration for the table:

```bash
dox make:model Blog      # only the model
dox make:model Blog -m   # the model and a migration for the table `blogs`
dox make:model Blog -a   # the model, a migration, a factory, a seeder and a resource controller
```

This makes `lib/app/models/blog/blog.model.dart`. Other options are `-c` (controller), `-r` (resource controller), `--api` (resource controller without `create` and `edit`), `-f` (factory) and `-s` (seeder). You can join them, like `-mfs`. See the [CLI reference](../../reference/cli.md#dox-makemodel).

A model uses a generated class (`BlogGenerator`), so you must run the generator after you make or change a model:

```bash
dart run build_runner build
```

If you want it to run again each time you save a file, use `dart run build_runner watch`.

## Defining models

A model is a class with `@DoxModel()`. Each `@Column()` field is one column of the table:

```dart title="lib/app/models/blog/blog.model.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'blog.model.g.dart'; // (1)!

@DoxModel() // (2)!
class Blog extends BlogGenerator { // (3)!
  @Column() // (4)!
  String? title;

  @Column(beforeSave: makeSlug) // (5)!
  String? slug;

  @Column()
  String? status;

  @Column(name: 'body') // (6)!
  String? description;

  @Column(name: 'user_id')
  int? userId;

  static String? makeSlug(Map<String, dynamic> map) {
    return map['title']?.toString().toLowerCase().replaceAll(' ', '-');
  }
}
```

1.  `build_runner` writes this file. It holds the generated `BlogGenerator` class.
2.  Marks the class as a model. The options, like `table` and `softDelete`, go here.
3.  The generated class gives the model `id`, `createdAt` and `updatedAt`, and the query builder methods.
4.  The column name is the field name in snake_case. Digits stay as they are: `address2` is `address2`.
5.  `beforeSave` runs this static function before a save. See [Changing values on save and read](#changing-values-on-save-and-read).
6.  Use `name` when the column name is not the snake_case of the field. The name is used exactly as written.

Make every column field nullable (`String?`, `int?`), because a new model has no values yet.

### Table names

The default table name is the class name in snake_case and singular: `Blog` uses `blog`, and `BlogPost` uses `blog_post`. With the [`pluralTableNames` flag](../index.md#orm-flags) it is plural. If your table has another name, set `table`:

```dart
@DoxModel(table: 'blogs')
class Blog extends BlogGenerator {}
```

`dox make:model Blog` always sets `table: 'blogs'` for you, and the migration from `-m` uses the same table.

### Primary keys

The primary key is `id` by default. If your key has another name, set `primaryKey`. The field name is the key in camelCase, so `blog_id` becomes `blogId`:

```dart
@DoxModel(primaryKey: 'uid')
class Blog extends BlogGenerator {}
```

The key field is `int?` by default. If your key is a UUID string, set `primaryKeyType`:

```dart
@DoxModel(primaryKey: 'uuid', primaryKeyType: String)
class Device extends DeviceGenerator {}
```

```dart
Device device = Device();
device.uuid = '0b6f2c1e-1a2b-4c3d-8e9f-001122334455';
await device.save(); // insert
```

`save()` inserts a new model, even when you set the key yourself.

### Timestamps

`save()` sets `created_at` and `updated_at` to the current UTC time. You read them with `blog.createdAt` and `blog.updatedAt`. If your columns have other names, set them:

```dart
@DoxModel(createdAt: 'created', updatedAt: 'modified')
class Blog extends BlogGenerator {}
```

If the table has no timestamp columns, turn them off. To turn off only one, set it to `null`, like `@DoxModel(updatedAt: null)`:

```dart
@DoxModel(timestamps: false)
class Setting extends SettingGenerator {}
```

### Column types

The field type tells Dox how to read the value:

| Field type | Column |
|---|---|
| `String?` | text, varchar |
| `int?` | integer types |
| `double?` | float, double. MySQL also gives `DECIMAL` as `double`. Postgres gives `numeric` as `String`. |
| `bool?` | boolean, or a number like `tinyint` (0 is false) |
| `DateTime?` | date, datetime, timestamp |
| `Map<String, dynamic>?` or `List<dynamic>?` | JSON |
| an enum, like `Status?` | text with the enum name |

For other types, use a [cast](casts.md).

### Changing values on save and read

Sometimes a column needs a small change when you save or read it. `beforeSave` and `beforeGet` take a static function of the model. The function gets a map and returns the value:

- `beforeSave` gets the model values (column name => value) and returns the value to save.
- `beforeGet` gets the row from the database and returns the value for the field.

```dart
@DoxModel()
class Blog extends BlogGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? title;

  // beforeSave: make the slug from the title
  @Column(beforeSave: makeSlug)
  String? slug;

  // beforeGet: old rows have no status, show them as draft
  @Column(beforeGet: readStatus)
  String? status;

  static String? makeSlug(Map<String, dynamic> map) {
    return map['title']?.toString().toLowerCase().replaceAll(' ', '-');
  }

  static String? readStatus(Map<String, dynamic> map) {
    return map['status'] as String? ?? 'draft';
  }
}
```

## Retrieving models

A model has all the [query builder](../query-builder.md) methods, so you read rows with them:

```dart
Blog? found = await Blog().find(1);
```

### Starting a new query

A model object keeps the parts of its query (`where`, `orderBy`, ...). If you want to start another query from it, use `query()`. It gives a new, empty model:

```dart
Blog blog = Blog();
List<Blog> active = await blog.where('status', 'active').get();

// a new query, without the where above
List<Blog> deleted = await blog.query().where('status', 'deleted').get();
```

### Refreshing models

Sometimes the row changed in the database after you read it. `refresh()` reads the row again into this model, and loads its relations again. `fresh()` gives a new model of the row and leaves this one as it is:

```dart
Blog? blog = await Blog().find(1);
await blog!.refresh();          // this model now has the values of the table
Blog? now = await blog.fresh(); // a new model, or null when the row is gone
```

## Inserting and updating models

### Inserts

To add a row, make a new model, set its fields and call `save()`:

```dart
Blog blog = Blog();
blog.title = 'My first blog';
await blog.save();
print(blog.id); // the new id
```

Fields that are `null` are not sent, so the database default is used.

### Updates

`save()` also updates a model that was read from the table or saved before. Only the fields that changed are sent:

```dart
Blog? found = await Blog().find(1);
found?.title = 'New title';
await found?.save();
```

To clear a column, set the field to `null` and save:

```dart
found?.status = null;
await found?.save(); // status is now NULL in the database
```

`model.exists` tells you if `save()` will insert or update. `save()` returns `false` when a [model event](events.md) cancels it.

### Creating from a map

`create()` makes a new row from a map and returns the model as it is in the table. The model needs `fillable`, see [Mass assignment](#mass-assignment):

```dart
Blog created = await Blog().create(<String, dynamic>{
  'title': 'My first blog',
  'status': 'draft',
});
```

`create()` works like `save()` on a new model: it saves only the `@Column` fields, runs `beforeSave`, sets the timestamps and fires the [model events](events.md).

To change some columns of a loaded model from a map, use `blog.update(<String, dynamic>{...})`. It changes only that row and sets `updated_at`, but it fires no model events.

### Mass assignment

`create()`, `insert()`, `update()`, `upsert()` and the find or create methods take their keys from a map. If they took every key, `User().create(req.body)` with `{"is_admin": 1}` would make an admin. So a model is guarded by default, and you must say which keys may come from a map:

```dart
@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  // only these keys are taken from a map
  @override
  List<String> get fillable => <String>['name', 'email'];

  // or: every key but these is taken from a map
  @override
  List<String> get guarded => <String>['is_admin'];
}
```

- With `fillable`, other keys are dropped.
- A model with no `fillable` (and the default `guarded`) throws a `MassAssignmentException` when it gets a map with keys.
- Fields you set in code and save with `save()` are always saved.

If you want to take every key, set `guarded` to an empty list. This is not safe with user input:

```dart
@override
List<String> get guarded => const <String>[];
```

#### Skip the fillable check

Sometimes your own code must set a guarded column, like `is_admin`. These methods ignore `fillable` and `guarded`, so never pass user input like `req.body` to them.

`forceCreate()` creates a row with every key of the map:

```dart
User admin = await User().forceCreate(<String, dynamic>{'name': 'Ann', 'is_admin': true});
```

`forceUpdate()` updates the rows of a query with every key of the map:

```dart
await User().where('id', 1).forceUpdate(<String, dynamic>{'is_admin': true});
```

`forceFill()` sets fields on a model. It does not save, so call `save()` after it:

```dart
User? user = await User().find(1);
await user!.forceFill(<String, dynamic>{'is_admin': true}).save();
```

`Model.unguarded()` turns the check off for everything inside the callback. Other requests that run at the same time still use `fillable`. Await everything inside the callback, because work that finishes later also runs with the check off:

```dart
await Model.unguarded(() async {
  await User().create(<String, dynamic>{'name': 'Bob', 'is_admin': true});
  await User().where('id', 2).update(<String, dynamic>{'is_admin': true});
});
```

### Find or create

Sometimes you want a row if it exists, and a new one if it does not. These methods find a row by the first map. When there is no row, they use both maps.

`firstOrCreate()` finds the row, or creates it:

```dart
User user = await User().firstOrCreate(
  <String, dynamic>{'email': 'ann@example.com'},
  <String, dynamic>{'name': 'Ann'},
);
```

`firstOrNew()` finds the row, or makes a new model that is not saved yet:

```dart
User other = await User().firstOrNew(<String, dynamic>{'email': 'bob@example.com'});
if (!other.exists) {
  await other.save();
}
```

`updateOrCreate()` updates the row, or creates it:

```dart
User updated = await User().updateOrCreate(
  <String, dynamic>{'email': 'ann@example.com'},
  <String, dynamic>{'name': 'Ann Lee'},
);
```

`firstOrCreate()` and `updateOrCreate()` fire the [model events](events.md). `firstOrNew()` does not save, so no event fires. See also the [query builder](../query-builder.md#finding-or-creating-a-row).

### Incrementing and decrementing

If you want to add to a number column, like a view count, use `increment()` and `decrement()`. They change the column in one query, and the model field gets the new value too:

```dart
Blog? blog = await Blog().find(1);
await blog!.increment('views');      // views + 1
await blog.increment('views', 5);    // views + 5
await blog.decrement('views');       // views - 1
print(blog.views);
```

They return the number of changed rows. They fire no model events and do not set `updated_at`.

### Touch and replicate

`touch()` sets `updated_at` to now. Give a column name to set another column. It fires the save events, and `touchQuietly()` does the same with no events:

```dart
Blog? blog = await Blog().find(1);
await blog!.touch();               // updated_at = now
await blog.touch('published_at');  // published_at = now
```

`replicate()` makes an unsaved copy of a model. It has no primary key and no timestamps, so `save()` inserts a new row. Relations are not copied:

```dart
Blog? blog = await Blog().find(1);
Blog copy = blog!.replicate()..title = 'Copy of ${blog.title}';
await copy.save();
```

If you do not want some columns in the copy, list them. They are set to `null`:

```dart
Blog other = blog.replicate(<String>['slug']);
```

### Checking changed columns

Sometimes you need to know what changed before or after a save. A model tracks this. The names are column names, like `user_id`, not the Dart field names:

```dart
Blog? blog = await Blog().find(1);
blog!.title = 'New title';

blog.isDirty();                     // true
blog.isDirty('title');              // true
blog.isDirty(<String>['body']);     // false
blog.isClean('body');               // true
blog.getDirty();                    // {title: New title}
blog.getOriginal('title');          // the old title
```

After a save, `wasChanged()` and `getChanges()` tell you what the last save changed:

```dart
await blog.save();
blog.wasChanged('title');           // true
blog.getChanges();                  // {title: New title, updated_at: ...}
```

## Deleting models

Call `delete()` on a model to delete its row. It returns the number of deleted rows: `1`, or `0` when the row was not there or a [model event](events.md) cancelled it:

```dart
Blog? blog = await Blog().find(1);
int count = await blog!.delete(); // deletes only this record
```

A model with no primary key value throws a `StateError` and runs no query, so `Blog().delete()` can not delete every row by mistake. To delete the rows of a query, add a `where`, like `Blog().where('status', 'draft').delete()`. A [global scope](scopes.md#global-scopes) counts as a `where`. To delete every row on purpose, see [write every row](../query-builder.md#writing-every-row).

### Soft deleting

Sometimes you want to keep deleted rows, so you can bring them back later. Turn on `softDelete`:

```dart
@DoxModel(softDelete: true)
class Blog extends BlogGenerator {}
```

The table needs a nullable `deleted_at` column. In a migration, add `table.softDeletes();`.

Now `delete()` sets `deleted_at` to the current time and keeps the row. Queries leave out soft deleted rows. Use `withTrash()` to get them too, or `onlyTrashed()` to get only them.

`trashed()` tells you if a model is soft deleted, and `restore()` brings it back:

```dart
Blog? blog = await Blog().withTrash().find(1);
if (blog!.trashed()) await blog.restore();
```

To really remove a soft deleted row, use `forceDelete()`:

```dart
Blog? trashed = await Blog().withTrash().find(1);
await trashed?.forceDelete(); // deletes the row, also with softDelete
```

## Converting to a map or JSON

`toMap()` gives all columns and computed values. `toJson()` gives the same without hidden fields:

```dart
Blog? blog = await Blog().find(1);

Map<String, dynamic>? map = blog?.toMap();  // all columns and computed values
Map<String, dynamic>? json = blog?.toJson(); // the same, without hidden fields
Map<String, dynamic>? row = blog?.toMap(original: true); // the raw database row
```

`jsonEncode(blog)` uses `toJson()`, so you can return a model, or a list of models, from a controller.

### Hide fields

You should never send fields like a password to the client. Put them in `hidden`, and `toJson()` leaves them out. Use the column names:

```dart
@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @override
  List<String> get hidden => <String>['password', 'remember_token'];
}
```

If you prefer a list of the fields to keep, use `visibleFields`. When it is empty (the default), every field is kept:

```dart
@override
List<String> get visibleFields => const <String>['id', 'name'];
```

To change this for one model, or for a list of models, use `makeHidden()` and `makeVisible()`. `makeVisible()` also shows a field that is in `hidden`:

```dart
return user.makeVisible(<String>['email']).toJson();
return users.makeHidden(<String>['phone']);
```

### Computed values

Sometimes you want a value in the JSON that is not a column, like a full name. Add `@Computed()` to a getter, then run `dart run build_runner build`:

```dart
@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @Column(name: 'first_name')
  String? firstName;

  @Column(name: 'last_name')
  String? lastName;

  @Computed() // json key: full_name
  String get fullName => '$firstName $lastName';

  @Computed(name: 'initials') // custom json key
  String get shortName => '${firstName?[0]}${lastName?[0]}';
}
```

```dart
User? user = await User().find(1);
print(user?.toJson());
// {id: 1, first_name: John, last_name: Wick, ..., full_name: John Wick, initials: JW}
```

The key is the getter name in snake_case, or the `name` you give. A computed value is never read from or written to the database. `hidden` also hides it, by its json key. The getter runs each time `toJson()` or `toMap()` is called, so keep it fast.

## Relationships

A model can load related models. See [HasOne](relationship/has-one.md), [HasMany](relationship/has-many.md), [BelongsTo](relationship/belongs-to.md), [ManyToMany](relationship/many-to-many.md), [HasManyThrough](relationship/through.md) and [Polymorphic](relationship/polymorphic.md).

The relationship pages use these tables:

```mermaid
erDiagram
    user ||--o| user_info : "HasOne"
    user ||--o{ post : "HasMany"
    user ||--o{ comment : "BelongsTo, from comment"
    artist ||--o{ artist_song : "ManyToMany"
    song ||--o{ artist_song : "ManyToMany"
    user {
        int id PK
        string name
    }
    user_info {
        int id PK
        int user_id FK
        string address
    }
    post {
        int id PK
        int user_id FK
        string title
    }
    comment {
        int id PK
        int user_id FK
        string content
    }
    artist_song {
        int id PK
        int artist_id FK
        int song_id FK
    }
```

### Preloading nested relations

A dot path also loads the relations of the loaded rows. It runs one query for each level:

```dart
List<User> users = await User().preload('posts.comments').get();
```

### Filtering a preload

If you want only some related rows, give a callback. It adds conditions to the query of the relation. With a dot path, it is for the last relation:

```dart
await User().preload('posts', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('published', true);
}).get();
```

```dart
// all posts, and only the approved comments of each post
await User().preload('posts.comments', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('approved', true);
}).get();
```

### Saving through a relation

These methods save a related model and set the foreign key for you. They work with `@HasMany`, `@HasOne`, `@MorphMany` and `@MorphOne`:

```dart
Blog blog = (await Blog().find(1))!;
Comment c = await blog.createRelated<Comment>('comments', <String, dynamic>{'body': 'hi'});
await blog.saveRelated('comments', Comment()..body = 'hi');
await blog.saveManyRelated('comments', <Comment>[c1, c2]);
```

`createRelated()` uses `create()`, so `fillable`, events and timestamps work. The foreign key does not need to be in `fillable`.

For a `@BelongsTo`, `comment.associate('blog', blog)` sets the key and `comment.dissociate('blog')` sets it to `null`. Call `save()` after them.

## Debugging queries

If you want to see the SQL of a model, use `debug(true)`. It prints the SQL in the terminal:

```dart
Blog blog = Blog();
blog.debug(true);
blog.title = 'John Wick';
await blog.save();
```

## Details

This section is for special cases. Most apps do not need it.

### All options

All options go in `@DoxModel(...)`.

| Option | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `table` | class name in snake_case | The table name. |
| `primaryKey` | `'id'` | The primary key column. |
| `primaryKeyType` | `int` | The Dart type of the primary key, like `String` for a UUID. |
| `createdAt` | `'created_at'` | The column that keeps the create time. |
| `updatedAt` | `'updated_at'` | The column that keeps the last update time. |
| `timestamps` | `true` | `false` turns off `createdAt` and `updatedAt`. |
| `softDelete` | `false` | `delete()` sets `deleted_at` and keeps the row. |

### Saving

- `create()` can write `NULL` for a key that is `null` in the map, with the [`createWritesNull` flag](../index.md#orm-flags).
- On update, a field is compared to its value from the last load or save. A `Map` or `List` field is always sent, because it can change in place.
- On update, a field is set to `NULL` only when it had a value before. Fields that were not loaded, for example with `select()`, are not changed.
- When nothing changed, `save()` runs no query and `updated_at` stays as it is. It still fires `updating` and `updated`, unless the [`skipCleanUpdateEvents` flag](../index.md#orm-flags) is on.
- When you set `updatedAt` yourself, `save()` keeps your value.
- `getChanges()` and `wasChanged()` also count `update()`, `increment()`, `decrement()`, `touch()`, `restore()` and a soft delete on the model as a save.
- A soft delete and `restore()` also set `updated_at` when the model has timestamps.

### Mass assignment

- `forceFill()` skips a key that is not a column. A value of the wrong type throws an `ArgumentError`.
- `Model.unguarded()` also covers timers, futures that are not awaited and stream listeners that start inside the callback.
- A query `update()` keeps the check, so `update(req.body)` stays safe.
- Model events that fire inside `forceCreate()` and `forceUpdate()` also run with the check off. So a `create()` or `update()` inside such a hook skips `fillable` too.

### Increment, touch and replicate

- A third argument to `increment()` sets other columns in the same query: `increment('views', 1, <String, dynamic>{'status': 'hot'})`. Keys that `fillable` and `guarded` do not allow are dropped.
- `touch()` returns the number of changed rows. It returns `0` when the model has no `updated_at` column and you give no column, or when a hook throws `CancelModelEvent`.
- `replicate()` copies `deleted_at`, so a copy of a soft deleted model is soft deleted too. A column in its list that can not be `null`, or that is not a column, throws an `ArgumentError`.

### Rows with no primary key

`update()`, `increment()`, `decrement()`, `touch()` and `delete()` on a model with no primary key value and no `where` throw a `StateError`. This happens on a model that was never saved, or that was read without its key.

### Refreshing

- `refresh()` and `fresh()` read by primary key from the write database. They find a soft deleted row too, and skip global scopes.
- `refresh()` throws a `StateError` on a model that is not in the table, and a `ModelNotFoundException` when the row is gone.

### Relations after a reload

`await user.reload()` and a preload set the relation fields again, also when there is no related row. A to-one field that can be `null` becomes `null`. A to-many field becomes `[]`. A to-one field that can not be `null` keeps its old value.

### Other cases

- `create:model` is another name for `make:model`.
- Computed values of loaded relations are in the nested JSON too. `toMap(original: true)` has no computed values.


---

# Model events

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/database/model/events/

# Model events

A model fires events when you save, delete or restore it, so you can run your own code at these moments.

There are two ways to listen:

- **Hooks** are methods in the model class. Use them for code that belongs to the model, like filling a value.
- **Observers** are separate classes. Use them for code that needs other services, like a mailer.

Events fire only on one model object. A query write like `Post().where('draft', true).update({...})`, `Post().where(...).delete()`, `insertMultiple()`, `upsert()`, `increment()`, `decrement()` or `Post().where(...).touch()` runs one query and fires no events.

## Defining hooks

Override an `on...` method in the model, then run `dart run build_runner build`. The hooks must be in the model class itself, because the generator looks there:

```dart title="lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart"
@DoxModel()
class Post extends PostGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? title;

  @Column()
  String? slug;

  @override
  Future<void> onSaving() async {
    slug = title?.trim().toLowerCase().replaceAll(' ', '-');
  }
}
```

```dart
Post post = Post()..title = 'Hello World';
await post.save(); // onSaving runs first, so slug is 'hello-world'
```

Hooks come in pairs. A before hook runs before the query, so you can change values or [cancel the operation](#cancelling-an-operation). An after hook runs after the query, when the row is written and a new model has its `id`. Use it for side effects.

| Before hook | After hook | Runs on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `onSaving` | `onSaved` | every `save()`: a new or a loaded model |
| `onCreating` | `onCreated` | `save()` or `create()` on a new model (INSERT) |
| `onUpdating` | `onUpdated` | `save()` on a loaded model (UPDATE) |
| `onDeleting` | `onDeleted` | `delete()` |
| `onForceDeleting` | `onForceDeleted` | `forceDelete()`: really removes a soft-deleted row |
| `onRestoring` | `onRestored` | `restore()`: brings back a soft-deleted row |

`onTrashed` runs after `onDeleted` when a soft delete changed the row. It has no before hook.

### Setting a value only on create

If a value should be set once, when the row is new, use `onCreating`. Updates do not run it:

```dart
@override
Future<void> onCreating() async {
  status ??= 'draft';
  publicId = Uuid().v4(); // from package:uuid
}
```

### Doing something after a change

After hooks are good for side effects, because the row is already in the database:

```dart
@override
Future<void> onSaved() async {
  await Cache().forget('post:$id'); // the next read gets the new data
}
```

```dart
@override
Future<void> onDeleted() async {
  if (coverPath != null) {
    await Storage().delete(coverPath!); // remove the file of the post
  }
}
```

## Cancelling an operation

Sometimes a save or delete must not happen. Throw `CancelModelEvent` in a before hook, and the query does not run:

```dart title="lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart"
@override
Future<void> onDeleting() async {
  if (status == 'published') {
    throw CancelModelEvent('unpublish the post first');
  }
}
```

The caller sees the cancel in the return value. `save()` and `restore()` return `false`, and `delete()` and `forceDelete()` return `0`:

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/post.controller.dart"
Future<Map<String, String>> destroy(DoxRequest req, int id) async {
  Post? post = await Post().find(id);
  if (post == null) throw NotFoundHttpException();

  int deleted = await post.delete();
  if (deleted == 0) {
    throw BadRequestException(message: 'Unpublish the post first');
  }
  return <String, String>{'message': 'deleted'};
}
```

`create({...})` returns the unsaved model, so its `id` is `null`. Any other error from a hook is thrown to the caller.

## Observers

An observer is a class that listens to one model. Use it when the code needs other objects, like a mailer, or when you do not want the code in the model.

Extend `ModelObserver<T>` and override only the methods you need. They have the same names as the hooks, and each one gets the model:

```dart title="lib/app/observers/user.observer.dart"
class UserObserver extends ModelObserver<User> {
  final Mailer mailer;

  UserObserver(this.mailer);

  @override
  Future<void> onCreated(User model) async {
    await mailer.sendWelcome(model.email!);
  }
}
```

A before method, like `onCreating(T model)`, can also cancel the operation with `CancelModelEvent`.

### Registering observers

Add the observer in the `setup()` of a [provider](../../digging-deeper/providers.md). Observers live in memory, and each isolate has its own memory, so this must run in every isolate. A provider does this for you:

```dart title="lib/providers/observer_provider.dart"
class ObserverProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Model.observe<User>(UserObserver(Mailer()));
  }
}
```

Dox finds `ObserverProvider` by itself, like every `DoxProvider`. Run `dart run build_runner build` after you add it. You can add more than one observer to a model.

### Listening to soft deletes

If you want to know when a row is soft deleted, add the `TrashedObserver` mixin and override `onTrashed(T model)`:

```dart
class PostObserver extends ModelObserver<Post> with TrashedObserver<Post> {
  @override
  void onTrashed(Post post) => print('trashed ${post.id}');
}
```

## Saving without events

Sometimes you do not want the events to run, for example in imports, seed data or tests. `saveQuietly()` saves one model with no events:

```dart
await user.saveQuietly(); // save without events
```

`Model.withoutEvents()` turns off events for everything inside the callback:

```dart
await Model.withoutEvents(() async {
  await user.save();
  await post.delete();
});
```

## Events and transactions

`save()` does not start a transaction, so if an after hook throws, the row stays written. If you want to undo the row when a hook fails, wrap the call in a [transaction](../transactions.md):

```dart
await QueryBuilder.transaction(() async {
  await user.save(); // if onCreated() throws, the INSERT is rolled back
});
```

## Details

### Order of events

| Call | Events, in order |
|------|------------------|
| `save()` on a new model | `saving` → `creating` → *INSERT* → `created` → `saved` |
| `save()` on a loaded model | `saving` → `updating` → *UPDATE* → `updated` → `saved` |
| `create({...})` | the same as `save()` on a new model |
| `firstOrCreate()`, `updateOrCreate()` | the same as `save()` when they create or update a row |
| `delete()` | `deleting` → *DELETE or soft delete* → `deleted` (→ `trashed` after a soft delete) |
| `forceDelete()` | `forceDeleting` → `deleting` → *DELETE* → `deleted` → `forceDeleted` |
| `restore()` | `restoring` → *UPDATE deleted_at = NULL and updated_at* → `restored` |
| `touch()` | `saving` → `updating` → *UPDATE updated_at* → `updated` → `saved` (`touchQuietly()` fires none) |

The model hook runs first. Then the observers run, in the order you added them.

### Other cases

- `save()` on a loaded model with no changes fires the same events, but runs no UPDATE. A model with a `Map` or `List` field is always sent, because the field can change in place.
- With the [`skipCleanUpdateEvents` flag](../index.md#orm-flags), a save with no changes fires only `saving` and `saved`. With this flag on, a save with changes runs `beforeSave` two times, and a save with no changes runs it one time.
