- When a model has events, `create({...})` saves only the `@Column` fields.
- `Model.forgetObservers<User>()` removes the observers of `User`. `Model.forgetObservers()` removes all.
- A model with no hooks and no observers does no event work.


---

# Query scopes

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/database/model/scopes/

# Query scopes

A scope is a query part that you use again and again, like "only active users", written once in the model and called like a query method.

## Local scopes

Add a static method with `@Scope()` to the model. It takes the query first and returns the query. Then run `dart run build_runner build`:

```dart
@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @Column()
  bool? active;

  @Column()
  int? age;

  @Scope()
  static QueryBuilder<User> isActive(QueryBuilder<User> q) {
    return q.where('active', true);
  }

  @Scope()
  static QueryBuilder<User> olderThan(QueryBuilder<User> q, int age) {
    return q.where('age', '>', age);
  }
}
```

The generator adds each scope as a method on the query of the model, so you can chain it with other query methods:

```dart
List<User> users = await User().isActive().get();

List<User> adults = await User()
    .where('name', 'like', 'a%')
    .isActive()
    .olderThan(18)
    .get();
```

A scope can take more arguments: required, optional (`[...]`) and named (`{...}`). The generated method takes the same arguments, without the query.

The scope name must not be a field or a method of the model. For example, a scope `active` next to a field `active` does not work, so name it `isActive`. A scope named like a query method (`count`, `get`) is never called.

## Global scopes

Sometimes every query of a model needs the same condition, like "leave out archived posts". Use `@Scope(global: true)` for this:

```dart
@DoxModel()
class Post extends PostGenerator {
  @Column()
  bool? archived;

  /// every query leaves out archived posts
  @Scope(global: true)
  static QueryBuilder<Post> notArchived(QueryBuilder<Post> q) {
    return q.where('archived', false);
  }
}

await Post().get(); // ... WHERE ("archived" = false)
```

The scope is added to every query: `get()`, `find()`, `all()`, `count()`, `paginate()`, query updates and deletes, and relation queries. The scope goes in brackets, so an `orWhere()` in your query can not skip it.

A global scope counts as a `where`, so `Post().delete()` deletes only the rows in the scope.

### Removing global scopes

If one query needs the rows outside the scope, remove the scope by its method name with `withoutGlobalScope()`. To remove all of them, use `withoutGlobalScopes()`:

```dart
await Post().withoutGlobalScope('notArchived').get();
await Post().withoutGlobalScopes().find(1);
```

## Details

- `save()`, `delete()` and `restore()` on a model object work on that one row. They do not use the global scopes.
- A query write with `withoutGlobalScopes()` and no `where` throws a `StateError`.
- Soft deletes are not a global scope. Use `withTrash()` for them.


---

# Attribute casts

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/database/model/casts/

# Attribute casts

A cast changes a column value between the database and Dart, for example to read JSON text as a map or to save an enum by its name.

Casts work the same on Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite. A cast runs when a row is read (`get()`, `find()` and others), when the model is saved, and in `toJson()`.

## Defining casts

Set a cast with `cast` on `@Column()`, then run `dart run build_runner build`:

```dart
enum Status { draft, live }

enum Level { low, mid, high }

@DoxModel()
class Item extends ItemGenerator {
  @Column(cast: JsonCast())
  Map<String, dynamic>? meta;

  @Column(cast: ListCast<String>())
  List<String>? tags;

  @Column()
  bool? active; // gets BoolCast()

  @Column()
  Status? status; // gets EnumCast(Status.values)

  @Column(cast: EnumCast<Level>(Level.values, byIndex: true))
  Level? level;
}
```

A `bool` field gets `BoolCast()` and an enum field gets `EnumCast(values)` by itself, so you do not need `cast` for them. `DateTime` fields need no cast either.

A cast does not change a `where()` value, so use the database value there:

```dart
where('status', Status.live.name)
```

## Built-in casts

| Cast | Dart value | Database value |
|---|---|---|
| `JsonCast()` | a map or a list | JSON, or JSON in a text column |
| `ListCast<E>()` | a typed list, like `List<String>` | JSON, or JSON in a text column |
| `BoolCast()` | `bool` | boolean, or a number like `tinyint` (0 is false), or the text `1`, `0`, `true`, `false`, `t`, `f` |
| `EnumCast<E>(E.values)` | an enum | text with the enum name |
| `EnumCast<E>(E.values, byIndex: true)` | an enum | a number, the enum index |

## Unknown enum values

A row can hold a value that the enum does not have, like an old name `archived`, or an index out of range. One such row does not fail the query.

- A nullable field reads it as `null`. The ORM logs one `[db]` warning for each table, column and value.
- A field that can not be null throws a `StateError` that names the column and the stored value.

To get a value of your own instead of `null`, give `unknown`. It works for a field that can not be null too:

```dart
@Column(cast: EnumCast(Status.values, unknown: Status.draft))
Status status = Status.draft;
```

Saving the model does not overwrite the stored value. Setting the field back to the value it read (`null`, or the `unknown` value) does not change it either. To replace a bad stored value, set a real enum value.

This is only for rows from the database. A value you give to `create()`, `firstOrNew()` or `updateOrCreate()` must be a name (or an index) of the enum, or it throws an `ArgumentError`.

## Custom casts

If no built-in cast fits, write your own. Extend `Cast<T>`: `get()` gets the database value and returns the Dart value, and `set()` gets the Dart value and returns the value to save. The class needs a const constructor:

```dart
class Money {
  final int cents;
  const Money(this.cents);
}

class MoneyCast extends Cast<Money> {
  const MoneyCast();

  @override
  Money? get(dynamic value) => value == null ? null : Money(value as int);

  @override
  dynamic set(Money? value) => value?.cents;
}

@DoxModel()
class Product extends ProductGenerator {
  @Column(cast: MoneyCast())
  Money? price;
}
```

A cast can take const arguments, like `EnumCast` does. The generator copies the `cast` code into the generated file, so the names in it must be imported in the model file.

## Details

- A column with `beforeGet` does not use its cast.


---

# Counting relations

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/database/model/counting-relations/

# Counting relations

`withCount()` adds the number of related rows to each model, without loading the rows.

This is useful when a page shows "3 posts" next to each user. It adds a subquery to the select, so you get the counts with the same query.

## Counting related rows

Give `withCount` the relation name (the field name). Then read the count with `countOf`:

```dart
@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @HasMany(Post)
  List<Post> posts = <Post>[];
}

List<User> users = await User().withCount('posts').get();

users.first.countOf('posts'); // 3
users.first.toJson();         // {..., "posts_count": 3}
```

In JSON, the key is the relation name in snake_case and `_count`, like `posts_count`.

It works with `hasOne`, `hasMany`, `hasOneThrough`, `hasManyThrough`, `manyToMany`, `morphOne` and `morphMany` relations. It is not for `belongsTo` relations, and there it throws an `UnsupportedError`.

### Counting only some rows

Sometimes you only want to count some related rows, like the published posts. Give a function with conditions, and use `as` to give the count its own key:

```dart
List<User> users = await User()
    .withCount('posts')
    .withCount('posts as published_count', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
      q.where('published', true);
    })
    .get();

users.first.countOf('posts');               // all posts
users.first.aggregate('published_count');   // published posts
```

The global scopes and soft deletes of the related model are used in the count.

### Counting and loading together

`withCount()` works with `where()`, `orderBy()`, `find()`, `getFirst()`, `paginate()`, and with `preload()` or eager relations:

```dart
User? user = await User().preload('posts').withCount('posts').find(1);
user?.posts;              // the posts
user?.countOf('posts');   // the number of posts
```

## Sum, average, min and max

If you need a total of one column, like all views of a user's posts, use `withSum()`, `withAvg()`, `withMin()` or `withMax()`. They work like `withCount()`. Read the value with `aggregate`. It is null when there is no related row:

```dart
User? user = await User()
    .withSum('posts', 'views')
    .withAvg('posts', 'views')
    .withMin('posts', 'views')
    .withMax('posts', 'views')
    .find(1);

user?.aggregate('posts_sum_views');
user?.aggregate('posts_avg_views');
user?.aggregate('posts_min_views');
user?.aggregate('posts_max_views');
```

## Checking if related rows exist

If you only need to know whether there is a related row, use `withExists()`. It adds `<relation>_exists`, which is `true` when there is at least one related row. It takes a function and `as`, like `withCount()`:

```dart
User? user = await User()
    .withExists('posts')
    .withExists('posts as has_published', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
      q.where('published', true);
    })
    .find(1);

user?.aggregate('posts_exists');   // true or false
user?.aggregate('has_published');  // true or false
```

If you want to keep only the rows that have related rows, use `whereHas()` or `has()` instead. See [Query by relations](relation-queries.md).

## Details

- It works for a relation to the same table, like the children of a category.


---

# Query by relations

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/database/model/relation-queries/

# Query by relations

`whereHas()`, `whereDoesntHave()` and `has()` keep the rows of a query by their related rows.

For example, you may want only the users that have a post. These methods do not load the related rows. They add a subquery to the `where` part, so it is still one query. If you also want to load the related rows, use `preload()`. See [HasMany](relationship/has-many.md).

The examples on this page use these models:

```dart
@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @HasMany(Post)
  List<Post> posts = <Post>[];
}

@DoxModel()
class Post extends PostGenerator {
  @Column()
  bool? published;

  @BelongsTo(User)
  User? user;

  @HasMany(Comment)
  List<Comment> comments = <Comment>[];
}
```

Use the relation name (the field name), like `'posts'`. Start the query with a model, like `User()`. A query from `QueryBuilder.table()` throws a `StateError`.

## Rows that have a relation

`whereHas` keeps the rows that have at least one related row:

```dart
List<User> users = await User().whereHas('posts').get();
// WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM "post" WHERE ...)
```

If only some related rows should count, give a function with conditions. This keeps the users that have at least one published post:

```dart
List<User> users = await User().whereHas('posts', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('published', true);
}).get();
```

## Rows that do not have a relation

`whereDoesntHave` keeps the rows that have no related row. It also takes a function:

```dart
List<User> users = await User().whereDoesntHave('posts').get();
// WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM "post" WHERE ...)

List<User> noDrafts = await User().whereDoesntHave('posts', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('published', false);
}).get();
```

## Joining with or

`orWhereHas` and `orWhereDoesntHave` do the same, but they join the condition with `OR`:

```dart
List<User> users = await User()
    .where('name', 'Ann')
    .orWhereHas('posts')
    .get();
// WHERE "name" = @name_p0 OR EXISTS (...)

await User().where('name', 'Ann').orWhereDoesntHave('posts').get();
```

## Counting related rows

Sometimes you need a number of related rows, like "three posts or more". `has` takes an operator and a number. The default is `'>='` and `1`, so at least one related row:

```dart
// at least one post
await User().has('posts').get();

// three posts or more
await User().has('posts', '>=', 3).get();

// no post
await User().has('posts', '=', 0).get();

// more than one published post
await User().has('posts', '>', 1, (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('published', true);
}).get();
```

The operator must be one of `=`, `!=`, `<>`, `<`, `>`, `<=` or `>=`. Any other operator throws an `ArgumentError`.

## Relations of relations

If you want to check a relation of a relation, use a dot. The function is for the last relation (`comments`):

```dart
// users that have a post with a comment
await User().whereHas('posts.comments').get();

// users that have a post with a comment by user 1
await User().whereHas('posts.comments', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('user_id', 1);
}).get();

// users that have no post with a comment
await User().whereDoesntHave('posts.comments').get();
```

With `has()`, the count is for the last relation of one row. So `has('posts.comments', '>=', 2)` keeps the users that have a post with two comments or more.

## A relation to the same table

It also works for a relation to the same table, like a `Category` with a parent `Category`:

```dart
// categories that have at least one child category
List<Category> parents = await Category().whereHas('children').get();

// categories whose parent is named 'Books'
List<Category> books = await Category()
    .whereHas('parent', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
      q.where('name', 'Books');
    })
    .get();
```

In the function, write the column without the table name: `name`, not `categories.name`. With the table name, the column points to the parent row, not to the related row.

## Details

- It works with `hasOne`, `hasMany`, `hasOneThrough`, `hasManyThrough`, `belongsTo`, `manyToMany`, `morphOne` and `morphMany` relations. A `morphTo` relation throws an `UnsupportedError`.
- Soft deleted related rows do not count. To count them, set `q.withTrashed = true` in the function.
- The global scopes and the `onQuery` function of the relation are used.
- It works with `where()`, `count()`, `paginate()`, `withCount()` and the other query methods.
- A name that is not a relation of the model throws an `ArgumentError`.
- For a relation to the same table, the subquery gives the table its own name, so each row is not compared with itself.


---

# HasOne

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/database/model/relationship/has-one/

# HasOne

Use `HasOne` when one row of this table has one row in another table.

For example, a user has one user info row. The other table keeps the foreign key (`user_info.user_id`).

## Defining the relation

Add a field with `@HasOne(...)` to the model. The field type is the related model, and it is nullable:

```dart title="lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../user_info/user_info.model.dart';

part 'user.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? name;

  @HasOne(UserInfo)
  UserInfo? userInfo;
}
```

The related model has the foreign key column:

```dart title="lib/app/models/user_info/user_info.model.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'user_info.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class UserInfo extends UserInfoGenerator {
  @Column()
  int? userId; // column user_id

  @Column()
  String? address;
}
```

Run `dart run build_runner build` after you add a relationship.

### Custom keys

By default the foreign key is the class name in snake_case and `_id`, so `User` gives `user_id`. This is also true when the table is `users`. If your columns have other names, set `foreignKey` and `localKey`:

```dart
@HasOne(UserInfo, foreignKey: 'owner_id', localKey: 'id')
UserInfo? userInfo;
```

## Loading the relation

The relation is not loaded by default. Use the field name (`'userInfo'`) as the relation name.

### Preloading

Use `preload` when you load the models with a query. For a list of users, it runs one query for all of them:

```dart
User? user = await User().preload('userInfo').find(1);
print(user?.userInfo?.address);
```

`preload` works with `find`, `get`, `all` and `getFirst`.

### Loading on a model you have

If you already have the model, use `$getRelation`:

```dart
User? user = await User().find(1);
await user?.$getRelation('userInfo');
print(user?.userInfo?.address);
```

### Querying the relation

Sometimes you need more conditions on the related row. `related` gives you a query for it. It does not set `user.userInfo`:

```dart
User? user = await User().find(1);
UserInfo? info = await user
    ?.related<UserInfo>('userInfo')
    ?.where('address', '!=', '')
    .getFirst();
```

### Always loading the relation

If every query of `User` should load the relation, set `eager: true`. Then you do not call `preload`:

```dart
@HasOne(UserInfo, eager: true)
UserInfo? userInfo;
```

## Filtering by the relation

`whereHas()` keeps the users that have a `user_info` row. `whereDoesntHave()` keeps the users without one. They do not load the `UserInfo`:

```dart
List<User> users = await User().whereHas('userInfo').get();

List<User> inParis = await User().whereHas('userInfo', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('address', 'Paris');
}).get();

List<User> noInfo = await User().whereDoesntHave('userInfo').get();
```

See [Query by relations](../relation-queries.md).

## Changing the relation query

Sometimes the relation should only load some rows. Give `onQuery` a static function in the same model class. It gets the query of the related model and returns it:

```dart
@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @HasOne(UserInfo, onQuery: onlyActive)
  UserInfo? userInfo;

  static QueryBuilder<UserInfo> onlyActive(UserInfo q) {
    return q.where('status', 'active');
  }
}
```

## Details

### All options

| Option | Default | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `foreignKey` | `{this model}_id`, like `user_id` | The column in the related table that points to this model. |
| `localKey` | the primary key of this model | The column in this table that `foreignKey` points to. |
| `onQuery` | none | A static function that changes the query. |
| `eager` | `false` | Load the relation on every query. |

### Other cases

- A relation with `eager: true` is always in `toJson()`. A relation loaded with `preload` is in `toJson()` of that query. The JSON key is the field name in snake_case: `user_info`.
- `reload()` and a preload set the relation fields again, also when there is no related row. See [Relationships](../index.md#relationships).
- The load runs one query like this:

```sql
SELECT *, "user_id" as "_owner_id" FROM "user_info" WHERE "user_id" IN (@user_id_p0)
```


---

# HasMany

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/database/model/relationship/has-many/

# HasMany

Use `HasMany` when one row of this table has many rows in another table.

For example, a user has many posts. The other table keeps the foreign key (`post.user_id`).

## Defining the relation

Add a field with `@HasMany(...)` to the model. The field type is a list of the related model. Start it as an empty list:

```dart title="lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../post/post.model.dart';

part 'user.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? name;

  @HasMany(Post)
  List<Post> posts = <Post>[];
}
```

The related model has the foreign key column:

```dart title="lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'post.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class Post extends PostGenerator {
  @Column()
  int? userId; // column user_id

  @Column()
  String? title;

  @Column()
  String? status;
}
```

Run `dart run build_runner build` after you add a relationship.

### Custom keys

By default the foreign key is the class name in snake_case and `_id`, so `User` gives `user_id`. This is also true when the table is `users`. If your columns have other names, set `foreignKey` and `localKey`:

```dart
@HasMany(Book, foreignKey: 'author_code', localKey: 'code')
List<Book> books = <Book>[];
```

## Loading the relation

The relation is not loaded by default. Use the field name (`'posts'`) as the relation name.

### Preloading

Use `preload` when you load the models with a query. For a list of users, it runs one query for all of them. A user without posts gets an empty list:

```dart
User? user = await User().preload('posts').find(1);
print(user?.posts.length);

List<User> users = await User().preload('posts').get();
```

`preload` works with `find`, `get`, `all` and `getFirst`.

### Loading on a model you have

If you already have the model, use `$getRelation`:

```dart
User? user = await User().find(1);
await user?.$getRelation('posts');
print(user?.posts.length);
```

### Querying the relation

Sometimes you need more conditions on the related rows. `related` gives you a query for them. It does not set `user.posts`:

```dart
User? user = await User().find(1);
List<Post> activePosts = await user
        ?.related<Post>('posts')
        ?.where('status', 'active')
        .orderBy('id', 'desc')
        .get() ??
    <Post>[];
```

### Always loading the relation

If every query of `User` should load the relation, set `eager: true`. Then you do not call `preload`:

```dart
@HasMany(Post, eager: true)
List<Post> posts = <Post>[];
```

## Filtering by the relation

`whereHas()` keeps the users that have a post. `whereDoesntHave()` keeps the users with no post. `has()` counts the posts. They do not load the posts:

```dart
List<User> writers = await User().whereHas('posts', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('status', 'active');
}).get();

List<User> noPosts = await User().whereDoesntHave('posts').get();
List<User> busy = await User().has('posts', '>=', 10).get();
```

See [Query by relations](../relation-queries.md).

## Changing the relation query

Sometimes the relation should only load some rows, or load them in an order. Give `onQuery` a static function in the same model class. It gets the query of the related model and returns it.

You can have two fields for the same model with different queries:

```dart
@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @HasMany(Post)
  List<Post> posts = <Post>[];

  @HasMany(Post, onQuery: onlyActive)
  List<Post> activePosts = <Post>[];

  static QueryBuilder<Post> onlyActive(Post q) {
    return q.where('status', 'active').orderBy('id', 'desc');
  }
}
```

## Details

### All options

| Option | Default | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `foreignKey` | `{this model}_id`, like `user_id` | The column in the related table that points to this model. |
| `localKey` | the primary key of this model | The column in this table that `foreignKey` points to. |
| `onQuery` | none | A static function that changes the query. |
| `eager` | `false` | Load the relation on every query. |

### Other cases

- A relation with `eager: true` is always in `toJson()`. A relation loaded with `preload` is in `toJson()` of that query. The JSON key is the field name in snake_case.
- `reload()` and a preload set the relation fields again, also when there is no related row. See [Relationships](../index.md#relationships).
- The load runs one query like this:

```sql
SELECT *, "user_id" as "_owner_id" FROM "post" WHERE "user_id" IN (@user_id_p0, ...)
```


---

# BelongsTo

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/database/model/relationship/belongs-to/

# BelongsTo

Use `BelongsTo` when this table keeps the foreign key to another table.

For example, a comment belongs to a user, so the comment table has the column `user_id`. `BelongsTo` is the other side of [HasOne](has-one.md) and [HasMany](has-many.md).

## Defining the relation

Add a field with `@BelongsTo(...)` to the model. The field type is the related model, and it is nullable:

```dart title="lib/app/models/comment/comment.model.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../user/user.model.dart';

part 'comment.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class Comment extends CommentGenerator {
  @Column()
  int? userId; // column user_id

  @Column()
  String? content;

  @BelongsTo(User)
  User? user;
}
```

The related model needs nothing special:

```dart title="lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'user.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? name;

  @Column()
  String? status;
}
```

Run `dart run build_runner build` after you add a relationship.

### Custom keys

By default the foreign key is the class name of the related model in snake_case and `_id`, so `User` gives `user_id`. This is also true when the table is `users`. It is not taken from the field name, so a field named `author` still uses `user_id`. In that case, set `foreignKey`:

```dart
@BelongsTo(User, foreignKey: 'author_id', localKey: 'id')
User? author;
```

## Loading the relation

The relation is not loaded by default. Use the field name (`'user'`) as the relation name.

### Preloading

Use `preload` when you load the models with a query. It runs one query for all comments, not one query per comment:

```dart
List<Comment> comments = await Comment().preload('user').all();
for (Comment comment in comments) {
  print(comment.user?.name);
}
```

`preload` works with `find`, `get`, `all` and `getFirst`. Each user is read once, also when it has many comments. Comments of the same user get the same `User` object.

### Loading on a model you have

If you already have the model, use `$getRelation`. Do not call it in a loop over many models, because it runs one query each time. Use `preload` for a list:

```dart
Comment? comment = await Comment().find(1);
await comment?.$getRelation('user');
print(comment?.user?.name);
```

### Querying the relation

Sometimes you need more conditions on the related row. `related` gives you a query for it. It does not set `comment.user`:

```dart
Comment? comment = await Comment().find(1);
User? activeUser = await comment
    ?.related<User>('user')
    ?.where('status', 'active')
    .getFirst();
```

### Always loading the relation

If every query of `Comment` should load the relation, set `eager: true`. Then you do not call `preload`:

```dart
@BelongsTo(User, eager: true)
User? user;
```

## Filtering by the relation

`whereHas()` keeps the comments by a user that matches. It does not load the users:

```dart
List<Comment> comments = await Comment().whereHas('user', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('name', 'Ann');
}).get();
```

See [Query by relations](../relation-queries.md).

## Changing the relation query

Sometimes the relation should only load some rows. Give `onQuery` a static function in the same model class. It gets the query of the related model and returns it:

```dart
@DoxModel()
class Comment extends CommentGenerator {
  @Column()
  int? userId;

  @BelongsTo(User, onQuery: onlyActive)
  User? activeUser;

  static QueryBuilder<User> onlyActive(User q) {
    return q.where('status', 'active');
  }
}
```

## Details

### All options

| Option | Default | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `foreignKey` | `{related model}_id`, like `user_id` | The column in this table that points to the related model. |
| `localKey` | the primary key of the related model | The column in the related table that `foreignKey` points to. |
| `onQuery` | none | A static function that changes the query. |
| `eager` | `false` | Load the relation on every query. |

### Other cases

- The [`belongsToKeyFromRelation` flag](../../index.md#orm-flags) takes the default foreign key from the relation name (`author_id`). The model generator does not pass the relation name yet, so set `foreignKey` when it is not the class name.
- A relation with `eager: true` is always in `toJson()`. A relation loaded with `preload` is in `toJson()` of that query. The JSON key is the field name in snake_case: `user`.
- `reload()` and a preload set the relation fields again, also when there is no related row. See [Relationships](../index.md#relationships).
- The load runs one query like this:

```sql
SELECT * FROM "user"
  WHERE "user"."id" IN (@userid_p0, ...)
```


---

# ManyToMany

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/database/model/relationship/many-to-many/

# ManyToMany

Use `ManyToMany` when rows on both sides can have many rows on the other side.

For example, an artist has many songs, and a song has many artists. The link is kept in a third table, the pivot table. It has one foreign key to each side.

## Tables

| Table | Columns |
|---|---|
| `artist` | `id`, `name` |
| `song` | `id`, `title` |
| `artist_song` (pivot) | `id`, `artist_id`, `song_id` |

A migration for the pivot table:

```dart
await schema.create('artist_song', (Table table) {
  table.id();
  table.foreignId('artist_id').constrained('artist').cascadeOnDelete();
  table.foreignId('song_id').constrained('song').cascadeOnDelete();
});
```

By default the pivot table name is the two class names in snake_case, in A-Z order, joined with `_`. So `Artist` and `Song` give `artist_song`, and `BlogPost` and `Tag` give `blog_post_tag`. The table names of the models do not change this.

## Defining the relation

Add a field with `@ManyToMany(...)` to each model that needs it. The field type is a list of the related model. Start it as an empty list:

```dart title="lib/app/models/artist/artist.model.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../song/song.model.dart';

part 'artist.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class Artist extends ArtistGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? name;

  @ManyToMany(Song)
  List<Song> songs = <Song>[];
}
```

```dart title="lib/app/models/song/song.model.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../artist/artist.model.dart';

part 'song.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class Song extends SongGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? title;

  @ManyToMany(Artist)
  List<Artist> artists = <Artist>[];
}
```

Run `dart run build_runner build` after you add a relationship.

### Custom keys

If your pivot table or columns have other names, set them:

```dart
@ManyToMany(
  Song,
  pivotTable: 'artist_song',
  pivotForeignKey: 'artist_id',
  pivotRelatedForeignKey: 'song_id',
  localKey: 'id',
  relatedKey: 'id',
)
List<Song> songs = <Song>[];
```

## Loading the relation

The relation is not loaded by default. Use the field name (`'songs'`) as the relation name.

### Preloading

Use `preload` when you load the models with a query. For a list of models, it runs one query for all of them. A model without links gets an empty list:

```dart
Artist? artist = await Artist().preload('songs').find(1);
print(artist?.songs.length);

List<Song> songs = await Song().preload('artists').get();
```

`preload` works with `find`, `get`, `all` and `getFirst`.

### Loading on a model you have

If you already have the model, use `$getRelation`:

```dart
Artist? artist = await Artist().find(1);
await artist?.$getRelation('songs');
print(artist?.songs.length);
```

### Querying the relation

Sometimes you need more conditions on the related rows. `related` gives you a query for them. It does not set `artist.songs`.

The query joins the pivot table, so write `table.column` for column names:

```dart
Artist? artist = await Artist().find(1);
List<Song> songs = await artist
        ?.related<Song>('songs')
        ?.orderBy('song.title')
        .get() ??
    <Song>[];
```

### Always loading the relation

If every query of `Artist` should load the relation, set `eager: true`. Then you do not call `preload`. Do not set `eager: true` on both sides, because each side would load the other side again and again:

```dart
@ManyToMany(Song, eager: true)
List<Song> songs = <Song>[];
```

## Reading pivot columns

The pivot table can have more columns, like a `role`. List them in `withPivot`:

```dart
@ManyToMany(Song, withPivot: <String>['role'])
List<Song> songs = <Song>[];
```

Then read them with `pivot` on each related model:

```dart
Artist? artist = await Artist().preload('songs').find(1);
for (Song song in artist!.songs) {
  print(song.pivot['role']);
}
```

`pivot` also has the two pivot keys, like `artist_id` and `song_id`. It is filled when the rows are loaded by the relation: with `preload`, `$getRelation`, `eager` or `related('songs')!.get()`. A model that was not loaded by the relation has an empty `pivot`.

### Pivot timestamps

If you want `created_at` and `updated_at` on the pivot rows, set `withTimestamps: true`. The pivot table needs both columns (`table.timestamps()`). Then `attach()`, `sync()` and `toggle()` set them, and `updateExistingPivot()` sets `updated_at`.

## Changing the links

These methods add and remove rows in the pivot table. The first argument is the relation name, like `'songs'`. Save the model first, because a model without an id throws a `StateError`.

The ids can be:

- one id: `1`
- a model: `song`
- a list of ids or models: `[1, 2, song]`
- a map of `id => pivot values`: `{1: {'role': 'singer'}, 2: {}}`

Each id is used once, so `[1, 1, '1']` adds one row.

### Attaching

`attach` adds a pivot row for each id. The third argument has the pivot values for every new row:

```dart
await artist.attach('songs', 1);
await artist.attach('songs', <int>[2, 3], <String, dynamic>{'role': 'singer'});
await artist.attach('songs', <int, Map<String, dynamic>>{
  4: <String, dynamic>{'role': 'writer'},
});
```

`attach` does not check for a row that is already there. If the row may be there, use `sync` or `syncWithoutDetaching`.

### Detaching

`detach` deletes the pivot rows of the ids and returns how many rows it deleted. With no ids argument, it deletes every pivot row of the model. The songs stay in the `song` table:

```dart
await artist.detach('songs', <int>[1, 2]);
await artist.detach('songs');
```

### Syncing

`sync` makes the pivot rows match the ids. It adds a row for each new id, deletes the rows of the ids that are not in the list, and sets changed pivot values on the rows that are already there.

It returns a `PivotSyncResult` with the ids of each change:

```dart
PivotSyncResult result = await artist.sync('songs', <int>[1, 2, 3]);
print(result.attached); // ids that got a new row
print(result.detached); // ids whose row was deleted
print(result.updated);  // ids whose pivot values changed
```

If you only want to add links and never delete, use `syncWithoutDetaching`:

```dart
await artist.syncWithoutDetaching('songs', <int>[4]);
```

### Toggling

`toggle` adds a row for each id that has none, and deletes the row of each id that has one. It returns a `PivotSyncResult` with `attached` and `detached`:

```dart
await artist.toggle('songs', <int>[1, 2]);
```

### Updating pivot values

`updateExistingPivot` sets pivot values on the rows of one id or a list of ids. It returns how many rows changed:

```dart
await artist.updateExistingPivot('songs', 1, <String, dynamic>{'role': 'writer'});
```

## Filtering by the relation

`whereHas()` keeps the artists that have a song. It checks the pivot table `artist_song` for you, and it does not load the songs:

```dart
List<Artist> artists = await Artist().whereHas('songs', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('title', 'Yesterday');
}).get();

List<Artist> noSongs = await Artist().whereDoesntHave('songs').get();
```

See [Query by relations](../relation-queries.md).

## Changing the relation query

Sometimes the relation should only load some rows. Give `onQuery` a static function in the same model class. It gets the query of the related model and returns it. Write `table.column`, because the query joins the pivot table:

```dart
@DoxModel()
class Artist extends ArtistGenerator {
  @ManyToMany(Song, onQuery: onlyPublished)
  List<Song> songs = <Song>[];

  static QueryBuilder<Song> onlyPublished(Song q) {
    return q.where('song.status', 'published');
  }
}
```

## Details

### All options

The examples are for `@ManyToMany(Song)` in the `Artist` model.

| Option | Default | Example value | What it is |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pivotTable` | the two model names in A-Z order, joined with `_` | `artist_song` | The pivot table. |
| `pivotForeignKey` | `{this model}_id` | `artist_id` | The pivot column that points to this model. |
| `pivotRelatedForeignKey` | `{related model}_id` | `song_id` | The pivot column that points to the related model. |
| `localKey` | the primary key of this model | `id` | The column in `artist` that `pivotForeignKey` points to. |
| `relatedKey` | the primary key of the related model | `id` | The column in `song` that `pivotRelatedForeignKey` points to. |
| `withPivot` | none | `['role']` | Extra pivot columns to read. See [Reading pivot columns](#reading-pivot-columns). |
| `withTimestamps` | `false` | `true` | Read and set `created_at` and `updated_at` in the pivot table. |
| `onQuery` | none | | A static function that changes the query. |
| `eager` | `false` | | Load the relation on every query. |

### Null and unsaved ids

- `null` means no ids. So `attach('songs', null)` and `detach('songs', null)` change nothing, and `sync('songs', null)` deletes every link, like `sync('songs', [])`.
- In a list, a `null` id or a model that is not saved is skipped by `attach`, `detach`, `toggle`, `syncWithoutDetaching` and `updateExistingPivot`.
- `sync` throws an `ArgumentError` for one, before it changes anything, because it would delete every other link.

### How ids match

- Two texts only match when the text is the same. So on a text key column, `'007'` and `'7'` are two ids.
- When one id is a number, Dart reads the other one as a number too. So on a number key column, `'01'` matches song `1`.
- A bool id is `1` or `0`. A whole double like `2.0` is sent as the int `2`. A `BigInt` that fits is an `int`.
- Other doubles (like `1.5`), a text number at or past ±2^53, a `BigInt` that does not fit, and any other type throw an `ArgumentError`. `sync` checks every id before its first write.
- In `PivotSyncResult`, a number id is an `int`, also when you gave `'3'`. A text like `'03'` stays text.
- On a text key that ignores case (MySQL and MariaDB by default, SQLite with `COLLATE NOCASE`), `sync` and `toggle` also ask the database about text ids that Dart did not match. So with a stored `'ABC'`, `sync('songs', ['abc'])` keeps that row.
- Text ids are sent to the database as they are. The database may read some texts in its own way, for example `'0x1'`.

### Other cases

- `toJson()` of a model loaded by a ManyToMany relation has a `pivot` key. Dates are ISO text. Put `'pivot'` in `hidden` to leave it out. If the model has its own `pivot` column, the key keeps the column value.
- A relation with `eager: true` is always in `toJson()`. A relation loaded with `preload` is in `toJson()` of that query. The JSON key is the field name in snake_case: `songs`.
- `reload()` and a preload set the relation fields again, also when there is no related row. See [Relationships](../index.md#relationships).
- The load runs one query like this. With `withPivot` or `withTimestamps`, it also selects those pivot columns, like `"artist_song"."role" as "_pivot_role"`:

```sql
SELECT "song".*, "artist_song"."artist_id" as "_owner_id" FROM "song"
  LEFT JOIN "artist_song" on "artist_song"."song_id" = "song"."id"
  WHERE "artist_song"."artist_id" IN (@artist_songartist_id_p0, ...)
```


---

# HasManyThrough

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/database/model/relationship/through/

# HasManyThrough

Use `HasManyThrough` to read rows that are two steps away, through a model in the middle. `HasOneThrough` is the same, but it gives one row.

For example, a country has many users, and a user has many posts. So a country has many posts through its users.

## Tables

| Table | Columns |
|---|---|
| `country` | `id`, `name` |
| `user` | `id`, `country_id` |
| `post` | `id`, `user_id`, `title` |

## Defining the relation

Add the field to the first model. The `through` option is the model in the middle:

```dart title="lib/app/models/country/country.model.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../post/post.model.dart';
import '../user/user.model.dart';

part 'country.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class Country extends CountryGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? name;

  @HasManyThrough(Post, through: User)
  List<Post> posts = <Post>[];

  @HasOneThrough(Post, through: User, onQuery: newest)
  Post? latestPost;

  static Model<Post> newest(Post q) {
    q.orderBy('post.id');
    return q;
  }
}
```

With `HasOneThrough`, when several rows match, the last row of the query wins. So `newest` orders by `post.id` from low to high, and the highest id is the last row.

Run `dart run build_runner build` after you add a relationship.

### Custom keys

If your columns have other names, set the four keys:

```dart
@HasManyThrough(
  Post,
  through: User,
  foreignKey: 'home_country_id', // on user, points to the country
  localKey: 'id', // on country
  throughForeignKey: 'author_id', // on post, points to the user
  throughLocalKey: 'id', // on user
)
List<Post> posts = <Post>[];
```

## Loading the relation

It loads like the other relations. `preload` runs one query for all countries. `withCount`, `whereHas`, `whereDoesntHave` and `has` work too:

```dart
Country? country = await Country().preload('posts').find(1);
print(country?.posts.length);

List<Country> countries = await Country().withCount('posts').get();
List<Country> active = await Country().whereHas('posts').get();
```

See [Counting relations](../counting-relations.md) and [Query by relations](../relation-queries.md).

Soft deleted rows are left out, in the middle table and in the far table.

## Writing column names

The query joins the two tables, and a column like `title` can be in both. So in `onQuery` and in a `whereHas` function, write the table in front of the column:

```dart
List<Country> countries = await Country().whereHas('posts', (QueryBuilder<dynamic> q) {
  q.where('post.title', 'Hello');
}).get();
```

## Details

### All options

| Option | Default | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `foreignKey` | `{this model}_id`, like `country_id` | The column in the middle table that points to this model. |
| `localKey` | the primary key of this model | The column in this table that `foreignKey` points to. |
| `throughForeignKey` | `{middle model}_id`, like `user_id` | The column in the far table that points to the middle model. |
| `throughLocalKey` | the primary key of the middle model | The column in the middle table that `throughForeignKey` points to. |
| `onQuery` | none | A static function that changes the query. |
| `eager` | `false` | Load the relation on every query. |


---

# Polymorphic

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/database/model/relationship/polymorphic/

# Polymorphic

Use a polymorphic relation when one model can belong to more than one other model.

For example, a comment can belong to a photo or to a video. The `comment` table does not have a `photo_id` and a `video_id`. Instead it has two columns:

- `commentable_id`: the id of the photo or the video.
- `commentable_type`: the type, like `photo` or `video`.

`commentable` is the morph name. You pick it.

## Tables

| Table | Columns |
|---|---|
| `photo` | `id`, `title` |
| `video` | `id`, `title` |
| `comment` | `id`, `body`, `commentable_id`, `commentable_type` |

`morphs()` adds both columns and an index:

```dart
await schema.create('comment', (Table table) {
  table.id();
  table.string('body');
  table.morphs('commentable');
  table.timestamps();
});
```

## The morph map

The morph map gives each model a type name. The type name is the value in the `commentable_type` column.

Set it in the `setup()` of a [provider](../../../digging-deeper/providers.md). Dox runs providers in every isolate, before the first request. The map is kept per isolate, so setting it only in `main()` is not enough:

```dart
class MorphMapProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Model.morphMap(<String, Model<dynamic> Function()>{
      'photo': Photo.new,
      'video': Video.new,
    });
  }
}
```

A queue worker or a CLI command that reads these relations must call it too.

You should always use a morph map, because without it the class name is stored, like `Photo`. The class name changes when you rename the class or build with `--obfuscate`, and then the old rows do not match. For the same reason, do not change a type name later. `@MorphTo` needs the map and throws without it.

## Defining the relation

### Has many

A photo has many comments. Use `@MorphMany`. The second argument is the morph name:

```dart title="lib/app/models/photo/photo.model.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

import '../comment/comment.model.dart';

part 'photo.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class Photo extends PhotoGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? title;

  @MorphMany(Comment, 'commentable')
  List<Comment> comments = <Comment>[];
}
```

### Has one

A photo has one cover image. Use `@MorphOne`. It works like `@MorphMany`, but the field is one model:

```dart
@MorphOne(Image, 'imageable')
Image? cover;
```

When there are many rows, it keeps the last row the query returns. Add an `orderBy` in `onQuery` to pick the row, like with [HasOne](has-one.md).

### The other side

A comment belongs to a photo or a video. Use `@MorphTo`. The field type is `Model<dynamic>?`, and the morph name is the field name in snake_case: `commentable`.

The `commentable_id` and `commentable_type` columns must be `@Column` fields, or the relation is always `null`:

```dart title="lib/app/models/comment/comment.model.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'comment.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel()
class Comment extends CommentGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? body;

  @Column()
  int? commentableId;

  @Column()
  String? commentableType;

  @MorphTo()
  Model<dynamic>? commentable;
}
```

Run `dart run build_runner build` after you add a relationship.

## Saving a row

There is no `associate()`, so set the two columns yourself. Use `Model.morphTypeOf()` for the type, so it is the same as the morph map:

```dart
Comment comment = Comment()
  ..body = 'Nice'
  ..commentableId = photo.id
  ..commentableType = Model.morphTypeOf(photo);
await comment.save();
```

## Loading the relation

Load it like the other relations: with `preload`, `$getRelation`, `related` or `eager`. On a `@MorphTo` field, check the type of the loaded model:

```dart
Photo? photo = await Photo().preload('comments').find(1);
print(photo?.comments.length);

List<Comment> comments = await Comment().preload('commentable').get();
for (Comment c in comments) {
  if (c.commentable is Photo) {
    print((c.commentable as Photo).title);
  }
}
```

A comment with a type that is not in the morph map throws a `StateError`. A comment with no type, or an empty type `''`, gets `null`.

## Filtering by the relation

`whereHas()`, `whereDoesntHave()` and `withCount()` work with `@MorphMany` and `@MorphOne`:

```dart
List<Photo> photos = await Photo().whereHas('comments').get();
List<Video> videos = await Video().withCount('comments').get();
```

They do not work with `@MorphTo`. It throws an `UnsupportedError`.

## Details

### Morph map helpers

Two helpers read the map:

```dart
String type = Model.morphTypeOf(Photo()); // 'photo'
Model<dynamic> model = Model.morphModel('video'); // a new Video()
```

`Model.morphMap(map, merge: false)` removes the names you set before.

### Options of `@MorphMany` and `@MorphOne`

The examples are for `@MorphMany(Comment, 'commentable')` in the `Photo` model.

| Option | Default | Example value | What it is |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` (2nd argument) | | `commentable` | The morph name. |
| `typeColumn` | `{name}_type` | `commentable_type` | The type column in `comment`. |
| `idColumn` | `{name}_id` | `commentable_id` | The id column in `comment`. |
| `localKey` | the primary key of this model | `id` | The column in `photo` that `idColumn` points to. |
| `onQuery` | none | | A static function that changes the query. |
| `eager` | `false` | | Load the relation on every query. |

### Options of `@MorphTo`

| Option | Default | Example value | What it is |
|---|---|---|---|
| `name` | the field name in snake_case | `commentable` | The morph name. |
| `typeColumn` | `{name}_type` | `commentable_type` | The type column in this table. |
| `idColumn` | `{name}_id` | `commentable_id` | The id column in this table. |
| `ownerKey` | the primary key of the related model | `id` | The column in the related table that `idColumn` points to. |
| `onQuery` | none | | A static function that changes the query of each type. It runs for every type, so it takes and returns `Model<dynamic>`. |
| `eager` | `false` | | Load the relation on every query. |

### Other cases

- `@MorphMany` and `@MorphOne` run one query for all models, with `where commentable_type = 'photo'`. `@MorphTo` runs one query for each type in the list.
- `related<Photo>('commentable')` on one comment gives the query of its photo.
- A relation with `eager: true` is always in `toJson()`. A relation loaded with `preload` is in `toJson()` of that query. The JSON key is the field name in snake_case: `comments`, `commentable`.
- `reload()` and a preload set the relation fields again, also when there is no related row. See [Relationships](../index.md#relationships).


---

# Authentication

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/security/authentication/

# Authentication

`dox_auth` lets users register, log in and log out, and it protects routes so only logged in users can use them.

It gives you a password login against your user table, three ways to keep a user logged in (access tokens, JWT and sessions), `AuthMiddleware` to protect routes, and `req.auth` to get the user in your controller.

`dox_auth` has no password reset, no email check, no "remember me" and no two-step login (2FA). Your app builds these, and the tools on this page help, for example the [two-step login recipe](#change-the-abilities-of-a-token). Rules about who may do what are on the [Authorization](authorization.md) page.

## Choosing a guard

A **guard** is a named way to log in, like `api` or `web`. It says how the login is kept and which model holds the users. Pick the guard driver that fits your app:

| Your app | Use |
| --- | --- |
| An API for a mobile app, a front end on another domain, or scripts | [Access tokens](#access-tokens). You can revoke each token, give it abilities and renew it. |
| An API where other services check the token with a key | [JWT](#jwt-tokens). The token is signed, so there is no token table. |
| Web pages served by this app (forms, Inertia) | [Session](#session-login-for-web-pages). The browser sends the session cookie. |
| Web pages and an API in one app | [More than one guard](#more-than-one-guard). |

If you are not sure, use access tokens for an API.

## Setup

These steps start from a new app made with `dox create my_app`. It has a SQLite database, a `User` model and a `users` table with `name`, `email` and `password` columns.

### Installing

Run `dox add auth`, then run the migration it writes:

```bash
dox add auth
```

The command adds the `dox_auth` package, writes the auth config, writes the provider that loads the config, and writes the [token table](#creating-the-token-table) migration. Run `dox migrate` after it. It needs the ORM and a `User` model, which a new app has. It never overwrites a file, so it is safe to run twice.

If you do not use the command, add the package with `dart pub add dox_auth` and write the config and provider below yourself. The command does not write the DTOs, so you always add them yourself.

### The user model

The password hash must never leave the server. So put it in `hidden`, and `toJson()` leaves it out. The model of a new app already does this:

```dart title="lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart"
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

part 'user.model.g.dart';

@DoxModel(table: 'users', softDelete: true)
class User extends UserGenerator {
  @override
  List<String> get fillable => <String>['name', 'email', 'password'];

  @override
  List<String> get hidden => <String>['password'];

  @Column()
  String? name;

  @Column()
  String? email;

  @Column()
  String? password;
}
```

### Configuration {#4-add-the-auth-config}

The config lists the guards. Each guard has a driver (how the login is kept) and an `AuthProvider` (which model holds the users). This config has one guard, `api`, with access tokens:

```dart title="lib/config/auth.dart"
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

AuthConfig authConfig = AuthConfig(
  defaultGuard: 'api',
  guards: <String, AuthGuard>{
    'api': AuthGuard(
      driver: AccessTokenAuthDriver(expiresIn: const Duration(days: 30)),
      provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
    ),
  },
);
```

`Auth()` and `AuthMiddleware()` use the `defaultGuard`. All options are in the [reference](#reference).

### Loading the config {#5-load-the-config-when-the-app-starts}

A `DoxProvider` gives the config to `dox_auth` when the app starts. Dox finds every `DoxProvider` by itself, so you do not register it. Do not mix it up with the `AuthProvider` of the config:

```dart title="lib/providers/auth_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/auth.dart';

class AppAuthProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Auth.initialize(authConfig);
  }
}
```

### Validating the input {#3-add-the-input-checks}

You should check the register and login body with [DTOs](../the-basic/validation.md). Bad input then gets a `422`, and the controller does not run:

```dart title="lib/app/dtos/auth/auth.dto.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart' hide Schema;

part 'auth.dto.g.dart';

/// The body of a register request.
@Dto()
class RegisterUser {
  @Trim()
  @Length(min: 1, max: 255)
  final String name;

  @Trim()
  @Lowercase()
  @Email()
  @Unique('users', column: 'email')
  final String email;

  /// bcrypt reads at most 72 bytes
  @Length(min: 8, max: 72)
  final String password;

  const RegisterUser({
    required this.name,
    required this.email,
    required this.password,
  });

  static const DtoSchema<RegisterUser> schema = $RegisterUserDto;
}

/// The body of a login request.
@Dto()
class LoginUser {
  @Trim()
  @Lowercase()
  @Email()
  final String email;

  final String password;

  const LoginUser({required this.email, required this.password});

  static const DtoSchema<LoginUser> schema = $LoginUserDto;
}
```

Then run the code generator. It writes the DTO code and adds `AppAuthProvider` to `lib/generated/container.g.dart`:

```bash
dart run build_runner build
```

## Access tokens

An access token is an API token that you can revoke at any time. A token looks like `oat_12.<secret>`, where `12` is the row id in the token table. The table keeps only a SHA-256 hash of the secret, so you see the plain token only once, when you make it.

The [setup](#setup) above already added the `api` guard with `AccessTokenAuthDriver`.

### Creating the token table

The tokens live in the `auth_access_tokens` table. `dox add auth` already wrote its migration. If you set up by hand, write it with this command:

```bash
dox auth:tokens-table --users-table=users
dox migrate
```

`--users-table=users` adds a foreign key with cascade delete, so when you delete a user, the user's tokens are deleted too. For users with uuid or text ids, see [Users with uuid or text ids](#users-with-uuid-or-text-ids).

### Issuing tokens

The controller makes a token on register and on login. `Hash.makeAsync` and `attempt` run bcrypt in another isolate, so they do not block the server:

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/auth.controller.dart"
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/dtos/auth/auth.dto.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

@Inject()
class AuthController {
  /// POST /api/auth/register: make an account and give a token.
  Future<DoxResponse> register(RegisterUser body) async {
    User user = User()
      ..name = body.name
      ..email = body.email
      ..password = await Hash.makeAsync(body.password);
    await user.save();

    AccessToken token = await Auth().createAccessToken(user, name: 'login');
    return response(<String, dynamic>{
      'token': token.value,
      'user': user,
    }).statusCode(201);
  }

  /// POST /api/auth/login: check the email and password, give a token.
  Future<Map<String, dynamic>> login(DoxRequest req, LoginUser body) async {
    Auth auth = Auth(ip: req.ip());
    String? token = await auth.attempt(<String, dynamic>{
      'email': body.email,
      'password': body.password,
    });
    if (token == null) {
      throw UnAuthorizedException(message: 'Wrong email or password');
    }
    return <String, dynamic>{'token': token, 'user': auth.user<User>()};
  }

  /// GET /api/auth/me: the logged-in user.
  User? me(DoxRequest req) {
    return req.auth?.user<User>();
  }

  /// POST /api/auth/logout: the token of this request stops working.
  Future<Map<String, bool>> logout(DoxRequest req) async {
    await (req.auth as Auth).revokeToken(req);
    return <String, bool>{'logged_out': true};
  }
}
```

`attempt` finds the user by email and checks the password. It gives a new token with all abilities, or `null` when the login is wrong. `Auth(ip: req.ip())` gives the client ip to the [login throttle](#login-throttle).

### Protecting the API routes

Add `AuthMiddleware()` to a route to protect it. A request with no good token stops with a `401`. You should also put a [rate limit](rate-limiting.md) on register and login, because it slows down password guessing:

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/api.controller.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/auth.controller.dart';

class ApiRouter extends Router {
  @override
  String get prefix => 'api';

  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    Route.get('/ping', (ApiController c) => c.pong);

    // for guests
    Route.post('/auth/register', <dynamic>[
      RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'register'),
      (AuthController c) => c.register,
    ]);
    Route.post('/auth/login', <dynamic>[
      RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'login'),
      (AuthController c) => c.login,
    ]);

    // for logged-in users
    Route.get('/auth/me', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(), (AuthController c) => c.me]);
    Route.post('/auth/logout', <dynamic>[
      AuthMiddleware(),
      (AuthController c) => c.logout,
    ]);
  }
}
```

Run `dart run build_runner build` again, then start the app with `dox s`.

### Sending the token

The client sends the token in the `Authorization` header. You can try the flow with curl:

```bash
# log in, and keep the token in TOKEN
curl -X POST localhost:3000/api/auth/login -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"ada@example.com","password":"secret-pass"}'
# 200 {"token":"oat_2.OTAG...","user":{"id":1,...}}
TOKEN='oat_2.OTAG...'

curl localhost:3000/api/auth/me -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"
# 200 {"id":1,"name":"Ada","email":"ada@example.com",...}

curl localhost:3000/api/auth/me
# 401 {"code":"unauthorized","message":"Authentication failed"}
```

### Token abilities {#abilities}

An **ability** is a name like `posts:read` on a token. It says what the token may do. Sometimes you want a token that can do only a few things, for example a token for a script that only reads posts. Give the abilities when you make the token. The default is `*`, which means all abilities:

```dart
AccessToken token = await auth.createAccessToken(
  auth.user<User>()!,
  name: 'script',
  abilities: <String>['posts:read'],
  expiresIn: const Duration(days: 90),
);
```

Check an ability in the controller with `tokenCan`. It is `true` when the token has the ability or `*`:

```dart
if (!(req.auth as Auth).tokenCan('posts:read')) {
  throw ForbiddenHttpException();
}
```

`AuthMiddleware` only checks that the token is good. So a route with no `tokenCan` check takes every token, and you must check the ability on each route that needs one. `tokenCan` is always `false` for a session or JWT login.

You should also guard the routes that make or renew tokens with an ability like `tokens:manage`. A login token has `*`, so it passes. A script token does not, so a leaked script token can not make new tokens.

### Listing and revoking tokens

Use these methods to manage the tokens of a user. A revoked token is deleted from the table, so it stops working at once:

```dart
await Auth().accessTokens(user);           // all tokens of the user, newest first, expired ones too
await Auth().revokeAccessToken(user, id);  // false when the user has no token with this id
await Auth().revokeAllAccessTokens(user);  // all tokens of the user, eg. after a password change
await Auth().revokeToken(req);             // the token of this request (a logout)
```

`token.toJson()` has no hash and no plain token, so you can send a token list to the client.

Expired tokens stay in the table until you delete them. Run `pruneExpiredAccessTokens` from a [scheduled task](../digging-deeper/scheduler.md):

```dart
await Auth().pruneExpiredAccessTokens();   // delete expired tokens, eg. from a scheduled job
```

### Rotating tokens {#rotate-a-token}

Rotate a token to renew it before it expires. `rotateAccessToken` makes a new token with the same user, name and abilities, and the old token stops working at once:

```dart
/// POST /api/auth/refresh: a new token in place of the token of this
/// request. The old token stops working at once.
Future<Map<String, dynamic>> refresh(DoxRequest req) async {
  Auth auth = req.auth as Auth;
  if (!auth.tokenCan('tokens:manage')) {
    throw ForbiddenHttpException();
  }
  AccessToken next = await auth.rotateAccessToken(auth.currentAccessToken!);
  return <String, dynamic>{
    'token': next.value,
    'expires_at': next.expiresAt?.toIso8601String(),
  };
}
```

A token can be rotated only once. A second rotate, or a rotate of a revoked or expired token, throws an `UnAuthorizedException` (`401`).

If one client sends requests in parallel, a request that is still on the way with the old token would fail. In that case give a short `grace`, so the old token works a few more seconds. Keep it short, because a stolen old token works on every route in that time:

```dart
rotateAccessToken(token, grace: const Duration(seconds: 10))
```

Each rotate gives the token a full new life. So a client that rotates again and again stays logged in forever. If you want a limit, keep the first login time yourself, or ask for the password again after some time.

## JWT tokens

A JWT is a signed token. The server keeps no list of tokens, so a token works until it expires, unless you turn on [revocation](#revoke-tokens). The user is still loaded from the database on each request, by the id in the token. This way needs no token table.

For a longer walkthrough, see the [JWT auth guide](../guides/jwt-auth.md).

### Configuring the JWT guard

Change the guard driver to `JwtAuthDriver`:

```dart title="lib/config/auth.dart"
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

AuthConfig authConfig = AuthConfig(
  defaultGuard: 'api',
  guards: <String, AuthGuard>{
    'api': AuthGuard(
      driver: JwtAuthDriver(
        secret: SecretKey(env.appKey),
        expiresIn: const Duration(days: 7),
        // the token holds only the user id
        minimalPayload: true,
        // lets logout stop a token before it expires
        revocation: true,
      ),
      provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
    ),
  },
);
```

`secret` signs the tokens. `APP_KEY` is fine, because it must be at least 32 bytes. `dox key:generate` makes a new one. `expiresIn` is one hour by default.

### Issuing JWT tokens

The controller and routes are the same as for [access tokens](#issuing-tokens), with two changes. On register, `Auth().login(user)` gives a token with no password check:

```dart
String? token = Auth().login(user);
```

On logout, revoke the token. This needs `revocation: true`:

```dart
await Auth().revokeToken(req);
```

Login with `attempt` works the same: it checks the password and gives a JWT.

### Small tokens

Anyone can read a JWT payload, because it is signed, not secret. By default the token holds the user (`toJson()` without `hidden` fields). You should set `minimalPayload: true`, so the token holds only the user id (the `sub` claim). Then load the user with `req.auth?.user<User>()`, not from the token.

### Revoking tokens {#revoke-tokens}

By default a JWT works until it expires. Turn on revocation if you want logout to stop a token at once. The driver then keeps revoked tokens in a [cache store](../digging-deeper/cache.md):

```dart
JwtAuthDriver(
  secret: SecretKey(env.appKey),
  revocation: true,
  revocationStore: 'auth',
)
```

Use `revokeToken` for a logout:

```dart
await Auth().revokeToken(req);     // revoke the bearer token of this request (a logout)
```

Use `revokeAllTokens` to log a user out everywhere, for example after a password change or a ban:

```dart
await Auth().revokeAllTokens(id);  // revoke all tokens of a user, eg. after a password change or a ban
```

Give auth its own cache store, like `redis` with its own prefix, and never flush it. A flush brings revoked tokens back until they expire. With revocation off, these methods throw a `StateError`, so no one thinks a token is revoked when it is not.

### Changing the secret {#change-the-jwt-secret}

Sometimes you must change the signing secret. New tokens are always signed with `secret`, and old tokens are checked with the old secrets too.

If the secret is `APP_KEY`, follow [Change the key](encryption.md#change-the-key-key-rotation). The old keys in `AppConfig.previousKeys` are used, so you need nothing more.

If you use a separate JWT secret, give the old one to the driver:

```dart
JwtAuthDriver(
  secret: SecretKey(env.jwtSecret),
  previousSecrets: <JWTKey>[SecretKey(env.jwtOldSecret)],
)
```

Remove the old secret once `expiresIn` has passed. To log out everyone at once, change the secret and keep no old secrets. Never keep a leaked secret, because anyone who has it can make tokens.

## Session login for web pages

For web pages, keep the login in the session instead of a token. The browser sends the session cookie, so the client does nothing. This needs `SessionMiddleware` and `CsrfMiddleware`. See [Session](../the-basic/session.md) and [CSRF protection](csrf.md).

### Configuring the session guard

Use `SessionAuthDriver`:

```dart title="lib/config/auth.dart"
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

AuthConfig authConfig = AuthConfig(
  defaultGuard: 'web',
  guards: <String, AuthGuard>{
    'web': AuthGuard(
      driver: SessionAuthDriver(),
      provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
    ),
  },
);
```

### Logging in

`attemptSession` checks the password and keeps the user id in the session. `loginSession` logs a user in with no password check. `logout` removes the login and all session data. Login and logout also give the session a new id and a new CSRF token.

This controller answers JSON, for a front end with axios or Inertia. axios sends the CSRF token by itself:

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/session.controller.dart"
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/dtos/auth/auth.dto.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

@Inject()
class SessionController {
  /// POST /register: make an account and log in.
  Future<DoxResponse> register(DoxRequest req, RegisterUser body) async {
    User user = User()
      ..name = body.name
      ..email = body.email
      ..password = await Hash.makeAsync(body.password);
    await user.save();

    Auth().loginSession(req, user);
    return response(user).statusCode(201);
  }

  /// POST /login: check the email and password, keep the login in the session.
  Future<User?> login(DoxRequest req, LoginUser body) async {
    Auth auth = Auth();
    bool ok = await auth.attemptSession(req, <String, dynamic>{
      'email': body.email,
      'password': body.password,
    });
    if (!ok) {
      throw UnAuthorizedException(message: 'Wrong email or password');
    }
    return auth.user<User>();
  }

  /// GET /me: the logged-in user.
  User? me(DoxRequest req) {
    return req.auth?.user<User>();
  }

  /// POST /logout: remove the login and all session data.
  Map<String, bool> logout(DoxRequest req) {
    Auth().logout(req);
    return <String, bool>{'logged_out': true};
  }
}
```

For an HTML form, answer with a redirect instead. The method then returns `Future<DoxResponse>`. See [CSRF protection](csrf.md#html-forms) for the form token:

```dart
if (!ok) {
  req.session.flashErrors(<String, dynamic>{'email': 'Wrong email or password'});
  return back(req);
}
return redirect('/dashboard');
```

### Adding the routes

Put the session and CSRF middleware on the web router only, so the API routes stay without a session:

```dart title="lib/routes/web.dart"
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/session.controller.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/web.controller.dart';

class WebRouter extends Router {
  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[
    const SessionMiddleware(),
    const CsrfMiddleware(),
  ];

  @override
  void register() {
    Route.get('/ping', (WebController c) => c.pong);

    Route.post('/register', <dynamic>[
      RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'register'),
      (SessionController c) => c.register,
    ]);
    Route.post('/login', <dynamic>[
      RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'login'),
      (SessionController c) => c.login,
    ]);
    Route.get('/me', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(), (SessionController c) => c.me]);
    Route.post('/logout', <dynamic>[
      AuthMiddleware(),
      (SessionController c) => c.logout,
    ]);
  }
}
```

### Redirecting guests

On web pages you often want to send a guest to the login page instead of a `401`. Use `redirectTo` for this:

```dart
AuthMiddleware(redirectTo: '/login')
```

With the `jsonNoRedirect` [flag](authorization.md#auth-flags) on, a JSON or XHR client gets a `401` and no redirect.

### Ending sessions when the password changes {#end-other-sessions-when-the-password-changes}

By default, a session stays logged in after the user changes the password, so a stolen session still works. Turn on the `endSessionsOnPasswordChange` [flag](authorization.md#auth-flags) to fix this. A password change then ends all sessions of the user on their next request through `AuthMiddleware`:

```dart title="lib/config/auth.dart"
AuthConfig authConfig = AuthConfig(
  defaultGuard: 'web',
  guards: guards,
  flags: const AuthFlags(endSessionsOnPasswordChange: true),
);
```

This also ends the current session. If your app changes the password itself, keep the current session with `updateSessionPasswordHash` after `save()`:

```dart
user.password = await Hash.makeAsync(newPassword);
await user.save();
Auth().updateSessionPasswordHash(req, user);
```

Pass a fully loaded user. A user from a `select()` with no password column looks like a user with no password, so the session ends.

### Logging out other devices

`logoutOtherDevices` ends all other sessions of the user and keeps this one. It checks the password, so it needs the password from a form. It needs a session guard and the flag above:

```dart
/// POST /logout-others: end the sessions on other devices.
Future<Map<String, bool>> logoutOthers(DoxRequest req, ConfirmPassword body) async {
  await (req.auth as Auth).logoutOtherDevices(req, body.password);
  return <String, bool>{'done': true};
}
```

`ConfirmPassword` is a DTO with one `password` field, like `LoginUser`. A wrong password throws an `UnAuthorizedException` (`401`, code `wrong_password`). Because it checks a password, put a rate limit on the route, like on a login.

## Protecting routes

### More than one guard

Sometimes one app needs more than one kind of login. For example, a session for web pages, access tokens for the API, and admins in their own table. Each guard has its own driver and its own user model:

```dart title="lib/config/auth.dart"
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/admin/admin.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

AuthConfig authConfig = AuthConfig(
  defaultGuard: 'web',
  guards: <String, AuthGuard>{
    'web': AuthGuard(
      driver: SessionAuthDriver(),
      provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
    ),
    'api': AuthGuard(
      driver: AccessTokenAuthDriver(),
      provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
    ),
    'admin': AuthGuard(
      driver: AccessTokenAuthDriver(table: 'admin_access_tokens'),
      provider: AuthProvider(model: () => Admin()),
    ),
  },
);
```

Pick a guard by name with `guard:`:

```dart
String? token = await Auth(guard: 'admin').attempt(credentials);

Route.get('/admin', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(guard: 'admin'), (AdminController c) => c.index]);
```

To accept more than one guard on a route, use `guards:`. The first guard with a good login sets `req.auth`:

```dart
// try the guards in order
Route.get('/me', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(guards: <String>['web', 'api']), (UserController c) => c.me]);
```

A token of one guard does not work on another guard. Give each user model its own token table, with `table:` on the driver and in the migration (`AccessTokenTables.up(schema, table: 'admin_access_tokens')`).

### Optional login

A public page may still want to know the user. `AuthMiddleware(optional: true)` sets `req.auth` when the login is good, and lets guests through with `req.auth` as `null`:

```dart
Route.get('/posts', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(optional: true), (PostController c) => c.index]);
```

### Pages for guests only

Login and register pages are for guests only. `GuestMiddleware` sends a logged-in user to `redirectTo`. With no `redirectTo`, the answer is a `403`:

```dart
Route.get('/login', <dynamic>[GuestMiddleware(redirectTo: '/dashboard'), (PageController c) => c.login]);
```

### Getting the logged in user

After `AuthMiddleware`, `req.auth` holds the login. It is `null` for a guest:

```dart
User? user = req.auth?.user<User>();
```

`req.auth?.id()` gives the primary key of the user. For `tokenCan` and `currentAccessToken`, cast it: `req.auth as Auth`.

## Login throttle {#login-throttle}

You should limit failed logins, because it stops password guessing on one account. The login throttle is off by default. Turn it on in your auth provider:

```dart title="lib/providers/auth_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/auth.dart';

class AppAuthProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Auth.initialize(authConfig);
    // 5 failed logins a minute. Change it with maxAttempts: and decay:
    Auth.throttle = LoginThrottle();
  }
}
```

After `maxAttempts` failed logins for the same email and ip, the next try throws `LoginThrottledException` (`429`) until `decay` has passed. A good login clears the count.

Always pass the ip with `Auth(ip: req.ip())`. Without an ip, the count is per account only, so anyone can lock an account. `attemptSession` takes the ip from the request.

The counts live in the app cache. If you run many isolates or servers, use a shared store with `LoginThrottle(store: 'redis')`. The throttle does not stop many tries sent at the same time, so also keep a `RateLimit` on the login route.

## Password hashing {#password-hash-cost}

Passwords use bcrypt with cost 10 by default. Each step up doubles the time of a login. If you raise it, set the cost for new hashes and tell the driver, so a login for an unknown email takes as long as a wrong password:

```dart
Hash.rounds = 12;
JwtAuthDriver(secret: SecretKey(env.appKey), hashRounds: 12);
SessionAuthDriver(hashRounds: 12);
AccessTokenAuthDriver(hashRounds: 12);
```

Old hashes keep their own cost, so they still work. Hash them again on the next good login:

```dart
if (Auth.needsRehash(user.password!)) {
  user.password = await Hash.makeAsync(password);
  await user.save();
  // with a session login and the endSessionsOnPasswordChange flag:
  // Auth().updateSessionPasswordHash(req, user);
}
```

bcrypt reads at most 72 bytes. A longer password throws an `ArgumentError`, so limit the length in the DTO. See [Hashing](hashing.md).

## Recipes

### Logging in with another field

`attempt` searches the user by `identifierFields` and checks the column in `passwordField`. Change them if your users log in with a username, or the hash is in another column:

```dart
AuthProvider(
  model: () => User(),
  identifierFields: <String>['username'],
  passwordField: 'password_hash',
)
```

### Users with uuid or text ids

Access tokens keep the user id in the `tokenable_id` column, which is a big int by default. If your users have other ids, use the same choice in the migration and on the driver:

- uuid ids: `dox auth:tokens-table --uuid` and `AccessTokenAuthDriver(uuidIds: true)`.
- text ids: `dox auth:tokens-table --string-ids` and `AccessTokenAuthDriver(stringIds: true)`.

Session and JWT guards need nothing for this.

### Two-step login (2FA) {#change-the-abilities-of-a-token}

A two-step login asks for a password, then for a code from a mail or an app. Your app makes and checks the code. `dox_auth` helps with tokens:

1. Step one checks the password with `once()`, and gives a short token with only the `2fa:pending` ability.
2. Step two checks the code, rotates the token, and gives the new token all abilities with `setAccessTokenAbilities`.
3. Each route that needs the second step uses a middleware that refuses `2fa:pending` tokens.

The controller with both steps:

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/two_factor.controller.dart"
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/dtos/auth/auth.dto.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/dtos/two_factor_code/two_factor_code.dto.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

@Inject()
class TwoFactorController {
  /// POST /api/auth/login, step one: check the password. The token
  /// works 10 minutes, and only for step two.
  Future<Map<String, dynamic>> login(DoxRequest req, LoginUser body) async {
    Auth auth = Auth(ip: req.ip());
    bool ok = await auth.once(<String, dynamic>{
      'email': body.email,
      'password': body.password,
    });
    if (!ok) {
      throw UnAuthorizedException(message: 'Wrong email or password');
    }
    AccessToken token = await auth.createAccessToken(
      auth.user<User>()!,
      name: 'login',
      abilities: <String>['2fa:pending'],
      expiresIn: const Duration(minutes: 10),
    );
    // send the code to the user here, for example by mail
    return <String, dynamic>{'token': token.value, 'two_factor': true};
  }

  /// POST /api/auth/two-factor, step two: check the code. Give a new
  /// token for a full login. The step-one token ends.
  Future<Map<String, dynamic>> verify(DoxRequest req, TwoFactorCode body) async {
```
