```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/two_factor.controller.dart"
    Auth auth = req.auth as Auth;
    AccessToken token = auth.currentAccessToken!;
    if (!token.abilities.contains('2fa:pending')) {
      throw ForbiddenHttpException();
    }
    if (!_codeIsGood(auth.user<User>()!, body.code)) {
      throw UnAuthorizedException(message: 'Wrong code');
    }
    // a new token with the expiresIn of the driver. It still has 2fa:pending.
    AccessToken full = await auth.rotateAccessToken(token);
    // all abilities, like a normal login
    await auth.setAccessTokenAbilities(full, <String>['*']);
    return <String, dynamic>{'token': full.value};
  }

  /// Check the code with your own two-step code. Make each code expire,
  /// and limit the wrong tries per user.
  bool _codeIsGood(User user, String code) {
    throw UnimplementedError('check the two-step code');
  }
}
```

`verify` checks `abilities.contains('2fa:pending')`, not `tokenCan`, because `tokenCan` is also `true` for `*`. Rotate first, then set the abilities, so no token ever has `*` when a step fails.

The middleware for the routes of a logged-in user. Put it after `AuthMiddleware()`:

```dart title="lib/app/http/middleware/two_factor.middleware.dart"
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

/// Lets a request through only when its token did the second step.
/// Put it after AuthMiddleware.
dynamic requireTwoFactor(DoxRequest req) {
  Auth? auth = req.auth as Auth?;
  if (auth == null || auth.currentAccessToken == null) {
    throw UnAuthorizedException();
  }
  if (auth.currentAccessToken!.abilities.contains('2fa:pending')) {
    throw ForbiddenHttpException();
  }
  return req;
}
```

Use `TwoFactorController.login` as the login route, and add the step-two route with a rate limit:

```dart
Route.post('/auth/login', <dynamic>[
  RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'login'),
  (TwoFactorController c) => c.login,
]);
Route.post('/auth/two-factor', <dynamic>[
  RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'two-factor'),
  AuthMiddleware(),
  (TwoFactorController c) => c.verify,
]);
```

A route without `requireTwoFactor` still takes a step-one token. Register must give no token, and any other place that gives a token must also do both steps.

### Checking a login with no request {#check-a-login-with-no-request}

Code that has no request, like a [Socket.IO](../packages/socketio.md#log-in-a-socket) login, can check a token or a session itself. Both give `null` when the login is not good:

```dart
User? user = await Auth(guard: 'api').userFromToken(token);
User? user = await Auth(guard: 'web').userFromSession(session);
```

`userFromToken` runs the same checks as a request, for JWT and access token guards. Give the token without the `Bearer ` prefix. For `userFromSession`, load the session with `SessionMiddleware().fromCookie(value)`. See [Session](../the-basic/session.md#other-cases).

### Writing your own guard

Sometimes you want to log users in your own way, like with an API key in a header. Write a driver: extend `AuthDriver` and return the user from `verifyToken`. `AuthMiddleware` and `req.auth` then work as with the other drivers.

This driver finds the user by a SHA-256 hash of the key, so a leak of the table does not leak the keys. It uses the `crypto` package:

```dart title="lib/app/auth/api_key_auth_driver.dart"
import 'dart:convert';

import 'package:crypto/crypto.dart';
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';

/// `Authorization: Bearer <api key>` gives the user with this key.
class ApiKeyAuthDriver extends AuthDriver {
  @override
  Future<Model<dynamic>?> verifyToken(IDoxRequest req, String guard) async {
    String header = req.header('Authorization') ?? '';
    if (!header.startsWith('Bearer ')) return null;
    String key = header.substring(7).trim();
    String hash = sha256.convert(utf8.encode(key)).toString();
    Model<dynamic> model = AuthEngine().guard(guard).provider.model();
    return await model.where('api_key_hash', hash).getFirst();
  }

  /// no password login for this guard
  @override
  Future<Model<dynamic>?> attempt(Map<String, dynamic> credentials, String guard) async => null;

  /// no token to make: the key is the token
  @override
  String? createToken(Map<String, dynamic>? userPayload, String guard) => null;
}
```

Add it as a guard, and use the guard on the route:

```dart
'key': AuthGuard(
  driver: ApiKeyAuthDriver(),
  provider: AuthProvider(model: () => User()),
),

Route.get('/me', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(guard: 'key'), (DoxRequest req) => req.auth?.user<User>()]);
```

Make each key long and random, like `openssl rand -hex 32`. Then a fast hash like SHA-256 is safe. Do not use bcrypt here, because you can not search by a bcrypt hash.

If you already have your own middleware, set the user with `Auth().setUser(req, user)`. Then `req.auth` gives this user:

```dart
Auth(guard: 'api').setUser(req, user);
```

### When the database fails

The access token check reads the database. When the database fails, the request gets a `401` by default, and the error is reported. But many clients take a `401` as "you are logged out", so a short database problem logs users out. Turn on `throwOnError` to throw the error instead:

```dart
AccessTokenAuthDriver(
  expiresIn: const Duration(days: 30),
  throwOnError: true,
)
```

The error then goes to your [exception handler](../the-basic/errors.md), which answers `500` by default. To answer `503`, so the client tries again, catch the database errors in `render`:

```dart title="lib/app/exception_handler.dart"
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_orm/dox_orm.dart';
import 'package:sqlite3/sqlite3.dart' show SqliteException;

class AppExceptionHandler extends ExceptionHandler {
  const AppExceptionHandler();

  @override
  dynamic render(Object error, HttpRequest req) {
    // a database error: ask the client to try again
    if (error is SqliteException ||
        error is PgException ||
        error is MysqlException) {
      return HttpStatusException(503, headers: <String, String>{'retry-after': '5'});
    }
    return super.render(error, req);
  }
}
```

`SqliteException` comes from the `sqlite3` package (`dart pub add sqlite3`). On Postgres or MySQL only, drop it. Set the handler with `exceptionHandler: const AppExceptionHandler()` in `AppConfig`.

## Testing {#test-it}

`DoxTestClient` runs your app in the test, and `withToken` sends `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. This test works for access tokens and JWT. It uses the database of `.env`, so it runs the migrations first:

```dart title="test/auth_test.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/testing.dart';
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/app.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/database.dart';
import 'package:test/test.dart';

import '../db/migration/migrations.dart';

void main() {
  late DoxTestClient client;

  setUpAll(() async {
    Dox().initialize(appConfig);
    await Migrator(
      migrations: migrations,
      config: databaseConfig.getConnectionConfig(),
    ).migrate();
    client = await DoxTestClient.start(appConfig);
  });

  tearDownAll(() async {
    await client.close();
  });

  test('register, then use the token', () async {
    String email = 'test-${DateTime.now().microsecondsSinceEpoch}@example.com';
    TestResponse register = await client.post(
      '/api/auth/register',
      body: <String, dynamic>{
        'name': 'Test',
        'email': email,
        'password': 'secret-pass',
      },
    );
    register.expectStatus(201);
    String token = register.json['token'] as String;

    TestResponse me = await client.withToken(token).get('/api/auth/me');
    me.expectStatus(200);
    expect(me.json['email'], email);
    expect(me.json.containsKey('password'), isFalse);
  });

  test('no token gives 401', () async {
    (await client.get('/api/auth/me')).expectStatus(401);
  });
}
```

To act as a user with no HTTP login, make a token in the test with `await Auth().createAccessToken(user)`, then use `client.withToken(token.value!)`. For a session app, use `client.withSession()`, which keeps cookies and sends the CSRF token. See [Testing](../digging-deeper/testing.md).

## Problems

| Error | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `LateInitializationError: Field 'config' has not been initialized.` | `Auth.initialize` did not run. `AppAuthProvider` is missing, or the generator did not run. | Add [`AppAuthProvider`](#5-load-the-config-when-the-app-starts), then run `dart run build_runner build`. |
| `401` `Authentication failed` | No `Authorization` header, a bad, expired or revoked token, a deleted user, or a token of another guard. | Send `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. Log in again. |
| `403` `Forbidden` | The token does not have the ability. | Use a token with the ability. See [Token abilities](#abilities). |
| `Invalid argument (guard): no auth guard with this name: "admin"` | A guard name that is not in `guards`. | Fix the name, or add the guard. |
| `Bad state: The auth guard 'api' does not use SessionAuthDriver. ...` | `logout`, `attemptSession` or `loginSession` on a token guard. | Use `revokeToken(req)` to log out a token. |
| `Bad state: The auth guard 'api' does not use AccessTokenAuthDriver.` | An access token method on a JWT or session guard. | Use a guard with `AccessTokenAuthDriver`. |
| `Bad state: The auth guard 'web' does not use JwtAuthDriver.` | `revokeAllTokens`, `forgetUser`, `userFromToken` or `revokeToken` on a session guard. | A session logs out with `logout(req)`. |
| `Bad state: AccessTokenAuthDriver makes tokens with Auth().createAccessToken(user), not login().` | `Auth().login(user)` on an access token guard. | Use `createAccessToken(user)`. |
| `Bad state: revokeToken needs token revocation. ...` | A revoke method on a JWT guard without revocation. | Set `revocation: true`. See [Revoking tokens](#revoke-tokens). |
| `Bad state: The table 'auth_access_tokens' has no rotated_at column. ...` | `rotateAccessToken` on an old token table. | Add the column. See [A token table without `rotated_at`](#a-token-table-without-rotated_at). |
| `401` `The access token was already rotated.` | A second rotate of the same token. | Rotate the new token, not the old one. |
| `401` `The access token is expired.` or `is revoked or does not exist.` | Rotate of an expired or revoked token. | Log in again. |
| `Invalid argument(s) (secret): The JWT secret is empty. ...` | `JwtAuthDriver` with an empty secret. | Set `APP_KEY` with `dox key:generate`. |
| `Invalid argument(s) (secret): The JWT secret is <n> bytes. ...` | A secret shorter than 32 bytes. In `development`, `local`, `test` and `testing` it is only a warning. | Run `dox key:generate`. |
| `Invalid argument(s) (password): The password is too long. ...` | A password longer than 72 bytes. | Limit the length in the DTO. |
| `Invalid argument(s): Set guard or a non-empty guards list, not both.` | `AuthMiddleware` with both `guard` and `guards`, or `guards: []`. | Set one of them. |
| `429` `Too many login attempts. ...` | The [login throttle](#login-throttle). | Wait `retryAfter`. |
| `419` `CSRF token mismatch` | A session `POST` without the CSRF token. | See [CSRF protection](csrf.md). |
| `403` `Already logged in` | `GuestMiddleware` with no `redirectTo`, for a logged-in user. | Set `redirectTo`, or log out first. |
| `401` `wrong_password` | `logoutOtherDevices` with a wrong password. | Show an error on the form. |
| `Bad state: logoutOtherDevices() needs the endSessionsOnPasswordChange flag` | `logoutOtherDevices` with the flag off. | Turn the [flag](#end-other-sessions-when-the-password-changes) on. |

## Details

### 401, 403, 419 and 429

- `401`: the user is not logged in. The client should log in again.
- `403`: the user is logged in, but may not do this, like a missing ability or a failed [policy](authorization.md).
- `419`: a session request with no CSRF token.
- `429`: too many failed logins.

### Access tokens

- `attempt` always gives a token with `*`.
- `revokeToken(req)` on the `Auth` of `AuthMiddleware` uses the token that was already checked.
- `last_used_at` is written at most once a minute per token. A failed write is reported and the request goes on.
- `tokenable_type` is the table name of the user model. If you rename the users table, old tokens stop working.
- Each token has a `type`, which is the guard name. If you rename a guard, set `AccessTokenAuthDriver(type: 'old-name')` to keep its tokens.
- When you delete a user without `--users-table`, call `revokeAllAccessTokens(user)`, so old tokens can not match a new user with the same id.
- The migration makes the table on the default connection. For `AccessTokenAuthDriver(connection: 'other')`, make it on that connection.
- `rotateAccessToken` runs in one transaction. When two rotates of one token run at the same time, only one works. `expiresIn:` and `name:` change the new token.
- A uuid is kept and compared in lower case. Text ids are compared exactly.
- A token name over 255 characters throws an `ArgumentError`.
- On MySQL, `expires_at` is rounded to the second.

### A token table without `rotated_at`

A token table without the `rotated_at` column works for everything except rotate. To add it, stop `dox s`, run `dox make:migration add_rotated_at_to_auth_access_tokens`, and put this in the new file. Then run `dox migrate`:

```dart
// ignore_for_file: file_names
import 'package:dox_migration/dox_migration.dart';

class AddRotatedAtToAuthAccessTokens extends Migration {
  @override
  Future<void> up(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.table('auth_access_tokens', (Table t) {
      t.dateTimeTz('rotated_at').nullable();
    });
  }

  @override
  Future<void> down(Schema schema) async {
    await schema.table('auth_access_tokens', (Table t) {
      t.dropColumn('rotated_at');
    });
  }
}
```

### JWT

- A token is checked with `secret` first, then with each old secret. An expired token fails at once.
- The token keeps the guard name in its `aud` claim, so a token of one guard does not work on another.
- `userCacheTtl` keeps the user in memory for this time and skips the query. A deleted or changed user is seen only after it ends, unless `forgetUser(id)` runs. Each isolate has its own cache.
- With revocation on, each token check reads the revocation store. Use `memory` for one isolate, or `redis` for many. When the store can not be read, the token is checked without it, and a warning is printed once.
- A revoked token stays on the deny list only until it expires. `revokeAllTokens` keeps tokens made after the call. It uses the server clock, so keep clocks in sync.
- The HMAC key is made from `secret` with HKDF-SHA256 and the label `dox:jwt`. Another service that checks the tokens needs `driver.signingKey`.
- `JwtAuthDriver.bearerToken(req)` gives the token of a request.

### Sessions

- The session keeps only the user id. `AuthMiddleware` loads the user on each request, so a deleted user is logged out.
- With the default `cookie` session driver, an old copy of the cookie works until the session `lifetime` ends. If logout must end old cookies, use the `cache` session driver.
- With `endSessionsOnPasswordChange`, a session made while the flag was off gets its fingerprint on its first checked request. To end all old sessions at once, change `APP_KEY` without `previousKeys`, or clear the `cache` session store.
- The password column must give the same value on every read, or every session ends.
- A rehash on login also changes the hash, so call `updateSessionPasswordHash` after it.

### Other cases

- `attempt` runs bcrypt also when no user is found, so the answer time does not tell if an email has an account.
- `once` checks the password like `attempt`, but makes no token and does not touch the session.
- With `optional: true`, a database error in the JWT or access token check goes on as a guest and is reported. With the session driver, it gives a `500`.
- `Auth.throttle` is static, so set it in a provider. If you set it in `main()`, only the first isolate throttles.
- `Auth.needsRehash(hash, rounds: 12)` checks against another cost. `Auth.hashCost(hash)` gives the cost of a hash.

### Reference

#### `AuthConfig` and `AuthGuard`

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AuthConfig(defaultGuard:)` | required | the guard that `Auth()` and the middleware use when no guard is given |
| `AuthConfig(guards:)` | `{}` | the guards, by name |
| `AuthConfig(flags:)` | `AuthFlags()` (all off) | opt-in behaviors. See [Auth flags](authorization.md#auth-flags) |
| `AuthGuard(driver:)` | required | `AccessTokenAuthDriver`, `JwtAuthDriver`, `SessionAuthDriver`, or your own `AuthDriver` |
| `AuthGuard(provider:)` | required | the `AuthProvider`: which model holds the users |

#### `AuthProvider`

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `model` | required | a function that makes a new model, like `() => User()` |
| `identifierFields` | `['email']` | the fields `attempt` searches by |
| `passwordField` | `'password'` | the column with the bcrypt hash |

#### `Auth`

| Method | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `Auth.initialize(AuthConfig)` | sets the config. Call it once, in a `DoxProvider` |
| `Auth(guard: 'admin')` | uses another guard from `guards`. Without `guard`, it uses `defaultGuard` |
| `Auth(ip: req.ip())` | gives the client ip to `attempt`, for the [login throttle](#login-throttle) |
| `Auth.throttle` | the [login throttle](#login-throttle). `null` (off) by default |
| `await attempt(credentials)` | finds the user and checks the password. Gives a token (a JWT, or an access token with all abilities), or `null` |
| `await once(credentials)` | checks the password like `attempt`. Gives `true` or `false`. It makes no token and does not touch the session |
| `login(user)` | gives a JWT for this user, with no password check |
| `setUser(req, user)` | sets this user on `req.auth`, with no token and no password check |
| `user<T>()` | the user after `attempt`, `once` or `login` |
| `isLoggedIn()`, `check()` | `true` when there is a user |
| `guest()` | `true` when there is no user |
| `id()` | the primary key of the user, or `null`. It works when the key is in `hidden` |
| `await userFromToken(token)` | the user of a JWT or access token, with no request |
| `await userFromSession(session)` | the user of a session, with no request |
| `await attemptSession(req, credentials)` | checks the password and keeps the user id in the session. Gives `true` or `false`. Session guard only |
| `loginSession(req, user)` | keeps this user in the session, with no password check. Session guard only |
| `logout(req)` | removes the session login and all session data. Session guard only |
| `await logoutOtherDevices(req, password)` | checks the password and ends all other sessions of the user. Needs the `endSessionsOnPasswordChange` flag |
| `updateSessionPasswordHash(req, user)` | keeps the current session logged in after your app changed the password |
| `await revokeToken(req)` | revokes the bearer token of this request. JWT (needs [revocation](#revoke-tokens)) or access token |
| `await revokeAllTokens(id)` | revokes all JWTs of this user made before the current second. Needs revocation |
| `await forgetUser(id)` | drops this user from the `userCacheTtl` cache. Needs revocation |
| `await createAccessToken(user, name:, abilities:, expiresIn:)` | a new access token. `token.value` is the plain token. `abilities` default to `['*']`, `expiresIn` to the driver `expiresIn` |
| `await rotateAccessToken(token, grace:, name:, expiresIn:)` | a new access token in place of `token`. See [Rotating tokens](#rotate-a-token) |
| `await setAccessTokenAbilities(token, abilities)` | replaces the whole abilities list of a token |
| `await accessTokens(user)` | all access tokens of the user, newest first |
| `await revokeAccessToken(user, id)` | deletes one access token of the user. `false` when the user has no such token |
| `await revokeAllAccessTokens(user)` | deletes all access tokens of the user. Gives how many |
| `await pruneExpiredAccessTokens()` | deletes the expired tokens of the table. Gives how many |
| `currentAccessToken` | the `AccessToken` of this request, or `null` |
| `tokenCan(ability)` | `true` when the access token of this request has the ability, or `*` |
| `Auth.needsRehash(hash)` | `true` when the hash was not made with the cost of `Hash.rounds` |
| `Auth.hashCost(hash)` | the bcrypt cost of a hash, or `null` when it is not a bcrypt hash |

#### `req.auth`

| Code | What it gives |
| --- | --- |
| `req.auth` | an `IAuth?`. `null` for a guest, and on a route with no `AuthMiddleware`. A query or body field can not set it |
| `req.auth as Auth` | the `Auth`, for `tokenCan`, `currentAccessToken` and `revokeToken` |
| `req.auth?.isLoggedIn()` | `true` when a user is loaded |
| `req.auth?.id()` | the primary key of the user, or `null` |
| `req.auth?.user<User>()` | the user model |
| `req.auth?.toJson()` | the user as a map, without `hidden` fields |

#### `AccessTokenAuthDriver`

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `table` | `'auth_access_tokens'` | the table of the tokens |
| `connection` | the default connection | the `dox_orm` connection name |
| `expiresIn` | `null` (no end) | how long a new token works |
| `hashRounds` | `10` | the bcrypt cost of your stored hashes, for `attempt` |
| `type` | the guard name | the type of the tokens. A token works only on a guard with the same type |
| `stringIds` | `false` | `true` for users with text ids. Use the same value in the migration |
| `uuidIds` | `false` | `true` for users with uuid ids. Use the same value in the migration |
| `throwOnError` | `false` | `true`: an error in a token check is thrown, not turned into a `401`. See [When the database fails](#when-the-database-fails) |

#### `AccessTokenTables.up` and `dox auth:tokens-table`

| Option | Flag | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `table` | none (edit the migration) | `'auth_access_tokens'` | the table name. Use the same name as the driver `table` |
| `uuidIds` | `--uuid` | `false` | `tokenable_id` is a uuid column (`UUID` on Postgres) |
| `stringIds` | `--string-ids` | `false` | `tokenable_id` is text. Do not use it with `--uuid` |
| `usersTable` | `--users-table=users` | none | adds a foreign key from `tokenable_id` to `usersKey` of this table, with cascade delete. The two id columns must have the same type |
| `usersKey` | `--users-key=uid` | `'id'` | the key column of `usersTable` |

`AccessTokenTables.down(schema, table: 'auth_access_tokens')` drops the table. The table has these columns: `id`, `tokenable_type`, `tokenable_id`, `type`, `name`, `hash`, `abilities`, `last_used_at`, `expires_at`, `rotated_at`, `created_at`, `updated_at`. `auth:tokens-table` is a [package command](../digging-deeper/package-commands.md) of `dox_auth`, and it never overwrites a migration that is already there.

#### `AccessToken`

| Field | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `id` | the row id |
| `value` | the plain token. Only set by `createAccessToken` and `rotateAccessToken`. It is not kept |
| `name`, `type` | the name and the type |
| `tokenableType` | the table name of the user model |
| `tokenableId` | the user id: an `int`, or a `String` with `stringIds` or `uuidIds` |
| `abilities` | the list of abilities |
| `lastUsedAt`, `expiresAt`, `createdAt`, `updatedAt` | times, in UTC |
| `user` | the user. Set by `createAccessToken` and by a token check. `null` in `accessTokens(user)` |
| `can(ability)`, `cannot(ability)` | checks one ability (`*` passes every check) |
| `toJson()` | the token without the hash and the plain value |

#### `JwtAuthDriver`

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `secret` | required | the key that signs tokens, like `SecretKey(env.appKey)`. It must be at least 32 bytes |
| `algorithm` | `JWTAlgorithm.HS256` | the signing algorithm. A token with another algorithm in its header is rejected |
| `expiresIn` | `Duration(hours: 1)` | how long a token is valid |
| `issuer` | `null` | the `iss` claim. When set, the check also reads it |
| `hashRounds` | `10` | the bcrypt cost of your stored hashes. Use the same value as `Hash.rounds` |
| `userCacheTtl` | `null` (off) | keep the user of a token in memory for this time |
| `previousSecrets` | `null` | old secrets, only to check tokens after a key change. `null` with `secret` = `APP_KEY`: the old keys come from `AppConfig.previousKeys`. `[]` turns it off |
| `minimalPayload` | `false` | put only the user id (the `sub` claim) in new tokens |
| `revocation` | `false` | turn on token revocation |
| `revocationStore` | `null` | the cache store for revoked tokens. `null` is the default app store |

#### `SessionAuthDriver`

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `hashRounds` | `10` | the bcrypt cost of your stored hashes |

#### `AuthMiddleware` and `GuestMiddleware`

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `AuthMiddleware(guard:)` | `defaultGuard` | the guard to check |
| `AuthMiddleware(guards:)` | none | several guards, tried in order. Do not set `guard` too |
| `AuthMiddleware(redirectTo:)` | none (`401`) | send a guest to this page instead of a `401`. Not used with `optional` |
| `AuthMiddleware(optional:)` | `false` | let guests through too |
| `GuestMiddleware(guard:)` | `defaultGuard` | the guard to check |
| `GuestMiddleware(redirectTo:)` | none (`403`) | send a logged-in user to this page instead of a `403` |

#### `LoginThrottle`

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `maxAttempts` | `5` | failed logins allowed per login field and ip |
| `decay` | `Duration(minutes: 1)` | how long the count is kept, from the first failed login |
| `store` | `null` | the cache store for the counts. `null` is the default app store |

# Authorization

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/security/authorization/

# Authorization

`dox_auth` lets you decide what a logged in user may do, with gates and policies.

[Authentication](authentication.md) tells you who the user is. Authorization tells you what this user may do. For example, a user may edit their own post, but not the post of another user.

There are two ways to write the rules:

- A **gate** is one rule, written as a function.
- A **policy** is a class with all the rules of one model, like `Post`.

## Registering the rules

Gates and policies are kept per isolate. Dox runs many isolates, so add them in the `setup()` of a provider, because it runs in every isolate:

```dart title="lib/providers/gate_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/post/post.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/policies/post_policy.dart';

class GateProvider extends DoxProvider {
  @override
  void setup() {
    Gate.define('update-post', (User user, Post post) => post.userId == user.id);
    Gate.policy<Post>(PostPolicy());
  }
}
```

Dox finds the provider by itself. Run `dart run build_runner build` to add it to `lib/generated/container.g.dart`.

## Writing gates

A gate gets the user and a subject, and gives `true` when the user may do it. The user and subject types come from the function, so a check with another type is denied:

```dart
Gate.define('update-post', (User user, Post post) => post.userId == user.id);
```

If the gate needs no subject, use `_` for the second parameter:

```dart
Gate.define('create-post', (User user, _) => user.verified == true);
```

A gate can also be async:

```dart
Gate.define('publish-post', (User user, Post post) async {
  return await user.canPublishIn(post.categoryId);
});
```

## Checking a gate

Use `Gate.allows` to check if the user may do something:

```dart
if (await Gate.allows(user, 'update-post', post)) {
  // the user may update the post
}
```

`Gate.denies` is the opposite:

```dart
if (await Gate.denies(user, 'create-post')) {
  // the user may not create a post
}
```

If you want to stop the request when the check fails, use `Gate.authorize`. It throws, and the client gets a `403`:

```dart
await Gate.authorize(user, 'update-post', post);
```

To check many abilities at once, use `Gate.any` (at least one) or `Gate.all` (all of them):

```dart
await Gate.any(user, <String>['update-post', 'delete-post'], post);
await Gate.all(user, <String>['update-post', 'delete-post'], post);
```

An ability with no gate and no policy is always denied.

### Giving a reason

Sometimes you want to tell the user why they may not do something. Return a `GateResponse` instead of a `bool`. The reason of `GateResponse.deny` becomes the message of the `403` answer:

```dart
Gate.define('delete-post', (User user, Post post) {
  if (post.published == true) {
    return GateResponse.deny('You can not delete a published post.');
  }
  return post.userId == user.id;
});
```

`Gate.inspect` gives you the full answer:

```dart
GateResponse response = await Gate.inspect(user, 'delete-post', post);
print(response.allowed);
print(response.message);
```

## Writing policies

When a model has many rules, put them in a policy. Write one method per ability. A method takes the user, and the model when the ability needs one. Then list the methods in `abilities`:

```dart title="lib/app/policies/post_policy.dart"
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/post/post.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

class PostPolicy extends Policy<User, Post> {
  bool create(User user) => user.verified == true;

  bool update(User user, Post post) => post.userId == user.id;

  bool delete(User user, Post post) => post.userId == user.id;

  @override
  Map<String, Function> get abilities => <String, Function>{
    'create': create,
    'update': update,
    'delete': delete,
  };
}
```

The `abilities` map is needed because compiled Dart apps can not find a method by its name.

Register the policy for its model:

```dart
Gate.policy<Post>(PostPolicy());
```

Now a check with a `Post` as the subject uses the policy. For an ability with no model, like `create`, pass the type `Post`:

```dart
await Gate.allows(user, 'update', post);
await Gate.allows(user, 'create', Post);
await Gate.authorize(user, 'delete', post);
```

Each method must take `(User user)` or `(User user, Post post)`. A method with another signature fails at `Gate.policy`, so you see the mistake when the app starts.

### Using the ability constants

Use the `Ability` constants when you want the compiler to find a wrong ability name. `Ability` has the five usual names: `Ability.viewAny`, `Ability.view`, `Ability.create`, `Ability.update` and `Ability.delete`.

```dart
Map<String, Function> get abilities => <String, Function>{
  Ability.update: update,
};

await Gate.allows(user, Ability.update, post);
```

Each constant is the same text as its name. Thus, `Ability.update` and `'update'` are the same ability.

## Authorizing in a controller

In a controller, use `req.authorize`, `req.can` and `req.cannot`. They use the logged in user of `req.auth`, so put the route after `AuthMiddleware`:

```dart
Future<Post> update(DoxRequest req, Post post) async {
  await req.authorize('update', post);
  post.title = req.input('title');
  await post.save();
  return post;
}
```

`req.can` gives a `bool`, for example to tell the front end what the user may do:

```dart
Future<Map<String, dynamic>> show(DoxRequest req, Post post) async {
  return <String, dynamic>{
    'post': post,
    'can_edit': await req.can('update', post),
  };
}
```

`req.authorize` answers `401` for a guest and `403` for a user who may not do it.

## Authorizing on a route

The `Can` middleware checks an ability before the controller runs. Put it after `AuthMiddleware`:

```dart
// a gate with no subject
Route.get('/admin', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(), Can('view-admin'), adminController.index]);
```

For a policy method with no model, pass the type with `subject`:

```dart
// a policy method with no model
Route.post('/posts', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(), Can('create', subject: Post), postController.store]);
```

For a policy method with a model, use `param`. The subject is then the value that `Route.bind` gives for that route param. When `Route.bind` finds nothing, the answer is `404`:

```dart
// a policy method with the model of the route param
Route.bind<Post>('post', (String id) => Post().find(id));
Route.put('/posts/{post}', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(), Can('update', param: 'post'), postController.update]);
```

A guest who may not do it gets `401`, and a logged in user who may not do it gets `403`.

## Guest users

A guest has no user, so a gate or policy is denied for a guest. If you want a rule that also works for guests, make the user type nullable:

```dart
Gate.define('view-post', (User? user, Post post) {
  return post.published == true || post.userId == user?.id;
});
```

The same works in a policy:

```dart
class CommentPolicy extends Policy<User?, Comment> {
  bool view(User? user, Comment comment) => comment.visible == true;

  @override
  Map<String, Function> get abilities => <String, Function>{'view': view};
}
```

On a public route, use `AuthMiddleware(optional: true)`. It loads the user when the login is good, and lets guests through. Without it, nothing loads the user, so a logged in user is a guest too:

```dart
Route.get('/posts/{post}', <dynamic>[AuthMiddleware(optional: true), Can('view-post', param: 'post'), postController.show]);
```

## Before and after hooks

Sometimes one user may do everything, like an admin. `Gate.before` runs before every check. Return `true` or `false` to decide at once, or `null` to go on with the normal check:

```dart
Gate.before((User user, String ability) => user.isAdmin == true ? true : null);
```

A hook runs only for users of its type, so a `User` hook does not run for guests.

`Gate.after` sees the answer of every check, for example to log it. It can not change the answer:

```dart
Gate.after((User user, String ability, GateResponse response) {
  print('${user.id} $ability ${response.allowed}');
});
```

A policy can have its own `before`. It runs before the methods of that policy:

```dart
class PostPolicy extends Policy<User, Post> {
  @override
  bool? before(User user, String ability) => user.isAdmin == true ? true : null;

  // ...
}
```

## Auth flags

Some behaviors are opt-in. Turn them on with `flags:` in `AuthConfig`. All flags are off by default:

```dart
AuthConfig authConfig = AuthConfig(
  defaultGuard: 'web',
  guards: guards,
  flags: const AuthFlags(forbidGuest: true, jsonNoRedirect: true),
);
```

- `forbidGuest`: `req.authorize` and `Can` give a guest `403` with the gate message, not `401`. `AuthMiddleware` still gives a guest `401`.
- `jsonNoRedirect`: `AuthMiddleware(redirectTo: '/login')` gives a JSON or XHR client a `401`, not a redirect. An Inertia request still gets the redirect.
- `endSessionsOnPasswordChange`: a session login ends when the user's password changes. It also turns on `logoutOtherDevices`. See [Ending sessions when the password changes](authentication.md#end-other-sessions-when-the-password-changes).

`AuthFlags.all()` turns on every flag:

```dart
AuthConfig(defaultGuard: 'web', guards: guards, flags: const AuthFlags.all());
```

## Testing

`Gate.flush()` removes all gates, policies and hooks. Call it in `setUp` when each test adds its own rules.

## Details

- A JSON client is a request with a json `Accept` header, a JSON body, or `X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest`.
- When a policy has no method for an ability, the gate with that name is used.
- Policy methods are normal typed Dart methods, so you can also call them directly in a test.
- The flags are part of `AuthConfig`, and `Auth.initialize` runs in every isolate, so every isolate gets the same flags.


---

# CORS

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/security/cors/

# CORS

CORS headers let a web page on another domain call your API.

A browser blocks a request from `https://my.app` to `https://api.my.app` by default. The API must send CORS headers to allow it. Dox adds these headers from `CORSConfig`.

## Setup

The config is in `lib/config/cors.dart`. A new app has this file with `enabled: false`, so it sends no CORS headers. Set `origin` to the URL of your front end, and set `enabled: true`:

```dart title="lib/config/cors.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

CORSConfig cors = CORSConfig(
  enabled: true,
  origin: 'https://my.app',
  methods: <String>['GET', 'POST', 'PUT', 'PATCH', 'DELETE'],
  headers: <String>['Content-Type', 'Authorization'],
  exposeHeaders: <String>['Content-Disposition'],
  credentials: true,
  maxAge: 600,
);
```

Then pass it to `AppConfig`:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  cors: cors,
  // ...
);
```

You do not need an `OPTIONS` route. Dox answers the browser's preflight `OPTIONS` request with `204 No Content` and the CORS headers of the route the browser asks about.

## Options

Each option sets one response header. All options except `enabled` are `null` by default, and a `null` option sends no header. So with no `origin`, the browser blocks pages on other domains.

| Option | Header | Value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `enabled` | - | `true` adds the headers to every route. Default: `true` |
| `origin` | `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` | one origin, a `List<String>` of origins, or `'*'` for all |
| `methods` | `Access-Control-Allow-Methods` | a `List<String>` or a text like `'GET,POST'`. `'*'` allows all |
| `headers` | `Access-Control-Allow-Headers` | a `List<String>` or a text. `'*'` allows all |
| `exposeHeaders` | `Access-Control-Expose-Headers` | the response headers the page may read |
| `credentials` | `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials` | `true` lets the browser send cookies |
| `maxAge` | `Access-Control-Max-Age` | how many seconds the browser keeps the preflight answer |

## Allowing more than one origin

If your API has more than one front end, give `origin` a list. Do not put many origins in one text, because a text is sent as it is:

```dart
CORSConfig cors = CORSConfig(
  origin: <String>['https://my.app', 'https://admin.my.app'],
);
```

The header accepts only one origin, so Dox checks the `Origin` header of the request. When the origin is in the list, Dox sends back that one origin. When it is not, Dox sends no header, and the browser blocks the call.

## Sending cookies

If the front end sends cookies, set `credentials: true`. Then do not use `origin: '*'`, because the browser blocks every call with cookies when the origin is `*`. Set `origin` to your real front end URL, or a list of URLs.

A page on an allowed origin can send requests with the cookies of your users, so list only sites you trust.

## CORS for some routes

`enabled` is the default for all routes. You can change it for a group of routes:

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
// CORS headers only on these routes (use with enabled: false)
Route.enabledCors(() {
  Route.get('/public/posts', (PostController c) => c.index);
});

// no CORS headers on these routes
Route.disabledCors(() {
  Route.post('/webhooks/stripe', (WebhookController c) => c.handle);
});
```

## Details

- For `methods`, `headers` and `exposeHeaders`, a list is joined with commas.
- With an `origin` list, Dox also sends `Vary: Origin`, so caches know the answer depends on the origin. A list with `'*'` sends `*`.


---

# CSRF protection

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/security/csrf/

# CSRF protection

`CsrfMiddleware` stops other sites from sending forms to your app in the name of your logged in users.

This attack is called cross site request forgery (CSRF). Another site makes the browser of your user send a form to your app. The browser sends your session cookie with it, so the request looks real.

To stop it, each session has a secret token. A request that changes data must send the token back. Another site can not read the token, so it can not send it.

## Setup

The middleware needs a session, so put it right after `SessionMiddleware`:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[
    const SessionMiddleware(),
    const CsrfMiddleware(except: <String>['/api/*', '/webhooks/stripe']),
  ],
  // ...
);
```

Now every `POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` and `DELETE` request must send the token. A request with no token, or a wrong one, gets a `419` with `{"code": "csrf_token_mismatch", "message": "CSRF token mismatch"}`.

`GET`, `HEAD` and `OPTIONS` requests are not checked, so never change data in a `GET` route.

## Sending the token

Dox reads the token from the `_token` field of the body, or from the `X-CSRF-TOKEN` or `X-XSRF-TOKEN` header. In your code the token is `req.session.token`.

Do not put the token in a URL, because URLs end up in logs and in the browser history. For the same reason, Dox does not read `_token` from the query string.

### HTML forms

Put the token in a hidden field. With [views](../the-basic/views.md#forms), `@csrf` writes this field for you:

```html
<form method="POST" action="/posts">
  @csrf
  ...
</form>
```

`@csrf` must be alone on its line. In the middle of a line, use `{{ csrfField() }}`, which prints the same field. If you only need the token, for example for a `<meta>` tag, use `csrfToken()`.

### axios and Inertia

Dox also sets an `XSRF-TOKEN` cookie with the token. It is not `HttpOnly`, so page scripts can read it. axios reads this cookie and sends it in the `X-XSRF-TOKEN` header by itself. Inertia uses axios, so it works with no code.

With `fetch`, read the cookie and send the header yourself:

```js
const token = document.cookie
  .split('; ')
  .find((c) => c.startsWith('XSRF-TOKEN='))
  ?.split('=')[1];

fetch('/posts', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'X-XSRF-TOKEN': token, 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify({ title: 'Hi' }),
});
```

## Excluding paths

Some routes can not send the token, like webhooks that other servers call, or APIs that use tokens. List them in `except`:

```dart
const CsrfMiddleware(except: <String>['/api/*', '/webhooks/stripe']);
```

A path that ends with `*` matches everything that starts with it, so `/api/*` matches `/api/posts` and `/api/users/5`. Any other path must match exactly.

Only skip paths that do not use the session login. A webhook should check its own signature instead.

## After login

`req.session.regenerate()` also makes a new token, and Dox sends the new `XSRF-TOKEN` cookie with the same response. So after login, the client must use the new token.

## Details

- An excluded path is not checked and gets no `XSRF-TOKEN` cookie.
- `regenerate(keepToken: true)` keeps the token, so forms open in other tabs keep working. Do not use it at login, because a token from before the login would stay valid.


---

# Encryption

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/security/encryption/

# Encryption

`Crypt` and `AESEncryptor` encrypt and decrypt text with AES-256-GCM, so you can store or send data that nobody else can read or change.

Dox uses the same encryption for cookies and the `cookie` session driver, with your `APP_KEY`.

## Configuration

The key is the `APP_KEY` in `.env`. Make a new one with the CLI. It writes a random key of 32 letters and digits:

```bash
dox key:generate
```

Keep `APP_KEY` in `.env` or in the secrets of your host. Never put it in code or in git.

At startup Dox checks `APP_KEY`. When it is empty, not exactly 32 bytes, or a public sample key, the app stops. In `development`, `local`, `test` and `testing` it only prints a warning.

## Encrypting values

`Crypt` uses the `APP_KEY` of the app, so you do not pass a key. Use `encryptString` for text:

```dart
String secret = Crypt.encryptString('card-1234');
```

Use `encrypt` for any JSON value:

```dart
String data = Crypt.encrypt(<String, dynamic>{'id': 5}); // any JSON value
```

The result is base64 text. The same value gives a different result each time.

## Decrypting values

Use `decryptString` or `decrypt` to get the value back:

```dart
String card = Crypt.decryptString(secret); // 'card-1234'

Map<String, dynamic> map = Crypt.decrypt(data);
```

They throw a `DecryptException` when the text was changed or made with another key. The client then gets a `400`. They also try the old keys in `AppConfig.previousKeys`, so values still work after you [rotate the key](#change-the-key-key-rotation).

## Using your own key

Sometimes you want a key that is not the `APP_KEY`. Use `AESEncryptor` and pass the key yourself:

```dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

String secret = env.appKey;

String encoded = AESEncryptor.encode('Hello world', secret);
String decoded = AESEncryptor.decode(encoded, secret); // 'Hello world'
```

`decode` throws a `DecryptException` when the text was changed or the key is wrong.

### One key per purpose

Dox does not use your key as it is. It makes a 32-byte key from it with HKDF-SHA256 and a label. The default label is `dox:encrypt`. You should pick your own label with `purpose:`, so a value made for one purpose can not be used for another. `decode` needs the same `purpose`:

```dart
AESEncryptor.encode(text, secret, purpose: 'app:invoice')
```

Dox uses these labels for its own keys:

| Label | Used for |
| --- | --- |
| `dox:cookie` | encrypted cookies, and the `cookie` session driver |
| `dox:jwt` | the HMAC key of `JwtAuthDriver` (with a `SecretKey`) |
| `dox:encrypt` | `AESEncryptor` when you give no `purpose` |
| `dox:signed-url` | for signed URLs |

## Encrypted cookies

`DoxCookie` encrypts its value with `APP_KEY` by default, and `req.cookie(key)` decrypts it:

```dart
return response().cookie(DoxCookie('theme', 'dark'));  // encrypted

String? theme = req.cookie('theme');                    // decrypted
```

If you need a plain text cookie, turn encryption off. Read the raw value with `decrypt: false`:

```dart
DoxCookie('theme', 'dark', encrypt: false);             // plain text

String? raw = req.cookie('theme', decrypt: false);      // as sent
```

`req.cookie(key)` returns `null` when the cookie was changed, made with another `APP_KEY`, or made for another cookie name. The cookie name is bound to the value, so a value can not be copied from one cookie to another. To decrypt a raw cookie value yourself, use `DoxCookie.decrypt(name, value)`.

## Rotating the key {#change-the-key-key-rotation}

You should change `APP_KEY` from time to time, or when someone who knew it leaves the team. If you just change it, old cookies and sessions can not be read, so every user is logged out, and JWT tokens signed with it stop working. With `previousKeys`, users stay logged in while you change it:

1. Copy the current `APP_KEY` to `APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS`.
2. Run `dox key:generate`. It writes a new `APP_KEY`. Now `.env` has both:

    ```bash title=".env"
    APP_KEY=<the new key from dox key:generate>
    APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS=<the old APP_KEY>
    ```

3. Read it in the env class, and give it to `AppConfig`:

    ```dart title="lib/config/env.dart"
    List<String> get appPreviousKeys => <String>[]; // APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS=a,b
    ```

    ```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
    AppConfig(
      appKey: env.appKey,
      previousKeys: env.appPreviousKeys,
    )
    ```

4. Deploy. Every instance must get the new env at the same time.
5. Wait until the old cookies have expired: the session `lifetime`, and the `maxAge` of your own cookies.
6. Remove the old key from `APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS` and deploy again.

`APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS` can hold more than one key, comma separated. Dox writes a cookie with the new key the next time it sends it, so a user who comes back during step 5 moves to the new key without noticing.

The old keys are used to read encrypted cookies, the `cookie` session driver, the CSRF token, `Crypt.decrypt`, and JWT tokens signed with `APP_KEY`. A JWT secret that is not `APP_KEY` needs its own `previousSecrets`, see [Authentication](authentication.md#change-the-jwt-secret). Your own `AESEncryptor.decode` calls read old keys only when you pass `previousSecrets: Dox().config.previousKeys`.

### When the key leaked

Do **not** put a leaked key in `previousKeys`, because anyone who has it can still make cookies and JWT tokens that Dox accepts. Change `APP_KEY` with no `previousKeys`. Every user is logged out, and that is what you want.

## Details

- To store passwords, do not encrypt them. Hash them. See [Hashing](hashing.md).
- `Crypt.encryptString(v)` gives the same as `AESEncryptor.encode(v, appKey)`.
- The flag `decryptServerError` makes a `DecryptException` a reported `500` instead of a `400`. See [Core flags](../reference/app-config.md#core-flags).
- `KeyDerivation.forAppKey(label)` gives the 32-byte key of a label.
- The work runs in Rust with the AES instructions of the CPU. One cookie takes about 1–2 µs.
- Each message gets a new random 12-byte nonce. The output is base64 of `nonce + encrypted text + tag`. The 16-byte tag makes `decode` throw if one byte is changed.
- `encode` and `decode` also take `associatedData`, like a cookie name. It is not in the output, but `decode` needs the same value.


---

# Hashing

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/security/hashing/

# Hashing

`Hash` turns a password into a bcrypt hash that you can store, and checks a password against it later.

A hash is one-way: you can not turn it back into the password. `Hash` uses bcrypt with a new random salt each time. It is in `package:dox_core/dox_core.dart`.

You do not need `Hash` for a normal login, because `Auth().attempt()` from `dox_auth` checks the password for you. See [Authentication](authentication.md).

## Hashing passwords

Hash the password before you save it:

```dart
user.password = await Hash.makeAsync(body.password);
await user.save();
```

`makeAsync` runs bcrypt in another isolate, so it does not block the server. The result looks like `$2a$10$...`. It holds the salt, so you only store this one string.

Never send the hash to the client. Put the column in the `hidden` list of the model.

## Verifying passwords

Use `verifyAsync` to check a password against a hash. It gives `true` when they match:

```dart
bool ok = await Hash.verifyAsync('secret', user.password!);
```

It gives `false` when the password does not match, or when the hash is not a valid bcrypt hash, like an empty string.

`Hash.make` and `Hash.verify` do the same, but they block the request isolate while bcrypt runs. Use them only outside request handlers. `Hash.check` is the same as `Hash.verify`:

```dart
bool ok = Hash.verify('secret', user.password!);
```

## Changing the cost

`Hash.rounds` is the bcrypt cost for new hashes. The default is `10`, and each step up doubles the time. The cost must be from 4 to 31. Do not go below 10:

```dart
Hash.rounds = 12;
String hash = Hash.make('secret', rounds: 12); // or per call
```

Old hashes keep their own cost, so they still verify. If you change the cost, also set `hashRounds` on your auth driver to the same value. See [Authentication](authentication.md#password-hash-cost).

## Long passwords

bcrypt reads at most 72 bytes. So `Hash.make` and `Hash.makeAsync` throw an `ArgumentError` for a longer password, and `Hash.verify` gives `false`. Limit the length in your DTO, like `@Length(min: 8, max: 72)`.

`@Length` counts characters, but a letter outside ASCII can use up to 4 bytes. So such a password can still be too long. Catch the error and answer `422`, or use a smaller `max`.

## Comparing secrets

To check an API key or a token, use `Hash.equals(given, expected)`, not `==`. `==` stops at the first wrong character, so the time can tell how much of the key was right. `Hash.equals` takes the same time for every value of the same length:

```dart
bool ok = Hash.equals(req.header('X-Api-Key') ?? '', Env.get<String>('API_KEY'));
```

## Storing tokens

For a long random secret that you keep in the database, like an API key, store only `Hash.sha256(token)`. Then find the row by the hash of what the client sends. SHA-256 gives the same hash for the same input, so a unique index works on it:

```dart
String stored = Hash.sha256(token);          // save this, never the token
Token? row = await Token().where('hash', Hash.sha256(given)).getFirst();
```

Never use `Hash.sha256` for passwords. A password is short and can be guessed, so use bcrypt.

## Details

- The error text of a too long password does not hold the password, so it is safe in logs.
- bcrypt is slow on purpose, so guessing is slow too. Do not hash in a loop on hot paths.


---

# Rate limiting

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/security/rate-limiting/

# Rate limiting

`RateLimit` is a middleware that stops a client that sends too many requests.

You should use it on login, sign up and other routes that bots like to hammer.

## Limiting a route

Add `RateLimit` to the route. The defaults are `max: 60` and `per: Duration(minutes: 1)`:

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
Route.post('/auth/login', <dynamic>[
  RateLimit(max: 5, per: Duration(minutes: 1)),
  (AuthController c) => c.login,
]);
```

Now each client (by ip) can send 5 login requests per minute. The 6th request gets a `429`:

```text
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 42
X-RateLimit-Limit: 5
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 0

{"code":"too_many_requests","message":"Too Many Requests"}
```

`Retry-After` is the number of seconds until the client can try again. Every answer, also a normal one, has the `X-RateLimit-Limit` and `X-RateLimit-Remaining` headers. The error goes through your exception handler, so it has the same JSON shape as your other errors.

## Limiting every route

To limit all routes, put it in `globalMiddleware`:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[
    RateLimit(max: 120),
  ],
  // ...
);
```

## Counting by user

By default each ip has its own count. Sometimes you want to count per user instead. Give a `key` function, which returns any `String`. For example, count by user id after `AuthMiddleware`:

```dart
Route.get('/reports', <dynamic>[
  AuthMiddleware(),
  RateLimit(
    max: 100,
    key: (DoxRequest req) => '${req.auth?.user<User>()?.id ?? req.ip()}',
  ),
  (ReportController c) => c.index,
]);
```

Do not count by a raw header, like `req.header('X-Api-Key')`. A client can send a new value with each request and get a new count each time. Count by a value that you checked first, like the id of the logged in user.

## Two limits with the same settings

Two `RateLimit` with the same `max` and `per` share one count for the same client. If you want separate counts, give each one a `name`:

```dart
Route.post('/auth/login', <dynamic>[
  RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'login'),
  (AuthController c) => c.login,
]);
Route.post('/auth/register', <dynamic>[
  RateLimit(max: 5, name: 'register'),
  (AuthController c) => c.register,
]);
```

## Behind a proxy

Behind Caddy, nginx or a load balancer, every request comes from the proxy ip, so all clients share one count. Add the proxy to `AppConfig.trustedProxies`, so `req.ip()` is the real client ip. See [App config](../reference/app-config.md).

## IPv6 clients

A home or a server with IPv6 often gets a whole /64 block. That is 2^64 addresses. By default each address has its own count, so such a client can send from a new address each time and never hit the limit.

Turn on `rateLimitIpv6Prefix` in `CoreFlags` to count each IPv6 client by its /64 prefix:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  flags: CoreFlags(rateLimitIpv6Prefix: true),
  // ...
);
```

All clients in one /64 then share one count. An IPv4 address stays as it is. A `key` function you give is used as it is. To use the same rule in your own key, call `RateLimit.ipBucket(req.ip())`.

## Where the counts live

When the default [cache](../digging-deeper/cache.md) store is Redis, the counts are in Redis, so all isolates and all servers share them. Use this when you run more than one server. To set a command timeout or other Redis options, see [Redis options](../digging-deeper/cache.md#redis-options).

With any other default store, the counts are kept in the main isolate of each server. All isolates of one server share them, but each server has its own counts. So with 3 servers, a client can send up to 3 times `max`.

To use a store by name, pass `store`:

```dart
RateLimit(max: 10, store: 'redis')
```

## Sliding window

By default the count starts at 0 at the start of each window. So a client can send `max` requests at the end of one minute, and `max` more at the start of the next. That is fine for most apps.

If you want to stop this burst, set `sliding: true`:

```dart
RateLimit(max: 5, per: Duration(minutes: 1), sliding: true)
```

The count is then the count of this window, plus a part of the window before. That part gets smaller as the window goes on. It costs one more read per request.

## Details

- A blocked request still counts, so a client that keeps sending while it is blocked stays blocked.
- In the main isolate mode, each limited request sends one small message to the main isolate.
- In the main isolate mode, the counter keeps at most 100,000 clients (about 15 MB). When it is full, it first drops the expired counts, then the oldest ones. A dropped client starts again at 0. New clients are never turned away, so a flood of fake clients can not lock out real users.
- A `memory` store named in `store` also counts in the main isolate. A store passed in `cacheStore` is used as it is.
- Sliding window example: 4 requests last minute, 1 this minute, 15 seconds in: the count is `4 x 45/60 + 1 = 4`. `X-RateLimit-Remaining` is `max` minus this count, rounded up. Each count is kept for 2 windows.

## See also

- [Middleware](../the-basic/middleware.md)
- [Security headers](security-headers.md)
- [Production checklist](../reference/production-checklist.md)


---

# Security headers

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/security/security-headers/

# Security headers

`SecurityHeaders` is a middleware that adds safe HTTP headers to every answer.

The browser reads these headers and blocks some common attacks, like showing your page in a frame on another site.

## Setup

Put it first in `globalMiddleware`. Then an error from a later middleware, like a `419` or a `429`, also gets the headers:

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  globalMiddleware: <dynamic>[
    const SecurityHeaders(),
  ],
  // ...
);
```

Every answer now has these headers:

| Header | Default value | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `X-Content-Type-Options` | `nosniff` | The browser does not guess the file type. |
| `X-Frame-Options` | `DENY` | No site can show your page in a frame. |
| `Referrer-Policy` | `strict-origin-when-cross-origin` | Other sites only see your domain, not the full url. |
| `Permissions-Policy` | `camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=()` | The page can not use the camera, the microphone or the location. |
| `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy` | `same-origin` | A page of another site that opens yours can not reach it. |
| `Strict-Transport-Security` | `max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains` | The browser uses only https for one year. Sent only on https requests. |

`Content-Security-Policy` is off by default, because a good policy depends on your pages.

## Changing a header

Each header has an option. Give a new value to change it, or `null` to remove it. Use `extra` for other headers:

```dart
const SecurityHeaders(
  frameOptions: 'SAMEORIGIN', // allow frames from your own site
  permissionsPolicy: null, // do not send this header
  contentSecurityPolicy: "frame-ancestors 'none'",
  extra: <String, String>{'Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy': 'same-origin'},
)
```

| Option | Header |
| --- | --- |
| `contentTypeOptions` | `X-Content-Type-Options` |
| `frameOptions` | `X-Frame-Options` |
| `referrerPolicy` | `Referrer-Policy` |
| `permissionsPolicy` | `Permissions-Policy` |
| `crossOriginOpenerPolicy` | `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy` |
| `strictTransportSecurity` | `Strict-Transport-Security` |
| `contentSecurityPolicy` | `Content-Security-Policy` |
| `xssProtection` | `X-XSS-Protection` (default `'0'`) |
| `extra` | any other headers, name to value. A `null` value removes that header |

## HSTS behind a proxy

Dox serves plain http, and a proxy (Caddy, nginx, a load balancer) does the https part. Dox sends `Strict-Transport-Security` only when the request came in over https. It knows this from the `X-Forwarded-Proto: https` header, but it only believes this header from a trusted proxy. So add your proxy to `AppConfig.trustedProxies`, or Dox never sends HSTS:

```dart
AppConfig(trustedProxies: <String>['127.0.0.1', '::1']);
```

See [App config](../reference/app-config.md).

## Details

- Without this middleware, the server already sends `X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and `X-XSS-Protection: 0` on every answer. `SecurityHeaders` replaces them, and `null` also removes them.
- `X-XSS-Protection: 0` turns off the old XSS filter of browsers, because in old browsers it can make holes. Use `Content-Security-Policy` instead.
- Middleware runs only for routes that exist. So a `404` for an unknown URL and a preflight `OPTIONS` answer get only the three server headers.

## See also

- [Middleware](../the-basic/middleware.md)
- [CORS](cors.md)
- [Rate limiting](rate-limiting.md)


---

# Signed URLs

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/security/signed-urls/

# Signed URLs

A signed URL has a `signature` in its query, so nobody can change the URL without your `APP_KEY`.

You need it for links in emails, like "unsubscribe" or "download your file", where the user is not logged in.

## Creating signed URLs

Give the route a name and add the `ValidateSignature` middleware:

```dart title="lib/routes/web.dart"
Route.get('/unsubscribe/{user}', <dynamic>[
  const ValidateSignature(),
  (UserController c) => c.unsubscribe,
]).name('unsubscribe');
```

Then make the URL with `Route.signedUrl`:

```dart
String url = Route.signedUrl(
  'unsubscribe',
  params: <String, Object>{'user': 5},
);
// https://example.com/unsubscribe/5?signature=3f9a...
```

A URL with no `signature`, a wrong one, or a changed path or query gets `403 Forbidden`.

### URLs that expire

Sometimes a link should work only for a while. Give `expires`. The URL then gets a signed `expires` query param, and after that time it gets a `403`:

```dart
String url = Route.signedUrl(
  'download',
  params: <String, Object>{'file': 12},
  expires: Duration(hours: 1),
);
```

## Relative URLs

By default the URL is absolute. Dox puts `APP_URL` in front, and the scheme and host are signed too. Give `baseUrl:` to use another one. The `Host` and the scheme of the request must match the URL it was made with: `APP_URL`, or the `baseUrl`.

If you want to sign only the path and the query, use `absolute: false`, and check it with `ValidateSignature(absolute: false)`:

```dart
Route.get('/files/{id}', <dynamic>[
  const ValidateSignature(absolute: false),
  (FileController c) => c.show,
]).name('files.show');

String url = Route.signedUrl(
  'files.show',
  params: <String, Object>{'id': 3},
  absolute: false,
);
// /files/3?signature=...
```

Behind a proxy that ends TLS, add the proxy to `AppConfig.trustedProxies`, so Dox sees that the scheme is https.

## Checking in a controller

If you want to answer a bad link in your own way, use `ValidateSignature.hasValidSignature(req)`. It gives `true` or `false`:

```dart
if (!ValidateSignature.hasValidSignature(req)) {
  return redirect('/link-expired');
}
```

## Details

- The signature is HMAC-SHA256 of the URL, with a key made from `APP_KEY`. Dox compares it in constant time.
- URLs made with an old key still work when the old key is in `AppConfig.previousKeys`.
- `signature` is a reserved query param. Any other param added to a signed URL makes it invalid.
- The `Host` must match the host of `APP_URL`, with the same port.
