# Socket.IO

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/packages/socketio/

# Socket.IO

`dox_socketio` is a Socket.IO v4 server for Dart, and it is the way to do realtime in Dox.

The official clients connect to it with no changes: `socket.io-client` (JavaScript v4) and the Dart `socket_io_client` package. It has acks, rooms, namespaces, binary data and long-polling.

In a Dox app, Socket.IO runs on the same port as your HTTP routes, at `/socket.io/`. It can also run on its own, see [Without Dox](#without-dox).

## In a Dox app

### Install

The quick way is the CLI:

```bash
dox add socketio
```

It adds the package, the provider, the config and the env key (steps 1, 2, 3 and 5 below). It never overwrites a file, so it is safe to run twice. Then write a namespace (step 4) and connect a client (step 6). Add `--broadcasting` to also turn on [broadcasting](../digging-deeper/broadcasting.md).

### Set it up by hand

If you do not use `dox add socketio`, do all the steps below.

### 1. Install

```bash
dart pub add dox_socketio
```

### 2. The provider

The provider starts Socket.IO in every isolate. Put it in `lib/providers/`, so the generated container finds it:

```dart title="lib/providers/socketio_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_socketio/dox_socketio.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/socketio.dart';

class AppSocketIoProvider extends SocketIoProvider {
  AppSocketIoProvider() : super(socketIoConfig);
}
```

### 3. The config

The config says which namespaces to serve:

```dart title="lib/config/socketio.dart"
import 'package:dox_socketio/dox_socketio.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/socket/chat.namespace.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

SocketIoConfig socketIoConfig = SocketIoConfig(
  enabled: env.socketioEnabled,
  namespaces: <NamespaceHandler>[ChatNamespace()],
);
```

| `SocketIoConfig` option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `enabled` | `true` | serve Socket.IO at `options.path` |
| `options` | `ServerOptions()` | see [Options](#options) |
| `namespaces` | `[]` | `NamespaceHandler` classes to register |
| `adapter` | `null` | makes one adapter in each isolate, see [Many isolates](#many-isolates) |

### 4. A namespace

A namespace handles the events of one path, like `/chat`:

```dart title="lib/app/socket/chat.namespace.dart"
import 'package:dox_socketio/dox_socketio.dart';

class ChatNamespace extends NamespaceHandler {
  @override
  String get path => '/chat';

  @override
  void onConnection(Socket socket) {
    socket.emit('welcome', <String, dynamic>{'id': socket.id});
    socket.join('lobby');
    socket.on('message', onMessage);
  }

  void onMessage(SocketEvent event) {
    event.socket.to('lobby').emit('message', event.data); // everyone in lobby but me
    event.ack('sent'); // answer the client callback
  }
}
```

### 5. Turn it on

Add a getter for the `SOCKETIO_ENABLED` key to `lib/config/env.dart`:

```dart title="lib/config/env.dart"
  /// serve Socket.IO on the app port
  bool get socketioEnabled => false;
```

```bash title=".env"
SOCKETIO_ENABLED=true
```

Then run `dart run build_runner build` and `dox serve`.

### 6. Connect a client

```js
import { io } from 'socket.io-client';

const socket = io('http://localhost:3000/chat', { transports: ['websocket'] });
socket.on('welcome', (data) => console.log(data.id));
socket.emit('message', 'hi', (answer) => console.log(answer)); // 'sent'
```

Use `transports: ['websocket']`, because long-polling does not work with many isolates. See [Many isolates](#many-isolates).

Requests to `/socket.io/` go to Socket.IO before the router, so route middleware does not run for them. To log users in, see [Log in a socket](#log-in-a-socket).

## Namespaces

A namespace is a class, so its dependencies come in through the constructor:

```dart
class ChatNamespace extends NamespaceHandler {
  ChatNamespace(this.messages);

  final MessageService messages;

  @override
  String get path => '/chat';

  @override
  void onConnection(Socket socket) {
    socket.on('message', onMessage);
  }

  void onMessage(SocketEvent event) {
    event.ack(messages.save(event.data));
  }
}

// in lib/config/socketio.dart
namespaces: <NamespaceHandler>[ChatNamespace(MessageService())],
```

### Namespace middleware

Sometimes you want to check a client before it joins. Add a middleware to the namespace. When it throws a `SocketIoException`, the client gets `connect_error` with the message and the data:

```dart
@override
List<Middleware> get middleware => <Middleware>[checkToken];

void checkToken(Socket socket) {
  if (socket.handshake.auth['token'] != 'secret') {
    throw SocketIoException('unauthorized', data: <String, dynamic>{'reason': 'bad token'});
  }
}
```

Any other error is written to stderr, and the client only gets `{"message": "Internal error"}`. So private text, like SQL, never reaches the client.

## Sending events

### Sending from a controller or a service

`SocketIoProvider.server` is the Socket.IO server of this isolate:

```dart
await SocketIoProvider.server?.of('/chat').to('lobby').emit('news', data);
```

From a queue job or another program, use the [emitter](#emit-from-other-programs).

### Common methods

The API follows the Node.js server. This table shows the few places where Dart is different:

| Node.js | Dart |
| --- | --- |
| `socket.on('e', (a, cb) => ...)` | `socket.on('e', (SocketEvent e) => ...)`, then `e.data`, `e.args`, `e.ack(x)` |
| `socket.emit('e', a, b)` | `socket.emit('e', a)` or `socket.emitArgs('e', [a, b])` |
| `await socket.timeout(5000).emitWithAck('e', a)` | `await socket.emitWithAck('e', a, timeout: Duration(seconds: 5))` |
| `socket.join(r)` / `socket.leave(r)` | the same |
| `socket.to(r).emit(...)` | the same |
| `socket.broadcast.emit(...)` | the same |
| `io.to(r).except(x).emit(...)` | the same |
| `io.of('/chat')`, `io.use(fn)` | the same |
| `socket.handshake` | `.headers`, `.query`, `.auth`, `.address`, `.token`, `.cookie(name)`, `.session()` |
| `socket.data` | `socket.data` (a `Map`) |
| `await io.in(r).fetchSockets()` | `await io.to(r).fetchSockets()` (all servers) |
| `await io.timeout(5000).emitWithAck('e', a)` | `await io.timeout(Duration(seconds: 5)).emitWithAck('e', a)` |
| `io.serverSideEmit('e', a)` | `await io.serverSideEmit('e', [a])` |
| `io.on('e', (a, cb) => ...)` (from other servers) | `io.onServerSideEmit('e', (ServerSideEvent e) => ...)`, then `e.data`, `e.ack(x)` |

To send binary data, send a `Uint8List`. It can be anywhere in lists and maps. The `disconnecting` and `disconnect` events give the reason in `event.data`, like `transport close`.

## Log in a socket

Socket.IO gets its requests before the router, so route middleware like session and auth does not run. Use `SocketAuth` as a namespace middleware instead. Your function gets the handshake and returns the user, or `null`:

```dart title="lib/app/socket/chat.namespace.dart"
class ChatNamespace extends NamespaceHandler {
  @override
  String get path => '/chat';

  @override
  List<Middleware> get middleware => <Middleware>[SocketAuth(findUser).handle];

  static Future<User?> findUser(Handshake handshake) async {
    String? token = handshake.token;
    if (token == null) return null;
    return User().where('api_token', token).getFirst();
  }

  @override
  void onConnection(Socket socket) {
    User user = socket.user! as User;
    socket.join('user:${user.id}');
  }
}
```

The client sends the token in `auth`. Browsers can not set headers on a websocket, so use `auth` and not a header:

```js
const socket = io('http://localhost:3000/chat', {
  transports: ['websocket'],
  auth: { token: 'the-user-token' },
});
socket.on('connect_error', (err) => console.log(err.message)); // 'Unauthorized'
```

When the function returns a user, it is kept in `socket.user`. When it returns `null`, the client gets a `connect_error` with the message `Unauthorized`, and `onConnection` does not run.

The handshake gives you these helpers:

- `handshake.token` is `auth.token` from the client, else the `Authorization: Bearer` header.
- `handshake.cookie('name')` reads a cookie and decrypts it with the `APP_KEY`. Use `decrypt: false` for a plain cookie.
- `await handshake.session()` gives the Dox session of the client, from its session cookie.

### With dox_auth

[dox_auth](../security/authentication.md#check-a-login-with-no-request) can check a JWT or the web login session for you:

```dart
static Future<User?> findUser(Handshake handshake) async {
  // an API client or a mobile app sends a JWT
  String? token = handshake.token;
  if (token != null) return Auth(guard: 'api').userFromToken(token);

  // a browser that logged in on a web page sends the session cookie
  Session session = await handshake.session();
  return Auth(guard: 'web').userFromSession(session);
}
```

`userFromToken` runs the same checks as `AuthMiddleware`, so a bad, expired or revoked token gives `null`. `handshake.session()` runs the same checks as `SessionMiddleware`.

The session is read once, when the socket connects. A logout later does not close the socket, so call `socket.disconnect()` yourself if you need that.

!!! warning "Cookie login needs `allowedOrigins`"
    A browser sends its cookies on a websocket from any website. So if you log users in with a cookie, set [`allowedOrigins`](#allowed-origins) to your own sites. Without it, another website can open a socket as your user.

## Many isolates

Dox runs one isolate per CPU core, and each isolate has its own Socket.IO server. A client is connected to one of them.

With many isolates, the provider uses the `IsolateAdapter` by default. It sends each broadcast to the other isolates of the process, so it reaches every client. `socketsJoin`, `fetchSockets`, `serverSideEmit` and broadcast acks work across isolates too. You need no Redis for this.

| Adapter | Reaches |
|---|---|
| `InMemoryAdapter` (one isolate) | the clients of this isolate |
| `IsolateAdapter` (many isolates, the default) | the clients of every isolate of this process |
| `RedisAdapter` | the clients of every isolate of every server |

Clients should connect with websocket only. One websocket stays on one isolate, but long-polling sends many requests that can reach different isolates. Long-polling only works with `totalIsolate: 1`, or with sticky sessions in front of many single-isolate servers.

Add each namespace in the config, so it is added in every isolate. A namespace that only one isolate adds with `io.of('/x')` gets no answer from the others, so `fetchSockets` and `serverSideEmitWithAck` wait 5 seconds and throw.

## Many servers: Redis adapter

If you run more than one server process, or Dox next to Node.js servers, use the Redis adapter. Then a broadcast on one server reaches the clients of all servers.

Add the `ioredis` package:

```bash
dart pub add ioredis
```

Then make the adapter in each isolate with a factory, because a Redis connection can not be sent to another isolate:

```dart title="lib/config/socketio.dart"
import 'package:dox_socketio/dox_socketio.dart';
import 'package:ioredis/ioredis.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/socket/chat.namespace.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

SocketIoConfig socketIoConfig = SocketIoConfig(
  enabled: env.socketioEnabled,
  namespaces: <NamespaceHandler>[ChatNamespace()],
  adapter: const RedisSocketAdapterFactory(),
);

/// makes the Redis adapter inside each isolate.
/// A Redis connection can not be sent to another isolate.
class RedisSocketAdapterFactory extends SocketAdapterFactory {
  const RedisSocketAdapterFactory();

  @override
  Adapter create() {
    Redis redis = Redis(); // 127.0.0.1:6379. Or Redis(RedisOptions(host: ..., port: ...))
    return RedisAdapter(subscriber: redis.duplicate(), publisher: redis);
  }
}
```

The subscriber needs its own connection, because a Redis connection in subscribe mode can not run other commands.

The adapter uses the format of `@socket.io/redis-adapter`, so Node.js servers with that adapter can share one Redis with Dox servers. If your Node.js servers use a JSON parser, set `format: RedisFormat.json`.

### Acting on all servers

With the Redis adapter, these methods work on the sockets of all servers:

```dart
// sockets of every server. Sockets of this server are `Socket`s.
List<RemoteSocket> sockets = await io.to('room1').fetchSockets();
for (RemoteSocket socket in sockets) {
  socket.emit('hello', socket.data['name']);
}

await io.to('room1').socketsJoin('room2');
await io.to('banned').disconnectSockets();
```

To get one ack from each client on all servers, set a timeout:

```dart
List<Object?> answers = await io
    .timeout(const Duration(seconds: 5))
    .emitWithAck('ping', 'are you there?');
```

`fetchSockets` throws a `TimeoutException` when a server does not answer within `requestsTimeout` (5 seconds by default).

### Events between servers

Sometimes the servers need to tell each other something, like "reload the config". `serverSideEmit` sends an event to the other servers. Clients do not get it:

```dart
// on every server
io.onServerSideEmit('reload-config', (ServerSideEvent event) {
  reloadConfig(event.data);
  event.ack('done'); // only when the sender waits for an answer
});

// on one server
await io.serverSideEmit('reload-config', <Object?>['v2']);
```

To wait for one answer from each other server, use `serverSideEmitWithAck`. When a server does not answer in time, it throws an `AckTimeoutException`, and its `responses` holds the answers that came back:

```dart
List<Object?> answers = await io.serverSideEmitWithAck('reload-config', <Object?>['v2']);
```

## Emit from other programs

Sometimes you want to send an event from a queue worker, a cron job or a service in another language. An emitter does this without a Socket.IO server. It writes to Redis, and every server with the Redis adapter sends the event to its clients:

```dart
import 'package:dox_socketio/dox_socketio.dart';
import 'package:ioredis/ioredis.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  Redis redis = Redis(RedisOptions(host: '127.0.0.1', port: 6379));
  SocketIoEmitter emitter = SocketIoEmitter(redis);

  await emitter.emit('news', <String, dynamic>{'title': 'hello'}); // all clients of `/`
  await emitter.to('room1').except('room2').emit('news', 'hi room1');
  await emitter.of('/chat').to('vip').emit('notice', 'for vip');

  await emitter.to('room1').socketsJoin('room3'); // sockets in room1 join room3
  await emitter.to('room3').socketsLeave('room1');
  await emitter.to('banned').disconnectSockets();

  await redis.disconnect();
}
```

The emitter does not wait for an answer, so it can not know if a client got the event.

The emitters of other languages use the same format, so they work too. For example, Node.js with [`@socket.io/redis-emitter`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@socket.io/redis-emitter):

```js
import { Emitter } from '@socket.io/redis-emitter';
import { createClient } from 'redis';

const redis = createClient({ url: 'redis://127.0.0.1:6379' });
await redis.connect();

const emitter = new Emitter(redis);
emitter.to('room1').emit('news', { title: 'hello' });
emitter.of('/chat').emit('notice', 'for everyone in /chat');
```

## Broadcasting

To send events to public, private and presence channels, see [Broadcasting](../digging-deeper/broadcasting.md).

## Options

Pass `ServerOptions` as `options` to `SocketIoConfig` in a Dox app, or to `SocketIoServer` without Dox:

```dart
SocketIoServer(
  options: ServerOptions(
    path: '/socket.io/',
    pingInterval: Duration(seconds: 25),
    pingTimeout: Duration(seconds: 20),
    maxHttpBufferSize: 1000000,
    transports: <String>['polling', 'websocket'],
    cors: CorsOptions(origins: <String>['https://my.app'], credentials: true),
  ),
);
```

| Option | Default | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `path` | `/socket.io/` | the URL path |
| `pingInterval` | 25 s | how often the server sends a ping |
| `pingTimeout` | 20 s | how long to wait for the pong before the client is gone |
| `upgradeTimeout` | 10 s | how long an upgrade from polling to websocket may take |
| `connectTimeout` | 45 s | how long the client has to join a namespace |
| `maxHttpBufferSize` | 1,000,000 bytes | the biggest message. A bigger websocket message closes the connection |
| `maxAttachments` | `10` | the most binary parts in one packet |
| `transports` | `['polling', 'websocket']` | allowed transports |
| `allowUpgrades` | `true` | let polling clients move to websocket |
| `cors` | `null` | CORS headers for polling requests. With a list of origins, it also checks the origin of websockets |
| `allowedOrigins` | `null` | the sites that may connect, see [Allowed origins](#allowed-origins) |
| `allowRequest` | `null` | accepts or refuses each request, see [Allow requests and limit sessions](#allow-requests-and-limit-sessions) |
| `maxSessions` | `null` | the most open sessions per isolate. Set it in production |
| `maxAttachmentBytes` | `null` | the most bytes of all binary parts of one packet. A bigger packet closes the client |
| `maxAuthSize` | `null` | the most bytes of the `auth` payload of a connect. A bigger one gets `connect_error` (`auth payload too large`) |
| `maxWriteBufferSize` | `null` | the most bytes kept for a client that does not read, like a polling client that stopped. Above it, the session closes |
| `ackTimeout` | `null` | the default timeout of `emitWithAck`. With `null`, it waits until the client answers or leaves |

### Waiting for acks

`socket.waitingAcks` is the number of acks a socket still waits for. Use it to see a client that never answers:

```dart
int waiting = socket.waitingAcks;
```

### Allowed origins

`allowedOrigins` says which websites may open a socket. You should set it when you log users in with cookies:

```dart
ServerOptions(allowedOrigins: <String>['https://app.example.com']);
```

- `null` (the default): no extra check. Dox logs a warning at start.
- `[]`: only pages of the same host can connect.
- A list of sites: the same host and those sites can connect.
- `['*']`: every site can connect.

Other sites get 403. A client with no `Origin` header (not a browser) is always allowed.

### Allow requests and limit sessions

`allowRequest` runs for every handshake and every websocket upgrade. It gets an `EngineRequest` with the headers, query and address, and returns `true` or `false`. `maxSessions` is the most open sessions:

```dart title="lib/config/socketio.dart"
SocketIoConfig socketIoConfig = SocketIoConfig(
  options: ServerOptions(
    allowRequest: (EngineRequest req) => req.query['key'] == 'secret',
    maxSessions: 10000,
  ),
);
```

When `allowRequest` gives `false` or throws, the client gets `403`. At the limit, a new handshake gets `503` and open sessions keep working. The count is per isolate, so with 4 isolates the app allows 4 times `maxSessions`. Without `maxSessions`, every GET request makes a session that lives about 45 seconds, so Dox logs one warning at start.

## Without Dox

`dox_socketio` also runs on its own, with no Dox app:

```dart
import 'package:dox_socketio/dox_socketio.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  SocketIoServer io = SocketIoServer();
  io.register(ChatNamespace());
  await io.listen(3001);
}
```

- `io.listen(port)` starts a native server on its own port. Run it in its own small program, like `bin/socket.dart`, behind the same proxy as the HTTP server.
- `io.attach(httpServer)` uses a server you already have: a `NativeHttpServer` or a `dart:io` one.
- In your own server, call `io.handle(request)` when `io.matches(request)` is true.
- `io.on('connection', (Socket socket) {...})` handles the default namespace `/` with no class.
- `io.use(SocketAuth(findUser).handle)` logs users in on the default namespace.

To use the Redis adapter, pass it to the server:

```dart
Redis redis = Redis(RedisOptions(host: '127.0.0.1', port: 6379));
SocketIoServer io = SocketIoServer(
  adapter: RedisAdapter(subscriber: redis.duplicate(), publisher: redis),
);
```

## Details

- With no provider, or with `enabled: false`, there is no extra work per request.
- Need a plain WebSocket with no Socket.IO protocol? `Route.websocket(path, handler)` in `dox_core` gives you the raw socket.
- Dox logs a hint at startup when it runs many isolates and polling is allowed.
- A client that a middleware refuses is closed after `connectTimeout`, unless it joins another namespace.
- `socket.user` stays on this server. `fetchSockets()` on other servers does not get it.
- `SocketAuth(findUser, message: '...')` changes the `Unauthorized` message.
- `handshake.session()` uses `AppConfig.session`. Pass another `SessionConfig` like `handshake.session(config)`. The session is read only, so changes are not saved. It prints a warning once when `allowedOrigins` is `null` or has `'*'`.
- With `userCacheTtl` on in `dox_auth`, a deleted or banned user can still connect until the cache time ends, unless `forgetUser` runs.
- With the `cookie` session driver, an old copy of the session cookie still works after logout until the `lifetime` ends. Use the `cache` driver if a logout must stop old cookies.
- `cors` with `*` in `origins`, or `cors: null`, allows websockets from any origin. `*` with `credentials: true` throws an `ArgumentError`.
- Websocket compression is off. A message bigger than `maxHttpBufferSize` closes with code 1009. On a plain `dart:io` server, the whole message is read before the size check, so also set a size limit in your proxy.
- A packet with more than `maxAttachments` binary parts closes that client.
- `allowRequest` does not run again for the polling requests of an open session. A client that leaves while it runs still holds a `maxSessions` slot until the ping timeout. A browser client only sees a connect error, not the `403` or `503` body.
- The Redis adapter reads msgpack and JSON, and writes msgpack. Long-polling with it needs sticky sessions too.
- The emitter `key` must be the same as the adapter `key`. Both default to `socket.io`. Binary data (`Uint8List`, or `Buffer` in Node.js) arrives as binary.

# PDF Library

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/packages/pdf-lib/

# PDF Library

Create, load and edit PDF files in Dart with `dox_pdf_lib`, and send them from a Dox controller.

`dox_pdf_lib` draws text, shapes, SVG paths, JPEG and PNG images. It also does forms, attachments, metadata, custom fonts, and PDF/A and PDF/X. It has the API of the pdf-lib JavaScript library.

The package is standalone. It does not need Dox, and Dox does not need it. To fill pdfme templates, see [pdfme](pdfme.md).

## Install

```bash
dart pub add dox_pdf_lib
```

## Sending a PDF from a controller

A controller can return a `DownloadableFile`. Dox streams the bytes and sets `Content-Type` and `Content-Disposition`. The browser saves the file. See [Response](../the-basic/response.md).

Use `StreamFile` instead to show the PDF in the browser tab.

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/report.controller.dart"
import 'dart:io';
import 'dart:typed_data';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_pdf_lib/dox_pdf_lib.dart';

@Inject()
class ReportController {
  Future<DownloadableFile> show(DoxRequest req) async {
    PDFDocument doc = await PDFDocument.create();
    PDFFont font = await doc.embedFont(StandardFonts.helvetica);
    PDFPage page = doc.addPage(PageSizes.A4);
    page.drawText('Monthly report', x: 50, y: 750, font: font, size: 24);

    Uint8List bytes = await doc.save();
    return DownloadableFile(
      ContentType('application', 'pdf'),
      Stream<List<int>>.value(bytes),
      'report.pdf',
      length: bytes.length,
    );
  }
}
```

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
Route.get('/report.pdf', (ReportController c) => c.show);
```

## Using other fonts

The 14 standard PDF fonts, like Helvetica, are built in. They only have Latin letters. For other languages, embed your own TrueType or OpenType font. Use `subset: true` to put only the letters you use into the file.

```dart
Uint8List bytes = File('NotoSansThai-Regular.ttf').readAsBytesSync();
PDFFont thai = await doc.embedFont(bytes, subset: true);
page.drawText('สวัสดีครับ', x: 50, y: 700, font: thai, size: 20);
```

Thai, Myanmar, Khmer, Lao, Arabic, Hebrew and Hindi text is laid out correctly. Line breaks in Myanmar, Thai, Khmer and Lao go between words.

## PDF/A and PDF/X

PDF/A is for long-term archives. PDF/X is for print. One call, `setConformance`, sets up a document for the standard you pick.

You bring the ICC profile. The package ships none.

```dart
Uint8List srgb = File('sRGB2014.icc').readAsBytesSync();

PDFDocument doc = await PDFDocument.create();
doc.setTitle('Annual report');
doc.setConformance(
  PDFStandard.pdfA2b,
  iccProfile: srgb,
  outputConditionIdentifier: 'sRGB IEC61966-2.1',
);

// PDF/A needs fonts from a font file. Standard fonts do not work.
PDFFont font = await doc.embedFont(
  File('NotoSans-Regular.ttf').readAsBytesSync(),
  subset: true,
);
doc.addPage().drawText('Kept for a long time', x: 50, y: 750, font: font);

for (ConformanceIssue issue in doc.checkConformance(PDFStandard.pdfA2b)) {
  print(issue);
}
```

`checkConformance` lists what is still wrong. For PDF/X, use `PDFStandard.pdfX1a`, `pdfX3` or `pdfX4`, and give each page a trim box. The [dox_pdf_lib README](https://pub.dev/packages/dox_pdf_lib) has the full list of rules.

## Platforms

`dox_pdf_lib` uses `dart:ffi` and a small native library. It runs in Dart programs on macOS, Linux and Windows.

It does not run on the web, iOS or Android.

A ready-built native library is downloaded for you, so you do not need Rust.

On Linux, the ready-built library needs glibc 2.35 or newer, for example Ubuntu 22.04 or Debian 12. On older Linux, or on Alpine, build the library yourself. The [dox_pdf_lib README](https://pub.dev/packages/dox_pdf_lib) shows how.

## Without Dox

The same code works in any Dart program. Call `PDFDocument.create()`, then write the bytes to a file:

```dart
import 'dart:io';

import 'package:dox_pdf_lib/dox_pdf_lib.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  PDFDocument doc = await PDFDocument.create();
  PDFFont font = await doc.embedFont(StandardFonts.helvetica);
  PDFPage page = doc.addPage(PageSizes.A4);
  page.drawText('Hello, PDF!', x: 50, y: 750, font: font, size: 30);
  File('hello.pdf').writeAsBytesSync(await doc.save());
}
```

## Learn more

- [`dox_pdf_lib` on pub.dev](https://pub.dev/packages/dox_pdf_lib): pages, forms, attachments, images, metadata and the full API.
- [Source on GitHub](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-pdf-lib)

# pdfme

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/packages/pdfme/

# pdfme

Make PDF files from [pdfme](https://pdfme.com) templates in Dart with `dox_pdf_me`, and send them from a Dox controller.

You design the template in the pdfme designer, then fill it with data on the server. `dox_pdf_me` reads the same template JSON as pdfme, and the PDF looks the same.

The package is standalone. It does not need Dox, and Dox does not need it. It is built on [PDF Library](pdf-lib.md).

## Install

```bash
dart pub add dox_pdf_me
```

## Filling a template

Design the template in the pdfme designer and save its JSON. Read it with `Template.fromJson`. The inputs are one map of strings for each copy of the template.

A controller can return a `DownloadableFile`. Dox streams the bytes and sets `Content-Type` and `Content-Disposition`. The browser saves the file. See [Response](../the-basic/response.md).

Use `StreamFile` instead to show the PDF in the browser tab.

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/invoice.controller.dart"
import 'dart:convert';
import 'dart:io';
import 'dart:typed_data';

import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_pdf_me/dox_pdf_me.dart';

@Inject()
class InvoiceController {
  Future<DownloadableFile> show(DoxRequest req) async {
    Map<String, Object?> json =
        jsonDecode(File('storage/invoice.template.json').readAsStringSync())
            as Map<String, Object?>;

    Uint8List bytes = await generate(
      template: Template.fromJson(json),
      inputs: <Map<String, String>>[
        <String, String>{'customer': 'Jane Doe', 'total': '120.00'},
      ],
      plugins: builtInPlugins,
    );
    return DownloadableFile(
      ContentType('application', 'pdf'),
      Stream<List<int>>.value(bytes),
      'invoice.pdf',
      length: bytes.length,
    );
  }
}
```

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
Route.get('/invoice.pdf', (InvoiceController c) => c.show);
```

`dox_pdf_me` supports text, image, svg, shapes, barcodes and QR codes, date and time, checkbox, radio group, select, table, multi variable text, signature and circle mark. Pass `builtInPlugins` to use all of them.

## Using other fonts

Text uses Roboto by default. For other languages, pass your fonts in `GenerateOptions`:

```dart
Uint8List noto = File('NotoSansJP-Regular.otf').readAsBytesSync();
Uint8List pdf = await generate(
  template: template,
  inputs: inputs,
  plugins: builtInPlugins,
  options: GenerateOptions(
    font: <String, FontSource>{
      'Roboto': FontStore.defaultFont,
      'NotoSansJP': FontSource(noto),
    },
  ),
);
```

Thai, Myanmar, Khmer, Lao, Arabic, Hebrew and Hindi text is laid out correctly. Line breaks in Myanmar, Thai, Khmer and Lao go between words.

## Platforms

`dox_pdf_me` uses `dox_pdf_lib`, which has a small native library. It runs in Dart programs on macOS, Linux and Windows.

It does not run on the web, iOS or Android.

A ready-built native library is downloaded for you, so you do not need Rust.

On Linux, the ready-built library needs glibc 2.35 or newer, for example Ubuntu 22.04 or Debian 12. On older Linux, or on Alpine, build the library yourself. The [dox_pdf_lib README](https://pub.dev/packages/dox_pdf_lib) shows how.

## Without Dox

The same code works in any Dart program. Call `generate(...)`, then write the bytes to a file:

```dart
import 'dart:io';
import 'dart:typed_data';

import 'package:dox_pdf_me/dox_pdf_me.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  Uint8List pdf = await generate(
    template: Template(
      basePdf: const BlankPdf(),
      schemas: <List<Schema>>[
        <Schema>[
          const TextSchema(name: 'title', position: Position(20, 20), width: 170, height: 15),
          BarcodeSchema(name: 'link', barcodeType: BarcodeType.qrcode, position: const Position(20, 40)),
        ],
      ],
    ),
    inputs: <Map<String, String>>[
      <String, String>{'title': 'Hello, PDF!', 'link': 'https://dartondox.dev'},
    ],
    plugins: builtInPlugins,
  );
  File('hello.pdf').writeAsBytesSync(pdf);
}
```

## Learn more

- [`dox_pdf_me` on pub.dev](https://pub.dev/packages/dox_pdf_me): schema types, tables, plugins, fonts and options, and how to build a template in Dart.
- [Source on GitHub](https://github.com/dartondox/dox-pdf-lib)

# MCP server

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/packages/mcp/

# MCP server

`dox_mcp` serves the tools of your app to AI clients, for example Claude, ChatGPT, and IDE agents, with the [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) (MCP).

A tool is an action that the AI can call, for example "add an expense". You write the tool in Dart. `dox_mcp` serves it from a normal Dox route over the Streamable HTTP transport.

- Tool arguments are `dox_validation` schemas. Clients see them as JSON Schema. Dox validates each call before your code runs.
- `APP_KEY` signs the session ids. Thus, a session works on all isolates and after a restart. You do not need a store.
- Replies are plain JSON. Tools do not need an SSE stream.

## Setup

Run:

```bash
dox add mcp
```

The command adds the package, `lib/config/mcp.dart` with an `McpServer`, and a sample tool in `lib/app/mcp/echo.tool.dart`. You add the route and the auth yourself. The command does not overwrite a file. It is safe to run it again.

To set up the package manually, add it:

```bash
dart pub add dox_mcp
```

## Write tools

A tool extends `McpTool`. A tool has these parts:

- `name`: the name of the tool.
- `description`: the text for the model.
- `input`: the schema of the arguments.
- `call`: the method that does the work.

```dart
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_mcp/dox_mcp.dart';

class AddExpense extends McpTool {
  @override
  String get name => 'add_expense';

  @override
  String get description => 'Record an expense. Amount is in dollars.';

  @override
  ObjectSchema get input => v.object(<String, Schema<Object?>>{
    'amount': v.num().positive().describe('Amount, like 12.50.'),
    'note': v.string().max(500).optional(),
  });

  @override
  Future<McpToolResult> call(Map<String, dynamic> args, McpContext context) async {
    User user = context.authAs<User>();
    // ... save it
    return McpToolResult.text('Recorded ${args['amount']} for ${user.email}.');
  }
}
```

If the arguments are not correct, the client gets a tool result with `isError: true`. This result lists each problem, so that the model can correct the call. If your tool throws an error, the client also gets a tool result with `isError: true` and the error text.

### Small tools

A small tool can be a function. Use `McpTool.of`:

```dart
McpTool.of(
  name: 'echo',
  description: 'Say the text back.',
  input: v.object(<String, Schema<Object?>>{'text': v.string()}),
  handler: (Map<String, dynamic> args, McpContext context) {
    return McpToolResult.text(args['text'] as String);
  },
);
```

### Tools that take a DTO

If you have a `@Dto` class, a tool can use it as its input. Extend `McpDtoTool<T>`. You write the rules of the DTO one time, for example `@Length` and `@HexColor`. The `handle` method gets the typed object, not a map.

Use `@Describe` on a field to explain the field to the model. Dox puts this text in the JSON Schema as `description`. It does not change the validation:

```dart
@Dto()
class NewCategory {
  @Describe('The category name, like Food.')
  @Length(min: 1, max: 50)
  final String name;

  @Describe('A color, like #1a2b3c.')
  @HexColor()
  final String color;

  const NewCategory({required this.name, required this.color});

  static const DtoSchema<NewCategory> schema = $NewCategoryDto;
}

class CreateCategory extends McpDtoTool<NewCategory> {
  @override
  String get name => 'create_category';

  @override
  String get description => 'Add a category.';

  @override
  DtoSchema<NewCategory> get dto => NewCategory.schema;

  @override
  Future<McpToolResult> handle(NewCategory input, McpContext context) async {
    // ... save it
    return McpToolResult.text('Added ${input.name}.');
  }
}
```

Dox validates the arguments the same as a DTO in a controller. This includes async rules, for example `@Unique` and `@Exists`. A call that is not correct gets a text like this:

```text
Input validation error: Invalid arguments for tool create_category: name: The name is required; color: The color must be a hex color like #1a2b3c
```

## Serve the tools

Make an `McpServer` with your tools, and call `handle` from a route. The MCP route has no auth. Thus, you must find the caller first. Get the user from a token, a header, or the URL, and give it as `auth`. The `scope` connects each session to that user:

```dart
final McpServer mcp = McpServer(
  name: 'my-app',
  version: '1.0.0',
  tools: <McpTool>[AddExpense()],
);

Route.match(<String>['GET', 'POST', 'DELETE'], '/mcp/{token}', (DoxRequest req) async {
  User? user = await User().where('mcp_token', req.param['token']).getFirst();
  if (user == null) return response('Invalid token').statusCode(401);
  return mcp.handle(req, auth: user, scope: 'user:${user.id}');
});
```

In a tool, `context.authAs<User>()` gives this user.

Proxies write a token in the URL to their logs. Thus, use a header when your clients can send one. If you want clients to sign in without your help, use [OAuth](#sign-in-with-oauth).

## Sign in with OAuth

With `McpOAuth`, you give the client only the address, for example `https://my.app/mcp`. The client finds the other data and signs in the user. The MCP spec asks for this sign-in: OAuth 2.1 with PKCE.

`dox_mcp` does the OAuth part. Your app does three things:

1. **Tokens.** Implement `McpOAuthTokens`. `issue` makes a token for a grant. `verify` gives the subject of a token, for example a user, or `null`. You choose the table and how to revoke a token. Keep only a hash of the token.
2. **The consent page.** Serve the page at `<issuer>/oauth/authorize`, or set `authorizePage`. The page reads `client_id`, `redirect_uri`, `state`, `code_challenge`, `code_challenge_method`, and `resource` from the query. The person signs in on this page with the usual login of your app.
3. **The answer.** Your page calls a route of your app, behind your login. If the person agrees, the route calls `oauth.approve(subject: ...)`. Then the route gives the page the address for the browser. If the person refuses, the route calls `await oauth.denyClient(...)`.

Then add the routes, and verify the token on the MCP route:

```dart
final McpOAuth oauth = McpOAuth(
  issuer: 'https://my.app',
  tokens: MyTokens(),
  codes: Cache().store('file'), // all isolates must share it
);

class McpRouter extends Router {
  @override
  void register() {
    oauth.routes(); // discovery, register and token
    Route.match(<String>['GET', 'POST', 'DELETE'], '/mcp', handleMcp);
  }
}

Future<DoxResponse> handleMcp(DoxRequest req) async {
  Object? user = await oauth.authenticate(req); // reads Authorization: Bearer
  if (user == null) return oauth.unauthorized(); // 401 with WWW-Authenticate
  return mcp.handle(req, auth: user, scope: '$user');
}
```

Call `oauth.routes()` in a router with no prefix, because clients look for `/.well-known/...` at the root of the host. All isolates must share the `codes` store. Use a file store on one host, or Redis on many hosts.

### Keep the consent page safe

The consent page controls who gets access. Obey these rules:

- Put the answer route behind [CSRF protection](../security/csrf.md). If you do not, a different site can make a signed-in person agree to a client. The person does not know about it.
- Use `await oauth.verifyClient(...)` to get the client for the page. This method throws an error when the client or the redirect address is not correct. In that case, do not send the browser to any address.
- Show `client.host` next to the client name, and show the redirect host. A client can choose any name, but not its host. Then the person sees who asks and where the browser goes.
- HTML-escape the client name before you show it. The client chose the name, so do not trust it.

There is no refresh token. To revoke a client, delete its token.

## Sessions

`SignedMcpSessions` is the default. It makes ids like `<random>.<signature>`. A key from `APP_KEY` signs each id. Thus, each isolate and each server with the same `APP_KEY` can verify an id, and Dox stores nothing. A new `APP_KEY` stops all sessions. Then clients start a new session automatically.

Dox stores nothing, so you cannot stop a signed id. If you want `DELETE` to stop a session, give a cache store that all isolates share. Use a file store or Redis, not memory:

```dart
SignedMcpSessions(ended: Cache().store('redis'))
```

For a different type of session, implement `McpSessions`.

## Security

- The MCP route has no auth. Find the caller before `handle`. `McpOAuth` is one way to do this.
- Set `allowedOrigins` when the server runs on a local or private network. This setting stops browser pages from other sites. This attack is DNS rebinding. If the `Origin` of a request is not in the list, the request gets `403`.
- Keep tokens out of logs.

## Details

This section gives special cases. Most apps do not need it.

### What the server answers

| Request | Answer |
| --- | --- |
| `POST` `initialize` | `200` with the server info and an `Mcp-Session-Id` header |
| `POST` a request with a valid `Mcp-Session-Id` | `200` with the JSON-RPC response (a list for a batch) |
| `POST` only notifications or responses | `202`, no body |
| `POST` with no session id | `400` |
| `POST` with an unknown session id, or one of another `scope` | `404`, so the client starts a new session |
| `POST` with an ended session id | `404`, only when `SignedMcpSessions` has an `ended` store. Without it, the id still works |
| `POST` with a body that is not valid JSON | `400` with the JSON-RPC error `-32700` |
| `POST` with an empty batch, or a message that is not JSON-RPC 2.0 | `400` with the JSON-RPC error `-32600` |
| `POST` with `initialize` in a batch with other messages | `400` with the JSON-RPC error `-32600`. Send `initialize` alone |
| `POST` with a batch of more than 50 messages | `400` with the JSON-RPC error `-32600`. No message runs |
| `POST` with an unsupported `MCP-Protocol-Version` header | `400` |
| `POST` with another `Content-Type` than JSON | `415` |
| Any request with an `Origin` header that is not in `allowedOrigins` | `403` |
| `GET` | `405`: there is no server-to-client stream |
| `DELETE` with a valid session id | `200`. The session ends only if `SignedMcpSessions` has an `ended` store (see [Sessions](#sessions)) |
| `DELETE` with no session id | `400` |
| `DELETE` with an unknown session id, or one of another `scope` | `404`. An ended id also gets `404` when there is an `ended` store |

- Methods: `initialize`, `ping`, `tools/list`, `tools/call`. Other methods get `-32601 Method not found`.
- An unknown tool gets a JSON-RPC error, `-32602`.
- `tools/list` sends the JSON Schema of a DTO tool as `inputSchema`. This schema comes from `toJsonSchema()`.
- `onToolError` gets the error of a tool that throws, for logs.
- Protocol versions: `2025-11-25`, `2025-06-18`, `2025-03-26`, and `2024-11-05`. If a client asks for a different version, it gets the newest version.
- The session signature is HMAC-SHA256 of the random part and the `scope`. Dox makes the key from `APP_KEY` with the label `dox:mcp`.

### OAuth routes

`oauth.routes()` adds these routes:

| Route | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource` (also with `/mcp` after it) | Names the MCP address and the issuer. |
| `GET /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` | Lists the endpoints. PKCE `S256` only, `authorization_code` only, no client secret. |
| `POST /oauth/register` | Dynamic client registration. Nothing is stored. The `client_id` is the name and the redirect addresses, signed with `APP_KEY`. |
| `POST /oauth/token` | Swaps a code for a token. The body is a form or JSON. The code works once, for `codeTtl` (1 minute). The client, the redirect address and the PKCE verifier must all match. An unknown `client_id` gets `401` with `invalid_client`. |

- The discovery file gives `<issuer>/oauth/register` and `<issuer>/oauth/token` as full addresses. A router prefix moves the routes, but not these addresses. Then clients cannot find the routes.
- A redirect address must use `https`, or `http` on `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, or `[::1]`. It must not have a `#fragment`. Its maximum length is 2048 characters (`McpOAuth.maxRedirectUriLength`).
- A `code_verifier` must have 43 to 128 characters from `A-Z a-z 0-9 - . _ ~`, as RFC 7636 says. Other verifiers get `invalid_request`. A `code_challenge` must have 43 base64url characters.
- Dox takes each code under a lock. Thus, two isolates cannot both swap the same code.
- These routes accept all origins, with CORS `*`, and read no cookie. They do not use the CORS list of the app.
- `issue` can throw `McpOAuthException`, for example `access_denied` when a person has too many clients. The client gets this error from the token endpoint.

# GraphQL

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/packages/graphql/

# GraphQL

GraphQL makes an API for your app from your models. You add annotations to a model, run the builder, and the API is ready.

A GraphQL API has one URL. The client writes the fields that it wants, and it gets JSON with only those fields. To learn GraphQL, read [graphql.org/learn](https://graphql.org/learn/).

## Install

Run the setup command in your app:

```bash
dox add graphql
```

The command adds the packages, `lib/config/graphql.dart` and `lib/providers/graphql_provider.dart`. It does not overwrite a file. For an app with no models, see [Without the ORM](#without-the-orm).

## Add a model to the API

Put `@GraphQL()` on a model. Then add one annotation for each operation that a client can use:

```dart title="lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart"
@DoxModel()
@GraphQL()
@GraphQLAll()
@GraphQLFind()
class Post extends PostGenerator {
  @Column()
  String? title;

  @Column()
  int? userId;

  @BelongsTo(User)
  User? user;
}
```

`@GraphQLAll()` adds the `posts` query, and `@GraphQLFind()` adds the `post` query. An operation with no annotation does not exist.

The `id`, the columns and the relations of the model are fields that a client can ask for. `Post` has a relation to `User`, so put `@GraphQL()` on `User` also.

Run the builder, and start the app again. Do these two steps after each change to an annotation:

```bash
dart run build_runner build
```

## Run a query

A query is a request that reads data. In development, open `http://localhost:3000/graphql` in a browser. This URL shows GraphiQL, a page where you write and run queries:

```graphql
{
  posts(limit: 10) {
    title
    user { name }
  }
}
```

The result has the same shape as the query:

```json
{ "data": { "posts": [{ "title": "Hello GraphQL", "user": { "name": "Ada" } }] } }
```

Dox loads the users of all ten posts with one database query.

Your client sends the same query as a `POST` request to `/graphql`. The JSON body is `{"query": "..."}`.

## All operations

Each annotation adds one query or one mutation. A mutation is a request that changes data.

| Annotation | GraphQL field | Function |
|---|---|---|
| `@GraphQLAll()` | `posts(limit, offset)` | Reads a list. |
| `@GraphQLPaginate()` | `posts(first, page)` | Reads a page of a list, with the total number of rows. |
| `@GraphQLFind()` | `post(id)` | Reads one row. |
| `@GraphQLCreate(dto:)` | `createPost(input)` | Adds a row. |
| `@GraphQLUpdate(dto:)` | `updatePost(id, input)` | Changes a row. |
| `@GraphQLDelete()` | `deletePost(id)` | Removes a row. |

Create and update use a [DTO](../the-basic/dto.md), so the input gets the same validation as your HTTP routes. For each annotation, see [Model annotations](#model-annotations).

## Write your own query

Write your own query when the annotations are not sufficient, for example for a search. Put `@GraphQLQuery()` on a method of a class in `lib/`:

```dart title="lib/app/graphql/post.resolver.dart"
class PostResolver {
  @GraphQLQuery()
  Future<List<Post>> latestPosts({int limit = 10}) {
    return Post().orderBy('id', 'desc').limit(limit).get();
  }
}
```

The method name is the query name, and the parameters are the values that a client can send:

```graphql
{ latestPosts(limit: 3) { title } }
```

For more, see [Your own resolvers](#your-own-resolvers).

## Protect the API

By default, all clients can use all operations. Set `guard: true` on an operation that a guest must not use. Give an ability with `can:`, and Dox asks the [policy](../security/authorization.md#writing-policies) of the model before the operation runs:

```dart title="lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart"
@DoxModel()
@GraphQL(filter: Ability.view)
@GraphQLAll(can: Ability.viewAny)
@GraphQLFind(can: Ability.view)
@GraphQLCreate(dto: PostInput, can: Ability.create, guard: true, owner: 'userId')
@GraphQLUpdate(dto: PostInput, can: Ability.update, guard: true)
@GraphQLDelete(can: Ability.delete, guard: true)
class Post extends PostGenerator {}
```

- `guard: true` makes the operation need a login.
- `can:` asks the policy if the user can do the operation.
- `filter:` hides the rows that the user cannot read.
- `owner: 'userId'` sets the owner of a new row to the logged-in user.

A guest that Dox refuses gets the error `UNAUTHENTICATED`. A user that Dox refuses gets the error `FORBIDDEN`. The other fields of the request still give their data.

To set this up, see [Authentication](#authentication) and [Authorization](#authorization).

## Production defaults and limits

In production, GraphiQL and introspection are off, and error details stay on the server. You do not set anything for this.

Limits stop a very large query before it causes much work on your server. For example, a query can nest 64 levels, and a list gives a maximum of 100 rows. Set lower limits when your API is open to the public:

```dart title="lib/config/graphql.dart"
GraphQLConfig graphqlConfig = GraphQLConfig(
  schema: graphqlSchema,
  maxDepth: 10,
  maxNodes: 10000,
);
```

For all settings, see [Configuration](#configuration).

## Model annotations

Each annotation can have these options:

| Option | Function |
|---|---|
| `name:` | A different name for the type or the field. |
| `description:` | The text that GraphiQL shows. |
| `guard: true` | A client must log in. See [Authentication](#authentication). |
| `can:` | The policy must allow the user. `@GraphQL` does not have this option. See [Authorization](#authorization). |

### @GraphQL

Use it to make the model a type of the API. All other model annotations need it.

```dart
@GraphQL()
```

A model with only `@GraphQL()` has no queries and no mutations. A client gets it only through a relation, for example `post.user`.

Dox does not show the fields in the `hidden` list of the model, so a password stays on the server. To hide a different field, put `@GraphQLIgnore()` above its `@Column()`.

`@GraphQL` also has `filter:`. See [Hide rows](#hide-rows).

### @GraphQLAll

Use it when a client must read a list with `limit` and `offset`:

```dart
@GraphQLAll()
```

```graphql
{ posts(limit: 10, offset: 20) { title } }
```

The default `limit` is `20`. A `limit` of more than `100` gives an error.

### @GraphQLPaginate

Use it when a client shows pages and needs the total number of rows. The client sends `first`, which is the number of rows on a page, and `page`:

```dart
@GraphQLPaginate()
```

```graphql
{
  posts(first: 10, page: 2) {
    data { title }
    paginatorInfo { total currentPage lastPage hasMorePages }
  }
}
```

```json
{
  "data": {
    "posts": {
      "data": [{ "title": "Hello GraphQL" }],
      "paginatorInfo": { "total": 11, "currentPage": 2, "lastPage": 2, "hasMorePages": false }
    }
  }
}
```

The default `first` is `20`, and the default `page` is `1`. A `first` of more than `100` gives an error.

`data` has the rows of the page. `paginatorInfo` has these fields:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| `total` | The number of rows on all pages. |
| `count` | The number of rows on this page. |
| `perPage` | The value of `first`. |
| `currentPage` | The number of this page. |
| `lastPage` | The number of the last page. |
| `hasMorePages` | `true` if there is a page after this page. |
| `firstItem` | The number of the first row of this page. The first row of page 1 is `1`. `null` on an empty page. |
| `lastItem` | The number of the last row of this page. `null` on an empty page. |

If the model also has `@GraphQLAll()`, the list is `posts` and the paged list is `postsPaginate`. To set a different name, use `name:`:

```dart
@GraphQLPaginate(name: 'postPages')
```

### @GraphQLFind

Use it when a client must read one row by its id:

```dart
@GraphQLFind()
```

```graphql
{ post(id: 1) { title } }
```

The result is `null` if no row has that id.

### @GraphQLCreate

Use it to let a client add a row. First, write a [DTO](../the-basic/dto.md) with the fields that the client can set:

```dart title="lib/app/dtos/post_input/post_input.dto.dart"
@Dto()
class PostInput {
  PostInput({required this.title});

  @MinLength(3, message: 'The title is too short')
  final String title;
}
```

Then give the DTO to the annotation:

```dart
@GraphQLCreate(dto: PostInput)
```

```graphql
mutation {
  createPost(input: { title: "My second post" }) { id title }
}
```

A client can set only the fields of the DTO. Thus, a client cannot set a different column, for example `userId`.

Dox applies the rules of the DTO before it saves the row. If the input is not correct, Dox saves nothing. The client gets the error `VALIDATION_FAILED`, with the message for each field in `extensions.fields`.

### Set the owner of a new row

Use `owner:` when each row belongs to the user that made it. Dox sets that column to the id of the logged-in user:

```dart
@GraphQLCreate(dto: PostInput, owner: 'userId')
```

With `owner:`, the client must log in to create a row. The owner column must not be a field of the DTO. An update never changes the owner column.

### @GraphQLUpdate

Use it to let a client change a row. It can use the same DTO as `@GraphQLCreate`:

```dart
@GraphQLUpdate(dto: PostInput, can: Ability.update, guard: true)
```

```graphql
mutation { updatePost(id: 1, input: { title: "A better title" }) { title } }
```

`updatePost` changes only the fields that the client sends, and Dox applies only the rules of those fields. The result is `null` if no row has that id.

!!! warning

    Without `can:`, each client that can call `updatePost` or `deletePost` can change or delete each row. Add `can:` to `@GraphQLUpdate` and `@GraphQLDelete`. The builder shows a warning if one of them has no `can:` and no `guard:`.

### @GraphQLDelete

Use it to let a client remove a row. It needs no DTO:

```dart
@GraphQLDelete(can: Ability.delete, guard: true)
```

```graphql
mutation { deletePost(id: 1) }
```

The result is `true`, or `false` if no row has that id.

## Authentication

Use `guard: true` when a client must log in. If your app does not have a login, set it up first with [`dox add auth`](../security/authentication.md).

Add `AuthMiddleware()` to the config. Dox uses it to read the user:

```dart title="lib/config/graphql.dart"
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:dox_graphql/dox_graphql.dart';
import 'package:my_app/generated/schema.g.dart';

GraphQLConfig graphqlConfig = GraphQLConfig(
  schema: graphqlSchema,
  middleware: <Object>[AuthMiddleware()],
);
```

The middleware does not stop a request. All fields stay public until you add `guard: true`. The client sends its token in the `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header, as usual.

### Make a query or mutation need a login

Set `guard: true` on each operation that a guest must not use:

```dart title="lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart"
@DoxModel()
@GraphQL()
@GraphQLAll()
@GraphQLFind()
@GraphQLCreate(dto: PostInput, guard: true)
@GraphQLUpdate(dto: PostInput, guard: true)
@GraphQLDelete(guard: true)
class Post extends PostGenerator {}
```

Here, a guest can read posts, but only a logged-in user can change them.

If a guest asks for a guarded field, the guest gets the error `UNAUTHENTICATED` for that field. The other fields in the same request still give their data.

`guard: true` needs `AuthMiddleware()` in the config. Without it, the app stops at start and shows the name of the type or field.

### Protect a model everywhere

Write `@GraphQL(guard: true)` on a model that a guest must never see, for example `User`:

```dart title="lib/app/models/user/user.model.dart"
@DoxModel()
@GraphQL(guard: true)
@GraphQLFind()
class User extends UserGenerator {}
```

Then each field that gives a user needs a login. This includes its queries, its mutations, each relation such as `post.user`, and your own resolvers.

### Read the logged-in user

Add a `DoxGraphQLContext` parameter to a resolver method. The client does not send this value. Dox puts the current request in it:

```dart title="lib/app/graphql/user.resolver.dart"
@GraphQLQuery()
Future<User?> me(DoxGraphQLContext context) {
  return context.user<User>();
}
```

`context.user<User>()` gives `null` for a guest.

## Authorization

`guard: true` is only a login check. Use a [policy](../security/authorization.md#writing-policies) when the answer is different for each user or each row.

### Write a policy

A policy is a class with one method for each rule. The `abilities` map gives a name to each method. This name is the ability. `Ability` has the usual names: `viewAny`, `view`, `create`, `update` and `delete`.

```dart title="lib/app/policies/post_policy.dart"
import 'package:dox_auth/dox_auth.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/post/post.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/user/user.model.dart';

class PostPolicy extends Policy<User, Post> {
  bool update(User user, Post post) => post.userId == user.id;

  @override
  Map<String, Function> get abilities => <String, Function>{
    Ability.update: update,
  };
}
```

Each ability section below adds one method to this policy. Add each new method to `abilities` also.

### Register the policy

Register the policy in the `setup()` of a provider. `dox add graphql` made the GraphQL provider, so you can use it. Keep the `super.setup()` call:

```dart title="lib/providers/graphql_provider.dart"
class AppGraphQLProvider extends GraphQLProvider {
  AppGraphQLProvider() : super(graphqlConfig);

  @override
  void setup() {
    Gate.policy<Post>(PostPolicy());
    super.setup();
  }
}
```

The config must have `AuthMiddleware()`. Without it, Dox cannot read the user, and each client is a guest.

When the app starts, Dox makes sure that the policy has each ability of `can:` and `filter:`. If one is missing, the app stops with an error that shows the available abilities:

```text
@GraphQLDelete(can: 'delete') on Post: PostPolicy has no ability 'delete'. Available: update.
```

### Use it on a model

Give an ability to an operation with `can:`. Dox asks the policy before the operation runs. An operation with no `can:` does not ask the policy.

```dart title="lib/app/models/post/post.model.dart"
@DoxModel()
@GraphQL(filter: Ability.view)
@GraphQLAll(can: Ability.viewAny)
@GraphQLPaginate(can: Ability.viewAny)
@GraphQLFind(can: Ability.view)
@GraphQLCreate(dto: PostInput, can: Ability.create, guard: true, owner: 'userId')
@GraphQLUpdate(dto: PostInput, can: Ability.update, guard: true)
@GraphQLDelete(can: Ability.delete, guard: true)
class Post extends PostGenerator {}
```

Some policy methods get a row, and some do not:

| Annotation | The policy method gets | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `@GraphQLAll(can:)`, `@GraphQLPaginate(can:)` | The user. | `Ability.viewAny` |
| `@GraphQLCreate(can:)` | The user. | `Ability.create` |
| `@GraphQLFind(can:)` | The user and the row. | `Ability.view` |
| `@GraphQLUpdate(can:)` | The user and the row. | `Ability.update` |
| `@GraphQLDelete(can:)` | The user and the row. | `Ability.delete` |
| `@GraphQL(filter:)` | The user and each row. | `Ability.view` |

Do not use an ability that needs a row, like `Ability.view`, on `@GraphQLAll`, `@GraphQLPaginate` or `@GraphQLCreate`.

When the policy refuses a user, the field is `null`. The other fields keep their data:

```json
{ "data": { "posts": null, "me": { "name": "Ada" } } }
```

The `errors` list of the result has one error for `posts`. Its code is `FORBIDDEN`, in `extensions.code`.

### viewAny

Use `viewAny` when some users must not get lists of the model:

```dart
@GraphQLAll(can: Ability.viewAny)
```

```dart
bool viewAny(User user) => user.banned != true;
```

### view

Use `view` when a user can read some rows and not others. Here, a user can read a published post and their own posts:

```dart
@GraphQLFind(can: Ability.view)
```

```dart
bool view(User user, Post post) {
  return post.status == 'published' || post.userId == user.id;
}
```

A refused user gets `FORBIDDEN` from `post(id)`.

### Hide rows

Use `filter:` on `@GraphQL` when a client must get only the rows that the user can read:

```dart
@GraphQL(filter: Ability.view)
```

Dox hides each row that the ability refuses, and gives no error. This applies to each field that gives the model:

- A list, a paged list, or a list relation such as `user.posts` does not include the row. Thus, a list can have fewer rows than `limit`.
- `post(id)` or a single relation such as `comment.post` gives `null`.
- Your own queries, mutations and fields that return the model do the same.

!!! warning

    `filter:` does not decide who can change a row. `updatePost` and `deletePost` ask only their `can:`. Give them a `can:`.

To get `null` and no error from `post(id)`, use `filter:` and no `can:` on `@GraphQLFind`.

### create

Use `create` when only some users can add a row. The method gets only the user, because no row exists yet:

```dart
@GraphQLCreate(dto: PostInput, can: Ability.create)
```

```dart
bool create(User user) => user.verified == true;
```

Dox asks the policy first. It applies the rules of the DTO only for a user that the policy allows. For a refused user, Dox saves nothing.

### update

Use `update` to decide who can change a row:

```dart
@GraphQLUpdate(dto: PostInput, can: Ability.update)
```

```dart
bool update(User user, Post post) => post.userId == user.id;
```

For a refused user, Dox writes nothing.

### delete

Use `delete` to decide who can remove a row:

```dart
@GraphQLDelete(can: Ability.delete)
```

```dart
bool delete(User user, Post post) => post.userId == user.id;
```

For a refused user, the row stays in the database.

### Add your own ability

Use your own ability when the five names of `Ability` are not sufficient. Write the name as a constant on the policy:

```dart title="lib/app/policies/post_policy.dart"
class PostPolicy extends Policy<User, Post> {
  static const String publish = 'publish';

  bool canPublish(User user, Post post) => user.editor == true;

  @override
  Map<String, Function> get abilities => <String, Function>{
    publish: canPublish,
  };
}
```

```dart
@GraphQLUpdate(dto: PostInput, can: PostPolicy.publish)
```

### Let guests in

A guest is a client that is not logged in. With `Policy<User, Post>`, Dox refuses each guest with the error `UNAUTHENTICATED`.

Use `Policy<User?, Post>` when a guest can read some rows. Then a guest gets to your methods, and `user` is `null`:

```dart
class PostPolicy extends Policy<User?, Post> {
  bool view(User? user, Post post) {
    if (post.status == 'published') return true;
    return user != null && post.userId == user.id;
  }

  @override
  Map<String, Function> get abilities => <String, Function>{Ability.view: view};
}
```

Now a guest can read the published posts, and a user can also read their own drafts. To refuse guests on one operation of this model, add `guard: true` to that operation.

## Your own resolvers

A resolver is a method that gives the result of a query or a mutation. Write one when the model annotations are not sufficient. The builder finds each class in `lib/` that has a resolver method.

```dart title="lib/app/graphql/post.resolver.dart"
import 'package:dox_graphql/dox_graphql.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/models/post/post.model.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/services/post.service.dart';

class PostResolver {
  PostResolver(this.postService);

  final PostService postService;

  @GraphQLQuery()
  Future<List<Post>> trendingPosts({int limit = 10}) {
    return postService.trending(limit);
  }
}
```

Dox gets the data of the query from the method:

- The method name is the query name: `trendingPosts`.
- The parameters are the values that a client can send. A parameter with a default value is optional.
- The return type is the type that the client gets.
- Dox gets the constructor parameters from the [container](../the-basic/dependency-injection.md).

A resolver annotation has `name:`, `description:` and `guard: true`, the same as a model annotation.

### Write your own mutation

Write your own mutation when one saved row is not sufficient. Put `@GraphQLMutation()` on a resolver method, and use a DTO for the input:

```dart title="lib/app/graphql/post.resolver.dart"
@GraphQLMutation()
Future<Post> importPost(PostInput input) {
  return postService.import(input);
}
```

Dox applies the rules of the DTO before your method runs.

### Send an error to the client

To send your own message, throw a `GraphQLError`:

```dart
throw GraphQLError('This post is not published yet');
```

For all other errors, the client sees "Internal server error" in production. Dox sends the real error to the `ExceptionHandler` of your app.

### Check a policy in a resolver

`can:` works only on the model annotations. To refuse a user in your own resolver, call [`Gate`](../security/authorization.md#checking-a-gate) yourself:

```dart title="lib/app/graphql/post.resolver.dart"
@GraphQLQuery()
Future<Post?> latestPost(DoxGraphQLContext context) async {
  Post? post = await postService.latest();
  User? user = await context.user<User>();
  if (post != null && await Gate.denies(user, Ability.view, post)) {
    throw GraphQLAuth.forbidden();
  }
  return post;
}
```

`GraphQLAuth.forbidden()` gives the same `FORBIDDEN` error as `can:`. `filter:` also hides rows in the result of your own resolvers.

## Configuration

All settings are fields of `GraphQLConfig` in `lib/config/graphql.dart`. Each setting has a default, so set only the settings that you want to change:

```dart title="lib/config/graphql.dart"
GraphQLConfig graphqlConfig = GraphQLConfig(
  schema: graphqlSchema,
  path: '/api/graphql',
);
```

| Setting | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `path` | `/graphql` | The URL of the API. |
| `middleware` | none | Route middleware, like `AuthMiddleware()`. |
| `graphiql` | on in development | The GraphiQL page. |
| `introspection` | on in development | Lets tools like GraphiQL read the list of your types and fields. |
| `showInternalErrors` | on in development | Sends the real text of an error to the client. |
| `maxDepth` | `64` | How deep a query can nest fields. |
| `maxQueryLength` | `1000000` | The most characters in the text of one query. |
| `maxFields` | `20000` | The most fields one query can ask for. |
| `maxNodes` | `100000` | The most values one request can load. |
| `maxRootFields` | `50` | The most top-level fields in one request. Each alias counts. |
| `maxRelationRows` | `50000` | The most rows that one list relation can load for all parent rows together. |

"On in development" means on when `APP_ENV` is `development`. For all other values, these three settings are off.

A request that is larger than a `max` setting gets an error. Set lower values when your API is open to the public.

## Without the ORM

If your app does not use models, install with `dox add graphql --no-orm`. Put `@GraphQL()` on a plain Dart class. Its public fields are the fields that a client can ask for. You write all the queries yourself:

```dart title="lib/app/graphql/product.resolver.dart"
@GraphQL()
class Product {
  Product({required this.id, required this.name, required this.shopId});

  final int id;
  final String name;

  @GraphQLIgnore()
  final int shopId;
}

class ProductResolver {
  ProductResolver(this.productRepository, this.shopRepository);

  final ProductRepository productRepository;
  final ShopRepository shopRepository;

  @GraphQLQuery()
  Future<List<Product>> products({int limit = 20}) {
    return productRepository.latest(limit);
  }

  @GraphQLResolveField()
  Future<Shop?> shop(Product product, DoxGraphQLContext context) {
    DataLoader<int, Shop> shops = context.loader<int, Shop>(
      'shops',
      () => DataLoader<int, Shop>(shopRepository.findByIds),
    );
    return shops.load(product.shopId);
  }
}
```

`@GraphQLResolveField()` adds a field to the class of its first parameter. Thus, `Product` gets a `shop` field, and `Shop` also needs `@GraphQL()`.

The `DataLoader` collects the shop ids of the full request. Thus, fifty products cause one shop query, not fifty queries. `findByIds` takes a `List<int>` and returns a `Future<List<Shop?>>`, in the same order as the ids.

## Performance

The same GraphQL API in Dox and in Go, on Postgres. The Dox app uses the ORM with `@GraphQLAll` and `@GraphQLFind`. The Go apps use gqlgen, one with pgx and one with GORM, and a dataloader for the relation.

All three queries at 256 connections, requests per second:

| Server               | One row by id | 20 rows | 20 rows with a relation | peak MB |
| -------------------- | ------------: | ------: | ----------------------: | ------: |
| Dox (ORM)            | 88,330        | 7,837   | 5,990                   | 223     |
| Go (gqlgen + pgx)    | 27,870        | 7,618   | 3,918                   | 132     |
| Go (gqlgen + GORM)   | 24,675        | 7,436   | 3,683                   | 105     |

- On one row by id, Dox is 3.2 times as fast as Go with pgx.
- On a list of 20 rows, all three are about the same. Postgres is the limit here.
- On a list with a relation, Dox is 1.5 times as fast.
- Dox uses more memory at the peak. After the load, its memory goes down again.

How it was run: the same rig as the [benchmark](../digging-deeper/performance.md#how-it-was-run) of the server. The server gets 2 CPUs, the database gets 2 CPUs and wrk gets the other 4. Each server has 8 database connections. Each query runs for 15 seconds, three times. The numbers are the median.

## Details

- **GET requests.** A client can also send a query as a `GET` request, with `query` in the URL. A mutation needs `POST`.
- **Computed fields.** Put `@GraphQLField()` on a getter of a `@GraphQL` class to make the getter a field. It has `guard: true` also.
- **Field types.** A field can be a `String`, `int`, `double`, `bool`, `DateTime`, an enum, a `@GraphQL` class, or a `List` of them. A different type stops the build. Put `@GraphQLIgnore()` on a field that the API does not need.
- **Paged lists with `filter:`.** `data` and `count` do not include the hidden rows. `total` and `lastPage` include them.
- **Results of mutations with `filter:`.** `createPost` always gives the new row. `updatePost` saves a hidden row, but its result is `null`.
- **Filtered types.** A field can give a model with `filter:` as `Post`, `Post?`, `List<Post>` or `List<Post>?`. A different shape stops the build.
- **An id that does not exist.** With `can:`, Dox asks the policy about an empty row. Thus, a refused user gets `FORBIDDEN` for each id. If your policy method allows an empty row, a client can find which ids exist.
- **Your own `AuthMiddleware`.** If you use a subclass of `AuthMiddleware`, override `asOptional()` to return your subclass. If you do not, your changes do not run.

| [Custom errors](custom-errors.md) | Your own exception classes, one JSON shape for every error, logging. |

# File upload

Source: https://dartondox.dev/latest/guides/file-upload/

# File upload

Accept an image from a form, check its size and type, save it to a disk, and return its URL.

You should never trust an uploaded file: it can be too big, or it can be a different type than its name says. So this guide checks the file in a [DTO](../the-basic/dto.md) first, and only then saves it.

## What you need

- A Dox app (`dox create my_app`). A new app has the `dox_storage` package, `lib/config/storage.dart` and `lib/providers/storage_provider.dart`.

## 1. Set up the disk

The `local` disk of a new app saves files in the `storage` folder. Give the disk a `url`, because `Storage().url()` uses it to build the public URL of a file:

```dart title="lib/config/storage.dart"
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/env.dart';

StorageConfig storageConfig = StorageConfig(
  defaultDisk: env.storageDisk,
  disks: <String, Map<String, dynamic>>{
    /// uploads go to the `storage` folder.
    /// `url` is the public address of `Storage.route('files', ...)`.
    'local': <String, dynamic>{
      'driver': 'local',
      'root': 'storage',
      'url': '${env.appUrl}/files',
    },
  },
);
```

`APP_URL` is a new key, so add a getter for it to the `AppEnv` class:

```dart title="lib/config/env.dart"
  /// the public URL of this app, used in file links
  String get appUrl => 'http://localhost:3000';
```

Run `dart run build_runner build` to update `env.g.dart`. Then add `APP_URL=http://localhost:3000` to your `.env`.

The provider of a new app sets up the disks. You do not need to change it:

```dart title="lib/providers/storage_provider.dart"
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';
import 'package:my_app/config/storage.dart';

class AppStorageProvider extends StorageProvider {
  AppStorageProvider() : super(storageConfig);
}
```

## 2. Write the DTO

The DTO checks the file before your controller runs. If the check fails, Dox answers `422` and the controller never sees the file.

```dart title="lib/app/dtos/upload_image/upload_image.dto.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';

part 'upload_image.dto.g.dart';

@Dto()
class UploadImage {
  /// jpg, jpeg, png, gif, webp or bmp. Dox reads the first bytes of the
  /// file to find the real type. The file name is not trusted.
  @Image()
  @MaxSize('5MB')
  final RequestFile image;

  const UploadImage({required this.image});

  static const DtoSchema<UploadImage> schema = $UploadImageDto;
}
```

If you want other file types, use `@Mimes(<String>['pdf', 'docx'])` in place of `@Image()`.

## 3. Write the controller

The controller saves the file with `putFile` and returns its path and URL. `putFile` gives the file a new UUID name, and on the local disk it does not read the whole file into memory.

```dart title="lib/app/http/controllers/upload.controller.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/dtos/upload_image/upload_image.dto.dart';

@Inject()
class UploadController {
  /// POST /api/upload (multipart/form-data, field `image`)
  Future<Map<String, String>> store(UploadImage body) async {
    // saves the file as /images/<uuid>.<ext> on the default disk
    String path = await Storage().putFile('images', body.image);
    String url = await Storage().url(path);
    return <String, String>{'path': path, 'url': url};
  }
}
```

!!! warning "Save the file before you return"
    Dox deletes the uploaded temp file when the response is sent.
    So call `putFile`, `store` or `moveTo` inside the controller, not later.

## 4. Add the routes

You need two routes. One route takes the upload, and `Storage.route` serves the saved files at `GET /files/{key*}`:

```dart title="lib/routes/api.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:my_app/app/http/controllers/upload.controller.dart';

class ApiRouter extends Router {
  @override
  String get prefix => 'api';

  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    Route.post('/upload', (UploadController c) => c.store);
  }
}
```

```dart title="lib/routes/web.dart"
import 'package:dox_core/dox_core.dart';
import 'package:dox_storage/dox_storage.dart';

class WebRouter extends Router {
  @override
  List<dynamic> get middleware => <dynamic>[];

  @override
  void register() {
    // GET /files/{key*}, any file of the default disk
    Storage.route('files', signed: false);
  }
}
```

`signed: false` makes every file public. If the files are private, leave it out, so the route serves only signed URLs. Then use `Storage().signedUrl(path)` in place of `Storage().url(path)`.

## 5. Register the DTOs

Dox finds a DTO in the `dtos` list of `AppConfig`. `build_runner` writes this list to `lib/generated/dtos.g.dart`. You add it only once, so skip this step if your `app.dart` already has `dtos: dtos`.

```dart title="lib/config/app.dart"
import 'package:my_app/generated/dtos.g.dart';

AppConfig appConfig = AppConfig(
  dtos: dtos,
  // ...
);
```

## 6. Build and run

```bash
dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs
dox serve
```

## Check it

Upload a PNG:

```bash
curl -F image=@photo.png http://localhost:3000/api/upload
```

```json
{"path":"/images/074aa0d0-ce21-11f1-938a-57265e28c4a3.png","url":"http://localhost:3000/files/images/074aa0d0-ce21-11f1-938a-57265e28c4a3.png"}
```

Open the `url` in the browser. The image shows.

Now upload a text file. You get `422`:

```bash
curl -F image=@notes.txt http://localhost:3000/api/upload
```

```json
{"image":"The image must be an image"}
```

If you send no file at all, you also get `422`, with `{"image":"The image is required"}`.

## Bigger files

A `multipart/form-data` body can be 100 MB by default. If you need more, change it in `AppConfig(maxMultipartSize: ...)`. Set the same limit in your proxy too (`client_max_body_size` in nginx).

## Details

- `@Image()` reads the first bytes of the file to find the real type. It does not trust the file name.
- A file bigger than 1 MB is written to a temp file while it arrives. That is the file Dox deletes after the response.
- On the local disk, `putFile` moves the temp file. With `permissions` on, it streams the file in place of a move.

## See also

- [Request: form data](../the-basic/request.md#form-data-file) for `RequestFile`
- [Validation rules: files](../the-basic/validation-rules.md#files) for `@Image`, `@Mimes`, `@MimeTypes`, `@MaxSize`, `@MinSize`, `@Dimensions`
- [File storage](../digging-deeper/file-storage.md) for S3 and signed URLs
